    An arcade fighting game generated from a single-sentence prompt requesting a King of Fighters remake, with no reference image (Figure 12). Two fighters trade combos under health bars, a round timer, and a neon-lit stage.

    Dungeon Roguelike

    A Soul Knight-style dungeon-shooter roguelike (Figure 13). The map is built from rooms and corridors; entering a room seals the doors and starts combat. The player picks up weapons from chests, carries up to two at a time, and aims toward the mouse, with health, shield, and mana as stats.

    Parkour Platformer

    A cartoon parkour platformer (Figure 14). The protagonist runs and dashes across a field of floating balloons; stepping on a balloon pops it and launches her upward, and the level is cleared by chaining precise balloon landings.

    Civilization prototype

    A simplified Civilization-style 4X strategy game on a hex map, rendered in a cartoon hand-drawn style with city management and unit combat (Figure 15). It runs on a separated frontend and backend with multiplayer support.

    AI Werewolf

    A single-player Werewolf game driven by the engine’s built-in LLM module (Figure 16). Eleven AI players fill a 12-role setup (villagers, werewolves, seer, hunter, witch, idiot), conducting sheriff elections, day discussions, and night actions; each AI’s speech is rendered as on-screen text.

    Hollow Knight to Demon Slayer

    An IP transfer applied to the Hollow Knight-style boss-fight prototype from Appendix 9.1.2: the system restyled the entire game into a Demon Slayer theme, recreating the Mugen Train battle between Tanjiro and Upper Rank Three while keeping the underlying combat logic unchanged (Figure 17).

    11 Adversarial Agent Team Case Study

    Three defects from one run of VibeGame with GPT-6.1-Sol on the GameCraft-Bench task Open-World Beast Tamer [11], each reported by a different review role. Quotes are the agents’ own reports.

    Auditor (static review).

    The PRD asks the player to tap “when the timing indicator is inside its acceptance band” (beats at 1, 2, 4, and 5 s, ±0.3 s). Figure 18 shows the game before and after the repair.

    “AdventureUI.js:53–54 renders four equally spaced flex cards and an indicator at elapsed / 6 … Beat centers 1/2/4/5 and ±0.3/±0.45 exist only as text; no band-position/width … is computed from the scoring predicates. … This is a missing timing-to-presentation mapping, not a visual-quality judgment.”

    Player (runtime check).

    An independent VLM pass first flagged the completed map; the player confirmed it and measured it in the running game. Figure 19 shows the game before and after the repair.

    “completed-map owned opportunity buttons visibly truncate names and type/status qualifiers with ellipses. Examples: Heartcamp Frost Gate · P… … label-overflow.json shows actual scroll widths exceeding client widths.”

    Reviewer (final check).

    Found by stopping the game 120 frames after an ability and reading both characters’ positions. Figure 20 shows the game before and after the repair.

    “after a normal successful Fire Breath, waiting idle for two seconds leaves Emberlynx and the standing keeper at the exact same ground anchor, producing an inseparable/occluded central silhouette. VLM … FAIL: the orange body reads as flames attached to the keeper, not a companion.”

    12 Codex with the AI-Native Engine

    To isolate the effect of the AI-native engine, we equip the native Codex harness with the engine of VibeGame. Both settings use GPT-6.1-Sol on all 30 tasks in the PA2G setting with the same asset library. With the engine, the overall score of Codex rises from 64.44 to 67.13, with gains in all four categories (Table 5). Since the art in both settings comes from the same asset library, we attribute the improvement to the engine; the largest gain, in Content Depth, suggests that the structured project representation helps agents expand game content.

    13 Limitation of Self-Evolution

    We observe that when VibeGame continuously develops games of different types, the experience accumulated by self-evolution can instead lower agent performance. Future work should analyze this phenomenon further and separate general experience from genre-specific experience, so that each can be injected adaptively. This observation is also one of the motivations for our experimental design: the main experiments use VibeGame without any accumulated experience, and we evaluate self-evolution separately in the ablation study.

item.title: FVD、LPIPS 都正常，玩起来却完全不同：Kuration SDK 在 CS 对局数据上把 Virtual2Real 的根因挖出来 ｜ Kuration SDK: Addressing the Virtual2Real Gap via Data Curation
item.description:
一句话：可玩性与 FVD/LPIPS/JEDi 并不对应；把数据策展做成可测量诊断管线，比换 backbone 更管用。

要点：

  • 在 CounterStrike 对局数据上训练扩散世界模型，确认「可以玩」与 FVD、LPIPS、JEDi 这类指标并不对应，作者把这一落差命名为 Virtual2Real gap
  • SDK 对每段数据输出 action_state_anomaly 等诊断量（该窗口内违反基线的像素位移次数），让策展策略可以据此过滤、分箱或加权
  • SDK 追到了一个具体案例的根因：两个世界模型用同一张地图、同一动作与状态分布训练，LPIPS 与 FVD 都很接近，实际玩起来差异巨大

为什么值得看：世界模型的「能玩」不该靠指标猜。把数据策展做成可量化、可归因的诊断流程，在训练开始之前就能定位问题，这对做 AI 原生引擎的团队比再换个生成 backbone 更直接。

中文摘要：动作条件世界模型的评测指标正在从视觉相似度转向动作语义与物理合理性，但对领域无关的训练而言，现有 benchmark 的信号依然很弱。作者在 CounterStrike 对局数据上训练扩散世界模型，确认定性可玩性与 FVD、LPIPS、JEDi 并不对应，并把这一落差称为 Virtual2Real gap。他们的主张是：与其等一个可靠 benchmark，不如先把原始对局数据策展好，并在训练前测量多种诊断属性。Kuration SDK 就是这套数据策展工具箱，逐段输出 action、state 与异常诊断量。它最有说服力的用例是定位到「同数据分布、同指标、不同可玩性」两个模型的数据侧根因，说明问题可以查、而不是只能祈祷。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-07

本期推送：2026-10-27

Kuration SDK: Addressing the Virtual2Real Gap via Data Curation

Abstract

Benchmarks for measuring the quality of action-conditioned world models are still evolving and shifting away from visual similarity-based metrics to action-semantic and physically-grounded metrics. However, for domain and task-agnostic action-conditioned world model training, existing benchmarks provide a limited signal. By training and evaluating diffusion world models on CounterStrike gameplay data, we confirm that qualitative playability does not correspond with metrics such as FVD, LPIPS, and JEDi. We term this the Virtual2Real gap. We posit that, in lieu of reliable benchmarks, curating raw gameplay data and measuring a variety of diagnostic properties provides a more robust signal to bridge the gap, before the training even begins. We present several curation strategies and a general-purpose kit for physical AI data curation called Kuration SDK, which is being open-sourced with this paper 111 https://drive.google.com/file/d/1tbq9zW12YJTt9bw4UL2n3r576je1G0OU. The SDK was instrumental in uncovering the root cause of the virtual2real gap in a specific case: why two world models trained on identical gameplay map, action and state distribution, behaved very differently when played in spite of having very similar LPIPS and FVD scores. Thus, Kuration SDK has the potential to uncover the root causes of Virtual2Real gap in specific datasets and accelerate development of sample-efficient training datasets.

1 Introduction

In the case of LLMs, training data curation and data quality ablation experiments were critical in accelerating task performance of LLMs, e.g., large-scale web-text curation pipelines such as FineWeb [(Penedo et al., 2024)] that filter and deduplicate raw crawl data before it ever reaches a training run. Well-established and meaningful benchmark metrics for evaluating foundational language capability enabled that progress, and generative modeling more broadly has shown predictable improvements with more data and compute [(Henighan et al., 2020)]. However, meaningful metrics for action-conditioned world models are still evolving. State-of-the-art benchmarks are either task-specific and require an agent to be trained and evaluated on task performance or do not provide a meaningful signal on model capability. Then, what is the role of data curation for training foundational and task-agnostic action-conditioned world models? This is the central question this paper investigates.

Playing a pretrained DIAMOND [(Alonso et al., 2024)] model, a diffusion world model trained on CS:GO gameplay, makes the problem concrete. Rollouts are visually coherent for roughly the first thirty frames; beyond that horizon, the model loses track of the player’s position and teleports to a visually similar but geographically distinct part of the map, and it permits actions the game physics never allow, such as walking through parked cars or repeated double-jumps against a wall. We use playability throughout to mean exactly these observable failures, map teleportation, geometry clipping, physics-violating actions, and control responsiveness and recovery, judged by the authors via interactive rollout inspection rather than a formal protocol or external, blinded raters (Section 7.2). Such failures are attributed to the training data rather than the architecture: raw competitive gameplay rarely contains sustained collisions, since good players avoid walking into walls, and it contains double-jump exploits often enough for the model to treat them as normal transitions.

By training action-conditioned world models on two gameplay datasets having identical state and action distributions, identical game world map, identical volumes, frame rates, resolution, and near identical game engines (CounterStrike:GO and CounterStrike2), we show that state-of-the-art benchmarks do not correspond to qualitative "playability" of the models. Similar to the Sim2Real gap, we term this the Virtual2Real gap. Given the lack of meaningful benchmarks to investigate this gap, we built a set of data diagnostics and curation tools we call Kuration SDK. The SDK was instrumental in uncovering the root cause of the gap: the magnitude of visual shift per action differed by 1.4–2.1× across the two datasets. Section 2 situates this against prior world-model and benchmark work; Sections 3–5 present the controlled experiment and root-cause diagnosis; Section 7 evaluates curation strategies against FVD, LPIPS, and JEDi; Section 8 discusses the implications for benchmarking gameplay world models. Our contributions:

1.1 Contributions

  • •

    We demonstrate the Virtual2Real gap directly: two diffusion world models trained on format- and distribution-matched CS:GO and CS2 corpora diverge sharply in qualitative playability despite comparable or better scores on FVD, LPIPS, and JEDi.

  • •

    We survey emerging action-semantic and physically-grounded benchmarks and show none offers a general-purpose, domain-agnostic quality signal for gameplay world models, motivating data-level diagnostics as an alternative.

  • •

    Using the Kuration SDK, we test a set of curation hypotheses and identify action-state consistency, whether a given input reliably produces the same characteristic screen motion, and specifically its magnitude, as the leading candidate explanation: the two corpora differ by roughly 2× on this axis, a difference neither FVD nor LPIPS detects.

  • •

    We release the Kuration SDK, an open-source toolkit for gameplay data curation, together with the curation strategies and full evaluation results from this paper, so the community can reproduce, extend, or apply these diagnostics to new corpora.

    • 2 Related work

    World models for physical AI.

    World models predicting future observations conditioned on actions have been proposed as planning and policy-learning substrates without further real-world interaction [(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2023)]. Genie [(Bruce et al., 2024)] pursues data scale, pretraining on internet-scale video with no action labels. GameNGen [(Valevski et al., 2025)] and DIAMOND [(Alonso et al., 2024)], real-time diffusion game world models, are the closest comparisons; we use DIAMOND as our baseline. Reported failure modes (map teleportation, geometry clipping) are attributed to the training corpus, but, to our knowledge, no prior work tests this against a second, independently captured corpus matched on format and scale, the gap Section 4 closes.

    Sim2Real vs. Virtual2Real.

    Sim2Real [(Zhao et al., 2020; Tobin et al., 2017)] treats the gap as dynamics-fidelity, addressed via domain randomization. Virtual2Real is a data-distribution problem: a model trained on an uncurated virtual-environment sample inherits its degenerate corners regardless of simulator accuracy.

    Video generation metrics and their limits.

    FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2018)] and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] compute a Fréchet distance over I3D features and a per-frame perceptual distance; neither targets single-interaction physical violations. JEDi [(Luo et al., 2024)] replaces I3D with V-JEPA [(Bardes et al., 2024)] features, predicting future latent states rather than classifying actions, and so is, in principle, more sensitive to how a scene evolves (Sections 4, 7). Newer benchmarks targeting action-semantics or physical grounding directly are not yet general-purpose: ACT-Bench [(Turing Motors et al., 2025)] needs a per-game trajectory or pose estimator, built for continuous 3D ego-motion rather than discrete or hybrid action spaces; ARR [(Hu et al., 2026)] depends on an auxiliary probe trained and validated per game; Atari 100K [(Kaiser et al., 2019)] and similar task-specific benchmarks do not generalize; and long-horizon drift metrics [(Kwon et al., 2025)], an action sequence followed by its inverse checked for return to the start, are self-referential, a round trip can close on an arbitrarily wrong path since no step is individually verified.

    Data curation.

    Subset selection from a large corpus is well studied for language and vision-language data (semantic deduplication [(Abbas et al., 2023)], coverage-driven filtering [(Li et al., 2024)]) over fixed text or image embeddings, which do not expose the features that matter here, physical interaction, action-state consistency, spatial trajectory, thus motivating gameplay-specific operators.

    3 Establishing a training baseline: reproducing DIAMOND

    To attribute any downstream effect to data rather than to our own training or evaluation code, we first reproduced DIAMOND on its published CS:GO dataset.

    Architecture and setup.

    DIAMOND is a two-stage architecture: a denoiser conditioned on the previous four frames and actions, operating at 30×56, and an independently trained upsampler mapping denoiser output to 150×280. Actions are discrete, spanning 20 categories of mouse and keyboard input. We matched the published configuration (learning rate 10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻², 600 epochs of 400 steps), and effective batch size.

    Parity result.

    Our 600-epoch run reaches FVD 4.4% below DIAMOND’s reported value at epoch 300 and LPIPS 4.2% above it at epoch 420, both within evaluation stochasticity. Running the released DIAMOND weights through our own pipeline reproduces the paper’s numbers within 1%, confirming our evaluation code (Table 1; per-30-epoch curve in Figure 3, Appendix A). Interactive rollouts from the reproduced model match DIAMOND’s published qualitative standard at short horizons; the long-horizon spatial teleportation and geometry-clipping failure modes described in Section 1 are present but, being multi-frame phenomena, are not visible in any single frame, part of why frame-level and short-clip metrics struggle to detect them.

    The reproduction confirms two things before we touch curation: our training and evaluation pipeline is faithful, and it reproduces the published qualitative failures (Section 1), map teleportation and geometry clipping persist at the same visual standard as the original. Any difference observed once we swap in a new corpus (Section 4) can therefore be attributed to the data.

    4 Controlled replication: Training on partner CS2 data

    We obtained server-side-captured Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) gameplay from a data partner, matched to DIAMOND’s CS:GO corpus on map (de_dust2), capture rate (16 fps), action encoding, and corpus scale; the recorded content, which players, which matches, which moments, is the one variable that cannot be held fixed across an independently captured corpus.

    We trained an uncurated reference model, baseline_v1, on 8,635 raw CS2 episodes, identical architecture and hyperparameters to Section 3, no episode-level curation, evaluated on a held-out set of 1,090 CS2 episodes. Cross-evaluating DIAMOND’s weights on this CS2 test set (Table 2) gives LPIPS and FVD both markedly worse than its own native CS:GO-test-set scores (Table 1), a real domain gap despite the shared map and format.

    baseline_v1 improves LPIPS by 20.9% over DIAMOND on the CS2 test set by epoch 600, matching or exceeding DIAMOND on aggregate video-generation metrics (Table 2). It is nonetheless qualitatively less playable: in interactive rollouts it shows the same class of failures as CS:GO DIAMOND, geometry clipping and spatial discontinuity over longer horizons, more severely, with less responsive control and less clean recovery. FVD is also a poor stopping signal here: its best value occurs at epoch 60 and is not bettered over the remaining 540 epochs (Appendix A). Cross-evaluated back onto DIAMOND’s own test set, baseline_v1 scores FVD 4.7× worse than DIAMOND: it does not transfer even across two versions of the same game on the same map.

    Table 2 (Section 7) reports baseline_v1’s full metrics alongside DIAMOND and every curation strategy on the same test set.

    5 Action-State consistency: the signal behind the gap

    Section 4’s two corpora agree on map, resolution, frame rate, and action encoding, yet produced models with different specialization and the same class of playability failure. We formulate several hypotheses and evaluate them via Kuration SDK as shown later in Section 7. Of those hypotheses, the action_state_consistency hypothesis was validated as described here.

    The operator.

    An action-conditioned world model learns only the mapping between an input and the screen motion that follows it; if that mapping is inconsistent in the data, the model cannot distinguish a genuine rule from an anomaly. Game engines routinely break this contract for reasons unrelated to world dynamics, coyote time, input buffering, lag compensation, deliberate choices that make a game feel responsive to a human player. pixel_shift measures the optical-flow displacement following every uninterrupted key press, projected onto the axis that control should move the camera on; action_state_consistency aggregates this into a per-control, per-press-length response curve.

    Finding.

    Applying this to DIAMOND’s CS:GO corpus [(Alonso et al., 2024)] and the partner CS2 corpus shows the two are not interchangeable at the action level, despite matching every specification and distribution. Figure 2 summarizes single-tap responses for the four movement controls. Three differences stand out. Magnitude: CS:GO responses are 1.4–2.1× larger in peak pixel shift across all four controls. Momentum: on multi-frame holds, CS2 decelerates on release (76–78% of in-hold magnitude, matching physical expectation), while CS:GO accelerates through release (112–126%) and takes 2–3× longer to decay to zero. Symmetry: CS2’s backward (S) response is 80% of forward (W), close to physically expected near-symmetry; CS:GO’s is only 26%.

    Why this matters.

    This is a measurable difference neither FVD nor LPIPS can detect. It also tracks which model plays better: CS:GO DIAMOND, despite its own map-teleportation and clipping failures, is more responsive and controllable than baseline_v1, despite baseline_v1 matching or beating it on LPIPS and FVD. Of the three axes, magnitude is the most plausible driver: a larger, more visually salient pixel shift per action gives a denoising, action-conditioned model a stronger training signal to key its predictions on, relative to other sources of frame-to-frame variation; a weaker signal, as in CS2, is easier to under-weight, even though CS2 is arguably the more physically well-behaved corpus on momentum and symmetry. We have not yet run a controlled ablation isolating magnitude from momentum and symmetry, so we report magnitude as the leading hypothesis, not a proven one. CS:GO and CS2 also run on different engine generations (Source vs. Source 2), so part of this measured difference could in principle reflect an engine-level property rather than a purely curatable data-selection one; matching map, resolution, frame rate, and action encoding (Section 4) narrows this confound but does not eliminate it (Section 7.2). What is established without qualification: two corpora indistinguishable by format specification differ measurably in exactly the property an action-conditioned model depends on, and that difference tracks playability where FVD and LPIPS do not.

    6 Kuration SDK

    The action-state consistency finding above is one instance of a general capability: the Kuration SDK, an open-source, pip-installable toolkit we release with this paper for curating gameplay and other sequential data into training-ready shards.222 See the abstract for the access link. A pipeline windows a source into segments, measures per-segment features, filters or selects against a time or count budget under a leakage-free train/test split, and writes shards with a config, manifest, and checksum, so a curated dataset is exactly reproducible from its config alone.

    kuration.gameplay ships the operators used in this paper. pixel_shift and action_state_consistency implement Section 5 (pipeline example in Appendix B). collision finds and classifies wall-hits from an expected unobstructed-movement curve so they can be oversampled relative to their naturally low base rate, targeting the wall-clipping failure mode of Section 1. slam_reconstruct, slam_quality, and slam_motion_diversity recover a camera’s 3D trajectory from video with no positional metadata and score it for gaps, impossible motion, and turning and path-length diversity, turning spatial coverage into a curatable axis for footage that started with none. Three general-purpose selection recipes, equal coverage across quantile bins of any feature, oversampling a rare event to a target rate, and cluster-then-sample diversity selection, compose with any of the above without new code. All strategies used below, and the full evaluation results, are released alongside the SDK.

    7 Curation strategies and results

    The action-state consistency finding motivates curating for specific behavioral properties rather than simply collecting more data, but it was one of four hypotheses we tested, not a foregone conclusion. Using the SDK, we curated the CS2 corpus along four strategies and compared each against baseline_v1 as the uncurated control, judging every checkpoint by the same qualitative rollout inspection used in Section 4. Coverage-based sampling selects segments to uniformly cover quantile bins over aim velocity, input entropy, and movement speed, trained from scratch for 120 of a planned 600 epochs on 7,530 episodes. Rare-trajectory up-weighting selects segments where movement speed falls in the tail (mean 43.9 vs. corpus mean 27.2), fine-tuned 60 epochs from baseline_v1’s epoch-300 checkpoint. Collision-aware selection up-weights collision-flagged segments (impact rate weighted 2× movement speed, 4× aim velocity), fine-tuned 55 epochs from the same checkpoint. Action-state-consistency selection, the only strategy motivated directly by the Section 5 diagnosis, up-weights segments with the largest per-action pixel-shift magnitude, moving the training distribution toward CS:GO’s more salient action-to-motion contract.

    7.1 One strategy improves playability

    Of the four curation strategies tested, three, coverage-based, rare-trajectory, and collision-aware, produce no qualitative playability improvement over baseline_v1, despite each moving at least one metric in the direction that would ordinarily be read as progress: coverage-based reaches near-baseline LPIPS and FVD in a fifth of the training budget (105 of 120 epochs), and collision-aware improves JEDi over the comparably fine-tuned rare-trajectory run (Table 2), consistent with collision-rich data helping a metric sensitive to interaction dynamics. Only action-state-consistency selection, the strategy directly motivated by the Section 5 root-cause diagnosis rather than a plausible-sounding proxy, produces a noticeable improvement in playability over baseline_v1; we do not yet know whether it closes the gap to CS:GO DIAMOND or narrows it only partially, and we have not run the negative control of curating for the same axis in the wrong direction, so we cannot yet rule out that any sufficiently different fine-tune from the epoch-300 checkpoint would have moved playability. Curating along an axis that sounds physically relevant (rare, physically demanding trajectories; collision events) was not sufficient here, and metric movement on that axis was not a reliable sign that it worked either way.

    This is not a claim that FVD and LPIPS are useless: LPIPS tracks progress within a single run, and FVD crosses below DIAMOND’s reported value by epoch 180 of the reproduction (Figure 3), a coarse but real convergence signal. The claim is narrower: once models are individually competent, neither metric, nor JEDi, reliably flags which curation hypothesis actually fixes the targeted behavior, which is precisely the regime curation research operates in.

    7.2 Limitations

    Several caveats. Collision-aware LPIPS/FVD, coverage-based JEDi, and all three of action-state-consistency’s quantitative metrics were not completed at time of writing (shared GPU availability); blank cells in Table 2 should not be read as parity, and the action-state-consistency result, including its training schedule, is qualitative only so far. The playability judgments throughout this paper rest on rollout inspection rather than a labeled playability benchmark, since none exists for this setting to our knowledge; a labeled benchmark, or even a second independent rater, would let us report agreement rather than a single team’s judgment. Raters were the authors themselves and were not blinded to which strategy produced a given checkpoint, so expectation bias cannot be ruled out, a concern that applies most directly to the action-state-consistency result, the one motivated by our own root-cause diagnosis. Neither a systematic, shared-test-set sweep of the SDK’s full strategy space nor a statistical action-state-consistency comparison with confidence intervals per control and press length has been run; Section 5 reports single-tap summaries, and multi-tap presses show the same pattern but are omitted here for space. CS:GO and CS2 are also not the same engine: beyond the map, resolution, frame rate, and action encoding we matched, they differ in engine generation (Source vs. Source 2) and underlying physics and netcode, so part of the action-state consistency gap of Section 5 could reflect an engine-level property rather than a purely fixable data-selection one; we cannot yet separate the two with a single corpus pair. More broadly, every result in this paper comes from one map, one architecture (DIAMOND), and one game family; the "task-agnostic" motivation in Section 1 is the question this work investigates, not a generality we have yet demonstrated beyond this setting.

    8 Conclusion and Future Work

    With the example of two format and scale-matched CounterStrike gameplay corpora, we demonstrated the Virtual2Real gap: benchmarks improve slightly while playability gets significantly worse. Faced with no reliable benchmark to identify the root cause, we used the Kuration SDK to test curation hypotheses directly against qualitative playability rather than against metrics alone (Section 7); only the hypothesis grounded in a measured difference between corpora, not an intuition about which behaviors seemed important, moved playability. In our experience, the SDK’s value was in letting us test and discard hypotheses without one-off scripts for each, not in any single curation trick, though we have not measured this efficiency claim against an alternative workflow. We release the Kuration SDK, the curation strategy specifications, and the full evaluation results from this paper so other groups can reproduce, extend, or apply these diagnostics to new corpora.

    In next steps, we will build a physics-conformance metric directly from geometry pass-through and trajectory discontinuity, rather than learned video features. Also, a shared benchmark comparing the SDK’s full strategy space on one held-out set, against all metrics used here plus any physics-conformance metric will make the claims more conclusive. Generalization beyond CS2: whether the same curation axes (interaction density, spatial coverage, action-state consistency) transfer to real robot teleoperation or egocentric video would make the case for domain-general curation infrastructure concrete rather than analogical.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Full Per-Checkpoint Results

    Table 3 reports LPIPS, FVD, and JEDi at every 30-epoch checkpoint of our DIAMOND reproduction (Section 3), on the DIAMOND standard CS:GO test set (500 episodes, 1-step samplers), plotted in Figure 3. Denoiser train loss decreases monotonically from 0.0682 at epoch 30 to 0.0339 at epoch 600, and denoiser test loss (evaluated at every second checkpoint) decreases from 0.0469 at epoch 60 to 0.0240 at epoch 600, confirming that the model continues to improve on its core frame-prediction objective throughout training even as FVD and LPIPS plateau after epoch 300. JEDi on this run is noisier than on the CS2 run of Table 4 and does not improve monotonically, though its best value is also reached late in training.

    Table 4 reports LPIPS, FVD, and JEDi for baseline_v1 at each evaluated checkpoint on the CS2 test set (1,090 episodes). The epoch-510 checkpoint was unavailable due to a storage-retention error and is omitted rather than interpolated.

    Appendix B Action-State Consistency Pipeline Example

    The snippet below windows a source, measures pixel shift for the W control, scores each window, keeps only windows with at least one measured press, and samples a coverage-balanced curated set Importing kuration.gameplay registers .pixel_shift(...), which measures the optical-flow displacement behind every isolated key or mouse press (Section 5), and the action-state-consistency scorer, which checks each window’s own measured presses against a supplied baseline (an expected sign and magnitude range per control) and attaches a per-window anomaly count:

    import kuration.gameplay  # registers pixel_shift and the scorer
from kuration import input

curated = ( input({"clip1": rows}, schema=schema, fields={"action": action_columns}, time="t") .join_video({"clip1": "clip1.mp4"}) .window(64, stride=32) .pixel_shift(controls=["W"]) .score("aintropy/action-state-consistency", out="action_state_anomaly", baselines=baselines, controls=["W"]) .filter("w_shift_measured", ">=", 1) .bin("w_shift_mean", bins=8) .sample("equal", n=100) .output("out/gameplay")
)

    Every segment in the output carries action_state_anomaly, the count of that window’s own pixel-shift instances that violate the baseline, so a curation strategy can filter, bin, or weight on it directly.

一句话：可玩性与 FVD/LPIPS/JEDi 并不对应；把数据策展做成可测量诊断管线，比换 backbone 更管用。

要点：

  • 在 CounterStrike 对局数据上训练扩散世界模型，确认「可以玩」与 FVD、LPIPS、JEDi 这类指标并不对应，作者把这一落差命名为 Virtual2Real gap
  • SDK 对每段数据输出 action_state_anomaly 等诊断量（该窗口内违反基线的像素位移次数），让策展策略可以据此过滤、分箱或加权
  • SDK 追到了一个具体案例的根因：两个世界模型用同一张地图、同一动作与状态分布训练，LPIPS 与 FVD 都很接近，实际玩起来差异巨大

为什么值得看：世界模型的「能玩」不该靠指标猜。把数据策展做成可量化、可归因的诊断流程，在训练开始之前就能定位问题，这对做 AI 原生引擎的团队比再换个生成 backbone 更直接。

中文摘要：动作条件世界模型的评测指标正在从视觉相似度转向动作语义与物理合理性，但对领域无关的训练而言，现有 benchmark 的信号依然很弱。作者在 CounterStrike 对局数据上训练扩散世界模型，确认定性可玩性与 FVD、LPIPS、JEDi 并不对应，并把这一落差称为 Virtual2Real gap。他们的主张是：与其等一个可靠 benchmark，不如先把原始对局数据策展好，并在训练前测量多种诊断属性。Kuration SDK 就是这套数据策展工具箱，逐段输出 action、state 与异常诊断量。它最有说服力的用例是定位到「同数据分布、同指标、不同可玩性」两个模型的数据侧根因，说明问题可以查、而不是只能祈祷。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-07

本期推送：2026-10-27

Kuration SDK: Addressing the Virtual2Real Gap via Data Curation

Abstract

Benchmarks for measuring the quality of action-conditioned world models are still evolving and shifting away from visual similarity-based metrics to action-semantic and physically-grounded metrics. However, for domain and task-agnostic action-conditioned world model training, existing benchmarks provide a limited signal. By training and evaluating diffusion world models on CounterStrike gameplay data, we confirm that qualitative playability does not correspond with metrics such as FVD, LPIPS, and JEDi. We term this the Virtual2Real gap. We posit that, in lieu of reliable benchmarks, curating raw gameplay data and measuring a variety of diagnostic properties provides a more robust signal to bridge the gap, before the training even begins. We present several curation strategies and a general-purpose kit for physical AI data curation called Kuration SDK, which is being open-sourced with this paper 111 https://drive.google.com/file/d/1tbq9zW12YJTt9bw4UL2n3r576je1G0OU. The SDK was instrumental in uncovering the root cause of the virtual2real gap in a specific case: why two world models trained on identical gameplay map, action and state distribution, behaved very differently when played in spite of having very similar LPIPS and FVD scores. Thus, Kuration SDK has the potential to uncover the root causes of Virtual2Real gap in specific datasets and accelerate development of sample-efficient training datasets.

1 Introduction

In the case of LLMs, training data curation and data quality ablation experiments were critical in accelerating task performance of LLMs, e.g., large-scale web-text curation pipelines such as FineWeb [(Penedo et al., 2024)] that filter and deduplicate raw crawl data before it ever reaches a training run. Well-established and meaningful benchmark metrics for evaluating foundational language capability enabled that progress, and generative modeling more broadly has shown predictable improvements with more data and compute [(Henighan et al., 2020)]. However, meaningful metrics for action-conditioned world models are still evolving. State-of-the-art benchmarks are either task-specific and require an agent to be trained and evaluated on task performance or do not provide a meaningful signal on model capability. Then, what is the role of data curation for training foundational and task-agnostic action-conditioned world models? This is the central question this paper investigates.

Playing a pretrained DIAMOND [(Alonso et al., 2024)] model, a diffusion world model trained on CS:GO gameplay, makes the problem concrete. Rollouts are visually coherent for roughly the first thirty frames; beyond that horizon, the model loses track of the player’s position and teleports to a visually similar but geographically distinct part of the map, and it permits actions the game physics never allow, such as walking through parked cars or repeated double-jumps against a wall. We use playability throughout to mean exactly these observable failures, map teleportation, geometry clipping, physics-violating actions, and control responsiveness and recovery, judged by the authors via interactive rollout inspection rather than a formal protocol or external, blinded raters (Section 7.2). Such failures are attributed to the training data rather than the architecture: raw competitive gameplay rarely contains sustained collisions, since good players avoid walking into walls, and it contains double-jump exploits often enough for the model to treat them as normal transitions.

By training action-conditioned world models on two gameplay datasets having identical state and action distributions, identical game world map, identical volumes, frame rates, resolution, and near identical game engines (CounterStrike:GO and CounterStrike2), we show that state-of-the-art benchmarks do not correspond to qualitative "playability" of the models. Similar to the Sim2Real gap, we term this the Virtual2Real gap. Given the lack of meaningful benchmarks to investigate this gap, we built a set of data diagnostics and curation tools we call Kuration SDK. The SDK was instrumental in uncovering the root cause of the gap: the magnitude of visual shift per action differed by 1.4–2.1× across the two datasets. Section 2 situates this against prior world-model and benchmark work; Sections 3–5 present the controlled experiment and root-cause diagnosis; Section 7 evaluates curation strategies against FVD, LPIPS, and JEDi; Section 8 discusses the implications for benchmarking gameplay world models. Our contributions:

1.1 Contributions

  • •

    We demonstrate the Virtual2Real gap directly: two diffusion world models trained on format- and distribution-matched CS:GO and CS2 corpora diverge sharply in qualitative playability despite comparable or better scores on FVD, LPIPS, and JEDi.

  • •

    We survey emerging action-semantic and physically-grounded benchmarks and show none offers a general-purpose, domain-agnostic quality signal for gameplay world models, motivating data-level diagnostics as an alternative.

  • •

    Using the Kuration SDK, we test a set of curation hypotheses and identify action-state consistency, whether a given input reliably produces the same characteristic screen motion, and specifically its magnitude, as the leading candidate explanation: the two corpora differ by roughly 2× on this axis, a difference neither FVD nor LPIPS detects.

  • •

    We release the Kuration SDK, an open-source toolkit for gameplay data curation, together with the curation strategies and full evaluation results from this paper, so the community can reproduce, extend, or apply these diagnostics to new corpora.

    • 2 Related work

    World models for physical AI.

    World models predicting future observations conditioned on actions have been proposed as planning and policy-learning substrates without further real-world interaction [(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2023)]. Genie [(Bruce et al., 2024)] pursues data scale, pretraining on internet-scale video with no action labels. GameNGen [(Valevski et al., 2025)] and DIAMOND [(Alonso et al., 2024)], real-time diffusion game world models, are the closest comparisons; we use DIAMOND as our baseline. Reported failure modes (map teleportation, geometry clipping) are attributed to the training corpus, but, to our knowledge, no prior work tests this against a second, independently captured corpus matched on format and scale, the gap Section 4 closes.

    Sim2Real vs. Virtual2Real.

    Sim2Real [(Zhao et al., 2020; Tobin et al., 2017)] treats the gap as dynamics-fidelity, addressed via domain randomization. Virtual2Real is a data-distribution problem: a model trained on an uncurated virtual-environment sample inherits its degenerate corners regardless of simulator accuracy.

    Video generation metrics and their limits.

    FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2018)] and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] compute a Fréchet distance over I3D features and a per-frame perceptual distance; neither targets single-interaction physical violations. JEDi [(Luo et al., 2024)] replaces I3D with V-JEPA [(Bardes et al., 2024)] features, predicting future latent states rather than classifying actions, and so is, in principle, more sensitive to how a scene evolves (Sections 4, 7). Newer benchmarks targeting action-semantics or physical grounding directly are not yet general-purpose: ACT-Bench [(Turing Motors et al., 2025)] needs a per-game trajectory or pose estimator, built for continuous 3D ego-motion rather than discrete or hybrid action spaces; ARR [(Hu et al., 2026)] depends on an auxiliary probe trained and validated per game; Atari 100K [(Kaiser et al., 2019)] and similar task-specific benchmarks do not generalize; and long-horizon drift metrics [(Kwon et al., 2025)], an action sequence followed by its inverse checked for return to the start, are self-referential, a round trip can close on an arbitrarily wrong path since no step is individually verified.

    Data curation.

    Subset selection from a large corpus is well studied for language and vision-language data (semantic deduplication [(Abbas et al., 2023)], coverage-driven filtering [(Li et al., 2024)]) over fixed text or image embeddings, which do not expose the features that matter here, physical interaction, action-state consistency, spatial trajectory, thus motivating gameplay-specific operators.

    3 Establishing a training baseline: reproducing DIAMOND

    To attribute any downstream effect to data rather than to our own training or evaluation code, we first reproduced DIAMOND on its published CS:GO dataset.

    Architecture and setup.

    DIAMOND is a two-stage architecture: a denoiser conditioned on the previous four frames and actions, operating at 30×56, and an independently trained upsampler mapping denoiser output to 150×280. Actions are discrete, spanning 20 categories of mouse and keyboard input. We matched the published configuration (learning rate 10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻², 600 epochs of 400 steps), and effective batch size.

    Parity result.

    Our 600-epoch run reaches FVD 4.4% below DIAMOND’s reported value at epoch 300 and LPIPS 4.2% above it at epoch 420, both within evaluation stochasticity. Running the released DIAMOND weights through our own pipeline reproduces the paper’s numbers within 1%, confirming our evaluation code (Table 1; per-30-epoch curve in Figure 3, Appendix A). Interactive rollouts from the reproduced model match DIAMOND’s published qualitative standard at short horizons; the long-horizon spatial teleportation and geometry-clipping failure modes described in Section 1 are present but, being multi-frame phenomena, are not visible in any single frame, part of why frame-level and short-clip metrics struggle to detect them.

    The reproduction confirms two things before we touch curation: our training and evaluation pipeline is faithful, and it reproduces the published qualitative failures (Section 1), map teleportation and geometry clipping persist at the same visual standard as the original. Any difference observed once we swap in a new corpus (Section 4) can therefore be attributed to the data.

    4 Controlled replication: Training on partner CS2 data

    We obtained server-side-captured Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) gameplay from a data partner, matched to DIAMOND’s CS:GO corpus on map (de_dust2), capture rate (16 fps), action encoding, and corpus scale; the recorded content, which players, which matches, which moments, is the one variable that cannot be held fixed across an independently captured corpus.

    We trained an uncurated reference model, baseline_v1, on 8,635 raw CS2 episodes, identical architecture and hyperparameters to Section 3, no episode-level curation, evaluated on a held-out set of 1,090 CS2 episodes. Cross-evaluating DIAMOND’s weights on this CS2 test set (Table 2) gives LPIPS and FVD both markedly worse than its own native CS:GO-test-set scores (Table 1), a real domain gap despite the shared map and format.

    baseline_v1 improves LPIPS by 20.9% over DIAMOND on the CS2 test set by epoch 600, matching or exceeding DIAMOND on aggregate video-generation metrics (Table 2). It is nonetheless qualitatively less playable: in interactive rollouts it shows the same class of failures as CS:GO DIAMOND, geometry clipping and spatial discontinuity over longer horizons, more severely, with less responsive control and less clean recovery. FVD is also a poor stopping signal here: its best value occurs at epoch 60 and is not bettered over the remaining 540 epochs (Appendix A). Cross-evaluated back onto DIAMOND’s own test set, baseline_v1 scores FVD 4.7× worse than DIAMOND: it does not transfer even across two versions of the same game on the same map.

    Table 2 (Section 7) reports baseline_v1’s full metrics alongside DIAMOND and every curation strategy on the same test set.

    5 Action-State consistency: the signal behind the gap

    Section 4’s two corpora agree on map, resolution, frame rate, and action encoding, yet produced models with different specialization and the same class of playability failure. We formulate several hypotheses and evaluate them via Kuration SDK as shown later in Section 7. Of those hypotheses, the action_state_consistency hypothesis was validated as described here.

    The operator.

    An action-conditioned world model learns only the mapping between an input and the screen motion that follows it; if that mapping is inconsistent in the data, the model cannot distinguish a genuine rule from an anomaly. Game engines routinely break this contract for reasons unrelated to world dynamics, coyote time, input buffering, lag compensation, deliberate choices that make a game feel responsive to a human player. pixel_shift measures the optical-flow displacement following every uninterrupted key press, projected onto the axis that control should move the camera on; action_state_consistency aggregates this into a per-control, per-press-length response curve.

    Finding.

    Applying this to DIAMOND’s CS:GO corpus [(Alonso et al., 2024)] and the partner CS2 corpus shows the two are not interchangeable at the action level, despite matching every specification and distribution. Figure 2 summarizes single-tap responses for the four movement controls. Three differences stand out. Magnitude: CS:GO responses are 1.4–2.1× larger in peak pixel shift across all four controls. Momentum: on multi-frame holds, CS2 decelerates on release (76–78% of in-hold magnitude, matching physical expectation), while CS:GO accelerates through release (112–126%) and takes 2–3× longer to decay to zero. Symmetry: CS2’s backward (S) response is 80% of forward (W), close to physically expected near-symmetry; CS:GO’s is only 26%.

    Why this matters.

    This is a measurable difference neither FVD nor LPIPS can detect. It also tracks which model plays better: CS:GO DIAMOND, despite its own map-teleportation and clipping failures, is more responsive and controllable than baseline_v1, despite baseline_v1 matching or beating it on LPIPS and FVD. What is established without qualification: two corpora indistinguishable by format specification differ measurably in exactly the property an action-conditioned model depends on, and that difference tracks playability where FVD and LPIPS do not.

    6 Kuration SDK

    The action-state consistency finding above is one instance of a general capability: the Kuration SDK, an open-source, pip-installable toolkit we release with this paper for curating gameplay and other sequential data into training-ready shards.222 See the abstract for the access link. A pipeline windows a source into segments, measures per-segment features, filters or selects against a time or count budget under a leakage-free train/test split, and writes shards with a config, manifest, and checksum, so a curated dataset is exactly reproducible from its config alone.

    kuration.gameplay ships the operators used in this paper. pixel_shift and action_state_consistency implement Section 5 (pipeline example in Appendix B). collision finds and classifies wall-hits from an expected unobstructed-movement curve so they can be oversampled relative to their naturally low base rate, targeting the wall-clipping failure mode of Section 1. slam_reconstruct, slam_quality, and slam_motion_diversity recover a camera’s 3D trajectory from video with no positional metadata and score it for gaps, impossible motion, and turning and path-length diversity, turning spatial coverage into a curatable axis for footage that started with none. Three general-purpose selection recipes, equal coverage across quantile bins of any feature, oversampling a rare event to a target rate, and cluster-then-sample diversity selection, compose with any of the above without new code. All strategies used below, and the full evaluation results, are released alongside the SDK.

    7 Curation strategies and results

    The action-state consistency finding motivates curating for specific behavioral properties rather than simply collecting more data, but it was one of four hypotheses we tested, not a foregone conclusion. Using the SDK, we curated the CS2 corpus along four strategies and compared each against baseline_v1 as the uncurated control, judging every checkpoint by the same qualitative rollout inspection used in Section 4. Coverage-based sampling selects segments to uniformly cover quantile bins over aim velocity, input entropy, and movement speed, trained from scratch for 120 of a planned 600 epochs on 7,530 episodes. Rare-trajectory up-weighting selects segments where movement speed falls in the tail (mean 43.9 vs. corpus mean 27.2), fine-tuned 60 epochs from baseline_v1’s epoch-300 checkpoint. Collision-aware selection up-weights collision-flagged segments (impact rate weighted 2× movement speed, 4× aim velocity), fine-tuned 55 epochs from the same checkpoint. Action-state-consistency selection, the only strategy motivated directly by the Section 5 diagnosis, up-weights segments with the largest per-action pixel-shift magnitude, moving the training distribution toward CS:GO’s more salient action-to-motion contract.

    7.1 One strategy improves playability

    Of the four curation strategies tested, three, coverage-based, rare-trajectory, and collision-aware, produce no qualitative playability improvement over baseline_v1, despite each moving at least one metric in the direction that would ordinarily be read as progress: coverage-based reaches near-baseline LPIPS and FVD in a fifth of the training budget (105 of 120 epochs), and collision-aware improves JEDi over the comparably fine-tuned rare-trajectory run (Table 2), consistent with collision-rich data helping a metric sensitive to interaction dynamics. Only action-state-consistency selection, the strategy directly motivated by the Section 5 root-cause diagnosis rather than a plausible-sounding proxy, produces a noticeable improvement in playability over baseline_v1; we do not yet know whether it closes the gap to CS:GO DIAMOND or narrows it only partially, and we have not run the negative control of curating for the same axis in the wrong direction, so we cannot yet rule out that any sufficiently different fine-tune from the epoch-300 checkpoint would have moved playability. Curating along an axis that sounds physically relevant (rare, physically demanding trajectories; collision events) was not sufficient here, and metric movement on that axis was not a reliable sign that it worked either way.

    This is not a claim that FVD and LPIPS are useless: LPIPS tracks progress within a single run, and FVD crosses below DIAMOND’s reported value by epoch 180 of the reproduction (Figure 3), a coarse but real convergence signal. The claim is narrower: once models are individually competent, neither metric, nor JEDi, reliably flags which curation hypothesis actually fixes the targeted behavior, which is precisely the regime curation research operates in.

    7.2 Limitations

    Several caveats. Collision-aware LPIPS/FVD, coverage-based JEDi, and all three of action-state-consistency’s quantitative metrics were not completed at time of writing (shared GPU availability); blank cells in Table 2 should not be read as parity, and the action-state-consistency result, including its training schedule, is qualitative only so far. The playability judgments throughout this paper rest on rollout inspection rather than a labeled playability benchmark, since none exists for this setting to our knowledge; a labeled benchmark, or even a second independent rater, would let us report agreement rather than a single team’s judgment. Raters were the authors themselves and were not blinded to which strategy produced a given checkpoint, so expectation bias cannot be ruled out, a concern that applies most directly to the action-state-consistency result, the one motivated by our own root-cause diagnosis. Neither a systematic, shared-test-set sweep of the SDK’s full strategy space nor a statistical action-state-consistency comparison with confidence intervals per control and press length has been run; Section 5 reports single-tap summaries, and multi-tap presses show the same pattern but are omitted here for space. CS:GO and CS2 are also not the same engine: beyond the map, resolution, frame rate, and action encoding we matched, they differ in engine generation (Source vs. Source 2) and underlying physics and netcode, so part of the action-state consistency gap of Section 5 could reflect an engine-level property rather than a purely fixable data-selection one; we cannot yet separate the two with a single corpus pair. More broadly, every result in this paper comes from one map, one architecture (DIAMOND), and one game family; the "task-agnostic" motivation in Section 1 is the question this work investigates, not a generality we have yet demonstrated beyond this setting.

    8 Conclusion and Future Work

    With the example of two format and scale-matched CounterStrike gameplay corpora, we demonstrated the Virtual2Real gap: benchmarks improve slightly while playability gets significantly worse. Faced with no reliable benchmark to identify the root cause, we used the Kuration SDK to test curation hypotheses directly against qualitative playability rather than against metrics alone (Section 7); only the hypothesis grounded in a measured difference between corpora, not an intuition about which behaviors seemed important, moved playability. In our experience, the SDK’s value was in letting us test and discard hypotheses without one-off scripts for each, not in any single curation trick, though we have not measured this efficiency claim against an alternative workflow. We release the Kuration SDK, the curation strategy specifications, and the full evaluation results from this paper so other groups can reproduce, extend, or apply these diagnostics to new corpora.

    In next steps, we will build a physics-conformance metric directly from geometry pass-through and trajectory discontinuity, rather than learned video features. Also, a shared benchmark comparing the SDK’s full strategy space on one held-out set, against all metrics used here plus any physics-conformance metric will make the claims more conclusive. Generalization beyond CS2: whether the same curation axes (interaction density, spatial coverage, action-state consistency) transfer to real robot teleoperation or egocentric video would make the case for domain-general curation infrastructure concrete rather than analogical.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Full Per-Checkpoint Results

    Table 3 reports LPIPS, FVD, and JEDi at every 30-epoch checkpoint of our DIAMOND reproduction (Section 3), on the DIAMOND standard CS:GO test set (500 episodes, 1-step samplers), plotted in Figure 3. Denoiser train loss decreases monotonically from 0.0682 at epoch 30 to 0.0339 at epoch 600, and denoiser test loss (evaluated at every second checkpoint) decreases from 0.0469 at epoch 60 to 0.0240 at epoch 600, confirming that the model continues to improve on its core frame-prediction objective throughout training even as FVD and LPIPS plateau after epoch 300. JEDi on this run is noisier than on the CS2 run of Table 4 and does not improve monotonically, though its best value is also reached late in training.

    Table 4 reports LPIPS, FVD, and JEDi for baseline_v1 at each evaluated checkpoint on the CS2 test set (1,090 episodes). The epoch-510 checkpoint was unavailable due to a storage-retention error and is omitted rather than interpolated.

    Appendix B Action-State Consistency Pipeline Example

    The snippet below windows a source, measures pixel shift for the W control, scores each window, keeps only windows with at least one measured press, and samples a coverage-balanced curated set Importing kuration.gameplay registers .pixel_shift(...), which measures the optical-flow displacement behind every isolated key or mouse press (Section 5), and the action-state-consistency scorer, which checks each window’s own measured presses against a supplied baseline (an expected sign and magnitude range per control) and attaches a per-window anomaly count:

    import kuration.gameplay  # registers pixel_shift and the scorer
from kuration import input

curated = ( input({"clip1": rows}, schema=schema, fields={"action": action_columns}, time="t") .join_video({"clip1": "clip1.mp4"}) .window(64, stride=32) .pixel_shift(controls=["W"]) .score("aintropy/action-state-consistency", out="action_state_anomaly", baselines=baselines, controls=["W"]) .filter("w_shift_measured", ">=", 1) .bin("w_shift_mean", bins=8) .sample("equal", n=100) .output("out/gameplay")
)

    Every segment in the output carries action_state_anomaly, the count of that window’s own pixel-shift instances that violate the baseline, so a curation strategy can filter, bin, or weight on it directly.

item.title: 把「开/关」拆成可组合的槽位：SwitchSplat 让 3DGS 场景随便拼状态，还能换没拍过的机位 ｜ SwitchSplat: Learning Discrete Object States from Casually Captured Scenes
item.description:
一句话：共享静态基底加每物体一个状态槽，3DGS 从此能组合开关状态，而不是回放拍过的时序。

要点：

  • base+slot 分解：共享静态基底保留不变场景，每个可交互物体一个槽位，各自独立持有两种二值状态（on/off）
  • 高斯到槽位的归属完全可微，每个状态的几何直接从视频里学出来，不需要人工标注
  • 12 个真实场景（Insta360 X4 双鱼眼、抽帧 4 FPS）上优于静态与动态基线，并泛化到训练中没出现过的状态组合与陌生机位

为什么值得看：这是「3DGS 当资产格式」的关键一步：状态一旦可离散组合，引擎里就能直接做开门、开灯、切设备，而不必回到 4DGS 按时间回放。槽位数量与交互时间窗目前由 VLM 预填，也指出了下一步要补的自动化缺口。

中文摘要：现有 3DGS 表示都假设世界是静态的，而随手拍的真实场景里，用户会开门、拨开关、移动物体，这些都是离散状态变化。按时间条件化的 4DGS 会把「什么时候被观测到」和「处于什么状态」混在一起，只能回放见过的序列。SwitchSplat 提出 base+slot 分解：共享静态基底负责不变部分，每个可交互物体一个槽位独立持有 on/off 两态，高斯到槽位的归属可微，因此每个状态的几何能从视频里自动发现。推理时用户可自由组合槽位状态并从任意视角渲染。作者构建了 12 个场景的新数据集，方法在标准留出视角、新机位与新状态组合三种设置下都优于静态与动态基线。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-17

本期推送：2026-10-27

SwitchSplat: Learning Discrete Object States from Casually Captured Scenes

© cc

Abstract.

3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world. This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment – opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects – introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model. Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate when a state was observed with what state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations. We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base+slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object. Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation. At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io.

Keywords:

Novel View Synthesis, Gaussian Splatting, State-aware Rendering, 360^∘ Capture ††cc-license: by

1. Introduction

In inverse rendering, Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] has emerged as the leading representation for real-time, high-fidelity novel-view synthesis, enabling a new generation of interactive applications. Its combination of fast training and efficient rendering has driven broad adoption across academia as well as industry, from Matterport’s digital twins and Niantic Scaniverse’s mobile reconstruction to Meta’s Hyperscape111https://www.meta.com/experiences/meta-horizon-hyperscape-capture-beta/8798130056953686/.

While early 3DGS pipelines required meticulous data acquisition (fixed exposure and white balance, controlled lighting, and a perfectly static scene), recent works like 3DGRT [(Moenne-Loccoz et al., 2024)] and FullCircle [(Foroutan et al., 2026)] have unlocked casual capture: viewpoints need not be carefully curated – made possible by 360^∘ cameras held in a single hand – and the capturer’s pixels are automatically masked out to satisfy the static-scene assumption. This freedom naturally invites users to interact with the environment during capture – opening doors, toggling switches, or repositioning objects – turning the operator into both an active agent and a dynamic distractor within the scene.

Yet no existing reconstruction framework is equipped to handle these interactions. Many contemporary 3D representations enforce a strict static-world assumption: when an operator triggers a discrete state change – opening a door, flipping a switch, relocating an object – the model has no mechanism to account for the resulting geometric variation. As a result, even state-of-the-art pipelines can only represent a single, frozen scene configuration, and capturing multiple stable states requires re-recording the scene from scratch.

One could argue that the natural candidate to address this limitation is the family of 4D Gaussian Splatting methods [(Yang et al., 2024b)], which extend 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the scene representation on time. However, this design choice fundamentally conflates when a state was observed with what state the scene is in: the model learns to replay a specific sequence of observations, not to understand independent object configurations.

As a result, 4D methods are largely limited to novel-viewpoint synthesis of seen sequences; composing an unseen combination of object states—e.g., door open and light on—is not directly supported, since no single timestamp in the training data corresponds to that configuration. What is needed instead is a representation that de-correlates scene state from time, allowing the user to freely specify both the viewpoint and the desired configuration of each object independently.

To address these challenges, we propose SwitchSplat, a method that learns “state-aware” representations from casual captures featuring human-object interactions; see Figure1. SwitchSplat organizes the scene into a static base – the parts that never change throughout the capture – and a set of slots, one per interactable object. Each slot holds two 3D representations corresponding to the binary states of that object (“on” and “off”). For example, if a room was captured while a closet door was closed for part of the recording and open for another, a single slot would hold both the “off” state (door closed, interior hidden) and the “on” state (door open, interior visible), while the walls, floor, and furniture – unchanged throughout – are handled by the static base. To assign each Gaussian primitive to the right part of the scene, we attach a small learnable score vector that controls how strongly the primitive belongs to the base, or to either state of each slot.

This decomposition avoids data redundancy: without a shared static base, one would need to duplicate the full scene geometry for every slot, with no reusable structure across states. Instead, SwitchSplat shares the base across all configurations and only stores the geometry that actually differs per state.222 This is structurally analogous to PCA-based morphable models [(Blanz and Vetter, 2023)]: the static base plays the role of the mean face, each slot’s on/off representations correspond to the eigenvectors, and the state activations act as the blend-shape coefficients. Because the full pipeline is differentiable end-to-end, the model learns simultaneously which Gaussians belong to which slot and when each slot is active – directly from the input video, without any manual annotation. At inference, the user can query any combination of slot states independently – e.g., closet door open and desk lamp on – and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint.

To summarize our contributions: (1) We identify a novel problem in the 3DGS literature: existing representations cannot model scenes with discrete, user-triggered state changes (e.g., objects that can be opened, switched, or moved), and we show that naïvely applying dynamic methods such as 4DGS fails to address this. (2) We propose SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this problem via a base+slot decomposition, where a shared static base captures the invariant scene and each slot independently models the binary states of one interactable object. (3) We demonstrate on a new casual-capture dataset that SwitchSplat improves novel-view synthesis quality over static and dynamic baselines, and uniquely supports rendering arbitrary combinations of object states from unseen viewpoints.

2. Related Work

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] has become the dominant representation for novel-view synthesis, optimizing a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives that render at real-time rates. Extensions beyond the standard perspective-camera model are particularly relevant to our setting: 3DGRT [(Moenne-Loccoz et al., 2024)] reformulates rendering via ray tracing, and 3DGUT [(Wu et al., 2025a)] adds support for highly distorted cameras and secondary rays, enabling casual capture with wide field-of-view sensors. FullCircle [(Foroutan et al., 2026)] further shows that raw dual-fisheye 360^∘ video suffices for high-quality reconstruction, automatically masking the camera operator. Despite these advances, all of these pipelines represent the scene as a single, fixed configuration. When multiple object states are present in the capture—a door open in some frames and closed in others—the model either conflates them into averaged geometry and ghosting artifacts, or learns to discard the minority state as a distractor [(Sabour et al., 2025)]. Either way, only one configuration survives in the final model; there is no mechanism to retain, switch between, or compose multiple stable states at inference time.

Dynamic Gaussian Splatting

A large family of methods extends 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the representation on time. Dynamic 3D Gaussians [(Luiten et al., 2024)] tracks persistent primitives across frames, while Deformable 3D Gaussians [(Yang et al., 2024a)] and 4DGS [(Wu et al., 2024)] deform a canonical scene over time, with 4DGS using a learned space-time encoding. Spacetime Gaussians [(Li et al., 2024a)] further augments primitives with temporal opacity and parametric motion. Subsequent work improves efficiency, temporal consistency, or geometric accuracy via depth priors [(Yang et al., 2024b; Sun et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025b)]. Differently from our method, all of these methods are parameterized by time, not by object state: recovering a specific scene configuration requires locating the right moment in the recording, and rendering a novel combination of states—e.g., two objects in configurations never co-observed—is not supported.

Decomposed Gaussian Splatting

More recent dynamic Gaussian methods, such as SDD-4DGS [(Sun et al., 2025)], observe that applying deformation models to the entire scene is often inefficient, since most real-world scenes are largely static. This motivates methods that decompose scenes into static and dynamic components: GauFRe [(Liang et al., 2025)] combines a static Gaussian component with deformable dynamic Gaussians, while Swift4D [(Wu et al., 2025b)] improves efficiency by passing only dynamic Gaussians through the deformation model. DeGauss [(Wang et al., 2025a)] further uses dynamic-static decomposition to improve robustness to transient distractors. This observation is closely aligned with our setting, since object interactions usually affect only a small part of a 360^∘ environment. In contrast to our method, existing decomposition methods still treat the dynamic component as a temporally varying foreground: they separate dynamic regions from a static background, but provide no mechanism to independently switch or compose object states at inference time.

Controllable Scene Representation

A parallel line of work studies controllable and articulated 3D representations. Pre-Gaussian methods such as Watch It Move [(Noguchi et al., 2022)] discover articulated structure from object motion; PARIS [(Liu et al., 2023)] goes further by decoupling static and movable parts from two multi-view captures of the same scene. Gaussian-based approaches extend this to photorealistic settings: SC-GS [(Huang et al., 2024)] enables motion editing via sparse control points, Template-free Articulated Gaussian Splatting [(Wan et al., 2024)] supports re-posing with super-points, and RigGS [(Yao et al., 2025)] adds rig-based editing and interpolation. ArtGS [(Liu et al., 2025a)] and ArticulatedGS [(Guo et al., 2025)] further focus on part-level modeling of individual objects. Crucially, all of these methods aim to encode object motion or articulation—they model how parts move, rather than discarding motion entirely to focus on the discrete stable configurations of the scene. In contrast, our method treats object interactions as a nuisance to be factored out, retaining only the clean on/off states and ignoring the transient motion between them.

State-aware Scene Reconstruction

Closest to our setting are methods that reconstruct scenes across discrete object states. IGFuse [(Hu et al., 2026)] and RecurGS [(Hu et al., 2025)] address this by using semantic cues to detect state changes and aligning them via rigid transformations. GaussianCut [(Jain et al., 2024)] and DecoupledGaussian [(Wang et al., 2025b)] contribute related tools for object segmentation and scene decomposition. However, all of these methods assume that state changes can be described as rigid motions of segmented object entities—an assumption that breaks down for casual capture, where interaction boundaries are fuzzy and deformations are non-rigid. In contrast, SwitchSplat learns which Gaussians belong to each state directly from photometric supervision, without requiring object masks, or rigid-body assumptions.

3. Method

SwitchSplat learns a state-aware 3D representation from casual captures by decomposing the scene into controllable, state-conditioned components. In the following subsections, we detail our methodology by first formulating our state-conditioned Gaussian primitives and describing their integration within volume rendering (Sec.3.1). We then introduce the parameterization of the differentiable slot-table (Sec.3.2), followed by our slot initialization procedure (Sec.3.3). Finally, we describe our training pipeline and objectives that facilitate granular, state-controlled visualization during inference (Secs.3.4 and 3.5).

Terminology

A slot corresponds to one interactable object and holds two 3D representations for its binary states: “off” (e.g., door closed) and “on” (e.g., door open). A slot activation is a per-frame binary variable indicating which state is currently observed. All parts of the scene that remain constant throughout the capture are handled by the static base, which is shared across all configurations.

3.1. State-aware Gaussian Splat

Each 3D Gaussian primitive in our model is defined by its standard geometric and appearance attributes: mean μ, covariance Σ, opacity α, and view-dependent appearance c. To make our representation state-aware, we augment every Gaussian with a learnable categorical state distribution p=softmax(ℓ) over 1+2K channels, where K is the total number of object slots. These channels comprise a single static base channel ℓ[0], together with a pair of off (ℓ[2k-1]) and on (ℓ[2k]) channels for each slot k∈{1,…,K}. The two channels per slot — rather than one — let the softmax assign each Gaussian to a single configuration, so that disjoint subsets of primitives can independently model the geometry and appearance of an object in each of its two states (see Figure3). This separation is essential because the on/off configurations of an object generally differ not just in appearance, but also in spatial extent — a closed door and an open door, for instance, occupy different parts of the scene — which a single shared primitive simply cannot represent.

Test-time rendering

Assume we have trained our representation, and that we want to render an image corresponding to the slot configuration p̃∈{0,1}^K. This is achieved by computing the probability of each gaussian being present in the scene to be rendered:

(1)

ω(p̃)=p[0]+∑ₖ₌₁^K(p̃[k]·p[2k]+(1-p̃[k])·p[2k-1])

This formulation ensures that “base” Gaussians remain present across all frames, while the presence of the on/off state Gaussians is gated by the probability of the corresponding slot being on. We then gate the opacity of the gaussian by this probability:

(2)

α̃=α·ω(p̃),

which is then used to compute the final RGB color for a ray r via classical volume rendering [(Tagliasacchi and Mildenhall, 2022)]:

Î(r)=∑_i∈H(r)Tᵢ(r)·α̃ᵢ·cᵢ(r), Tᵢ(r)=∏_j

where H(r) represents the set of Gaussians intersected by the ray in depth order and cᵢ(r) denotes the view-dependent color. While p̃ will be selected by the user at test-time, the key question in training our representation lies in how to propagate the gradients from image Îₜ at time t to the (per-Gaussian) state distribution p.

3.2. Differentiable slot table

To achieve this, we exploit the key assumption that, within the video, the activation state of a slot is compactly supported in time. Let us denotes with the per-slot scalar πₖ(t)∈[0,1] the probability of slot k being in its on state at time t. Then, ∀k≠0 we have that πₖ(t) is zero everywhere outside some bounded, closed region. Without loss of generality, let us drop the indexing k, and focus on a single entry π(t). We can satisfy our compact support assumption by explicitly parameterizing π(t) as a smooth window function defined by its temporal endpoints (tₗ,tᵣ)333 To ensure tₗ≤tᵣ in practice we optimize auxiliary free variables u and v, and then remap them to tₗ=\min(u,v) and tᵣ=\max(u,v)., and a temperature parameter rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5) that controls the smoothness of transition; see Figure4.

By defining the midpoint as tₘ=(tₗ+tᵣ)/2, and σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(t)=σ(t/rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)), the probability of an interaction occurring at time t is computed via the normalized product of two sigmoid functions σ:

(3)π(t)=(σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(t-tₗ)·σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(tᵣ-t))/(σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(tₘ-tₗ)·σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(tᵣ-tₘ))

Therefore, to model the time window of each object interaction, we treat the state of the k-th slot at time t as a Bernoulli random variable S_k,t∈{0,1}, where S_k,t=1 denotes the slot being in its on state and S_k,t=0 its off state, whose probability mass function (PMF) for a specific state s∈{0,1} is given by:

(4)P(S_k,t=s)=πₖ(t)ˢ(1-πₖ(t))¹⁻ˢ

Train-time rendering

The quantity πₖ(t) defined above is our slot table, which we use to compute the probability of each Gaussian being present in the scene at time t:

(5)ω(t)=p[0]+∑ₖ₌₁^K(πₖ(t)·p[2k]+(1-πₖ(t))·p[2k-1])

from which, like before, we can compute a time-dependent effective opacity for volume rendering the predicted image Îₜ:

(6)α̃(t)=α·ω(t)

This differentiable rendering framework ensures that gradients propagate seamlessly to the slot activation probabilities, Gaussian state memberships, and geometric parameters, enabling stable and efficient joint optimization of the entire scene representation.

3.3. Initialization

In a casual capture setting, neither the total number of slots K, nor the precise slot transition timestamps are known a priori. Requiring the user to annotate them would defeat the very premise of a “casual” capture. To address this, we leverage the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and in particular GPT 5.6, to provide an approximate initialization for the slot-table. By prompting GPT 5.6 with a sequence of frames, we extract semantically grounded start and end timestamps for each distinct object interaction. These timestamps serve as the initial values for the endpoint parameters (tₗ,tᵣ) in our slot-table. This VLM-informed initialization allows the system to bypass exhaustive temporal searches or complex diagnostics, providing a clean and efficient configuration for final full-resolution training. To facilitate a robust optimization process, we initialize each interaction slot with a high temperature value rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5). This high-temperature initialization ensures that the Bernoulli random variable S_k,t begins with smooth transitions at the boundaries, allowing the gradients to flow more effectively over a wider temporal range during the initial stages of optimization.

3.4. Optimization

Leveraging the initial parameters derived from the VLM-based slot discovery phase, we proceed to optimize our final state-aware scene representation. We build our state-aware framework upon the 3D Gaussian Unscented Transform (3DGUT) architecture [(Wu et al., 2025a)]. Following the 3DGUT pipeline, we initialize the 3D Gaussian primitives using COLMAP-derived point clouds and augment each primitive with the learnable state logits ℓ. To provide an unbiased starting point for optimization, these logits are initialized such that the base/on/off state channels are assigned equal membership probabilities. Throughout this stage, we jointly optimize the geometric attributes of the Gaussians, their state logits, and the temporal parameters of the slot-table (tₗ,tᵣ,rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)). We strictly adhere to the optimization schedule established by 3DGUT, including its specialized densification and pruning protocols. To ensure consistent state behavior during optimization, we modify the standard densification process: whenever a Gaussian primitive is cloned or split, its state logits are inherited by the resultant primitives. This inheritance mechanism ensures that state-aware attributes remain spatially coherent even as the underlying scene geometry increases in complexity.

3.5. Training objective

Beyond the standard L₁ photometric and SSIM losses used to preserve perceptual fidelity, we employ two additional regularizers to mitigate floater artifacts, and prevent the emergence of redundant Gaussian primitives by supervising the optimization process via:

(7)L=L_rgb+λ₁L_SSIM+λ₂L_sparsity+λ₃L_compactness

Sparsity loss

To ensure a parsimonious partitioning of the scene, we regularize the Gaussian primitives to favor the static base state, thereby preventing unnecessary scene regions from being categorized as interactive. This is achieved by applying a negative log-likelihood penalty on the base state probability for all N Gaussians:

(8)L_sparsity=-1/N∑ₙ\logpₙ[0]

Compactness loss

To encourage Gaussians within slots to form spatially cohesive clusters, we first compute the opacity-weighted center of mass for primitives assigned to the on state of slot k:
