一句话：不合成伪视图，直接补密内部几何 token：3 视角输入也能超过 16 视角基线。

要点：

  • 不动重建头、也不合成假视图：把主干内部的几何 token 压进紧凑 latent，再用一步 flow matching 在相机几何条件下补齐未观测视角的 latent
  • 补完的 latent 解码回 token 交给原重建头，所以模块可以插进不同的前馈 3DGS 模型，主干保持冻结
  • 仅 3 个输入视角时，让 AnySplat 在 RealEstate10K 上的 PSNR 超过其 16 视角的稠密基线

为什么值得看：少视角就塌是前馈 3DGS 上线的最大障碍。常见做法是用图像/视频生成器补视图再编码，既贵又不保证 3D 一致；DensiTok 改的是「证据本身」，等于给现成模型加一个不改权重的外挂模块。

中文摘要：前馈 3DGS 用一次前向取代逐场景优化，但输入图像一少，质量就断崖下跌。作者指出瓶颈在重建头之前：几个无位姿视角提供的内部表示里，没有任何关于未观测区域的证据，于是出现空洞、浮点与模糊。常见补救是合成额外视角再编码，代价高且本质上不保证 3D 一致。DensiTok 换方向：把主干内部的几何 token 压进紧凑 latent 空间，条件于相机几何、用一步 flow matching 补全未观测视角的 latent，再解码回 token 交给原重建头，整个过程主干冻结。因此同一模块可插进不同前馈模型，用 3 个输入视角就能让 AnySplat 超过它 16 视角基线的 PSNR。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-06

本期推送：2026-10-27

DensiTok: Making Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting See More Views Than It Is Given

Abstract

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstructs a scene in a single forward pass, replacing per-scene optimization with a network trained across many scenes. Its quality, however, degrades sharply as the number of input images drops. The bottleneck is upstream of the reconstruction heads: from a few unposed views, the internal representation they read carries no evidence for unobserved regions, leaving holes, floaters, and blur. The common remedy supplies that evidence as pixels, synthesizing extra views with an image or video generator and re-encoding them, which is costly and not 3D-consistent by construction. We instead densify the evidence itself. We present DensiTok, a plug-in module for pretrained feed-forward 3DGS models that densifies their internal geometry tokens directly, making a frozen backbone behave as though it had observed many more views than it was given. DensiTok compresses those tokens into a compact latent space, completes the latents of the unobserved viewpoints in a single flow-matching step conditioned on camera geometry, and decodes them back into tokens that the original reconstruction heads. The same module design can be integrated into different pretrained predictors while keeping each backbone and its reconstruction heads frozen. Completion in a low-dimensional latent space requires no image synthesis or additional encoder passes. Across three pretrained backbones and two benchmarks, DensiTok consistently improves sparse-view reconstruction and recovers much of the gap to dense-view reconstruction. Project page: https://hydragon.co.kr/DensiTok.

1 Introduction

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting predicts cameras, geometry, and appearance in a single network pass, replacing per-scene optimization with a model amortized over many scenes. This makes reconstruction practical from unposed, unconstrained image collections, and recent backbones accept an arbitrary number of input views. Such models [(Jiang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025)] share a common anatomy: a geometry encoder maps the input images to a set of view-aligned geometry tokens, and camera, depth, and Gaussian heads decode that shared representation into the final reconstruction. Their quality, however, tracks the visual evidence they are given. The right side of Fig.1 plots reconstruction quality against the number of input views for several recent backbones, and it degrades in the few-view regime that motivated feed-forward reconstruction in the first place. The cause sits upstream of the heads: a handful of unposed images gives the encoder little cross-view evidence, so its tokens describe only the surfaces that were actually observed. Occluded and uncovered surfaces have no tokens at all, and the heads turn that gap into holes, floaters, and blurred novel views. What the model lacks, then, is not pixels but tokens. This suggests a different target: rather than acquiring the views it never saw, synthesize the geometry tokens those views would have produced.

Existing remedies differ mainly in where they supply the missing evidence. The dominant line of work operates in image space, either synthesizing extra input views with a multi-view or video diffusion model [(Gao et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2025)], or repairing those renderings, and refitting the scene to them [(Chen et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2025)]. Both incur two separate costs: running a large generative model at full image resolution, and then running the geometry encoder again over the enlarged set of views. Because pixels are not a shared 3D representation, consistency across generated views is encouraged but never enforced, so the reconstruction must fit views that disagree with one another. More fundamentally, pixels are a detour. The reconstruction needs only tokens for the missing viewpoints. These methods produce entire RGB frames instead, which the encoder then compresses into those tokens, so most of what the generator produced is discarded immediately. A second line of work supplies no new evidence at all, and instead trains feed-forward architectures specialized for sparse views, extracting as much as possible from the correspondences the input views do provide [(Chen et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2025a; Smart et al., 2024)]. Such models remain bounded by what those views cover, and they are standalone architectures tied to a small, fixed number of views. Closest to our setting, recent work [(Jang et al., 2026)] generates directly in token space, but without a compressed latent it must run cascaded multi-step generators on features with over a thousand channels, so generation stays expensive.

We introduce DensiTok, a plug-in that densifies the geometry tokens of a pretrained feed-forward 3DGS model so that its heads reconstruct as if from far more views. As shown in Fig.1, DensiTok sits between the geometry encoder and the reconstruction heads, with the encoder frozen and the heads either frozen or minimally adapted. The encoder’s output is naturally organized as a sequence of per-view token sets, one for each input image. DensiTok augments token sets for viewpoints that were never observed, so the heads receive the representation of a dense capture even though only a few images were encoded. Doing this directly on the tokens is costly: the heads read tokens from several layers of the encoder, and each layer has over a thousand channels in current backbones. DensiTok instead treats the whole stack of layers as one object: it compresses them into a single compact latent per view, completes the unobserved views in that latent space, and expands the result back into tokens for every layer.

Two components realize this design. The first is a variational autoencoder (VAE) [(Kingma and Welling, 2013)] with Level-Adaptive Modulation (LAM-VAE). Its encoder predicts how much each feature level should contribute for each token, fuses the features accordingly, and compresses the fused tokens into compact latents. This lets a single latent stand in for all layers without fixing in advance which layers matter, since that varies across backbones and even across scenes. The second is a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)] for Geometry Latent Augmentation: it extends the latent sequence with the unobserved views, generating their latents from the observed ones in a single flow-matching [(Lipman et al., 2022)] step, conditioned on their cameras. Since the input is unposed, these cameras are not given. The backbone’s own camera head predicts them for the observed views, and the cameras of the new views are interpolated along the path through those predictions, so the new views densify the captured trajectory rather than extrapolate beyond it. The VAE decoder then expands the completed latent sequence back into tokens at every layer the heads expect, and the camera, depth, and Gaussian heads decode them. Image-space methods supply the missing evidence indirectly, as pixels that the encoder must process again. DensiTok produces the evidence itself, once and in a compact latent space, in exactly the form the heads already consume.

We evaluate DensiTok on RealEstate10K [(Zhou et al., 2018)] and DL3DV [(Ling et al., 2024)] with three representative feed-forward 3DGS backbones: AnySplat [(Jiang et al., 2025)], WorldMirror [(Liu et al., 2025)], and Depth Anything 3 [(Lin et al., 2025)]. DensiTok consistently improves novel-view rendering quality from sparse, unposed inputs. This comes at a bounded cost: the encoder still processes only the sparse inputs, and generation is a single step in a compact latent space, so where DensiTok reaches dense-view quality, it does so in less time than dense-view reconstruction itself.

2 Related Work

2.1 Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting

Feed-forward 3DGS amortizes reconstruction across scenes by using a single network to predict Gaussian attributes, cameras, and depth from a set of images in one pass. Posed methods build explicit correspondence machinery, with pixelSplat [(Charatan et al., 2024)] using epipolar matching, MVSplat [(Chen et al., 2024a)] constructing cost volumes, and DepthSplat [(Xu et al., 2025a)] adding monocular depth priors. Splatt3R [(Smart et al., 2024)], NoPoSplat [(Ye et al., 2025)], PF3plat [(Hong et al., 2025)], and SelfSplat [(Kang et al., 2025)] remove the pose requirement for sparse unposed inputs. More recent general backbones, including AnySplat [(Jiang et al., 2025)], WorldMirror [(Liu et al., 2025)], and Depth Anything 3 [(Lin et al., 2025)], accept an arbitrary number of unconstrained views and jointly predict cameras, geometry, and Gaussians, typically by pairing a large geometry transformer with lightweight decoding heads. All of these models, however, are bounded by what their inputs show. With only a few views, overlap is limited, pose and depth are ambiguous, so the geometry tokens describe only the visible parts of the scene. Therefore, they render everything the tokens do not cover as holes, floaters, and blurred novel views. DensiTok instead treats sparse-view reconstruction as a completion problem inside the representation, augmenting token sets for additional viewpoints.

2.2 Generative Priors for 3D Reconstruction

Image-space generative priors are typically incorporated in two ways. The first augments the sparse input set with pose-controlled synthetic views before reconstruction, as in CAT3D [(Gao et al., 2024)], VistaDream [(Wang et al., 2025a)], and Bolt3D [(Szymanowicz et al., 2025)]. The second starts from a coarse 3DGS reconstruction, renders it along novel camera trajectories, and uses a video or multi-view generative model to refine or complete the rendered sequence, as in MVSplat360 [(Chen et al., 2024b)], FlowR [(Fischer et al., 2025)], VideoScene [(Wang et al., 2025b)], GSFixer [(Yin et al., 2025)], and G4Splat [(Ni et al., 2026)]. Both can synthesize plausible content for unobserved regions, but the generative step operates in RGB or generic video latent spaces with no shared 3D representation to respect. Consequently, inconsistencies across the generated views turn into geometric artifacts. Both also incur two separate costs: a generative model runs for many sampling steps at image resolution, and the scene must then be reconstructed from the enlarged set of views. DensiTok instead generates in the backbone’s own token space, so the completed representation is decoded into one Gaussian scene by the same heads, with no image synthesis and no second reconstruction.

2.3 Generation in 3D-Aware Latent Spaces

A separate line avoids image synthesis altogether by generating in a latent space that decodes straight to 3D. LN3Diff [(Lan et al., 2025)] diffuses a 3D-structured latent decoded into neural fields, Prometheus [(Yang et al., 2025)] generates multi-view RGB-D latents that a Gaussian decoder turns into pixel-aligned Gaussians, and Wonderland [(Liang et al., 2025)] lifts camera-controlled video latents directly to 3DGS. Most recently, GLD [(Jang et al., 2026)] uses the features of a pretrained geometry encoder [(Wang et al., 2025c)] as the latent space itself, applying flow matching to selected feature levels for feature-space novel-view synthesis and deriving the remaining levels by propagating the result through the frozen encoder. This removes the need for a VAE, but the generated levels keep the encoder’s full width of over a thousand channels. Therefore, GLD runs cascaded multi-step generators on them, decodes RGB with a separately trained decoder. DensiTok differs on each point. It compresses all feature levels into a single four-channel latent and completes the sequence in one step to produce a Gaussian scene rather than images.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Formulation

A feed-forward 3DGS model takes N unposed images I₁,…,I_N and reconstructs the scene in a single forward pass. Internally, a geometry encoder 𝔼_geo, a deep transformer, processes all N images jointly and represents each image as K tokens, each a d_f-dimensional vector. Such tokens exist after every layer of the encoder, but the pretrained reconstruction heads do not read only the last one: they read a fixed set of L intermediate layers (e.g., 4 of the 24 layers), chosen when the backbone was trained. We call these L layers levels and index them by ℓ=1,…,L from shallow to deep. The part of the encoder’s output that the heads consume is therefore

(F₁,…,F_L)=𝔼_geo(I₁,…,I_N), F_ℓ∈ℝ^N×K×d_f,

(1)

where F_ℓ collects the tokens of all N views at level ℓ. The camera, depth, and Gaussian heads decode (F₁,…,F_L) jointly into cameras, depth maps, and a Gaussian scene. Everything the heads know about the scene is contained in these tokens.

In our setting, only n~(

(Fᵒᵇˢ₁,…,Fᵒᵇˢ_L)=𝔼_geo({Iᵢ|mᵢ=1}), Fᵒᵇˢ_ℓ∈ℝ^n×K×d_f,

(2)

and the unobserved views have no tokens at all. DensiTok fills this gap. For every level ℓ it produces a full-size token tensor F̃_ℓ∈ℝ^N×K×d_f that covers all N views, generating the tokens of the (N-n) unobserved views from the observed ones. The target is what the encoder would have produced had all N images been available, so that the heads can decode (F̃₁,…,F̃_L) exactly as they decode (F₁,…,F_L) in the full-view case. We keep the geometry encoder and reconstruction heads frozen by default. However, due to the structure of feed-forward 3DGS reconstruction heads, we also consider minimal appearance adaptation, as detailed later.

3.2 VAE with Level-Adaptive Modulation

As shown in Fig.2, Level-Adaptive Modulation (LAM-VAE) combines level-adaptive fusion with the VAE encoder. We refer to this combined encoding module as the LAM-VAE encoder.

Because the heads read all L levels jointly, DensiTok has to produce F̃_ℓ for every level, and generating each level with its own model would multiply the cost of an already high-dimensional problem by L. We instead fuse the L levels of every token into a single vector before compressing it into a d_z-dimensional latent, so that one VAE and one generator handle all L levels. Which levels carry the most useful information can vary across backbones and even across scenes, so rather than fixing a subset of levels in advance [(Jang et al., 2026)], we let each token decide how much every level contributes. All operations in this paragraph act on one token at a time, so we drop the view and token indices and write f_ℓ∈ℝ^d_f for the token’s feature at level ℓ. Each f_ℓ is first normalized with a LayerNorm [(Ba et al., 2016)] specific to its level, so that no level dominates the others by magnitude. A gating network then decides how much each level contributes. It summarizes each f_ℓ with a shared linear layer, concatenates the L summaries, and outputs one logit per level through an MLP. Because the MLP sees all L summaries at once, the logit of each level depends on the others, so the gate compares levels rather than scoring each in isolation. A softmax turns the logits into weights α₁,…,α_L that sum to one. We use gains g_ℓ=L α_ℓ rather than the weights themselves: the gains average to one, so uniform weights recover the plain concatenation of all levels, and gating acts as a reweighting around that baseline instead of shrinking the input by a factor of L. The fused token is then a gain-weighted sum of level-wise linear projections,

h=∑_ℓ=1^Lg_ℓ W_ℓf_ℓ,

(3)

where W_ℓ is a learnable linear projection that maps level ℓ to the width of the VAE encoder transformer. Equivalently, one can concatenate the gain-weighted levels and apply a single linear layer. The fused tokens of all n observed views form one sequence that enters the VAE encoder transformer, which follows the alternating frame and global attention of VGGT [(Wang et al., 2025c)]. Frame blocks attend among the tokens of one view, global blocks attend across all views, and 2D rotary position embeddings [(Su et al., 2024)] encode each token’s position on the patch grid. For every token the transformer outputs a Gaussian posterior over a d_z-dimensional latent, parameterized by a mean μ₀∈ℝ^d_z and a log-variance \logσ²∈ℝ^d_z, with d_z=4 in our main setting.

Level-wise residual into the posterior mean.

Compressing the fused token h into a d_z-dimensional latent, is what makes generation in a compact latent space possible. However, such a narrow bottleneck can erase detail that is specific to a single level, especially since the levels have already been mixed in h before the transformer sees them. Each normalized level feature f_ℓ is projected into the latent space by a level-specific linear layer P_ℓ∈ℝ^d_z×d_f, and the projections are combined with the same weights α_ℓ from the fusion step,

μ=μ₀+∑_ℓ=1^Lα_ℓ P_ℓf_ℓ,

(4)

so the mean of each token is corrected by exactly the levels that dominate its fusion. The residual touches only the mean; the log-variance \logσ² predicted by the VAE encoder is kept as is. During VAE training, the latent of each token is sampled as z=μ+σ⊙εᵥₐₑ with εᵥₐₑ∼ℕ(0,I). At inference we drop the noise and use the mean itself as the deterministic latent representation, z=μ∈ℝ^d_z. Stacking the latents of all K tokens of all encoded N views gives Z∈ℝ^N×K×d_z; in the completion setting only the n observed views are encoded, yielding Zᵒᵇˢ∈ℝ^n×K×d_z, which is the input to the generator described next. The LAM-VAE encoder includes this level-wise residual, so its complete path from geometry tokens to Z comprises level-adaptive fusion, the VAE encoder transformer, and the residual into the posterior mean.

3.3 DiT for Geometry Latent Augmentation

We use a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)] for geometry latent augmentation: given the observed latents Zᵒᵇˢ, it generates latents for the (N-n) unobserved views and returns a completed tensor Z̃∈ℝ^N×K×d_z whose observed views are Zᵒᵇˢ. The generated views are trained to match the corresponding views of Z, the latents obtained when all N images are encoded, which are available only at training time. The DiT is conditioned on three inputs: the observed latents Zᵒᵇˢ; the mask m from the problem formulation (Sec.3.1), which marks the observed views; and cameras g₁,…,g_N for all N views, since an unobserved view has no image and its camera is the only information that specifies which view to generate. How the cameras are obtained differs between training, where ground truth exists for all N views, and inference, where only the cameras of the observed views can be predicted.

Latent sequence.

Zᵒᵇˢ covers only the n observed views, whereas the DiT works on all N views at once. We therefore lay out an N-view sequence along the camera path. The latents of each observed view sit at that view’s position and stay clean throughout; they are the condition. The positions of unobserved views are what the DiT fills in. We use rectified flow matching [(Lipman et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022)], with t=0 denoting clean latents and t=1 pure noise. During training, the latents of view i at time t are

x_t,i=mᵢ zᵒᵇˢᵢ+(1-mᵢ)[(1-t) zᵢ+t εᵢ], εᵢ∼ℕ(0,I),

(5)

where zᵢ and zᵒᵇˢᵢ∈ℝ^K×d_z are the latents of view i in Z and Zᵒᵇˢ. At inference, sampling starts from the t=1, which requires only Zᵒᵇˢ and noise. Each view carries its own time τᵢ=t(1-mᵢ): observed views stay at the clean time zero, unobserved views follow the global time t. This lets a single network handle both kinds of views in one sequence.

Camera conditioning and latent completion.

Unobserved views enter as pure noise, so their cameras are the only signal that tells the DiT which view to generate. We therefore encode the cameras of all N views as Plücker rays. For every patch token of every view, we compute the ray through that patch center, so the Plücker ray embedding has the same K-token layout as the latents. The few tokens that do not correspond to a patch, such as the camera token, receive a learnable embedding instead. These embeddings, together with the time τᵢ (zero for observed views, t for unobserved ones), condition every DiT block through adaptive LayerNorm (AdaLN) [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)]. The blocks alternate frame and global attention in the same pattern as the VAE encoder, so that noisy unobserved views gather evidence from the clean observed views in the global blocks. The DiT predicts the flow velocity with respect to increasing t, from clean latents toward noise, and the sampler integrates this velocity backward from t=1 to t=0 with Euler steps, resetting the observed views to Zᵒᵇˢ after every step so they never drift; the result is the completed tensor Z̃. Training supervises only the unobserved views, including the finetuning that reduces sampling to a single Euler step.

3.4 Camera Conditioning at Training and Inference

The DiT is conditioned on the cameras of all N views, yet at inference only the n observed views come with images, so the N cameras have to be obtained differently at training and inference. In both regimes, the backbone’s pretrained camera head first predicts the cameras of the observed views from the observed tokens Fᵒᵇˢ; we denote these predicted cameras by {ĝᵒᵇˢᵢ}ᵢ₌₁ⁿ.

Training.

During training, the dataset provides ground-truth cameras {gᵍᵗᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N for all N views. They cannot be used as n-view conditions directly: the backbone reconstructs at an arbitrary scale, so its predicted cameras {ĝᵒᵇˢᵢ}ᵢ₌₁ⁿ live in a differently scaled world, and a DiT trained on raw ground-truth cameras would face a mismatch at inference, where only predicted cameras exist. Both sets of cameras are expressed relative to the first observed view, following the convention of the backbone’s camera head, so the two worlds already share their global rotation and translation and differ only in scale. We remove this last difference by rescaling all ground-truth camera centers by a single factor, the ratio of the spread of the predicted centers to that of the ground-truth centers over the observed views, and denote the aligned cameras by {gᵃˡⁱᵍⁿᵉᵈᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N. The DiT is trained on these aligned cameras and thus only ever sees cameras in the world it will encounter at inference.

Inference.

At inference no ground-truth cameras exist, and the predicted cameras {ĝᵒᵇˢᵢ}ᵢ₌₁ⁿ are themselves the reference, so no alignment is needed. What is missing are the cameras of the (N-n) unobserved views. We obtain them by fitting a smooth trajectory through the predicted cameras, and sampling it at the unobserved views: camera centers are interpolated with a natural cubic spline, rotations with spherical interpolation. We denote the resulting cameras by {ĝⁱⁿᵗᵉʳᵖᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N-n for mᵢ=0. Because the unobserved views are virtual, we place all of them between the first and last observed cameras, so the trajectory is only ever interpolated to densify the observed camera path. In summary, the cameras that condition the DiT are the aligned ground-truth cameras {gᵃˡⁱᵍⁿᵉᵈᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N during training, and at inference {ĝᵒᵇˢᵢ}ᵢ₌₁ⁿ for observed views and {ĝⁱⁿᵗᵉʳᵖᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N-n for unobserved views.

3.5 Overall Training Strategy

DensiTok is trained in three stages, with the geometry encoder frozen throughout. In Stage 1, the VAE with Level-Adaptive Modulation is trained to reconstruct the geometry tokens of the frozen geometry encoder. In Stage 2, the DiT for geometry latent augmentation is trained on top of the frozen VAE with the rectified flow-matching objective on the unobserved views. At this stage, we can keep the Gaussian head frozen or minimally finetune it, as detailed in Appendix A.2. In Stage 3, the model is finetuned for one-step sampling by fixing the time of the unobserved views at t=1, so that a single Euler step maps noise directly to the completed latents.

item.title: 别再用多视图立体拼地形：OrTeN 把纹理高度图与线扫相机抖动放在一起做神经逆向渲染 ｜ OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction
item.description:
一句话：地形高度场与相机轨迹联合求解，4 个火星/月球场景里 3 个达到亚 GSD 对齐的 RMSE。

要点：

  • 直接对已标定的线扫卫星影像优化纹理高度图与相机改正，同时吃掉大尺度轨迹位姿误差与高频指向抖动
  • 用表面投影 patch 的归一化互相关（NCC）约束同一地形的多观测一致性，配合半经验反射率模型与阴影渲染拟合不同太阳光照下的外观
  • 4 个火星与月球场景中，3 个达到亚 GSD 对齐的地形 RMSE 并优于被测 ASP 重建；相比 EO-NeRF 的 30 万次迭代、10–20 小时收敛，效率明显更高

为什么值得看：「地形高度场 + 相机标定一起解」这套思路，对引擎侧的大世界地表重建同样成立：误差要联合求解，不要先重建再纠偏。给地形导入管线做多源卫星/航拍融合时可以直接借鉴。

中文摘要：行星探测用的数字地形图（DTM）现行做法是多视图立体，需要复杂管线处理相机误差、光照变化与视差不足。OrTeN 改用神经逆向渲染：直接在线扫卫星影像上联合优化一张纹理高度图与相机改正，在训练中同时修正大尺度轨迹位姿不一致与高频指向抖动。它用表面投影 patch 的 NCC 强制同一地形的多观测一致，并以半经验反射率模型加阴影渲染拟合多日期、不同太阳高度角下的外观。方法只需已标定的线扫影像，在 4 个火星/月球场景中 3 个达到亚 GSD 对齐的地形 RMSE，并优于被测的 ASP 重建基线，同时训练成本远低于常规 NeRF 式长迭代方案。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-16

本期推送：2026-10-27

OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction

Abstract

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are used for landing site selection, terrain-relative navigation, and geological analysis in planetary exploration. Existing state-of-practice reconstruction techniques for creating DTMs from satellite imagery use multi-view stereo, requiring complex pipelines for dealing with camera error, changing illumination, and images with limited disparity. This work introduces Orbital Terrain Networks (OrTeN), a DTM construction method that uses neural inverse rendering to jointly optimize a textured height map and orbital camera corrections from line-scan satellite images. OrTeN operates directly on calibrated line-scan images with pixel values expressed as radiance factor (I/F) and corrects both broad trajectory pose inconsistencies and high-frequency pointing jitter jointly with surface reconstruction during training. Surface-projected patch normalized cross-correlation (NCC) enforces consistency between observations of the same terrain, refining an initial rough reconstruction. A semi-empirical reflectance model and shadow rendering are used to fit surface appearance from multi-date imagery with differing solar illumination. OrTeN requires only calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses and does not use any structural priors including ranging/depth measurements or initial rough DTMs. OrTeN is evaluated on four planetary imagery datasets. Aligned terrain RMSEs are 2.35 m at Jezero Crater, 2.82 m at Gale Crater, 16.18 m at Olympus Mons, and 0.43 m at McGetchin Crater.

1 Introduction

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are an important supporting data product in space exploration. Accurate DTMs enable landing site selection and terrain-relative navigation (TRN) during entry, descent, and landing for modern autonomous space exploration missions such as Mars 2020 [11, 21]. They also provide the topographic context needed to interpret planetary landforms and their geological history [29].

Current pipelines for orbital DTM production used in the space science community rely on classical multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques to infer terrain structure—features are detected and matched between radiometrically calibrated images, bundle adjustment (BA) is performed to refine camera poses, and stereo correspondences are triangulated to produce a 3D terrain model [22, 7]. MVS can produce high-quality maps suitable for mission operations, but a number of challenges inherent to both MVS itself and its application to satellite datasets complicate the process. These challenges include the difficulty of getting reliable feature matches in the presence of shadows or low-texture regions, the line-scan geometry of most satellite images not admitting the epipolar constraints assumed by traditional MVS, and transients like dust storms or seasonal changes that alter the appearance of the terrain. Correcting for these effects can require labor-intensive preprocessing and careful manual intervention, making MVS pipelines cumbersome to use.

Neural inverse graphics provides a methodology for scene reconstruction that can address many of the challenges faced by classical MVS pipelines. For instance, satellite adaptations of neural radiance fields (NeRFs) model changing illumination and acquisition appearance while recovering scene geometry [15, 26, 27]. However, full 3D volumetric representations admit degenerate solutions—for instance, all scene density concentrated in front of cameras, explaining the observed images without recovering the true geometry—which can be particularly problematic when working with low-disparity orbital imagery where depth cues are weak. While structural priors can help mitigate these degeneracies [38, 36], these measurements are not always available or reliable.

OrTeN mitigates the shortcomings of classical MVS and volumetric neural reconstruction by optimizing a textured height map directly. Critically, OrTeN requires no structural priors to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction from images and approximate camera poses. It builds on Neural Terrain Maps (NTM) [8], adding direct bundle adjustment of line-scan camera extrinsics jointly with training, a semi-empirical photometric model, and geometric shadow modeling. The contributions of this work are:

  • 1.

    A pipeline for creating accurate DTMs through differentiable volume rendering of textured height maps including a first-order approximation of distance to the height map along the ray to improve performance at oblique angles.

  • 2.

    Joint terrain and line-scan camera optimization, including smooth trajectory adjustment and high-frequency jitter removal, and a semi-empirical, spatially varying photometric model including geometric shadow modeling with an image-space prior.

  • 3.

    An evaluation on four Mars and Moon scenes with varied relief and illumination, using the Context Camera (CTX) and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC).

    • OrTeN achieves aligned height errors below the ground sampling distance (GSD) in three scenes and improves on the tested Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP) reconstruction in those scenes.

    2 Related Work

    DTM creation with MVS.

    A number of well-established pipelines exist for creating DTMs from orbital imagery using MVS, including the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP), satellite stereo pipeline (s2p), and COLMAP [7, 13, 33, 34]. All of these methods use feature extraction and matching to constrain camera alignment before performing dense stereo matching to triangulate terrain. Orbital imagery is often taken by linescan cameras, and therefore integration into standard MVS pipelines requires particular care because each detector line is acquired at a different pose. This precludes the standard epipolar geometry assumptions used in perspective-camera MVS to make searching for correspondences straightforward. Linescan epipolar loci are generally curved, so the global rectification used for ideal perspective cameras must be replaced by local or sensor-specific constructions [14, 19]. ASP can also refine time-varying camera states to correct high-frequency jitter [4].

    Illumination changes, common in multi-date satellite data acquisitions, create an additional challenge for traditional MVS approaches. Shadows and surface reflectance can change between acquisitions even when terrain is static and make feature selection and matching more difficult. Therefore, masking shadows and other illumination-dependent artifacts is often necessary to improve the robustness of MVS matching. Shadows can also provide important geometric information which can be exploited in reconstruction, and shape-from-shading methods exploit this to further refine existing DTMs [3]. OrTeN performs trajectory bundle adjustment, including jitter removal, jointly with training, and uses a semi-empirical photometric model with explicit geometric shadow handling to improve terrain reconstruction.

    Neural reconstruction of orbital imagery.

    S-NeRF introduced illumination-aware neural rendering for satellite photogrammetry, and Sat-NeRF added rational polynomial coefficient (RPC) camera support and transient appearance modeling. EO-NeRF built on these previous methods to establish a baseline framework for general-purpose scenes on Earth by incorporating geometrically consistent shadows with learned radiometric and camera corrections and transient appearance embeddings [15, 26, 27]. Season-NeRF separated seasonal appearance from Sun and viewing geometry [17], while a semi-empirical bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) was incorporated into BRDF-NeRF [39]. Other methods address the geometry directly through depth supervision, surface constraints, or gravity-aligned and coarse-to-fine regularization [38, 31, 36]. Gaussian splatting for satellite imagery has also emerged as an alternative to methods utilizing volume rendering, offering efficient, high-quality neural scene representations [2, 9].

    More recent works have begun to focus on large-scale terrain reconstruction using neural inverse graphics. Both NTM and LNEM introduce direct rendering of linescan imagery for terrain reconstruction [8, 23]. For descent imagery, de Almeida et al. incorporate a neural height field into reconstruction from wide-angle cameras [12]. OrTeN eschews structural priors and retains the explicitly parameterized terrain representation, as is done in NTM, and adds ray-distance-based opacity and improved regularization with normalized cross-correlation (NCC). Its coarse-to-fine optimization follows the principle established by BARF: low-frequency structure should stabilize camera alignment before fine appearance is exposed [24].

    3 Methodology

    OrTeN represents the scene with a height field h_θ:ℝ²→ℝ in a local east–north–up (ENU) frame and learned surface appearance (Fig.2). The surface is x=(x,y,h_θ(x,y)), and unit-direction camera rays are given by r(t)=o+td. The origin is constructed as the common look point of all cameras, the horizontal bounds are set by the image footprints on the horizontal plane, enlarged by a factor of 1.5, and the vertical bounds are set by global planetary height limits.

    3.1 Rendering a height field

    OrTeN follows the lineage of NeuS, which derives opacity from the decrease of a logistic cumulative distribution function (CDF) along a ray through an implicit surface [37]. Applying this construction to distance along the ray rather than vertical height residual gives

    αⱼ=[1-(Φ_β(q(tⱼ₊₁)))/(Φ_β(q(tⱼ)))]₊,(1)
    Tⱼ=∏_k(2)

    Here Φ_β(q)=(1+e^-q/β)⁻¹, [z]₊=\max(z,0), αⱼ is interval opacity, Tⱼ is transmittance to that interval, and wⱼ is its rendering weight. The CDF ratio is evaluated on a log scale to improve numerical stability. Sampling locations are chosen with a proposal network as is done in Nerfacto [35].

    To obtain q, the effect of terrain slope and viewing direction on the height residual is considered:

    f(t)=r_z(t)-h_θ(r_xy(t)),(3)
    f^′(t)=d_z-∇h_θ(r_xy(t))^⊤d_xy,(4)
    q(t)=(f(t))/(\max(-f^′(t),10⁻³)).(5)

    Subscripts xy and z select horizontal and vertical components. For a plane, q(t)=t_⋆-t when the denominator clamp is inactive, where t_⋆ is the intersection distance. This formulation ensures the learned width β>0 has the same metric meaning across terrain slopes and viewing angles. Height derivatives are calculated by finite differences using a first-order formulation.

    3.2 Calibrated I/F image formation

    Training uses calibrated scalar radiance factor I/F=πL/F_⊙ images, where L is observed radiance and F_⊙ is solar irradiance at the body [6, 32]. Albedo a_ψ is aggregated over the ray samples:

    A=∑ⱼwⱼ, ā=(∑ⱼwⱼa_ψ(r_xy(t̄ⱼ)))/(\max(A,10⁻⁸)),

    		(6)

    where t̄ⱼ is the interval midpoint. A second network head predicts the spatial Lunar–Lambert mixture m_φ(x,y), integrated in the same way to give m̄. The normalized, weighted terrain normal n is used to compute positive incidence and emission cosines μ₀=[n^⊤s]₊ and μ=[n^⊤(-d)]₊, with s pointing toward the Sun. The direct-light factor is

    F(μ₀,μ,m)=(1-m)μ₀+(2mμ₀)/(\max(μ₀+μ,10⁻⁶)),(7)
    D=(F(μ₀,μ,m̄))/(F(\cos30^∘,1,m̄)).(8)

    This interpolates between Lambert and Lommel–Seeliger responses [28].

    Geometric shadows.

    Starting from the weighted camera-ray depth, a surface intersection is refined and traced toward the Sun until the ray leaves the scene bounds. Solar interval opacities αₖ^⊙ are converted to visibility using

    V=V_\rmatt∏ₖ(1-αₖ^⊙), V_η=(1-η)V_\rmatt+ηV.

    		(9)

    Here V_\rmatt smoothly suppresses light on back-facing slopes and is zero when the Sun is below the local horizon. The startup factor η ramps cast shadows in over 500 updates. Terrain outside the bounds cannot cast shadows in this model.

    OrTeN uses a semi-empirical image formation model inspired by EO-NeRF’s shadow-fill and affine brightness approach [27]. The predicted image for acquisition i is

    ŷᵢ=gᵢ[V_ηD+(1-V_η)a_\rmamb(s)]ā+bᵢ.

    		(10)

    The Sun-dependent ambient factor a_\rmamb∈(0,1) fills shadows without inheriting the direct-light angular response. Scalar gains gᵢ=e^uᵢ-ū and offsets absorb acquisition-wide brightness differences, with ū=M⁻¹∑ᵢuᵢ fixing the geometric mean gain to one across M acquisitions. The same image model is used throughout training.

    Histogram-valley shadow detection [1] is adopted to provide an initial image-space shadow estimate at startup. Only sufficiently dark, distinct pixels are accepted, and mask erosion is applied to remove boundary transients. For an ordinary rendering batch B, a regularizer is applied:

    L_\rmshadow=|B|⁻¹∑_p∈BzₚVₚ²,

    		(11)

    where zₚ=1 marks a detected core and zₚ=0 means unknown. This loss is one-sided, so unlabeled pixels are not treated as either shadow or sunlit.

    3.3 Linescan bundle adjustment

    A linescan pixel (ℓ,s) has nominal origin oᵢ⁰(ℓ) and direction dᵢ⁰(ℓ,s). Intrinsics and distortion are retained, and corrections are optimized in the local scene frame:

    oᵢ=oᵢ⁰+Δpᵢ(u),(12)
    dᵢ=\exp([Δωᵢ(u)]_×)dᵢ⁰,(13)
    Δpᵢ(u)=sₚ∑ₖ₌₀³Bₖ(u)Pᵢₖ,(14)
    Δωᵢ(u)=s_ω[∑ₖ₌₀³Bₖ(u)Wᵢₖ+rJᵢ(u)].(15)

    Here u∈[0,1] is normalized acquisition time and Bₖ are cubic Bernstein functions. The matrix [ω]_× implements the cross product with ω, and its exponential gives the corresponding rotation. The learned controls Pᵢₖ,Wᵢₖ use physical scales sₚ,s_ω which are constrained by soft priors based on expected trajectory error [11]. During the refinement phase (Sec.3.5), the ramp r introduces angular jitter Jᵢ, represented by a cubic B-spline with 64 intervals per acquisition. Its global cubic component is removed so it cannot duplicate the smooth trajectory correction.

    3.4 Surface-guided patch consistency

    In addition to uniformly sampled rays, at each training iteration 5×5 patches are sampled in source images and projected onto the current height field through the refined cameras. Each patch point is then projected from the surface into other acquisitions, where bilinear interpolation is used to calculate observed intensities. For accepted source–neighbor pairs, the normalized cross-correlation loss is

    L_\rmNCC=𝔼_P,i,j[1-(⟨Pᵢ-P̄ᵢ,Pⱼ-P̄ⱼ⟩)/(∥Pᵢ-P̄ᵢ∥₂ ∥Pⱼ-P̄ⱼ∥₂)].

    		(16)

    Here Pᵢ,Pⱼ contain the observed patch intensities and P̄ᵢ,P̄ⱼ are their means. ⟨·,·⟩ is the inner product. Invalid, occluded, low-contrast, and nearly parallel view pairs are rejected, and up to three of the best eligible neighbors are retained per source patch. NCC is active in both roughing and refinement (Sec.3.5).

    3.5 Architecture and losses

    Fig.3 shows the overall network architecture. Training progresses from images downsampled by 4× to 2×, then to native resolution. Active encoding levels are adjusted to approximately match the current image resolution. There are two training stages: roughing and refinement. Roughing ends when terrain and camera motion stabilize or the roughing update limit is reached. Refinement lowers the geometry learning rate, increases NCC sampling, and introduces jitter and local regularization.

    Let s_y=√𝔼_\rmtrain[y²] be the RMS brightness of all training pixels. The rendering loss is

    L_I/F=𝔼_p∈B[(ŷₚ-yₚ)²/s_y²].

    		(17)

    Albedo starts exactly at s_y, ambient at 0.2, and gains and offsets at one and zero. The remaining surface and appearance penalties are

    L_\rmbend=𝔼ₓ[sₕ²∥H_sₕh_θ(x)∥_F²],(18)
    L_\rmwidth=\log(1+(β/g₀)²),(19)
    L_\rmradio=𝔼ᵢ[((uᵢ-ū)/0.1)²+(bᵢ/0.01)²],(20)
    L_\rmamb=𝔼ₛ[[logita_\rmamb(s)-\log9]₊²].(21)

    Here H_sₕ is the finite-difference Hessian. In order, these losses regularize surface bending, control the rendering width, enforce radiometric calibration, and constrain the ambient illumination. The fixed scale g₀ is the initial training-image GSD. The optional ambient penalty acts only when the ambient factor exceeds 0.9.

    Camera regularization penalizes the dimensionless trajectory controls and, in refinement, the sampled jitter motion. Let cᵢ(u) concatenate the trajectory position and rotation corrections divided by sₚ and s_ω. Its second derivative penalizes trajectory curvature:

    L_\rmcamera=λ_C𝔼_i,k(∥Pᵢₖ∥₂²+∥Wᵢₖ∥₂²)
    +λ_C1_r>0𝔼_i,u∥Jᵢ(u)∥₂²
    +λ_K𝔼ᵢ∫₀¹∥cᵢ^′′(u)∥₂²du.(22)

    For each camera or solar ray, the proposal loss is the histogram-envelope objective used by Nerfstudio [35]:

    L_\rmenv=∑ₗ𝔼ⱼ([wⱼ-Wₗⱼ]₊²)/(wⱼ+10⁻⁷).

    		(23)

    Here Wₗⱼ is proposal level l’s total mass in bins overlapping final interval j. The camera and solar proposal losses are summed as L_\rmproposal. The complete objective is

    L=L_I/F+ηλ_NL_\rmNCC+λ_WL_\rmwidth+λ_RL_\rmradio
    +L_\rmcamera+L_\rmproposal
    +r(λ_BL_\rmbend+λ_SL_\rmshadow+λ_AL_\rmamb).(24)

    The refinement ramp r is zero during roughing and rises over 500 updates after transition.

    4 Experiments and Results

    4.1 Datasets

    Four lunar and Martian datasets were selected for their varied terrain and illumination and the availability of reference DTMs. Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and Olympus Mons each contain fifteen 1024×1024 CTX crops. McGetchin Crater contains ten LROC NAC crops of the same size. Images are calibrated to I/F using the Integrated Software for Imagers and Spectrometers (ISIS) and paired with initial line-scan camera states. Table1 gives additional details on the instruments and reference DTM quality for each dataset. The Olympus dataset reference uses a DTM separately reconstructed from the same image collection because a high-quality engineering DTM was unavailable.

    4.2 Evaluation protocol and metrics

    Metrics for each scene are calculated over a fixed reference footprint that is covered by at least five initial cameras. To resolve the gauge freedom inherent in the bundle adjustment process, reconstructed DTMs are aligned to the reference DTM using a six-degree-of-freedom rigid transformation. No scale change, local warping, or separate alignment for different metrics is applied. For aligned height errors eₚ=ĥₐ(p)-h_\rmref(p) on N valid posts, the metrics are

    RMSEₐ=√N⁻¹∑ₚeₚ², MAEₐ=N⁻¹∑ₚ|eₚ|.

    		(25)

    The subscript a denotes metrics applied to rigidly aligned DTMs, so these scores measure relative shape rather than absolute geolocation.

    Slope is evaluated using a local quadratic surface fit calculated over a 9×9 sliding window. This follows established practices in terrain analysis [18] and reduces sensitivity to reference DTM artifacts. Slope RMSEa is the RMS difference between slope angles in degrees, under the same rigid alignment. Although OrTeN permits direct network differentiation, the reported comparison differentiates polynomial fits to every method’s raster export to match spatial scale. Height RMSE and MAE use unsmoothed elevations.

    One 64×64 block per acquisition, at the full image resolution, is held out during training for perceptural metric calculation. This is necessary because of learned image-dependent radiometric calibration. PSNR is 10\log₁₀(R²/MSE) where R is the 99th minus 1st percentile of the pooled held-out observations per scene. SSIM uses the same range and 11×11 Gaussian windows (σ=1.5 pixels), averaged over valid window centers.

    4.3 Training details

    All training runs use a single seed, are limited to 15,000 iterations, and use a batch size of 8,192 rays. The same configuration for OrTeN is used across all four scenes. This includes enabling trajectory BA, jitter adjustment, and the detected-shadow prior with weight 0.01. The roughing stage iteration cap is set to 8,000 updates.

    Comparisons with depth-supervised EO-NeRF [27] and ASP [7] are reported. EO-NeRF uses the same camera-derived scene bounds as OrTeN, 8,192 rays per update, 128 depth samples per ray, and fixed cameras. Its depth targets come from the unaligned ASP stereo mosaics, without reference-terrain supervision or registration. ASP uses image-based BA, dense stereo, and jitter refinement anchored to its own stereo terrain estimates. The same ASP pipeline is used for all scenes.

    Mean setup-plus-training times are 52.7/41.2 minutes for OrTeN on NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation/RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, respectively. These include periodic evaluation and checkpointing, exclude final evaluation, and average different scene/configuration mixes across GPUs. OrTeN uses Adam with a 500-step warmup to learning rates of 3×10⁻³ for geometry and appearance, 10⁻³ for cameras, and 10⁻² for proposal networks. Geometry decays during roughing, then starts refinement at most 1.5×10⁻⁴ and decays to 5×10⁻⁵. Appearance and camera rates finish at 3×10⁻⁴ and 10⁻⁵.

    4.4 Results and ablations

    Tab.2 gives the results of the baseline OrTeN configuration on each scene. OrTeN attains sub-GSD height RMSEa in Jezero, Gale, and McGetchin scenes. On the Olympus Mons scene, the RMSEa remains at 2.91 × GSD. Its large relief (almost 3 km) and substantial cast shadows make reconstruction challenging. The lack of an independent, high-accuracy reference limits comparison with ASP, which performs similarly on this scene.

    Depth-supervised EO-NeRF fails to reconstruct accurate DTMs in any of the scenes despite access to structural supervision. It falls short of OrTeN both visually and in structural accuracy. Noting that the default EO-NeRF configuration trains for much longer (300,000 iterations) and takes 10-20 hours to converge, this comparison demonstrates that OrTeN’s approach achieves meaningful improvement in both efficiency and accuracy.

    ASP recovers sound DTMs for all four scenes, but performs worse than OrTeN on all scenes except Olympus Mons. as opposed to ASP, which typically processes images pairwise or in smaller subsets. OrTeN also benefits from its semi-empirical appearance modeling which allows it to better deal with shadows and varying illumination conditions which may confound feature matching in purely photogrammetric approaches.

    Four ablation studies were conducted to evaluate the impact of the three key features in this work: bundle adjustment with jitter, normalized cross-correlation (NCC) for photometric consistency, and semi-empirical appearance modeling with shadow modeling. The results of the ablation are summarized in Tab.3.

    Removing BA significantly degrades the quality of the reconstructed DTMs across all scenes, highlighting the importance of joint optimization of camera parameters and scene geometry. Fig.4 shows baseline and no-BA renderings of the same acquisition for the McGetchin Crater scene. The no-BA ablation shows clearly degraded visual reconstruction quality with a drop of more than 10 dB in reserved-pixel PSNR. The DTM is similarly impacted with RMSEa increasing from 0.43 to 10.36 m and the quality of the reconstruction visibly degrading, especially in the fine detail around the central crater region.

    Disabling NCC has an even more pronounced effect on the quality of the reconstructed DTMs. Fig.5 shows baseline and no-NCC renderings of the same acquisition for the Jezero Crater scene, and again illustrates the degradation of fine detail around the crater region. In some of the scenes, the PSNR improves in the no-NCC ablation compared to the baseline. Rendering loss alone can therefore be misleading when assessing terrain reconstruction, especially in low-disparity orbital scenes.

    Removal of geometric shadows produces a less pronounced effect on the quality of the reconstructed DTMs compared to the other ablations, but can be observed in reconstruction quality. Fig.6 shows baseline and no-shadow renderings of the same acquisition for the Olympus Mons scene. The baseline is able to reconstruct the large shadow cast by the cliff face while the ablated scene cannot.

    5 Conclusion

    OrTeN jointly reconstructs terrain and refines line-scan cameras from calibrated orbital images without depth supervision or stereo initialization. Across four Mars and Moon scenes, it achieves sub-GSD aligned terrain RMSE in three and improves on the tested ASP reconstruction in those same three scenes. The ablations demonstrate the importance of camera refinement and surface-patch NCC for achieving high geometric accuracy. They also show that an accurate image reconstruction can coexist with an incorrect surface. Comparison with EO-NeRF with depth supervision also demonstrates that structural priors are not sufficient to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction efficiently.

    However, a number of limitations remain. Without structural priors such as ranging measurements or known control points, absolute geolocation is not possible. Furthermore, it is possible that integrating structural priors into OrTeN could improve reconstruction accuracy and efficiency and should be tested. While the height map representation is an effective structural prior for the datasets considered here, when detail becomes sufficient, this representation becomes more limiting. For instance, height maps cannot represent overhangs or complex 3D structures like caves. Future work should work on mitigating these shortcomings to allow ground level imagery to be integrated into the terrain reconstruction process.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：地形高度场与相机轨迹联合求解，4 个火星/月球场景里 3 个达到亚 GSD 对齐的 RMSE。

要点：

  • 直接对已标定的线扫卫星影像优化纹理高度图与相机改正，同时吃掉大尺度轨迹位姿误差与高频指向抖动
  • 用表面投影 patch 的归一化互相关（NCC）约束同一地形的多观测一致性，配合半经验反射率模型与阴影渲染拟合不同太阳光照下的外观
  • 4 个火星与月球场景中，3 个达到亚 GSD 对齐的地形 RMSE 并优于被测 ASP 重建；相比 EO-NeRF 的 30 万次迭代、10–20 小时收敛，效率明显更高

为什么值得看：「地形高度场 + 相机标定一起解」这套思路，对引擎侧的大世界地表重建同样成立：误差要联合求解，不要先重建再纠偏。给地形导入管线做多源卫星/航拍融合时可以直接借鉴。

中文摘要：行星探测用的数字地形图（DTM）现行做法是多视图立体，需要复杂管线处理相机误差、光照变化与视差不足。OrTeN 改用神经逆向渲染：直接在线扫卫星影像上联合优化一张纹理高度图与相机改正，在训练中同时修正大尺度轨迹位姿不一致与高频指向抖动。它用表面投影 patch 的 NCC 强制同一地形的多观测一致，并以半经验反射率模型加阴影渲染拟合多日期、不同太阳高度角下的外观。方法只需已标定的线扫影像，在 4 个火星/月球场景中 3 个达到亚 GSD 对齐的地形 RMSE，并优于被测的 ASP 重建基线，同时训练成本远低于常规 NeRF 式长迭代方案。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-16

本期推送：2026-10-27

OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction

Abstract

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are used for landing site selection, terrain-relative navigation, and geological analysis in planetary exploration. Existing state-of-practice reconstruction techniques for creating DTMs from satellite imagery use multi-view stereo, requiring complex pipelines for dealing with camera error, changing illumination, and images with limited disparity. This work introduces Orbital Terrain Networks (OrTeN), a DTM construction method that uses neural inverse rendering to jointly optimize a textured height map and orbital camera corrections from line-scan satellite images. OrTeN operates directly on calibrated line-scan images with pixel values expressed as radiance factor (I/F) and corrects both broad trajectory pose inconsistencies and high-frequency pointing jitter jointly with surface reconstruction during training. Surface-projected patch normalized cross-correlation (NCC) enforces consistency between observations of the same terrain, refining an initial rough reconstruction. A semi-empirical reflectance model and shadow rendering are used to fit surface appearance from multi-date imagery with differing solar illumination. OrTeN requires only calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses and does not use any structural priors including ranging/depth measurements or initial rough DTMs. OrTeN is evaluated on four planetary imagery datasets. Aligned terrain RMSEs are 2.35 m at Jezero Crater, 2.82 m at Gale Crater, 16.18 m at Olympus Mons, and 0.43 m at McGetchin Crater.

1 Introduction

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are an important supporting data product in space exploration. Accurate DTMs enable landing site selection and terrain-relative navigation (TRN) during entry, descent, and landing for modern autonomous space exploration missions such as Mars 2020 [11, 21]. They also provide the topographic context needed to interpret planetary landforms and their geological history [29].

Current pipelines for orbital DTM production used in the space science community rely on classical multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques to infer terrain structure—features are detected and matched between radiometrically calibrated images, bundle adjustment (BA) is performed to refine camera poses, and stereo correspondences are triangulated to produce a 3D terrain model [22, 7]. MVS can produce high-quality maps suitable for mission operations, but a number of challenges inherent to both MVS itself and its application to satellite datasets complicate the process. These challenges include the difficulty of getting reliable feature matches in the presence of shadows or low-texture regions, the line-scan geometry of most satellite images not admitting the epipolar constraints assumed by traditional MVS, and transients like dust storms or seasonal changes that alter the appearance of the terrain. Correcting for these effects can require labor-intensive preprocessing and careful manual intervention, making MVS pipelines cumbersome to use.

Neural inverse graphics provides a methodology for scene reconstruction that can address many of the challenges faced by classical MVS pipelines. For instance, satellite adaptations of neural radiance fields (NeRFs) model changing illumination and acquisition appearance while recovering scene geometry [15, 26, 27]. However, full 3D volumetric representations admit degenerate solutions—for instance, all scene density concentrated in front of cameras, explaining the observed images without recovering the true geometry—which can be particularly problematic when working with low-disparity orbital imagery where depth cues are weak. While structural priors can help mitigate these degeneracies [38, 36], these measurements are not always available or reliable.

OrTeN mitigates the shortcomings of classical MVS and volumetric neural reconstruction by optimizing a textured height map directly. Critically, OrTeN requires no structural priors to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction from images and approximate camera poses. It builds on Neural Terrain Maps (NTM) [8], adding direct bundle adjustment of line-scan camera extrinsics jointly with training, a semi-empirical photometric model, and geometric shadow modeling. The contributions of this work are:

  • 1.

    A pipeline for creating accurate DTMs through differentiable volume rendering of textured height maps including a first-order approximation of distance to the height map along the ray to improve performance at oblique angles.

  • 2.

    Joint terrain and line-scan camera optimization, including smooth trajectory adjustment and high-frequency jitter removal, and a semi-empirical, spatially varying photometric model including geometric shadow modeling with an image-space prior.

  • 3.

    An evaluation on four Mars and Moon scenes with varied relief and illumination, using the Context Camera (CTX) and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC).

    • OrTeN achieves aligned height errors below the ground sampling distance (GSD) in three scenes and improves on the tested Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP) reconstruction in those scenes.

    2 Related Work

    DTM creation with MVS.

    A number of well-established pipelines exist for creating DTMs from orbital imagery using MVS, including the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP), satellite stereo pipeline (s2p), and COLMAP [7, 13, 33, 34]. All of these methods use feature extraction and matching to constrain camera alignment before performing dense stereo matching to triangulate terrain. Orbital imagery is often taken by linescan cameras, and therefore integration into standard MVS pipelines requires particular care because each detector line is acquired at a different pose. This precludes the standard epipolar geometry assumptions used in perspective-camera MVS to make searching for correspondences straightforward. Linescan epipolar loci are generally curved, so the global rectification used for ideal perspective cameras must be replaced by local or sensor-specific constructions [14, 19]. ASP can also refine time-varying camera states to correct high-frequency jitter [4].

    Illumination changes, common in multi-date satellite data acquisitions, create an additional challenge for traditional MVS approaches. Shadows and surface reflectance can change between acquisitions even when terrain is static and make feature selection and matching more difficult. Therefore, masking shadows and other illumination-dependent artifacts is often necessary to improve the robustness of MVS matching. Shadows can also provide important geometric information which can be exploited in reconstruction, and shape-from-shading methods exploit this to further refine existing DTMs [3]. OrTeN performs trajectory bundle adjustment, including jitter removal, jointly with training, and uses a semi-empirical photometric model with explicit geometric shadow handling to improve terrain reconstruction.

    Neural reconstruction of orbital imagery.

    S-NeRF introduced illumination-aware neural rendering for satellite photogrammetry, and Sat-NeRF added rational polynomial coefficient (RPC) camera support and transient appearance modeling. EO-NeRF built on these previous methods to establish a baseline framework for general-purpose scenes on Earth by incorporating geometrically consistent shadows with learned radiometric and camera corrections and transient appearance embeddings [15, 26, 27]. Season-NeRF separated seasonal appearance from Sun and viewing geometry [17], while a semi-empirical bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) was incorporated into BRDF-NeRF [39]. Other methods address the geometry directly through depth supervision, surface constraints, or gravity-aligned and coarse-to-fine regularization [38, 31, 36]. Gaussian splatting for satellite imagery has also emerged as an alternative to methods utilizing volume rendering, offering efficient, high-quality neural scene representations [2, 9].

    More recent works have begun to focus on large-scale terrain reconstruction using neural inverse graphics. Both NTM and LNEM introduce direct rendering of linescan imagery for terrain reconstruction [8, 23]. For descent imagery, de Almeida et al. incorporate a neural height field into reconstruction from wide-angle cameras [12]. OrTeN eschews structural priors and retains the explicitly parameterized terrain representation, as is done in NTM, and adds ray-distance-based opacity and improved regularization with normalized cross-correlation (NCC). Its coarse-to-fine optimization follows the principle established by BARF: low-frequency structure should stabilize camera alignment before fine appearance is exposed [24].

    3 Methodology

    OrTeN represents the scene with a height field h_θ:ℝ²→ℝ in a local east–north–up (ENU) frame and learned surface appearance (Fig.2). The surface is x=(x,y,h_θ(x,y)), and unit-direction camera rays are given by r(t)=o+td. The origin is constructed as the common look point of all cameras, the horizontal bounds are set by the image footprints on the horizontal plane, enlarged by a factor of 1.5, and the vertical bounds are set by global planetary height limits.

    3.1 Rendering a height field

    OrTeN follows the lineage of NeuS, which derives opacity from the decrease of a logistic cumulative distribution function (CDF) along a ray through an implicit surface [37]. Applying this construction to distance along the ray rather than vertical height residual gives

    αⱼ=[1-(Φ_β(q(tⱼ₊₁)))/(Φ_β(q(tⱼ)))]₊,(1)
    Tⱼ=∏_k(2)

    Here Φ_β(q)=(1+e^-q/β)⁻¹, [z]₊=\max(z,0), αⱼ is interval opacity, Tⱼ is transmittance to that interval, and wⱼ is its rendering weight. The CDF ratio is evaluated on a log scale to improve numerical stability. Sampling locations are chosen with a proposal network as is done in Nerfacto [35].

    To obtain q, the effect of terrain slope and viewing direction on the height residual is considered:

    f(t)=r_z(t)-h_θ(r_xy(t)),(3)
    f^′(t)=d_z-∇h_θ(r_xy(t))^⊤d_xy,(4)
    q(t)=(f(t))/(\max(-f^′(t),10⁻³)).(5)

    Subscripts xy and z select horizontal and vertical components. For a plane, q(t)=t_⋆-t when the denominator clamp is inactive, where t_⋆ is the intersection distance. This formulation ensures the learned width β>0 has the same metric meaning across terrain slopes and viewing angles. Height derivatives are calculated by finite differences using a first-order formulation.

    3.2 Calibrated I/F image formation

    Training uses calibrated scalar radiance factor I/F=πL/F_⊙ images, where L is observed radiance and F_⊙ is solar irradiance at the body [6, 32]. Albedo a_ψ is aggregated over the ray samples:

    A=∑ⱼwⱼ, ā=(∑ⱼwⱼa_ψ(r_xy(t̄ⱼ)))/(\max(A,10⁻⁸)),

    		(6)

    where t̄ⱼ is the interval midpoint. A second network head predicts the spatial Lunar–Lambert mixture m_φ(x,y), integrated in the same way to give m̄. The normalized, weighted terrain normal n is used to compute positive incidence and emission cosines μ₀=[n^⊤s]₊ and μ=[n^⊤(-d)]₊, with s pointing toward the Sun. The direct-light factor is

    F(μ₀,μ,m)=(1-m)μ₀+(2mμ₀)/(\max(μ₀+μ,10⁻⁶)),(7)
    D=(F(μ₀,μ,m̄))/(F(\cos30^∘,1,m̄)).(8)

    This interpolates between Lambert and Lommel–Seeliger responses [28].

    Geometric shadows.

    Starting from the weighted camera-ray depth, a surface intersection is refined and traced toward the Sun until the ray leaves the scene bounds. Solar interval opacities αₖ^⊙ are converted to visibility using

    V=V_\rmatt∏ₖ(1-αₖ^⊙), V_η=(1-η)V_\rmatt+ηV.

    		(9)

    Here V_\rmatt smoothly suppresses light on back-facing slopes and is zero when the Sun is below the local horizon. The startup factor η ramps cast shadows in over 500 updates. Terrain outside the bounds cannot cast shadows in this model.

    OrTeN uses a semi-empirical image formation model inspired by EO-NeRF’s shadow-fill and affine brightness approach [27]. The predicted image for acquisition i is

    ŷᵢ=gᵢ[V_ηD+(1-V_η)a_\rmamb(s)]ā+bᵢ.

    		(10)

    The Sun-dependent ambient factor a_\rmamb∈(0,1) fills shadows without inheriting the direct-light angular response. Scalar gains gᵢ=e^uᵢ-ū and offsets absorb acquisition-wide brightness differences, with ū=M⁻¹∑ᵢuᵢ fixing the geometric mean gain to one across M acquisitions. The same image model is used throughout training.

    Histogram-valley shadow detection [1] is adopted to provide an initial image-space shadow estimate at startup. Only sufficiently dark, distinct pixels are accepted, and mask erosion is applied to remove boundary transients. For an ordinary rendering batch B, a regularizer is applied:

    L_\rmshadow=|B|⁻¹∑_p∈BzₚVₚ²,

    		(11)

    where zₚ=1 marks a detected core and zₚ=0 means unknown. This loss is one-sided, so unlabeled pixels are not treated as either shadow or sunlit.

    3.3 Linescan bundle adjustment

    A linescan pixel (ℓ,s) has nominal origin oᵢ⁰(ℓ) and direction dᵢ⁰(ℓ,s). Intrinsics and distortion are retained, and corrections are optimized in the local scene frame:

    oᵢ=oᵢ⁰+Δpᵢ(u),(12)
    dᵢ=\exp([Δωᵢ(u)]_×)dᵢ⁰,(13)
    Δpᵢ(u)=sₚ∑ₖ₌₀³Bₖ(u)Pᵢₖ,(14)
    Δωᵢ(u)=s_ω[∑ₖ₌₀³Bₖ(u)Wᵢₖ+rJᵢ(u)].(15)

    Here u∈[0,1] is normalized acquisition time and Bₖ are cubic Bernstein functions. The matrix [ω]_× implements the cross product with ω, and its exponential gives the corresponding rotation. The learned controls Pᵢₖ,Wᵢₖ use physical scales sₚ,s_ω which are constrained by soft priors based on expected trajectory error [11]. During the refinement phase (Sec.3.5), the ramp r introduces angular jitter Jᵢ, represented by a cubic B-spline with 64 intervals per acquisition. Its global cubic component is removed so it cannot duplicate the smooth trajectory correction.

    3.4 Surface-guided patch consistency

    In addition to uniformly sampled rays, at each training iteration 5×5 patches are sampled in source images and projected onto the current height field through the refined cameras. Each patch point is then projected from the surface into other acquisitions, where bilinear interpolation is used to calculate observed intensities. For accepted source–neighbor pairs, the normalized cross-correlation loss is

    L_\rmNCC=𝔼_P,i,j[1-(⟨Pᵢ-P̄ᵢ,Pⱼ-P̄ⱼ⟩)/(∥Pᵢ-P̄ᵢ∥₂ ∥Pⱼ-P̄ⱼ∥₂)].

    		(16)

    Here Pᵢ,Pⱼ contain the observed patch intensities and P̄ᵢ,P̄ⱼ are their means. ⟨·,·⟩ is the inner product. Invalid, occluded, low-contrast, and nearly parallel view pairs are rejected, and up to three of the best eligible neighbors are retained per source patch. NCC is active in both roughing and refinement (Sec.3.5).

    3.5 Architecture and losses

    Fig.3 shows the overall network architecture. Training progresses from images downsampled by 4× to 2×, then to native resolution. Active encoding levels are adjusted to approximately match the current image resolution. There are two training stages: roughing and refinement. Roughing ends when terrain and camera motion stabilize or the roughing update limit is reached. Refinement lowers the geometry learning rate, increases NCC sampling, and introduces jitter and local regularization.

    Let s_y=√𝔼_\rmtrain[y²] be the RMS brightness of all training pixels. The rendering loss is

    L_I/F=𝔼_p∈B[(ŷₚ-yₚ)²/s_y²].

    		(17)

    Albedo starts exactly at s_y, ambient at 0.2, and gains and offsets at one and zero. The remaining surface and appearance penalties are

    L_\rmbend=𝔼ₓ[sₕ²∥H_sₕh_θ(x)∥_F²],(18)
    L_\rmwidth=\log(1+(β/g₀)²),(19)
    L_\rmradio=𝔼ᵢ[((uᵢ-ū)/0.1)²+(bᵢ/0.01)²],(20)
    L_\rmamb=𝔼ₛ[[logita_\rmamb(s)-\log9]₊²].(21)

    Here H_sₕ is the finite-difference Hessian. In order, these losses regularize surface bending, control the rendering width, enforce radiometric calibration, and constrain the ambient illumination. The fixed scale g₀ is the initial training-image GSD. The optional ambient penalty acts only when the ambient factor exceeds 0.9.

    Camera regularization penalizes the dimensionless trajectory controls and, in refinement, the sampled jitter motion. Let cᵢ(u) concatenate the trajectory position and rotation corrections divided by sₚ and s_ω. Its second derivative penalizes trajectory curvature:

    L_\rmcamera=λ_C𝔼_i,k(∥Pᵢₖ∥₂²+∥Wᵢₖ∥₂²)
    +λ_C1_r>0𝔼_i,u∥Jᵢ(u)∥₂²
    +λ_K𝔼ᵢ∫₀¹∥cᵢ^′′(u)∥₂²du.(22)

    For each camera or solar ray, the proposal loss is the histogram-envelope objective used by Nerfstudio [35]:

    L_\rmenv=∑ₗ𝔼ⱼ([wⱼ-Wₗⱼ]₊²)/(wⱼ+10⁻⁷).

    		(23)

    Here Wₗⱼ is proposal level l’s total mass in bins overlapping final interval j. The camera and solar proposal losses are summed as L_\rmproposal. The complete objective is

    L=L_I/F+ηλ_NL_\rmNCC+λ_WL_\rmwidth+λ_RL_\rmradio
    +L_\rmcamera+L_\rmproposal
    +r(λ_BL_\rmbend+λ_SL_\rmshadow+λ_AL_\rmamb).(24)

    The refinement ramp r is zero during roughing and rises over 500 updates after transition.

    4 Experiments and Results

    4.1 Datasets

    Four lunar and Martian datasets were selected for their varied terrain and illumination and the availability of reference DTMs. Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and Olympus Mons each contain fifteen 1024×1024 CTX crops. McGetchin Crater contains ten LROC NAC crops of the same size. Images are calibrated to I/F using the Integrated Software for Imagers and Spectrometers (ISIS) and paired with initial line-scan camera states. Table1 gives additional details on the instruments and reference DTM quality for each dataset. The Olympus dataset reference uses a DTM separately reconstructed from the same image collection because a high-quality engineering DTM was unavailable.

    4.2 Evaluation protocol and metrics

    Metrics for each scene are calculated over a fixed reference footprint that is covered by at least five initial cameras. To resolve the gauge freedom inherent in the bundle adjustment process, reconstructed DTMs are aligned to the reference DTM using a six-degree-of-freedom rigid transformation. No scale change, local warping, or separate alignment for different metrics is applied. For aligned height errors eₚ=ĥₐ(p)-h_\rmref(p) on N valid posts, the metrics are

    RMSEₐ=√N⁻¹∑ₚeₚ², MAEₐ=N⁻¹∑ₚ|eₚ|.

    		(25)

    The subscript a denotes metrics applied to rigidly aligned DTMs, so these scores measure relative shape rather than absolute geolocation.

    Slope is evaluated using a local quadratic surface fit calculated over a 9×9 sliding window. This follows established practices in terrain analysis [18] and reduces sensitivity to reference DTM artifacts. Slope RMSEa is the RMS difference between slope angles in degrees, under the same rigid alignment. Although OrTeN permits direct network differentiation, the reported comparison differentiates polynomial fits to every method’s raster export to match spatial scale. Height RMSE and MAE use unsmoothed elevations.

    One 64×64 block per acquisition, at the full image resolution, is held out during training for perceptural metric calculation. This is necessary because of learned image-dependent radiometric calibration. PSNR is 10\log₁₀(R²/MSE) where R is the 99th minus 1st percentile of the pooled held-out observations per scene. SSIM uses the same range and 11×11 Gaussian windows (σ=1.5 pixels), averaged over valid window centers.

    4.3 Training details

    All training runs use a single seed, are limited to 15,000 iterations, and use a batch size of 8,192 rays. The same configuration for OrTeN is used across all four scenes. This includes enabling trajectory BA, jitter adjustment, and the detected-shadow prior with weight 0.01. The roughing stage iteration cap is set to 8,000 updates.

    Comparisons with depth-supervised EO-NeRF [27] and ASP [7] are reported. EO-NeRF uses the same camera-derived scene bounds as OrTeN, 8,192 rays per update, 128 depth samples per ray, and fixed cameras. Its depth targets come from the unaligned ASP stereo mosaics, without reference-terrain supervision or registration. ASP uses image-based BA, dense stereo, and jitter refinement anchored to its own stereo terrain estimates. The same ASP pipeline is used for all scenes.

    Mean setup-plus-training times are 52.7/41.2 minutes for OrTeN on NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation/RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, respectively. These include periodic evaluation and checkpointing, exclude final evaluation, and average different scene/configuration mixes across GPUs. OrTeN uses Adam with a 500-step warmup to learning rates of 3×10⁻³ for geometry and appearance, 10⁻³ for cameras, and 10⁻² for proposal networks. Geometry decays during roughing, then starts refinement at most 1.5×10⁻⁴ and decays to 5×10⁻⁵. Appearance and camera rates finish at 3×10⁻⁴ and 10⁻⁵.

    4.4 Results and ablations

    Tab.2 gives the results of the baseline OrTeN configuration on each scene. OrTeN attains sub-GSD height RMSEa in Jezero, Gale, and McGetchin scenes. On the Olympus Mons scene, the RMSEa remains at 2.91 × GSD. Its large relief (almost 3 km) and substantial cast shadows make reconstruction challenging. The lack of an independent, high-accuracy reference limits comparison with ASP, which performs similarly on this scene.

    Depth-supervised EO-NeRF fails to reconstruct accurate DTMs in any of the scenes despite access to structural supervision. It falls short of OrTeN both visually and in structural accuracy. Noting that the default EO-NeRF configuration trains for much longer (300,000 iterations) and takes 10-20 hours to converge, this comparison demonstrates that OrTeN’s approach achieves meaningful improvement in both efficiency and accuracy.

    ASP recovers sound DTMs for all four scenes, but performs worse than OrTeN on all scenes except Olympus Mons. as opposed to ASP, which typically processes images pairwise or in smaller subsets. OrTeN also benefits from its semi-empirical appearance modeling which allows it to better deal with shadows and varying illumination conditions which may confound feature matching in purely photogrammetric approaches.

    Four ablation studies were conducted to evaluate the impact of the three key features in this work: bundle adjustment with jitter, normalized cross-correlation (NCC) for photometric consistency, and semi-empirical appearance modeling with shadow modeling. The results of the ablation are summarized in Tab.3.

    Removing BA significantly degrades the quality of the reconstructed DTMs across all scenes, highlighting the importance of joint optimization of camera parameters and scene geometry. Fig.4 shows baseline and no-BA renderings of the same acquisition for the McGetchin Crater scene. The no-BA ablation shows clearly degraded visual reconstruction quality with a drop of more than 10 dB in reserved-pixel PSNR. The DTM is similarly impacted with RMSEa increasing from 0.43 to 10.36 m and the quality of the reconstruction visibly degrading, especially in the fine detail around the central crater region.

    Disabling NCC has an even more pronounced effect on the quality of the reconstructed DTMs. Fig.5 shows baseline and no-NCC renderings of the same acquisition for the Jezero Crater scene, and again illustrates the degradation of fine detail around the crater region. In some of the scenes, the PSNR improves in the no-NCC ablation compared to the baseline. Rendering loss alone can therefore be misleading when assessing terrain reconstruction, especially in low-disparity orbital scenes.

    Removal of geometric shadows produces a less pronounced effect on the quality of the reconstructed DTMs compared to the other ablations, but can be observed in reconstruction quality. Fig.6 shows baseline and no-shadow renderings of the same acquisition for the Olympus Mons scene. The baseline is able to reconstruct the large shadow cast by the cliff face while the ablated scene cannot.

    5 Conclusion

    OrTeN jointly reconstructs terrain and refines line-scan cameras from calibrated orbital images without depth supervision or stereo initialization. Across four Mars and Moon scenes, it achieves sub-GSD aligned terrain RMSE in three and improves on the tested ASP reconstruction in those same three scenes. The ablations demonstrate the importance of camera refinement and surface-patch NCC for achieving high geometric accuracy. They also show that an accurate image reconstruction can coexist with an incorrect surface. Comparison with EO-NeRF with depth supervision also demonstrates that structural priors are not sufficient to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction efficiently.

    However, a number of limitations remain. Without structural priors such as ranging measurements or known control points, absolute geolocation is not possible. Furthermore, it is possible that integrating structural priors into OrTeN could improve reconstruction accuracy and efficiency and should be tested. While the height map representation is an effective structural prior for the datasets considered here, when detail becomes sufficient, this representation becomes more limiting. For instance, height maps cannot represent overhangs or complex 3D structures like caves. Future work should work on mitigating these shortcomings to allow ground level imagery to be integrated into the terrain reconstruction process.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 颜色自洽就能约束几何：跨射线一致性把原生 NeRF 的 Chamfer 距离拉低 30.8% ｜ Geometry Regularization for Vanilla NeRF via Self-Supervised Cross-Ray Consistency
item.description:
一句话：无需深度或法线监督，只靠多条虚拟射线在同一表面点的颜色一致性修密度场。

要点：

  • 从密度场采样候选表面点，从多个方向生成穿过该点的虚拟射线并渲染其外观，用可见性加权的颜色一致性约束隐式几何
  • 对颜色预测不一致的候选点惩罚不透明度，另加局部法线平滑项，全部来自 NeRF 自身预测，不需要深度或法线真值
  • 8 个 Replica 场景、30 万次累计迭代下，平均 Chamfer 距离比原生 NeRF 降低 30.8%，墙面与桌面等面的噪声明显减少

为什么值得看：很多团队的 NeRF/3DGS 资产问题不是分辨率不够，而是密度场本身含糊。这条自监督正则不需要额外采集或标注，就能换来更干净的表面与更少的「雾状体积」，属于低成本高回报的改造。

中文摘要：原生 NeRF 的密度场常常是噪声大、几何不准的，因为同一组输入图像可以被许多「形状 + 辐射」组合解释。作者给原生 NeRF 加了一条几何优化分支，核心是自监督的跨射线一致性：从密度场采样候选表面点，从不同方向生成穿过该点的虚拟射线，用这些射线渲染出的颜色在可见性加权下是否一致来约束几何。在此基础上再对颜色不一致的候选点惩罚不透明度、对局部法线加平滑，所有约束都由 NeRF 自己的预测导出，不需要深度或表面法线监督。在 8 个 Replica 场景上，该方法把平均 Chamfer 距离相对原生 NeRF 降低 30.8%，定性结果里墙面与桌面的不规则起伏也被显著抹平。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-27

Geometry Regularization for Vanilla NeRF via Self-Supervised Cross-Ray Consistency

© none

Abstract.

Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve high-quality novel-view synthesis by representing a scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field. However, the geometry encoded by the density field of vanilla NeRF can be noisy and inaccurate, since different combinations of shape and radiance may explain the same input images. To reduce this ambiguity, we augment vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch based on self-supervised cross-ray consistency. Specifically, this branch samples candidate surface points from the density field, generates virtual rays that intersect at each point from different directions, and renders their appearance using the NeRF network. Based on the visibility-weighted color consistency across these rays, we constrain the implicit geometry. We further regularize the implicit geometry by penalizing opacity at candidates with inconsistent appearance predictions and encouraging local normal smoothness. These geometric constraints are derived from the NeRF predictions and require no ground-truth depth or surface-normal supervision. Experiments on eight Replica scenes show that the proposed method reduces the mean Chamfer distance by 30.8% compared with vanilla NeRF.

Keywords:

neural radiance fields, implicit geometry, 3D reconstruction, cross-ray consistency

1. Introduction

Recovering 3D shape from 2D observations is a cornerstone problem of computer vision and graphics. This long-standing research topic supports various applications in AR, VR, games, movies, etc.[(Azinović et al., 2022; Boss et al., 2022)] With the advances of inverse graphics, differentiable renderer can be integrated in neural network pipelines, making it feasible to directly optimize the 3D geometric parameters using observed 2D images. Among various 3D geometry representations, implicit function represents 3D content continuously and without discretization. With its small memory footprint, implicit neural representation is popular in recent studies. One of the most successful approaches is NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)].
