    Appendix 0.A Text2PhyX Dataset Details

    0.A.1 Overview

    As introduced in the main text, Text2PhyX is a large-scale, text-conditioned 3D physical property dataset designed to resolve the inherent ambiguity of predicting object mechanics from pure visual inputs. The dataset is built upon a diverse collection of 1,700 unique 3D assets, which are sourced from two distinct domains to ensure both quality and real-world complexity: approximately 1,000 high-quality 3D meshes from the Objaverse dataset, and 700 3D gs (gs) models reconstructed from in-the-wild 2D images using SAM 3D Objects.

    To support flexible, text-driven physical predictions, we generate 8 distinct textual descriptions paired with corresponding physical parameters for each base object. Consequently, Text2PhyX comprises a total of 13,600 data triplets. Each triplet consists of:

  • 1.

    A 3D object representation (dense OpenCLIP semantic voxels extracted from multi-view renderings).

  • 2.

    A text description specifying the material or physical state of the object’s constituent parts.

  • 3.

    The ground-truth dense physical parameters, specifically Young’s Modulus (E), Poisson’s Ratio (ν), and Density (ρ), assigned at the voxel level.

    • The entire dataset is partitioned at the object level into a training set of 12,600 samples from 1,575 objects and a testing set of 1,000 samples from 125 held-out objects, providing a robust benchmark for text-conditioned 3D physical parameter regression.

    0.A.2 Gallery with Physics Property

    To intuitively demonstrate the diversity and granularity of Text2PhyX, Figure A5 provides a visual gallery showcasing various objects alongside their part-level segmentations and corresponding physical property heatmaps.

    Multi-View Renderings and Semantic Segmentation.

    To mitigate the ambiguity of single-view observations and extract robust 3D OpenCLIP voxels, we uniformly render multiple views from the upper hemisphere of each object. Based on these visual features and vlm-generated keywords, objects are accurately segmented into constituent parts. As shown in the second column of Figure A5, a snowman is segmented into its body, arms, and nose; a potted grass is separated into the planter and the green grass; and a bag is distinctly divided into the fabric body and plastic handles. This fine-grained part-level segmentation is crucial for applying localized, text-driven physical controls.

    Voxel-Wise Physical Property Heatmaps.

    Building upon the part segmentation, Text2PhyX provides dense, voxel-wise annotations for three key physical properties. As visualized in the rightmost three columns of Figure A5, different semantic parts within the same object exhibit distinctly different physical values, reflecting their assigned materials. For example, the wooden trunk of the tree shows a significantly higher Young’s Modulus (E) compared to its leaves, while the plastic handles of the bag exhibit different densities (ρ) and elasticity compared to the fabric body. These detailed heatmaps confirm that our automated, text-guided pipeline successfully assigns physically plausible and spatially accurate parameters across a wide variety of complex 3D objects.

    0.A.3 OpenCLIP-Driven 3D Semantic Segmentation

    Overview

    To endow our volumetric representation with open-vocabulary semantic understanding suitable for physics-based simulation, we distill dense, high-dimensional semantic features from a pre-trained 2D vision-language foundation model (specifically OpenCLIP) into a continuous 3D feature field. Furthermore, to ensure physical accuracy during stress propagation, we extend these surface features into the unobservable internal volume using a robust ray-casting strategy.

    2D Feature Extraction

    Given a set of multi-view RGB images {Iₖ} of the scene, we first extract 2D semantic feature maps using a pre-trained OpenCLIP image encoder. Since vision transformers typically output features at a lower resolution than the input image, we obtain a dense feature map Fₖ∈ℝ^512×512×768 for each image Iₖ, where 768 is the dimensionality of the OpenCLIP latent space.

    3D Feature Distillation via Volumetric Rendering

    Unlike heuristic multi-view projection methods that suffer from occlusion ambiguities, we lift the 2D semantic features into 3D using a physics-inspired volumetric rendering framework. We freeze the density field σ obtained from a pre-trained RGB NeRF and introduce a continuous 3D feature field Φ:ℝ³→ℝ^D, parameterized by a neural network or a feature grid.

    During optimization, we render the expected 3D feature F̂(r) along a camera ray r using the accumulated transmittance T(t). This naturally handles occlusions by dropping the transmittance to zero behind visible surfaces. We optimize the feature field Φ by minimizing the discrepancy between the rendered ray features F̂(r) and the corresponding ground-truth OpenCLIP features Fₖ(r) sampled from the 2D feature maps. We employ the negative cosine similarity loss as our distillation objective:

    L_distill=-1/N∑ₖ∑ᵣ(F̂(r)·Fₖ(r))/(∥F̂(r)∥₂∥Fₖ(r)∥₂)

    where N is the total number of sampled rays. By minimizing this loss, the 3D feature field learns to encode view-consistent semantic priors strictly on the visible surfaces.

    Internal Volume Filling via Even-Odd Rule

    While the volumetric rendering successfully distills features onto the object’s surface, physics-based simulations require semantic and physical properties (e.g., Young’s modulus E, Poisson’s ratio ν) to be defined throughout the object’s interior. Since internal voids are unobservable from external cameras, their features remain undefined.

    To bridge this gap, we employ a hierarchical ray-casting strategy based on the classic even-odd rule. For a given unassigned voxel v in the 3D space, we cast multiple rays uniformly distributed over a sphere towards infinity. Along each ray, we count the number of intersections with the object’s surface (defined by a density threshold on σ). If the intersection count is consistently odd across the majority of the casted rays, the voxel v is robustly classified as being inside the object, effectively handling complex concavities.

    Finally, for each identified internal voxel, we assign its semantic feature by performing nearest-neighbor interpolation from the optimized surface feature field Φ. This ensures that the internal volume inherits semantically and physically consistent properties from its closest bounding surface, yielding a complete volumetric representation ready for downstream simulation.

    Open-Vocabulary Querying

    Once the 3D feature distillation is complete, the scene can be queried using natural language. Given a user-provided text prompt (e.g., "a red apple" or "the handle of the mug"), we encode the text into a 768-dimensional embedding t using the OpenCLIP text encoder.

    To perform 3D semantic segmentation, we compute the cosine similarity between the text embedding t and the distilled 3D feature fₚ of each primitive: S(p,t)=(fₚ·t)/(∥fₚ∥₂∥t∥₂) Primitives with a similarity score S(p,t) exceeding a predefined threshold are segmented as belonging to the target object. This continuous similarity field not only enables robust part-level segmentation but also facilitates downstream tasks such as language-guided robotic grasping and interaction.

    0.A.4 vlm labeling

    To further illustrate the automated data generation pipeline described in Section 3.3, Figure A4 provides a concrete example of our text-guided property assignment process. As discussed in the main text, relying solely on visual inputs for physical parameter prediction is inherently ill-posed. To resolve this, we utilize a vlm to generate diverse, physically plausible textual descriptions and assign corresponding physical parameters.

    In this example, the input consists of multi-view RGB renderings of a soda can and its extracted 3D representation. During the augmentation phase, the vlm generates a novel semantic condition: “The soda can is now made of a very hard plastic.” Rather than blindly guessing the physical values, the vlm grounds its assignment by querying external knowledge bases. As shown in the generated JSON metadata, the model explicitly provides its reasoning trace (“from wiki”) to prevent hallucination.

    Based on this grounded knowledge, the vlm determines an appropriate scaling factor (multiplier: 0.113) for the material transition from standard aluminum to hard plastic. This multiplier is then applied to the default Young’s Modulus (E) of the object (“original_E_mean”: 249999920.0) to compute the updated physical parameter (“new_E_mean”: 28249996.8) for the specified part (“soda can”). This transparent, physics-aware reasoning process ensures that the generated text-parameter pairs in Text2PhyX remain strictly consistent and physically accurate across all 13,600 data triplets.

    Appendix 0.B Additional Evaluation and Analysis

    0.B.1 Human-Annotated Text Generalization

    To further evaluate text generalization beyond Text2PhyX, we construct a human-annotated test set of 30 objects. For each material category, we query The Engineering Toolbox to obtain plausible physical-property ranges, retrieve corresponding object images, and reconstruct 3D assets using SAM 3D Objects. We sample two material-property configurations from the queried ranges and run physics simulation for each sample. Human annotators then watch these videos and provide the corresponding natural language descriptions, making this evaluation independent of the text-generation pipeline used to build Text2PhyX.

    0.B.2 Unconditional Cross-Dataset Validation

    To evaluate whether our framework is tied only to Text2PhyX, we also compare Pixie, VoMP, and our model under an unconditional protocol using an empty text input. We train and test the methods on the Pixie dataset, the VoMP dataset, and Text2PhyX, respectively. This setting is not designed to test text controllability; rather, it checks whether the voxel-based feed-forward architecture remains competitive when reduced to the same unconditional setting as prior feed-forward methods.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：文本条件调制视觉特征，在体素场里预测空间变化的物理属性，兼容 mesh、点云、3DGS 与 NeRF。

要点：

  • 跨模态调制：用文本特征动态调制视觉特征做物理 grounding，在体素场里表示属性，因此对 mesh、点云、高斯与 NeRF 都可用
  • 配套一条部件可控的数据生成管线：把复杂 3D 资产拆成语义部件，配多样化且物理合理的参数与对应文本描述
  • Text2PhyX 上 PSNR 从 23.421 提到 26.012（比 Pixie 高约 2.6 dB），推理 2 秒内；真实数据 ABO-500 上 ADE 比次优方法低 20%

为什么值得看：物理参数一直是仿真资产里靠人猜、靠试错的一环。文本可条件化意味着关卡与资产可以按描述批量生成可仿真参数，而不是逐件手调；体素场表示则让它能挂到现有的各种资产格式上。

中文摘要：高保真 4D 仿真需要与材质一致的物理参数，但现有做法要么逐场景做昂贵优化，要么只看外观预测参数——而外观本身是有歧义的，比如仅凭样子分不清橡胶的软硬。AutoPhyX 用文本条件补上这层语义：先把复杂 3D 资产拆成语义部件，生成带多样化物理参数与文本描述的训练数据；再用跨模态调制让文本特征动态调制视觉特征，做精确的物理 grounding；属性在体素场里预测，因此兼容 mesh、点云、3DGS 与 NeRF 等多种表示。方法一次前向即可给出空间变化的物理参数，在自建 Text2PhyX 上 PSNR 从 23.421 提升到 26.012、推理 2 秒内，在真实 ABO-500 上把 ADE 比次优方法降低 20%。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-27

AutoPhyX: Automatic Text-Condition Physics Property Generation

Abstract

High-fidelity 4D physical simulation requires accurate physical parameter assignments that align with diverse material properties. Previous methods struggle with critical bottlenecks: they either rely on computationally intensive per-scene optimization or predict parameters from purely visual inputs. The latter suffers from inherent ambiguity, e.g., the inability to distinguish the stiffness of rubber from its appearance alone. To bridge this gap, we propose AutoPhyX, a text-conditioned framework for predicting spatially-varying physical properties. Since training robust feed-forward models requires fine-grained supervision, we first introduce a novel part-controllable data generation pipeline that decomposes complex 3D assets into semantically distinct components and pairs them with physically plausible, diverse parameters and corresponding text descriptions. Leveraging this dataset, AutoPhyX employs a cross-modal modulation mechanism where text features dynamically modulate visual features for precise physical grounding. By formulating property prediction within a voxel field, AutoPhyX ensures compatibility with diverse 3D representations, including meshes, point clouds, gs, and nerf. Experiments demonstrate that our method enables physically plausible, text-driven parameter assignment in a single forward pass. It achieves high accuracy and robust generalization to in-the-wild objects, paving the way for future physics-intensive embodied and robotic applications.

Keywords:

Physics Simulation Physical Parameter Prediction Cross-modal Modulation

1 Introduction

High-fidelity 4D physical simulation  [48, 36, 40, 27] has become a vital foundation for interactive digital environments, driving applications ranging from fem (fem) based [31, 5, 2, 4, 6] robotic policy training, to sph (sph) driven [32, 34, 33, 35, 43, 39, 26] complex fluid and glacier calving simulations, and mpm (mpm) powered [14, 3, 19, 46, 42, 9, 10, 46, 21, 47] real-time virtual reality (VR) experiences. Despite their ability to synthesize high-fidelity, realistic dynamics across diverse scenes, these physics-based approaches share a major bottleneck: they rely heavily on the manual assignment of physical parameters. This reliance on trial-and-error parameter design severely limits their scalability and applicability to complex scenes characterized by diverse, spatially varying materials.

Existing methods aiming to automate material acquisition primarily fall into two categories, each with its own limitations. Optimization-based methods [25, 17, 54, 51] leverage differentiable physics to iteratively refine material fields to match target observations. However, inferring particle-wise parameters from sparse supervision is ill-posed and computationally expensive, often requiring hours of per-scene optimization [25] and offering limited generalization across scenes. In contrast, feed-forward approaches such as Pixie [22] and VoMP [13] enable much faster inference; yet they rely purely on visual cues, which sacrifices semantic controllability and suffers from appearance ambiguity. For example, as shown in  Figure1, a tree could feature flexible branches that sway in the wind or brittle wood that fractures easily, while a biscuit box could be rigid cardboard or thin paper. Without explicit semantic guidance, it is difficult to disambiguate objects that are physically distinct but visually similar.

To address these critical limitations, we propose AutoPhyX, a feed-forward framework for fast, generalizable, and semantically controllable prediction of physical properties. Given a 3D asset and textual descriptions of its physical properties, the model predicts spatially dense physical parameters in a unified voxel field representation. This formulation provides a common physical abstraction that can be directly transferred to diverse downstream 3D formats, including gs (gs), meshes, and point clouds, without per-scene optimization. To resolve the material-level ambiguity and capture spatially varying properties across multi-part, multi-material assets, AutoPhyX modulates the intermediate visual representation with a feature-wise affine transformation conditioned on the encoded text features, coupling high-level semantic cues with fine-grained spatial representations. This cross-modal design enables the model to distinguish visually similar but physically different materials, while also assigning spatially coherent physical parameters to semantically distinct parts of the 3D asset.

Training such a robust, spatially-grounded model requires large-scale fine-grained supervision over multi-part, multi-material 3D assets with text descriptions, which is currently unavailable. To bridge this gap, we introduce an automated, part-controllable data generation pipeline. For each asset, we construct a 3D OpenCLIP [18] voxel representation, and leverage authoritative engineering databases (e.g., MatWeb and Wikipedia) and vlm to extract robust text-guided part segmentation, assign plausible material properties, and generate diverse part-aware textual descriptions. Our dataset, Text2PhyX, features 1,700 high-quality 3D assets, each paired with 8 distinct physical-parameter and text-description annotations, supplementing as training and testing data for text-conditioned physical property assignment.

We evaluate AutoPhyX extensively on Text2PhyX and the real-world ABO-500  [51, 11] dataset, achieving state-of-the-art quantitative results on both. Specifically, our method improves the PSNR from 23.421 to 26.012 on our dataset and reduces the Average Displacement Error (ADE) by 20% compared to the second-best method on ABO-500. Furthermore, our predicted properties support a wide range of physical simulators, which we demonstrate through extensive results using both MPM and fem. This versatility allows us to flexibly choose rendering and simulation pipelines on demand, e.g., gs for real-time dynamic rendering, mesh rendering in Blender, or Isaac Gym for robotic policy training.

In summary, our main contributions are:

  • •

    The first text-conditioned feed-forward framework for 3D physics prediction. We introduce AutoPhyX that achieves precise semantic and physical grounding through a novel cross-modal modulation architecture, resolving the inherent ambiguity of previous pure-vision methods.

  • •

    A large-scale, multi-part, multi-level 3D physics dataset. We build Text2PhyX with dense part-aware physical annotations and paired text descriptions, enabling supervised learning for text-conditioned property prediction with an automated vlm-driven generation pipeline.

  • •

    Extensive validation across diverse workflows. We demonstrate that AutoPhyX significantly outperforms existing baselines in physical accuracy. More importantly, our approach bridges the gap between static 3D assets and various physics solvers, providing a plug-and-play solution that generalizes across varied representations, platforms, and rendering engines.

    • 2 Related Work

    Physical simulation has long been a cornerstone of computer graphics . Typical simulation methods, e.g., fem, which models stress-strain responses for rigid and soft bodies, and mpm[19, 14], particularly suited for large deformations and complex materials, have been widely adopted. Despite their success, they all rely on accurate physical parameters as input. In this work, we are particularly interested in three canonical properties: Young’s modulus E, Poisson’s ratio ν, and density ρ, because they jointly govern a material’s stiffness, lateral deformation behavior, and inertial response, making them fundamental for a broad range of solid and deformable simulations. To eliminate the need for manual parameter assignment, prior efforts can be broadly grouped into the following directions.

    2.1 Physics Property Assignment via vlm

    Prior research, such as NeRF2Physics [51], directly prompts vlm to predict exact physical parameters from images [8, 51, 16, 7]. However, this direct approach struggles for three main reasons: vlm lacks accurate built-in physics knowledge, their outputs are highly random, and materials suffer from severe visual ambiguity, where objects that look identical can have completely different physical properties. To overcome these issues, we shift the vlm’s role from a direct physics calculator to a semantic reasoning engine supported by external tools. Specifically, instead of relying on the vlm to guess exact numbers, we give specific material requirements, e.g., more deformable or crisp, and prompt it to query external databases to find reasonable physical ranges. To handle the randomness of vlm outputs, we query the model multiple times and select the best result. Finally, we use the vlm to generate text descriptions that explicitly define the material, effectively solving the visual ambiguity problem.

    2.2 Test-time Physics Property Optimization

    Another prominent line of research focuses on test-time optimization, which iteratively refines physical parameters to align simulations with target observations. Observation-based optimization techniques [37, 23, 55, 20, 53, 50, 20, 28, 52, 24] typically minimize the discrepancy between simulated deformations and ground-truth data, such as multi-view videos or particle trajectories under known forces. While effective, these methods often require high-quality, dense supervision that is difficult to acquire in real-world settings.

    To alleviate this dependency, approaches [17, 54, 25] propose leveraging pretrained video diffusion models to guide physics discovery via motion distillation losses. Notable examples include PhysDreamer [54] and DreamPhysics [17], which optimize material fields by ensuring simulated dynamics remain consistent with realistic motion priors. Despite their ability to discover physics from sparse inputs, these optimization-based paradigms suffer from extensive computational overhead, often requiring hours of optimization to resolve hundreds of thousands of material points. Furthermore, these methods are characterized by heavy per-scene memorization; for each new scenario, the costly optimization must be executed from scratch, failing to generalize across diverse scenes.

    2.3 Feedforward Physics Property Prediction

    Feedforward methods such as Pixie [22] and VoMP [13] have recently emerged to bypass the computational burdens of test-time optimization by directly regressing physical attributes in a single pass. However, these methods rely exclusively on visual cues, which inherently lead to physical ambiguity, i.e., visually similar objects, such as fresh fruit and its plastic replica, can possess drastically different material properties. To resolve this limitation, AutoPhyX introduces textual constraints as a crucial semantic prior to resolve the visual ambiguities, enabling the differentiation of materials with similar appearances but distinct physical behaviors. Unlike previous models, our goal is to ensure that the predicted parameters are efficient to compute, controllable, and physically plausible, providing a versatile solution for augmenting diverse 3D representations, including meshes, point clouds, and gs.

    3 Method

    Given a 3D object represented with multi-view images and a text prompt, our goal is to predict a dense, physics-ready volumetric field of material parameters, specifically Young’s modulus E, Poisson’s ratio ν, and density ρ. To achieve this, we propose AutoPhyX that operates in two primary stages. First, it extracts 2D OpenCLIP features from multi-view images and lifts them into a dense 3D OpenCLIP voxel grid, explicitly handling self-occlusion via volume rendering and filling the unobservable interior regions to ensure a solid physical volume ( Sec.3.1). Second, we fuse these 3D visual features with textual embeddings to resolve inherent visual ambiguities, directly decoding this cross-modal representation into a unified voxel field of precise physical parameters ready for downstream simulation (Sec.3.2). We additionally generate a large-scale dataset to facilitate training and testing, as detailed in Sec.3.3.

    3.1 3D Feature Extraction from 2D Images

    Recent methods like VoMP [13] lift 2D features to 3D via naive multi-view averaging. However, ignoring visibility causes severe feature contamination, such as foreground leaves erroneously projecting features onto an occluded trunk, as shown in Figure3. To address these geometric ambiguities, we shift from heuristic projection to a volumetric rendering framework. We treat the 2D OpenCLIP [18] features as “feature radiance” and optimize a continuous 3D feature field Φ:ℝ³→ℝ^D via end-to-end differentiable rendering. Using a fixed density field σ from a pre-trained RGB nerf (nerf), we render the expected 2D feature F̂(r) along a camera ray r(t)=o+td as F̂(r)=∫_tₙ^t_fT(t)σ(r(t))Φ(r(t))dt, where tₙ and t_f denote the near and far bounds of the ray, and T(t)=\exp(-∫_tₙᵗσ(r(s))ds) represents the accumulated transmittance. Here, T(t) naturally suppresses occluded regions by dropping to zero behind surfaces, ensuring that the 3D feature field Φ is supervised from viewpoints where the surfaces are truly visible.

    While volume rendering captures surface features, physics-based simulations inherently require volumetric properties, such as (E,ν,ρ), defined throughout the object’s interior to accurately model stress propagation. To bridge this gap, we fill unobservable internal voids using a hierarchical ray-casting strategy inspired by PhysGaussian [49]. Specifically, following the classic even-odd rule in computer graphics, we identify internal voxels by casting multiple rays to infinity, where a consistently odd number of surface intersections across all rays indicates the voxel is inside, robustly handling complex concavities. Finally, these voxels inherit semantic features via nearest-neighbor interpolation from the surface, yielding a physically and semantically consistent volumetric representation.

    3.2 Text-conditioned Physical Parameter Prediction

    While vision-based 3D representations, such as 3D CLIP feature field [41], have proven highly effective for open-vocabulary localization and commonsense reasoning, relying solely on pure vision is fundamentally insufficient for predicting physical properties. This limitation arises from the inherent ambiguity of visual appearance. For instance, a rubber toy might look identical whether it is extremely stiff or highly deformable. Therefore, it is essential to introduce textual descriptions as a disambiguating condition, fusing the semantic priors of language with the spatial awareness of 3D visual features to guide the physical reasoning process.

    Specifically, the textual description is first processed by a frozen OpenCLIP text encoder to extract a dense semantic embedding, denoted as eₜₑₓₜ. Note that since both the 3D visual voxels and the textual embeddings are derived from the OpenCLIP latent space, they are inherently aligned, which avoids the need for complex cross-modal projection or pre-processing modules. To achieve the cross-modal fusion, we draw inspiration from Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) [38], which demonstrates remarkable success in visual reasoning tasks. Rather than naively concatenating this embedding with visual features, eₜₑₓₜ acts as a direct and highly effective global condition to modulate the 3D OpenCLIP visual voxels at multiple scales.

    In our design, eₜₑₓₜ is passed through dedicated Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLP) to predict layer-specific modulation parameters: the scaling factor γ and the shifting factor β. Let Fᵢ represent the intermediate 3D voxel feature map at the i-th layer of our U-Net. The FiLM layer applies a channel-wise affine transformation to modulate this feature map:

    Fᵢ^′=γᵢ(eₜₑₓₜ)·Fᵢ+βᵢ(eₜₑₓₜ).

    		(1)

    By interleaving these FiLM layers throughout the 3D U-Net, the network learns to dynamically emphasize or suppress specific visual feature channels based on linguistic cues. This multi-scale, text-driven modulation ensures that the final extracted features are highly attuned to the physical attributes specified in the text, thereby enabling the accurate regression of the target physical parameters. We present a detailed comparison between our design and other multi-modal fusion modules in the Supplementary Material.

    The physics loss L_phys is computed by enforcing supervision exclusively on the occupied voxels G. Let K={E,ν,ρ} denote the set of target physical properties, corresponding to Young’s modulus, Poisson’s ratio, and density, respectively. We formulate the total loss as:

    L_phys=(1)/(N_occ)∑_p∈G∑_k∈K∥k̂(p)-k^GT(p)∥²,

    		(2)

    where N_occ represents the total count of valid voxels, and k̂(p), k^GT(p) denote the predicted and ground-truth physical parameters at voxel p.

    3.3 Dataset Generation

    Unlike Pixie  [22] and VoMP  [13], which supervise the prediction of each object by a single deterministic set of physical parameters, our approach resolves the inherent ambiguity of prediction by introducing text description as conditioning signals. This formulation supports downstream applications that require flexible object physics, e.g., increasing the robustness of robot manipulation policy by varying the potential plausible physics for the same object during training. However, such text-conditioned training data are currently unavailable at scale, motivating our automated pipeline for large-scale data generation.

    Semantic Part Segmentation.

    To achieve precise text-driven control, e.g., accurately specifying whether a tree trunk is hardwood or softwood, or adjusting the stiffness of a car’s tires, it is required that our dataset provide accurate part-level segmentation. To this end, we first extract 3D OpenCLIP voxels for each 3D object as in Sec.3.1. OpenCLIP voxels have been successfully and widely adopted in object grounding and reasoning [41], and their text-aligned semantic features enable segmentation of objects based on corresponding text keywords.

    To mitigate the ambiguity associated with single-view observations, we uniformly render 15 images from the upper hemisphere of each object. We then prompt vlm[12] to generate a text list encompassing all constituent parts it identifies for the object. Upon obtaining these text keywords, we compute the segmentation on the OpenCLIP voxels based on the cosine similarity between the text-visual features. To ensure robustness, we repeatedly generate five distinct sets of keywords per object and render their corresponding 3D segmentations, as illustrated in  . The vlm finally selects the highest-quality segmentation from these five candidates, which effectively prevents incorrect segmentations caused by the use of uncommon vocabulary for part names.

    Text-Guided Property Assignment.

    After part-level segmentation, the next step is to generate the physical properties paired with text descriptions. To resolve the physical ambiguity from pure visual inputs, our guideline is to generate text first to guide the property assignment. For each object, we randomly select a subset of parts and prompt vlm[12] to generate physically diverse but plausible textual descriptions, which act as the guideline for parameter assignment. To ground these assignments and prevent potential vlm hallucination, for each description, we prompt vlm to query the corresponding physics parameter range from online databases, i.e., Matweb [30], Wikipedia [45], and The Engineering Toolbox [15]. Once the physics ranges are acquired, we leverage vlm to sample a corresponding parameter in the valid range. For instance, the description “This is mahogany that might sink to the bottom,” would lead to a density value near the upper end of the wood’s density range (800kg/m³ to 1300kg/m³), whereas “This is softwood that can float on water” yields a lower density. When an object comprises multiple parts, any unmentioned parts are assigned the mean value of their valid physical ranges. In addition, to ensure robust physical parameter assignment in the absence of detailed textual guidance, for each object, we include a simple default text description “This is a [object name],” where all parts are assigned the mean value in their valid ranges. We further filter generated assignments through simulation-based consistency checks: for each selected object and sampled physical setting, we generate a 100-frame simulation and reject cases with clear artifacts, poor segmentation, implausible property assignments, or behavior inconsistent with the generated description. The vlm may resample the assignment up to five times; objects that still fail this automatic check are discarded.

    4 Method

    To build a diverse and comprehensive dataset, we acquire our 3D assets from two distinct sources. First, we collect approximately 1,000 high-quality 3D meshes from the Objaverse dataset. Second, to capture the complexity of real-world objects, we gather diverse 2D images via Google Search and utilize SAM 3D Objects [44] to reconstruct approximately 700 3D Gaussian Splatting (gs) models. This yields a total base of 1,700 unique 3D assets. As detailed above, we generate 8 distinct textual descriptions and their corresponding physical parameters for each object. Consequently, our dataset, Text2PhyX, contains 1700×8=13600 data triplets, with each triplet comprising a 3D object representation, a text description, and the ground-truth physical parameters. We partition this collection at the object level into 1,575 training objects and 125 testing objects, corresponding to 12,600 training samples and 1,000 testing samples. The resulting category distribution is shown in Fig. 4, and additional dataset galleries are included in Supplementary Material.

    5 Experiment

    We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of AutoPhyX to validate its ability to recover accurate physical constants from visual and linguistic inputs. Our experiments focus on two primary objectives: (1) Quantitative Analysis, where we measure the precision of predicted physics properties on our dataset Text2PhyX and a real-world dataset ABO-500; and (2) Qualitative Simulation, where we demonstrate the practical utility of our framework by applying the predicted physics properties to realistic physics-based simulations, containing both gs and mesh. Through these evaluations, we show that AutoPhyX effectively bridges the gap between high-level semantic descriptions and low-level physical dynamics in an end-to-end manner.

    Dataset and Settings.

    We evaluate text-conditioned physical parameter prediction on the test set of Text2PhyX, detailed in Sec.3.3. We measure the discrepancy between the estimated and ground-truth physical parameters. Furthermore, we assess the visual and dynamic quality of renderings from simulations driven by the predicted properties and the ground-truth.

    Furthermore, to rigorously assess real-world generalization, we incorporate the ABO-500 dataset as an additional out-of- distribution test set. The ABO-500 dataset contains the density and mass of 500 real-world objects, which allows us to evaluate the discrepancy between our predicted physical properties and the real-world ground truth. Since this dataset lacks detailed physical descriptions, we solely use text prompts following the simple template: “This is a [object name].” We also include additional human-annotated and cross-dataset evaluations in Supplementary Material, where natural language descriptions are provided by annotators after observing simulated object behavior rather than generated by our data pipeline.

    Implementation Detail.

    AutoPhyX is trained using the Adam optimizer with the initial learning rate 10⁻⁴ on 2 NVIDIA RTX A800 GPUs. Training takes 2 days with a batch size of 4 per GPU and 100 epochs. Training hyperparameters are selected once using a small 3,000/300 train/test split drawn from the training objects and then kept fixed for all reported experiments. For both training and metric computation, we apply a log transform to E and ρ, and normalize all \logE, ν, and \logρ values to the range [-1,1]. The Supplementary Material contains the model architecture and OpenCLIP version.

    Baselines.

    We compare AutoPhyX against several representative methods. Both OmniPhysGS [25] and DreamPhysics [17] utilize video diffusion models to optimize the physics simulation process online. NeRF2Physics [51] uses GPT [1] to generate material text prompts and their physical properties, mapping them to 3D points via text-image CLIP similarity. We also test representative vlm, Gemini, which we ask to predict the part name and corresponding physics property, and then assign them back to the object corresponding to OpenCLIP feature similarity. To alleviate the randomness of vlm output, we conduct 5 queries and take the average as the final result of Gemini. Pixie [22] is a recent feed-forward physics generation method that relies solely on visual features. Since the original dataset for Pixie is not publicly available, we retrain it on our dataset to ensure a fair comparison. Furthermore, as Pixie does not support textual descriptions as input, we evaluate it exclusively under the default unconditional setting described in Sec.3.3. We additionally report unconditional cross-dataset comparisons with VoMP [13] in Supplementary Material.

    Evaluation Metrics.

    In Text2PhyX, we evaluate using physical and visual metrics. For physical accuracy, we compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) for Young’s modulus E, Poisson’s ratio ν, and density ρ. To handle large magnitude variations, E and ρ are evaluated in log-space (\log₁₀). This is especially important for Young’s modulus, which spans many orders of magnitude across materials; raw absolute error would be dominated by stiff materials and would underweight soft materials where small absolute changes can strongly alter dynamics. For visual fidelity, we simulate and render images with the predicted properties using PhysGaussian [49] for gs, and Isaac Sim [29] for meshes. The rendered frames are then evaluated against ground truth using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS).

    On the real-world ABO-500 mass dataset, we report four metrics: ADE (Average Displacement Error), ARE (Average Relative Error), ALDE (Average Log Displacement Error), and MnRE (Minimum Ratio Error). Specifically, ADE measures the absolute numerical difference in weight, while ARE captures the percentage of this error relative to the object’s true weight, which is crucial for lighter items. Furthermore, ALDE evaluates the error in logarithmic space. MnRE avoids bias toward systematic over- or underestimation and reduces sensitivity to outliers, making it particularly effective for evaluating physical quantity predictions across heterogeneous samples.

    Quantitative Result

    As shown in Tab.1, our method exhibits a significant performance margin over existing baselines. AutoPhyX with the OpenCLIP features achieves a PSNR of 26.012, outperforming the state-of-the-art Pixie by approximately 2.6 dB. This significant improvement is primarily attributed to our cross-modal modulation utilizing the text conditions, coupled with OpenCLIP’s richer semantic representations compared to standard CLIP; they together empower our model to make finer-grained physical predictions. Pixie, while making reasonable predictions, is constrained to the default physical conditions because it solely takes CLIP voxel features as input. This reliance on purely visual input suffers from inherent visual ambiguity, which is more evident on the ABO-500 object mass estimation benchmark. As shown in Tab.2, our method consistently improves accuracy over NeRF2Physics and Pixie, achieving lower ALDE, ADE, ARE, and higher MnRE, which suggests that AutoPhyX not only achieves a good performance on text-conditioned prediction on our dataset, but also generalizes well in the out-of-distribution real-world dataset across diverse physical scenarios.

    Since NeRF2Physics directly relies on GPT for physical property predictions, it inherits inaccurate physical priors and vlm hallucinations. As a result, its performance in terms of physical accuracy and visual fidelity is relatively low. Similar to NeRF2Physics, directly leveraging Gemini as an agent that predicts physics properties cannot achieve high precision. While Text2PhyX also employs Gemini for part segmentation and physical property retrieval during data generation, we mitigate these limitations through a multiple-sampling strategy for robust part segmentation and text-guided property assignment. Furthermore, we ground our queries in authoritative online databases rather than relying solely on the VLM’s internal knowledge for physical properties. This also highlights a key asymmetry: vlms can generate coherent part descriptions and then produce compatible physical parameters in a forward manner, but they struggle with the inverse problem that requires specific property estimation from a given text description, because their internal physics knowledge is not well calibrated for accurate, instance-specific parameter estimation. Consequently, although we utilize Gemini for data generation, our method leverages large-scale supervised training to improve generalizability and substantially outperform pure VLM-based baselines across all evaluation metrics.

    Since NeRF2Physics directly relies on GPT for physical property predictions, it inherits inaccurate physical priors and vlm hallucinations. As a result, its performance in terms of physical accuracy and visual fidelity is relatively low. Similar to NeRF2Physics, directly leveraging Gemini as an agent that predicts physics properties cannot achieve high precision. While Text2PhyX also employs Gemini for part segmentation and physical property retrieval during data generation, we mitigate these limitations through a multiple-sampling strategy for robust part segmentation and text-guided property assignment. Furthermore, we ground our queries in authoritative online databases rather than relying solely on the VLM’s internal knowledge for physical properties. This also highlights a key asymmetry: vlms can generate coherent part descriptions and then produce compatible physical parameters in a forward manner, but they struggle with the inverse problem that requires specific property estimation from a given text description, because their internal physics knowledge is not calibrated for accurate, instance-specific parameter estimation. Consequently, although we utilize Gemini for data generation, our method leverages large-scale training to improve generalizability and substantially outperform pure VLM-based baselines across all evaluation metrics.

    Runtime.

    Figure5 plots PSNR versus runtime (log-scale). Our method attains the highest PSNR (26.01) with 2s inference, while optimization-based baselines (DreamPhysics and OmniPhysGS) require minutes to hours, depending on the number of epochs, and yield lower PSNR. For Pixie, NeRF2Physics, and our method, we additionally show a second point that accounts for approximately 3 minutes of CLIP voxel feature extraction as input preprocessing.

    Qualitative Results

    As illustrated in Fig. 6, the versatility of our voxelized prediction approach allows the predicted physical properties to be integrated into diverse simulation pipelines. For the first six rows, we employ the mpm to drive the dynamic behavior of gs representations, capturing complex physical effects under varying material properties: from rigid rotation to elastic warping of the propeller (Rows 1-2), from gentle swaying to pronounced bending of the ficus in the wind (Rows 3-4), and from an intact collision to brittle fracture of the falling bread (Rows 5-6).

    Furthermore, to demonstrate the cross-representation capability, the final two rows present deformable object simulations conducted in Isaac Sim using the fem. Despite the change in both the physical solver and the 3D representation, our model consistently predicts accurate parameters that govern realistic material behaviors, such as volume-preserving bouncing versus large deformation. This highlights that our method learns intrinsic physical attributes that are independent of specific simulators or 3D representations.

    As illustrated in Fig. 7, our voxel-based prediction framework achieves significantly higher precision in material decomposition compared to existing methods. A key limitation of NeRF2Physics is its lack of structural granularity, which predicts nearly identical physical attributes for different parts, such as assigning uniform Young’s modulus values to both the foliage and the trunk. On the other hand, Pixie struggles with material boundaries at the base of the object, predicting that the soil and the ceramic pot have the same physical properties. In contrast, our method successfully recovers the sharp discontinuities between distinct materials. It accurately distinguishes the rigid trunk from the soft leaf clusters and maintains a clear boundary between the soil and the rigid container. This heatmap confirms that our model captures intrinsic semantic-physical correlations beyond simple global averages.

    6 Conclusion and Future Work

    We presented AutoPhyX, a text-conditioned feed-forward framework that automates dense physical property assignment for diverse 3D assets. Our method uses a unified voxel field representation to bridge high-level linguistic semantics with low- level physical dynamics in a scalable manner. To support this cross-modal paradigm, we designed an automated, vlm-driven generation pipeline and constructed Text2PhyX, a large-scale, multi-part 3D physics dataset for training and testing across diverse object categories.

    Extensive experiments validate AutoPhyX. Quantitatively, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on our dataset and the real-world ABO-500 benchmark. Qualitatively, our method integrates into simulation pipelines, including mpm and fem, across objects such as a bonsai, a propeller, and bread. These results demonstrate its potential for larger, complex interactive environments. In the future, we plan to extend our framework by incorporating additional physical properties, such as surface friction and damping coefficients, and by exploring higher-resolution fields for objects with very fine structures.

    Acknowledgements

    This work was supported in part by National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grant 62272011.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix 0.A Text2PhyX Dataset Details

    0.A.1 Overview

    As introduced in the main text, Text2PhyX is a large-scale, text-conditioned 3D physical property dataset designed to resolve the inherent ambiguity of predicting object mechanics from pure visual inputs. The dataset is built upon a diverse collection of 1,700 unique 3D assets, which are sourced from two distinct domains to ensure both quality and real-world complexity: approximately 1,000 high-quality 3D meshes from the Objaverse dataset, and 700 3D gs (gs) models reconstructed from in-the-wild 2D images using SAM 3D Objects.

    To support flexible, text-driven physical predictions, we generate 8 distinct textual descriptions paired with corresponding physical parameters for each base object. Consequently, Text2PhyX comprises a total of 13,600 data triplets. Each triplet consists of:

  • 1.

    A 3D object representation (dense OpenCLIP semantic voxels extracted from multi-view renderings).

  • 2.

    A text description specifying the material or physical state of the object’s constituent parts.

  • 3.

    The ground-truth dense physical parameters, specifically Young’s Modulus (E), Poisson’s Ratio (ν), and Density (ρ), assigned at the voxel level.

    • The entire dataset is partitioned at the object level into a training set of 12,600 samples from 1,575 objects and a testing set of 1,000 samples from 125 held-out objects, providing a robust benchmark for text-conditioned 3D physical parameter regression.

    0.A.2 Gallery with Physics Property

    To intuitively demonstrate the diversity and granularity of Text2PhyX, Figure A5 provides a visual gallery showcasing various objects alongside their part-level segmentations and corresponding physical property heatmaps.

    Multi-View Renderings and Semantic Segmentation.

    To mitigate the ambiguity of single-view observations and extract robust 3D OpenCLIP voxels, we uniformly render multiple views from the upper hemisphere of each object. Based on these visual features and vlm-generated keywords, objects are accurately segmented into constituent parts. As shown in the second column of Figure A5, a snowman is segmented into its body, arms, and nose; a potted grass is separated into the planter and the green grass; and a bag is distinctly divided into the fabric body and plastic handles. This fine-grained part-level segmentation is crucial for applying localized, text-driven physical controls.

    Voxel-Wise Physical Property Heatmaps.

    Building upon the part segmentation, Text2PhyX provides dense, voxel-wise annotations for three key physical properties. As visualized in the rightmost three columns of Figure A5, different semantic parts within the same object exhibit distinctly different physical values, reflecting their assigned materials. For example, the wooden trunk of the tree shows a significantly higher Young’s Modulus (E) compared to its leaves, while the plastic handles of the bag exhibit different densities (ρ) and elasticity compared to the fabric body. These detailed heatmaps confirm that our automated, text-guided pipeline successfully assigns physically plausible and spatially accurate parameters across a wide variety of complex 3D objects.

    0.A.3 OpenCLIP-Driven 3D Semantic Segmentation

    Overview

    To endow our volumetric representation with open-vocabulary semantic understanding suitable for physics-based simulation, we distill dense, high-dimensional semantic features from a pre-trained 2D vision-language foundation model (specifically OpenCLIP) into a continuous 3D feature field. Furthermore, to ensure physical accuracy during stress propagation, we extend these surface features into the unobservable internal volume using a robust ray-casting strategy.

    2D Feature Extraction

    Given a set of multi-view RGB images {Iₖ} of the scene, we first extract 2D semantic feature maps using a pre-trained OpenCLIP image encoder. Since vision transformers typically output features at a lower resolution than the input image, we obtain a dense feature map Fₖ∈ℝ^512×512×768 for each image Iₖ, where 768 is the dimensionality of the OpenCLIP latent space.

    3D Feature Distillation via Volumetric Rendering

    Unlike heuristic multi-view projection methods that suffer from occlusion ambiguities, we lift the 2D semantic features into 3D using a physics-inspired volumetric rendering framework. We freeze the density field σ obtained from a pre-trained RGB NeRF and introduce a continuous 3D feature field Φ:ℝ³→ℝ^D, parameterized by a neural network or a feature grid.

    During optimization, we render the expected 3D feature F̂(r) along a camera ray r using the accumulated transmittance T(t). This naturally handles occlusions by dropping the transmittance to zero behind visible surfaces. We optimize the feature field Φ by minimizing the discrepancy between the rendered ray features F̂(r) and the corresponding ground-truth OpenCLIP features Fₖ(r) sampled from the 2D feature maps. We employ the negative cosine similarity loss as our distillation objective:

    L_distill=-1/N∑ₖ∑ᵣ(F̂(r)·Fₖ(r))/(∥F̂(r)∥₂∥Fₖ(r)∥₂)

    where N is the total number of sampled rays. By minimizing this loss, the 3D feature field learns to encode view-consistent semantic priors strictly on the visible surfaces.

    Internal Volume Filling via Even-Odd Rule

    While the volumetric rendering successfully distills features onto the object’s surface, physics-based simulations require semantic and physical properties (e.g., Young’s modulus E, Poisson’s ratio ν) to be defined throughout the object’s interior. Since internal voids are unobservable from external cameras, their features remain undefined.

    To bridge this gap, we employ a hierarchical ray-casting strategy based on the classic even-odd rule. For a given unassigned voxel v in the 3D space, we cast multiple rays uniformly distributed over a sphere towards infinity. Along each ray, we count the number of intersections with the object’s surface (defined by a density threshold on σ). If the intersection count is consistently odd across the majority of the casted rays, the voxel v is robustly classified as being inside the object, effectively handling complex concavities.

    Finally, for each identified internal voxel, we assign its semantic feature by performing nearest-neighbor interpolation from the optimized surface feature field Φ. This ensures that the internal volume inherits semantically and physically consistent properties from its closest bounding surface, yielding a complete volumetric representation ready for downstream simulation.

    Open-Vocabulary Querying

    Once the 3D feature distillation is complete, the scene can be queried using natural language. Given a user-provided text prompt (e.g., "a red apple" or "the handle of the mug"), we encode the text into a 768-dimensional embedding t using the OpenCLIP text encoder.

    To perform 3D semantic segmentation, we compute the cosine similarity between the text embedding t and the distilled 3D feature fₚ of each primitive: S(p,t)=(fₚ·t)/(∥fₚ∥₂∥t∥₂) Primitives with a similarity score S(p,t) exceeding a predefined threshold are segmented as belonging to the target object. This continuous similarity field not only enables robust part-level segmentation but also facilitates downstream tasks such as language-guided robotic grasping and interaction.

    0.A.4 vlm labeling

    To further illustrate the automated data generation pipeline described in Section 3.3, Figure A4 provides a concrete example of our text-guided property assignment process. As discussed in the main text, relying solely on visual inputs for physical parameter prediction is inherently ill-posed. To resolve this, we utilize a vlm to generate diverse, physically plausible textual descriptions and assign corresponding physical parameters.

    In this example, the input consists of multi-view RGB renderings of a soda can and its extracted 3D representation. During the augmentation phase, the vlm generates a novel semantic condition: “The soda can is now made of a very hard plastic.” Rather than blindly guessing the physical values, the vlm grounds its assignment by querying external knowledge bases. As shown in the generated JSON metadata, the model explicitly provides its reasoning trace (“from wiki”) to prevent hallucination.

    Based on this grounded knowledge, the vlm determines an appropriate scaling factor (multiplier: 0.113) for the material transition from standard aluminum to hard plastic. This multiplier is then applied to the default Young’s Modulus (E) of the object (“original_E_mean”: 249999920.0) to compute the updated physical parameter (“new_E_mean”: 28249996.8) for the specified part (“soda can”). This transparent, physics-aware reasoning process ensures that the generated text-parameter pairs in Text2PhyX remain strictly consistent and physically accurate across all 13,600 data triplets.

    Appendix 0.B Additional Evaluation and Analysis

    0.B.1 Human-Annotated Text Generalization

    To further evaluate text generalization beyond Text2PhyX, we construct a human-annotated test set of 30 objects. For each material category, we query The Engineering Toolbox to obtain plausible physical-property ranges, retrieve corresponding object images, and reconstruct 3D assets using SAM 3D Objects. We sample two material-property configurations from the queried ranges and run physics simulation for each sample. Human annotators then watch these videos and provide the corresponding natural language descriptions, making this evaluation independent of the text-generation pipeline used to build Text2PhyX.

    0.B.2 Unconditional Cross-Dataset Validation

    To evaluate whether our framework is tied only to Text2PhyX, we also compare Pixie, VoMP, and our model under an unconditional protocol using an empty text input. We train and test the methods on the Pixie dataset, the VoMP dataset, and Text2PhyX, respectively. This setting is not designed to test text controllability; rather, it checks whether the voxel-based feed-forward architecture remains competitive when reduced to the same unconditional setting as prior feed-forward methods.

item.title: 着色器随游戏一起下载：Advanced Shader Delivery 覆盖四家 GPU，首启编译从几分钟压到几秒 ｜ Advanced Shader Delivery is Available Now Across Hardware and Coming Soon to Other Storefronts
item.description:
一句话：预编译 state object database 随下载下发，减少加载时间、着色器卡顿与功耗。

要点：

  • 把预编译的 state object database（SODB）随商店下载一起下发，官方给出三项收益：总体加载时间、游戏内着色器卡顿、功耗
  • 已覆盖 AMD / Intel / NVIDIA / Qualcomm，系统要求 Windows 11 24H2 及以上；《使命召唤：现代战争 4》首启只需几秒，典型 PC 原本要几分钟
  • 工具链进度：UE 5.8.4 现在就能把 SODB 接进构建流程，Unity 的集成要等到 2027；ASD 也将从 Microsoft Store / Xbox PC 扩展到 Epic 商店与 Steam

为什么值得看：首启着色器编译是 PC 上最大的一笔体验税。这条路线要求构建期把 PSO 集合枚举干净并上传，等于倒逼引擎的 PSO 收集与状态对象管理流程重构——这对任何自研渲染后端都是同一道题。

中文摘要：Advanced Shader Delivery（ASD）解决的是 PC 生态的老问题：首次启动时现场编译着色器，导致长时间等待与运行中的卡顿。做法是把预编译好的 state object database 随游戏下载一起发到玩家机器，官方口径是同时降低总体加载时间、游戏内着色器卡顿与功耗。该能力现已覆盖 AMD、Intel、NVIDIA、Qualcomm 四家硬件，要求 Windows 11 24H2 及以上与较新的驱动。《使命召唤：现代战争 4》作为示范：首启编译只需几秒，而典型 PC 原本要几分钟。工程侧，微软继续简化状态对象的枚举与编译，10 月 Agility SDK 将引入 partial programs；UE 5.8.4 已支持把 SODB 打进流程，Unity 要等到 2027，Epic 商店与 Steam 也即将支持。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：DirectX Dev Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-27

A few weeks ago, we announced that Advanced Shader Delivery (ASD) is available for Gears of War: E-Day and teased that the feature is coming to devices across Windows 11. Today, we’re proud to announce that Advanced Shader Delivery is broadly available across the Windows ecosystem on devices powered by AMD, Intel, Nvidia, and Qualcomm!

ASD addresses a PC ecosystem wide challenge by delivering shaders at download of a title- reducing overall loading time, reducing shader stutter in game, and saving on power consumption. Check out the system requirements below for supported hardware and graphics drivers.

What’s next?

We’re also excited to announce that ASD will soon expand beyond the Microsoft Store and XBOX PC app to the Epic Games Store and Steam to deliver a better Windows gaming experience to more players! Epic Games will also roll out ASD support in an upcoming update for Fortnite.

For game developers, we’re continuing to make it easier to enumerate and compile state objects. Our upcoming October Agility SDK release includes important improvements such as partial programs, which will more efficiently compile complex state objects in different configurations.

Today: Advanced Shader Delivery Comes to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4

We are also excited to showcase Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 as a great example of ASD working across devices. With ASD, shader compilation at first launch takes just a few seconds, compared to several minutes on a typical PC without ASD.

To experience ASD for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, install the XBOX PC app before downloading.  For the best experience for ASD across all supported titles, make sure your graphics drivers are up to date.

Call to Action

If you’re a game developer looking to solve shader compilation, take a look at our documentation on how to integrate ASD for your title. Here, you’ll find instructions on how to collect state object databases (SODB) and upload them to game storefronts to support pre-compilation for your title today.

For those using Unreal Engine 5.8.4 to develop their title, the ability to integrate SODBs into the process is available today. Here is a link to their documentation on how to easily build an SODB into the process.

For those using Unity, SODB integration will be available in 2027!

System Requirements:

OS: Windows 11 24H2 or higher

AMD:

GPUs supported:AMD RDNA ™ 1, RDNA 2, RDNA 3, RDNA 3.5, RDNA 4 architectures

Driver version:Adrenalin 26.6.1 or higher

Intel:

GPUs supported:Intel® Arc B-Series: B570, B580, Intel® Core™ Ultra Series 2, Intel® Core™ Ultra Series 3

Min driver version:32.0.101.9150 or higher

Nvidia:

GPUs supported:All RTX GPUs and RTX Spark

Driver version:621.01 or higher

Qualcomm:

GPUs supported:Qualcomm® Snapdragon® X2 Series

Driver version:2026.08.3 or higher

Feedback?

For feedback on the Advanced Shader Delivery experience, you can let us know via our DirectX Discord.

Category

  • Advanced Shader Delivery
  • DirectX

    • Author

    Join the discussion.

    Sort by :Newest

  • Hi Wendy, whats the expected behavior with an Optimus config?

    The Xbox app loads on the Low Power device in this scenario and users are reporting that supported games such as Gears E-day aren't showing the Precompiled shaders message.

    Should it be getting shaders for all present gpu's in the system?

    if that is the intent, is there a bug where an unsupported driver causes the download to fail on All devices?

    Edit: There is a bug in Gaming Services which does exactly this, if an unsupported adapter (old driver, or possibly no asd package for this driver) the whole request is destroyed and...

    Hi Wendy, whats the expected behavior with an Optimus config?

    The Xbox app loads on the Low Power device in this scenario and users are reporting that supported games such as Gears E-day aren’t showing the Precompiled shaders message.

    Should it be getting shaders for all present gpu’s in the system?

    if that is the intent, is there a bug where an unsupported driver causes the download to fail on All devices?

    Edit: There is a bug in Gaming Services which does exactly this, if an unsupported adapter (old driver, or possibly no asd package for this driver) the whole request is destroyed and there is no fail through onwards to other devices in the system.

    This also widens the issue to any system with an active igp with pre-asd drivers.

    • Stay informed

    Get notified when new posts are published.Follow this blog

item.title: 拿 BVH 当特征索引：位置编码的查表直接塞进光追加速结构，显存占用与场景复杂度脱钩 ｜ BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing
item.description:
一句话：同一棵 BVH 既是光追加速结构又是特征索引，用包围盒八角的特征三线性插值出编码。

要点：

  • 在已有 BVH 里取一个 cut，取 cut 节点包围盒八个角上存的可学习特征向量做三线性插值，得到该 3D 位置的编码
  • 同一棵 BVH 既作光追加速结构又作特征索引结构，编码天然贴合场景几何，支持一般几何图元
  • 特征显存有上界、与场景复杂度无关；论文以 neural radiance cache（NRC）作为应用验证

为什么值得看：神经缓存/神经光追真正卡住的是输入编码的存储与查表成本。复用已经在遍历的 BVH，意味着不需要再建一套空间结构，也不会随场景规模线性涨显存——这是让 NRC 类技术进得了真实关卡的关键工程点。

中文摘要：多反弹路径追踪在游戏里至今难落地，一个现实出口是用小型 MLP 当神经缓存（如 neural radiance cache）来承担部分光追工作。MLP 能否学到高频信号，关键在输入编码。这篇论文提出一种专为光追设计的编码：直接复用光追加速结构 BVH，先在树里取一个 cut，把可学习特征向量存在 cut 节点包围盒的八个角上，再对位置做三线性插值得到编码。这样一棵 BVH 同时承担加速结构与特征索引两个职责，编码自然贴合场景几何、支持一般图元，而且特征显存有固定上界、不随场景复杂度增长。作者在 NRC 场景中验证了该编码的有效性，为神经辅助光追提供了更实用的存储方案。

Right: We feed the result to a neural network. Abstract We propose a novel input encoding method of 3D positions for neural networks used in ray tracing algorithms. Our encoding technique utilizes the bounding volume hierarchy (BVH), which serves both as an acceleration data structure for ray tracing and as a spatial data struc- ture for indexing learnable latent feature vectors. Our method naturally adapts to scene ge- ometry, supports general geometric primitives, and maintains a bounded memory footprint independent of scene complexity. We demonstrate an application of our technique in the context of neural radiance cache (NRC).

  1. Introduction

Despite the capabilities of modern graphics hardware, multi-bounce path tracing in the game industry remains elusive. A simple neural network, such as a multilayer 49 ISSN 2331-7418 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org perceptron (MLP), has been proven to credibly learn quantities such as visibility [Bokˇsansk´y and Meister 2025] or radiance [M¨uller et al. 2021], which are commonly used in ray tracing-based algorithms. Thanks to its compact representation, an MLP can be efficiently implemented on the GPU, allowing for online training at real-time frame rates. Such a neural network can serve as a cache for these quantities, sig- nificantly reducing the ray tracing workload at the cost of a small error (bias). The crucial component that allows an MLP to learn high frequencies of a signal is the input encoding. In this article, we present a novel encoding method tailored for ray tracing. All modern ray tracing APIs rely on the bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) [Meister et al. 2021] as an acceleration data structure. We demonstrate that the same data structure can be used for indexing learnable feature vectors that are used for encoding 3D positions in virtual scenes. Specifically, we find a cut of a fixed size in the BVH, wherein feature vectors are stored in the corners of the cut nodes’ bounding boxes. In this manner, each geometric primitive belongs to a single cut node such that its bounding box can be used for interpolating the corresponding feature vectors [M¨uller et al. 2022]. The benefits of our approach include the following: (1) naturally adapting to geometry, (2) a bounded memory footprint, and (3) a support for general geometric primitives.

  1. Related Work

Spectral bias is a phenomenon when a neural network struggles to learn high fre- quencies of a low-dimensional input signal [Rahaman et al. 2019]. To address this problem, various encoding methods have been proposed, mapping the input data to a higher-dimensional space prior to being fed to the neural network. Frequency en- coding [Mildenhall et al. 2021] transforms each input value by a series of sines and cosines with different angular frequencies. Parametric encoding introduces latent fea- ture vectors that are trained together with weights of the neural network using back- propagation, where an input point is encoded by interpolating feature vectors in the proximity of the input point. The feature vectors are indexed by a spatial data struc- ture to efficiently identify the feature vectors in the proximity of the encoded point. Hadadan et al. [2021] proposed to use multi-resolution grid encoding, which stores feature vectors in a set of uniform grids of different resolutions, where the input is encoded by concatenating feature vectors from each grid. M ¨uller et al. [2022] pro- posed to store the uniform grids in a hashed form, considerably reducing memory requirements. Fujieda et al. [2023] combined the hash-grid encoding with frequency encoding. Weier et al. [2026] proposed spatio-directional encoding that hierarchi- cally encodes a position and direction using a 5D hashed multi-resolution grid. The position is encoded in a similar manner as hash-grid encoding does. The method 50 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org distributes the feature vectors on a triangulated unit sphere, using barycentric interpo- lation to encode the direction. Yoshimura et al. [2026] proposed an unbounded hash grid, allowing unnormalized inputs by modifying the hash function. Takikawa et al. [2021] proposed storing feature vectors in an octree. Bok ˇsansk´y et al. [2025] and Su et al. [2025] proposed storing and interpolating feature vectors directly on the trian- gles. This approach naturally adapts to the geometry distribution, but it is limited to triangles only and the number of feature vectors grows with the scene complexity in contrast to uniform grids or octrees. Alber et al. [2025] proposed to store Markov chain states in a multi-resolution hash grid that selects the level based on the distance from the camera, to ensure roughly constant projected area on the screen. Weier et al. [2024] proposed to ap- proximate subtrees in the bottom levels of a BVH by a neural network. The subtrees are found by refining the cut in the BVH, iteratively splitting the nodes with the high- est training error. Our method stores feature vectors in the bounding volume hierarchy, combining the advantages of the approaches discussed above. Compared to octrees or uniform grids, our method naturally adapts to the scene geometry, efficiently handling the teapot-in-a-stadium problem. Unlike triangle-based encoding, our method supports general geometric primitives and maintains a bounded memory footprint independent of the scene complexity (see Table 1).   1. BVH Encoding

In this section, we describe the details of our BVH encoding. We first define the BVH cut and how it can be used to index feature vectors. Then, we show how to encode an input point using the cut and how to optimize the feature vectors by backpropagation. 3.1. BVH Cut We define a cut in the BVH as a set of nodes that separates the leaves and the root (both inclusively). The root and the leaves are trivial cuts. An important property of the cut is that each leaf node is included in a single cut node. An example of the BVH cut is illustrated in Figure 2. We form the cut iteratively by opening nodes with the 51 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 0 9 10 1 2 3 BVH cut Feature vectors of cut node 8 0 1 2 3 Feature vector buffer Figure 2. An example of the BVH cut (blue nodes) and its memory layout. The sequential index of a cut node (the bottom-left numbers) determines, where the corresponding eight feature vectors are stored in the feature vector buffer. largest surface area starting from the root using a priority queue (in the same manner as Hendrich et al. [2017]). We keep opening the nodes until we fill a given maximum cut size. Besides the cut nodes, we also compute a mapping from each geometric primitive to the corresponding cut node index and the sequential index of the node within the cut that we later use for the encoding itself. In the case of a two-level BVH, we propose a simple heuristic that redistributes the cut size budget among individual bottom-level BVHs based on the surface area of the bottom-level BVH (in world space). Note that this is only a heuristic that does not take into account other factors such as the distance to the camera, visibility, and material properties. The cut is an inherent part of the bottom-level BVH rather than of an individual instance. All instances of a bottom-level BVH therefore share a single cut, whose budget is determined by the largest world-space surface area among those instances. Note that in many cases the instances are of the same size. The BVH cut can be generalized to multiple levels such that we start with an initial coarser cut that we further refine to get a finer cut. In this way, we can find multiple cuts, corresponding to multiple feature vectors that can be concatenated in the same way as multi-resolution grid encoding does. Since we form cuts only in the bottom-level BVHs, we do not care much about the construction times; as in real-time scenarios, only the top-level BVH is being rebuilt in each frame. 3.2. Encoding We assume that the input points are the hit points provided as results of ray tracing. Note that the input point could be spatially in multiple cut nodes since the bound- 52 Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques BVH Encoding for Neural-Assisted Ray Tracing V ol. 15, No. 2, 2026 http://jcgt.org ing boxes may overlap, but the determining factor is the BVH cut node where the corresponding intersected geometric primitive belongs. Feature vectors are stored on the application side outside the ray tracing frame- work. Each cut node has eight feature vectors corresponding to the corners of its bounding box. The feature vectors are stored using the sequential index that is re- turned in the hit structure (see Figure 2). The encoding procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1. We fetch the bounding box using the cut node index and the correspond- ing feature vectors using the sequential index. Then, we normalize the hit point (in the object space in the case of a two-level BVH) using the bounding box and tri-linearly interpolate the corresponding feature vectors. Since the shape of the bounding boxes is arbitrary in contrast to the grid cells, special care must be taken for flat bounding boxes (e.g., of an axis-aligned triangle) to avoid division by zero (see lines 16–20). In the case of a two-level BVH, we precompute offsets to the feature vector buffer for each object/instance (i.e., a prefix sum of the number of cut nodes in each object/in- stance). Note that each instance has its own set of feature vectors but uses the same BVH cut. 3.3. Training The feature vectors are optimized in two passes (in a similar manner as the grid en- coding). We first compute gradients with respect to a loss function L: ∂L ∂zk = ∂L ∂z ∂z ∂zk = wk ∂L ∂z , where z is the tri-linearly interpolated feature vector fed to the neural network, zk is a feature vector of the k-th corner, and wk is the corresponding interpolation weight. The gradients are accumulated over the whole training batch. Then, we compute the average gradient, which we use to update the feature values using an optimizer such as the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) or Adam.

  1. Implementation Details

To demonstrate that our method is compatible with modern ray tracing engines, we extend HIPRT [Meister et al. 2024], an open-source ray tracing framework in HIP. We need only three minor modifications of its API: (1) a build parameter specifying the maximum number of cut nodes in a bottom-level BVH, (2) an extension of the hit structure to return the cut node and sequential indices (see Algorithm 1), and (3) a function for normalizing the point given the instance and cut node indices. Alternatively, we could provide a function returning a bounding box, and normal- ize the point on the application side. However, the internal hardware format supports oriented bounding boxes, where we need to (inversely) transform the point into the space of the oriented bounding box prior to the interpolation.
