    1. 坐标系转换
    首先，防止你忘记不同空间的坐标变换，我让豆老师跑出一份Unity中的坐标转换关系：


    视图空间与裁剪空间的转换

    裁剪空间中的w分量实质上就是视线空间的z分量的相反数（小知识：如果我们把视线空间的xy分量除以裁剪空间中的w分量，得到的坐标中xy分量一定与NDC坐标成线性关系！）。


    NDC空间与视图空间的转换

    视线空间的z分量与NDC空间中的z分量不成线性关系，但是视线空间中的1/z是与NDC空间中的z分量成线性关系的！


    屏幕空间与NDC空间的转换

    从上面几个式子中可以看出来，屏幕空间z分量和视图空间1/z分量成线性关系（Unity中，经过变换之后的屏幕空间坐标的原点是在左上角，故我们应该对其进行反转），这也就是为什么我在屏幕空间插值的是1/z，而不是z。我们使用1/z可以轻松复原视图空间的z分量。

    2. 重点细节讲解
    1）为什么屏幕空间要用[0, w-1]，[0, h-1]？
    其实我开始看别人代码的时候想的是为什么不用[0, 1]范围的uv坐标，如果这样也方便采样，不用重新反向映射一次，直到我看到DDA算法要算1/屏幕空间增量（float invdx = dir / deltaSS.x;），我才反应过来。实际上我们横纵范围不能看作一样的，我们屏幕分辨率是不同的（全高清1920×1080，四倍高清2560×1440 ...），想要步进屏幕空间，必须精确到像素级别！

    2）为什么循环中做一次初始半步长迈进？

    从我们的相交判断条件来看：

  • 判断rayFarZ这个较远点是否被表面遮挡；
  • 判断rayNearZ是否在一定阈值（Thickness）内。

    • 只有两个都满足时，才能说明相交成功，进行采样。那么我们先迈进半步长，之后的判断都在Reflection Dir方向的半步长处进行步进，如下图：

    这样是十分舒服的判断，既可以防止首次的判断失误，又确保后面的判断正确！

    3）为什么要这个Thickness这个阈值？
    其实就是增大容错率，如下图：

    3. 问题解析
    1）相机向下看时，会有一个自反射圆圈，超出MaxDistance之后会消失。

    这个问题我仔细分析了一下，原因是在视图空间中，我们反射出来的最终位置，可能超出近裁面了，我们如果把这个点映射到屏幕空间就会出错（仔细思考MVP变换，如果有个点在你相机后面（不在视锥体内），变换之后的位置必然不在投影盒中，那么映射到屏幕空间必然会出错），所以我们必须要对这个最终反射点进行一次近裁剪面的判断，从而调整反射点的最终位置，如下：

    // 视图空间中射线起始位置和结束位置
float3 startVS = posVS;
float3 endVS = posVS + reflDirVS * maxDistance;
if (endVS.z > -_ProjectionParams.y)
    maxDistance = (-_ProjectionParams.y - startVS.z) / reflDirVS.z;
endVS = startVS + reflDirVS * maxDistance;

// inverse w
......

    2）屏幕信息缺失
    很好理解，毕竟我们在屏幕空间进行反射，那么必定会缺失信息，如下图：

    根据Games 202，闫老师给的思路，在屏幕空间进行一次衰减，不同的是，闫老师的思路是利用反射距离进行衰减，我的思路是利用反射点的uv进行衰减。

    那么实现步骤也是十分简单的，先在Render Pass传入一个控制衰减的参数attenuation，在Shader中，我使用暗角后处理的控制方法，如下：

    if (intersecting)
{
    float2 attUV = abs(hitUV - 0.5) * 1.8;
    attUV = pow(saturate(attUV), attenuation);
    float att = length(attUV);
    float edgeFading= pow(saturate(1 - att * att), 5);

    return GetSource(hitUV) * smoothness * edgeFading + GetSource(uv);
}

    这个效果简单来说就是做一次屏幕边缘的衰减，我的想法就是，如果我们hitUV打到了屏幕边缘，那么就肯定给一个小的权重，若打到屏幕中心，那么肯定要给一个大点的权重，同时需要考虑到屏幕长宽的影响，综合考虑之后，我决定使用暗角作为权重。

item.title: Bevy 0.20：实时路径追踪器 Solari 上 Metal 并接 DLSS，变更 tick 让 GPU 网格提取快 132 倍 ｜ Bevy 0.20
item.description:
一句话：227 位贡献者、817 个 PR：路径追踪、场景系统与 ECS 变更追踪同时推进。

要点：

  • Solari（Bevy 的实时路径追踪渲染器）更快、更准、支持的渲染特性更多，并且通过 Metal 跑上 macOS，同时接入 DLSS
  • BSN 场景系统语法重写，可读性与可组合性提升；子节点全部生成后会触发可观测的 Ready 事件
  • 实体级变更 tick 的取舍：写入变贵（要同时写列与实体两级），但对「常查少改」的实体，GPU 网格提取实测快 132 倍

为什么值得看：一个完全开源的引擎把「实时路径追踪 + DLSS + ECS 变更追踪」同时往前推，是观察未来引擎架构取舍的活样本：哪些该交给神经渲染、哪些该在数据层省，这里都能看到真实数字。

中文摘要：Bevy 0.20 由 227 位贡献者、817 个 PR 堆出来，重点在渲染与工程结构。Solari 是 Bevy 的实时路径追踪渲染器，这一版更快、更准、覆盖更多 Bevy 渲染特性，并通过 Metal 上了 macOS，同时接入了 DLSS。BSN 场景系统做了语法重写，更易读易组合，子实体全部生成后会触发可观测的 Ready 事件，方便挂初始化逻辑。Feathers UI 工具包补齐了颜色输入、可滚动列表、下拉选择与懒加载菜单等控件。ECS 侧引入实体级变更 tick：写入时要同时写列与实体两级，代价变高，但对那些被频繁查询、很少修改的实体，官方实测 GPU 网格提取快了 132 倍。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：Bevy（English）

原文发布：2026-10-08

本期推送：2026-10-27

Bevy 0.20

Posted on October 8, 2026 by Bevy Contributors

The Zorah scene rendered in Bevy Solari

Thanks to 227 contributors, 817 pull requests, community reviewers, and our generous donors, we're happy to announce the Bevy 0.20 release on crates.io!

For those who don't know, Bevy is a refreshingly simple data-driven game engine built in Rust. You can check out our Quick Start Guide to try it today. It's free and open source forever! You can grab the full source code on GitHub. Check out Bevy Assets for a collection of community-developed plugins, games, and learning resources.

To update an existing Bevy App or Plugin to Bevy 0.20, check out our 0.19 to 0.20 Migration Guide.

Since our last release a few months ago we've added a ton of new features, bug fixes, and quality of life tweaks, but here are some of the highlights:

  • Solari and DLSS: Solari, Bevy's realtime pathtraced renderer, is now faster, more accurate, supports more Bevy rendering features, and runs on macOS via Metal!
  • BSN Syntax Improvements: BSN, Bevy's new scene system, had some syntax changes that made it much easier to read and compose
  • Ready Event: BSN scene entities now trigger an observable 
    Ready
     event when all of their children have been spawned.
  • More UI Widgets: Bevy Feathers, Bevy's opinionated editor-centric UI toolkit, now has Color Input, Scrollable List View, Dropdown Selection, and Lazy Menu widgets. The Number Input widget is now scrubbable / draggable, and we've added Headless Tab Widgets.
  • WESL Shaders: Bevy has officially adopted the WESL shader language (a standardized extension of WGSL). WESL is already an improvement over Bevy's old custom WGSL dialect, and we've been working with the WESL team to plan out the future of shader development in Bevy.
  • Sprite Materials and Extended 2D Materials: It is now possible to create custom shader materials for Sprites, and 2D mesh materials can now be extended like they can in 3D.
  • Pan Orbit Camera: Bevy now has a "pan orbit camera", making it possible to navigate scenes in a CAD-like way.

    • Solari and DLSS #

    Authors:@JMS55, @mate-h, @stuartparmenterPRs:#24667, #24767, #25082, #25123, #25244, #25423, #25513, #25518, #25703, #25704, #25787, #25814

    Solari, Bevy's realtime pathtraced renderer, has seen major improvements to pretty much every aspect of the plugin!

    Read JMS55's blog for the technical details, or continue reading below for the high level overview.

    Improved Image Quality #

    Thanks to improvements in our ReSTIR implementation, rendering is now mostly unbiased, leading to much more accurate lighting.

    Additionally, thanks to some other changes, moving objects no longer have shadows that lag behind, and reflections now look significantly less shimmery in motion, especially for non-metallic materials.

    Improved Performance #

    DLSS-RR has gotten very good in recent updates, and for many scenes, ReSTIR costs a decent chunk of performance, and does not significantly improve image quality.

    As a result, we've decided to make ReSTIR optional, and turn it off by default.

    If you were using Solari in Bevy 0.19, check if the loss of ReSTIR affects your scene, and if so re-enable 

    SolariLighting::restir
    .

    With ReSTIR off, expect reduced shadow quality and missing shadows in motion in scenes with many lights. We are exploring cheaper ways of improving light sampling, without ReSTIR, to improve this in the future.

    In addition, Solari's scene management code is now retained (similar to retained render world optimizations in previous versions of Bevy), and overall much more optimized, leading to significantly reduced CPU costs.

    You may also want to take a look at the new fields in 

    SolariLighting
    . While we aim to set reasonable defaults that will work well across a wide variety of games, there are now many knobs (world cache size, per-pixel light sample count, temporal accumulation, and path tracing bounce count) that can be tweaked to improve performance or quality for your specific scene, project and hardware.

    Improved Compatibility #

    Solari now supports lighting from 

    Atmosphere
    and 
    EnvironmentMapLight
    s on cameras, in addition to the existing support for 
    DirectionalLight
     and emissive meshes. We're hoping to add support for the remaining 
    PointLight
    , 
    SpotLight
    , and 
    RectLight
     types in the near future.

    Solari now also runs on macOS, but note that there is currently no built-in denoiser included in 

    bevy_solari
    for macOS. MetalFX Ray Reconstruction might be a possible solution in the future (contributions welcome!)

    DLSS Updates #

    Finally, our 

    dlss_wgpu
    crate has been updated to support the latest version of DLSS, bringing support for DLSS-RR 4.5, which significantly improves denoising quality in Solari.

    If you were using DLSS in Bevy 0.19, make sure to download and setup the newest version of the DLSS SDK, else you will run into compiler errors.

    BSN Syntax Improvements #

    Authors:@cartPRs:#25318, #25626

    BSN landed with a few idiosyncrasies that caused friction in practice. We made some changes to BSN's syntax this cycle in the interest of improving its ergonomics and clarity. After this, the syntax should largely be nailed down.

    Explicit scene syntax #

    All scene references now require 

    @
    prefixes:
    // Before
bsn! {
    scene_variable
    scene_function()
    @SceneComponent
    {scene_expression}
}

// After
bsn! {
    @scene_variable
    @scene_function()
    @SceneComponent
    @{scene_expression}
}

    In addition to making it easier to spot scene inclusions (and unifying the syntax across cases), this freed us up to make component values much easier to work with!

    No more 
    template_value
    wrappers! #

    You can now remove all of those pesky 

    template_value
    wrappers from your component values:
    // Before
bsn! {
    template_value(component_variable)
    template_value(component_function())
}

// After
bsn! {
    component_variable
    component_function()
}

    Enums "just work" #

    Enums no longer require 

    VariantDefaults
    or 
    FromTemplate
    , provided they implement 
    Default
    and 
    Clone
    :
    // Before
#[derive(Component, Default, Clone, VariantDefaults)]
enum Foo {
    A { x: u32, y: u32 },
    #[default]
    B,
}

bsn! {
    Foo::B
}

// After
#[derive(Component, Default, Clone)]
enum Foo {
    A { x: u32, y: u32 },
    #[default]
    B,
}

bsn! {
    Foo::B
}

    If you were using an enum that didn't support 

    VariantDefaults
    , you can now remove the 
    template_value
    wrapper:
    // Before
bsn! {
    template_value(Foo::A)
}
// After
bsn! {
    Foo::A
}

    The removal of 

    VariantDefaults
    does mean that enums must now have every field specified:
    // Before (y field is initialized to its default value)
bsn! {
    Foo::A { x: 1 }
}

// After (y field must be manually specified)
bsn! {
    Foo::A { x: 1, y: 0 }
}

    We believe this tradeoff is worth it, as it increases BSN's compatibility with arbitrary Rust enums. Rust doesn't support "enum variant defaults" anyway!

    Chained method support #

    The "builder pattern" (and chained methods generally) previously required a 

    template_value
    wrapper. This can now be removed:
    // Before
bsn! {
    template_value(Transform::from_xyz(-2.5, 4.5, 9.0).looking_at(Vec3::ZERO, Vec3::Y))
}
// After
bsn! {
    Transform::from_xyz(-2.5, 4.5, 9.0).looking_at(Vec3::ZERO, Vec3::Y)
}

    Additionally, you can now remove the 

    template_value
    wrapper in cases like this:
    // Before
bsn! {
    template_value(node.clone())
}
// After
bsn! {
    node.clone()
}

    In general, you should now be able to remove all 

    template_value
    instances from your BSN declarations!

    Improved list syntax #

    BSN previously used commas to separate entities, with optional 

    ()
    around entities to make the boundaries clearer. This resulted in a lot of syntax noise, line noise, and over-indentation:
    bsn! {
    Node 
    Children [
        (
            #OkButton
            @button("Ok")
        ),
        (
            #CancelButton
            @button("Cancel")
        ),
    ]
}

    To avoid this, many developers opted for this syntax instead, which made it very hard to visually distinguish entities:

    bsn! {
    Node 
    Children [
        #OkButton
        @button("Ok"),
        #CancelButton
        @button("Cancel"),
    ]
}

    BSN now uses 

    --
    to separate entities in a list:
    bsn! {
    Node 
    Children [
        #OkButton
        @button("Ok")
        --
        #CancelButton
        @button("Cancel")
    ]
}

    This gives us the best of all worlds: entities are visually distinct, and there is no over-indentation, line noise, or syntax noise (the stats when compared to other competitors in the "markup format" space are very competitive!). Both 

    ()
    and 
    ,
    have been deprecated in this context.

    Using 

    []
    and 
    ()
    for 
    bsn_list!
     (and 
    bsn!
    ) is now discouraged / warned against (ex: 
    bsn_list! []
    ), as it can result in poor rustfmt autoformatting. Instead, use 
    bsn_list! {}
    , which is the only syntax that 
    rustfmt
    won't touch. Don't worry, we plan to build a BSN auto-formatter!
    bsn_list! {
    #Ok @button("Ok")
    --
    #Cancel @button("Cancel")
}

    Ready
    Event #

    Authors:@cartPRs:#25296

    We landed BSN, Bevy's next generation scene system, in our last release. It was missing a key piece though: the ability to easily run logic when a scene is fully "ready" and spawned (ex: all dependencies have loaded, the full hierarchy is present, and all of the initial components are inserted in the scene). This is a critical piece for building cohesive, standalone, composable scenes. It is also necessary to properly layer Bevy logic on top of other scene representations (like glTF).

    The closest we had was the 

    Add
    event for a given component, which runs "top down" (meaning children are not available). We needed a "bottom up" equivalent to enable building logic that relies on the complete loaded and spawned scene.

    The solution is pretty straightforward: trigger a new 

    Ready
    event for each entity in a spawned scene after the full spawn logic has run for that entity (including its descendants).

    This enables the following:

    #[derive(SceneComponent, Default, Clone)]
struct Widget;

impl Widget {
    fn scene() -> impl Scene {
        bsn! {
            Node { width: px(100), height: px(100) }
            on(|ready: On| {
                info!("The full scene, including 'widget.bsn' contents, is available here")
            })
            Children [
                Text("hello")
                --
                :"widget.bsn"
            ]
        }
    }
}

world.spawn(bsn! { @Widget })

    More Feathers Widgets #

    Authors:@viridia, @gagnus, @tmstoreyPRs:#25446, #25079, #24092, #24847, #24784, #24636, #24701

    Feathers, Bevy's opinionated editor-centric UI toolkit, now has more widgets for you to play with:

    Color Input #

    Bevy now has a compact color input selector that displays a color picker widget popup when clicked. This includes a color wheel selector, RGB, and HSL selectors, and a recently used colors grid.

    List View / Scrollbar #

    A scrollable, selectable list view.

    Dropdown Selection #

    A selection field that when clicked, displays a dropdown containing a list of options to select.

    Spawns a menu popup when the menu is opened and despawns it when it is closed. This is in contrast to the normal Menu widget, which just hides the menu.

    Number Input Widget Scrubbing / Dragging #

    The 

    FeathersNumberInput
    widget has been expanded to support both normal text input and scrubbing / dragging. There is a configurable "hard limit" (minimum and maximum value via any input method) and "soft limit" (minimum and maximum value via dragging), in addition to control over floating point precision and step sizes.

    Headless Tab Widgets #

    Authors:@jbuehler23PRs:#25515

    bevy_ui_widgets
    now has headless (bring-your-own-visuals) tab behavior: a 
    TabList
     container and 
    Tab
     headers.

    Selection is managed "externally". 

    SelectedTab
    on the list holds the selected tab; interaction emits 
    ValueChange>
     as a request, applied by the app or by the optional 
    tablist_self_update
     observer.

    Tabs support keyboard shortcuts and integrate with Bevy's focus, interaction, and accessibility systems.

    bsn! {
    TabList
    SelectedTab(Some(first_tab))
    on(tablist_self_update)
    Children [
        Tab Children [ Text("General") ]
        --
        Tab Children [ Text("Rendering") ]
    ]
}

    See the 

    headless_tabs
    example for controlled and self-updating tab lists in both orientations.

    WESL Shaders #

    Authors:@tychedelia, @BenjaminBrienenPRs:#25088

    Bevy's shaders are now written in WESL and the old "Custom Bevy Extended WGSL" language support has been removed.

    WESL is a language standard that extends WGSL to add important usability features like modules, imports, conditional compilation, and more. You can see what that looks like (and render pretty shader toys!) live in your browser in the WESL Playground.

    Bevy has historically handled these things in our own custom WGSL dialect, but we believe it is better for the wider shader ecosystem (and for us) to adopt a common standard where we can pool resources on language improvements, module ecosystems, and IDE tooling. We've been working closely with the WESL team to evolve the standard in a way that fits well into the Bevy picture.

    A critical part of that tooling is language server protocol support, in the form of wgsl-analyzer. That means syntax highlighting, go-to-definition, inlay hints, code folding, formatting and more, once installed for your IDE of choice.

    Custom shaders in the old Bevy WGSL dialect need to be translated to WESL and renamed from 

    .wgsl
    to 
    .wesl
    . Plain WGSL files with no preprocessor directives will keep working.

    Before: Custom Bevy Extended WGSL #

    #import bevy_pbr::forward_io::VertexOutput
#import "shaders/util.wgsl"::hsv_to_rgb
#ifdef VERTEX_COLORS
var tint: vec4;
#endif
@group(2) @binding(#{MATERIAL_BIND_GROUP}) var color: vec4;

    After: WESL #

    import bevy_pbr::render::forward_io::VertexOutput;
import super::util::hsv_to_rgb;
@if(VERTEX_COLORS)
var tint: vec4;
@group(2) @binding(constants::MATERIAL_BIND_GROUP) var color: vec4;

    Mesh Shaders #

    Authors:@ChristopherBiscardiPRs:#25627

    Mesh shaders are now integrated with Bevy's pipeline cache and are available for advanced users to take advantage of. Mesh shaders can be used to render:

  • Meshlets generated using tools like meshoptimizer
  • Procedural grass with dynamic level-of-detail, as seen here
  • Voxels, like nvidium
  • Particles
  • and more

    • Mesh shaders, at a high level, replace the classic vertex shader with a compute shader. This allows generating geometry directly on the GPU and passing those generated primitives directly to the fragment shader without using multiple pipelines or intermediary buffers (to pass data from a compute shader to a render pipeline).

    A 

    MeshPipeline
    contains:
  • an optional task shader (also known as amplification shader)
  • a mesh shader
  • a fragment shader

    • The new 

    MeshPipelineDescriptor
    can be used to define a 
    MeshPipeline
    . That 
    MeshPipeline
     is then used as a 
    RenderPipeline
    , which allows the re-use of Bevy's lower level rendering APIs such as 
    RenderContext::begin_tracked_render_pass
     to take advantage of the new 
    draw_mesh_tasks
     APIs.
    let mut pass = render_context.begin_tracked_render_pass(RenderPassDescriptor {
    label: Some("custom_mesh_shader_pass"),
    color_attachments: &[Some(target.get_color_attachment())],
    depth_stencil_attachment: Some(depth.get_attachment(StoreOp::Store)),
    ..default()
});

pass.set_render_pipeline(mesh_pipeline);
pass.set_bind_group(0, &bind_group, &[view_uniform_offset.offset]);

// draw_mesh_tasks dispatches the task shader if there is one,
// or dispatches the mesh shader if there is no task shader.
pass.draw_mesh_tasks(1, 1, 1);

    It is notable that mesh shaders are an advanced graphics approach with platform-specific performance considerations, and that this is the initial base support for the feature. Higher level user APIs, and easy integration with Bevy's 

    StandardMaterial
    , are left to future work.

    Mesh shaders are not supported on web platforms.

    Check out the new 

    mesh_shader_intro
    example for more usage examples.

    Sprite Materials #

    Authors:@cookie1170PRs:#25415

    Until now, Bevy's sprite renderer has been lacking a major feature: the ability to extend it with custom shaders! With this release, it's now possible to create custom materials for sprites by implementing the 

    MaterialExtension2d
    trait, inserting the 
    SpriteMaterial
     component and adding the 
    SpriteMaterialPlugin
     to your app.

    The shader can use functions exported from 

    bevy_sprite_render::sprite_mesh::functions
    , including:
    // Samples the sprite's final color, including the tint and alpha discard, at a given UV.
fn sample_final_color(uv: vec2, instance_index: u32) -> vec4;

// Samples the sprite's texture without tint and alpha discard at a given UV.
fn sample_sprite_texture(uv: vec2, instance_index: u32) -> vec4;

// Applies tint and alpha discard to the sprite's color.
fn get_final_color(sprite_color: vec4, instance_index: u32) -> vec4;

    Check out the 

    sprite_material
    example to see it in action!

    2D Extended Materials #

    Authors:@cookie1170PRs:#25183

    Bevy now provides a 2D analog to 3D's 

    ExtendedMaterial
    , which can be used to extend an existing material by implementing the 
    MaterialExtension2d
     trait:
    #[derive(AsBindGroup, Reflect, Clone)]
struct MyMaterial {
    #[uniform(20)]
    value: Vec4,
}

impl MaterialExtension2d for MyMaterial {
    fn fragment_shader() -> Option {
        Some("my_material.wesl".into())
    }
}

    This material can now be used in an 

    ExtendedMaterial2d
    struct:
    let handle = materials.add(ExtendedMaterial2d {
    base: ColorMaterial::from_color(Color::WHITE),
    extension: MyMaterial {
        value: Vec4::ZERO,
    },
});
commands.spawn((
    Mesh2d,
    MeshMaterial2d(handle),
));

    Sprite Render Backend Unification #

    Authors:@IceSentryPRs:#25432

    The sprite render backend was replaced by a new backend that reuses a lot of the infrastructure made for 3D. This resulted in improved performance in many cases and also makes future maintenance and improvements easier.

    Pan Orbit Camera #

    Authors:@aevyrie, @taishi-samaPRs:#25434

    We have upstreamed the awesome 

    bevy_editor_cam
    made by @aevyrie as the new 
    PanOrbitCamera
     in our 
    bevy_camera_controller
     crate!

    Usage #

    Add 

    MeshPickingPlugin
    and 
    DefaultPanOrbitCameraPlugins
    :
    app.add_plugins((
    MeshPickingPlugin,
    DefaultPanOrbitCameraPlugins,
))

    Then add the 

    PanOrbitCamera
    component on any 3D camera.
    commands.spawn((
    Camera3d::default(),
    PanOrbitCamera::default(),
))

    Full functionality is shown in the 

    camera/pan_orbit_camera_cad
    example.

    Weak System Ordering with 
    chain_weak
    #

    Authors:@JMS55PRs:#25128

    Ordering large groups of systems with 

    .chain()
    is convenient, but it can be overly strict. If system set 
    X
    is chained before system set 
    Y
    , every system in 
    X
    must finish before any system in 
    Y
    can start, even when the systems involved never touch the same data. This often leaves worker threads idle while they wait for a handful of stragglers at the end of a system set, a pattern that shows up frequently in the render world.

    The new 

    chain_weak()
    , 
    before_weak()
    , and 
    after_weak()
     functions provide a looser alternative. Like their regular counterparts, they request an ordering between successive elements, however that ordering is only kept between systems whose data accesses actually conflict. Systems that don't conflict are left unordered and may run in any order, including in parallel.
    schedule.configure_sets(
    (
        ExtractCommands,
        PrepareMeshes,
        CreateViews,
        Specialize,
        PrepareViews,
        Queue,
        PhaseSort,
        Prepare,
        Render,
        Cleanup,
        PostCleanup,
    )
        .chain_weak(),
);

    When two weakly-ordered systems actually conflict on their data access, a normal ordering is kept between them, so the earlier one still runs first. Two systems that conflict only through a non-conflicting system between them in the chain stay ordered as well. Non-conflicting systems, however, are left free to run in any order and overlap for increased parallelism!

    Two kinds of system are treated as always conflicting, so their ordering is always kept: an earlier system that produces deferred effects such as 

    Commands
    (so the later system observes them, with an 
    ApplyDeferred
     sync point inserted as usual), and exclusive systems (which cannot overlap anything regardless).

    Because the scheduler can only see accesses it tracks, dependencies expressed through interior mutability on read-only accesses, global state, or other untracked methods are not respected. Use 

    chain_weak
    only when your systems don't rely on such hidden ordering, otherwise stick with 
    chain
    .

    Contextual Theming #

    Authors:@viridiaPRs:#24969

    Feathers now supports "contextual theming", meaning that the theme variables can change depending on the parent entity. So widgets that are inside of a dialog box or subpanel can have different colors than widgets that are on a regular panel or window background.

    The design follows that of popular web toolkits like MUI, Radix, or Chakra. There's a new component, 

    ThemeContext
    , which lets you select which color scheme the widget's descendants should use; currently the available schemes are 
    Base
    , 
    Higher
    , 
    Highest
    , and 
    Floating
    , which correspond to the design plans for the Bevy scene editor.

    The theme context is used in conjunction with a new kind of design token, named 

    SemanticToken
    . The lookup process for a color now requires two stages: the 
    ThemeToken
     is converted into a 
    SemanticToken
    , and then the combination of 
    SemanticToken
    and 
    ThemeContext
     is used to look up a color.

    In addition to allowing context-specific color choices, this also makes it easier to design new themes! Instead of having to tediously choose colors for a hundred different theme tokens, the set of semantic tokens is much smaller, and the relationship between token and color is much more intuitive.

    Val::Em
    and 
    Val::Rem
    #

    Authors:@gagnusPRs:#25231

    Bevy UI now supports 

    em
    and 
    rem
     as sizing units. 
    em
    is the current font size (represented by an 
    EmSize
     component), 
    rem
    is a global "root" font size (represented by the existing 
    RemSize
     resource).

    EmSize
    is derived from 
    TextFont
     when one is on the same entity; propagating it down the hierarchy is left to your app.

    This is especially useful if you might want to vary your text size after authoring your UIs, for example as an accessibility feature or just to improve your UI on different devices.

    bsn! {
    Node { width: em(10) }
    Text("Hello")
    TextFont { font_size: FontSize::Rem(1.5) }
}

    The default font-size is now 

    rem(1)
    rather than 
    px(20)
    . This is a no-op if you're not changing 
    RemSize
     but it means your text will scale by default when you do.

    Per-Column Change Ticks #

    Authors:@pcwalton, @SkiFire13PRs:#25157, #25429

    Components can now opt-in to "column summary change ticks":

    #[derive(Component)]
#[component(summary_tick)]
struct MyComponent {
    /* fields here */
}

    When enabled, this will store a "column change tick" in addition to a "per-entity change tick", which allows cheaply skipping the whole column of entities when querying for changes, rather than needing to check every entity's component to see if it has changed.

    This makes mutations more expensive, as they need to write both the column change tick and the entity change tick, but for entities whose changes are queried often, but change infrequently, this tradeoff can easily be worth it! We've seen change ticks result in a 132x speedup in our GPU mesh extraction code!

    FixedNode
    #

    Authors:@ickshonpePRs:#24323

    FixedNode
    is a new marker component for Bevy UI.

    A UI node entity with the 

    FixedNode
    component is positioned relative to the target camera's viewport rather than its parent element. 
    FixedNode
    s don't inherit their parent's layout, clipping or transform context. They behave like a "root node".

    Elliptical Border Radius #

    Authors:@ickshonpePRs:#24779

    Bevy UI can now draw nodes with elliptical border geometry.

    The fields of 

    BorderRadius
    are now 
    CornerRadius
    s to enable different radius to be set for each axis.
    let a = BorderRadius::all(CornerRadius::circular(vh(10.)));
let b = BorderRadius::all(vh(10.)); // a == b
let c = BorderRadius::top_right(CornerRadius::new(px(10.), px(20.)));

    Schedule Randomization #

    Authors:@andriyDevPRs:#25094

    Before a schedule runs (and therefore, your systems), it first computes the system run order based on their ordering constraints (

    .before()
    , 
    .after()

一句话：227 位贡献者、817 个 PR：路径追踪、场景系统与 ECS 变更追踪同时推进。

要点：

  • Solari（Bevy 的实时路径追踪渲染器）更快、更准、支持的渲染特性更多，并且通过 Metal 跑上 macOS，同时接入 DLSS
  • BSN 场景系统语法重写，可读性与可组合性提升；子节点全部生成后会触发可观测的 Ready 事件
  • 实体级变更 tick 的取舍：写入变贵（要同时写列与实体两级），但对「常查少改」的实体，GPU 网格提取实测快 132 倍

为什么值得看：一个完全开源的引擎把「实时路径追踪 + DLSS + ECS 变更追踪」同时往前推，是观察未来引擎架构取舍的活样本：哪些该交给神经渲染、哪些该在数据层省，这里都能看到真实数字。

中文摘要：Bevy 0.20 由 227 位贡献者、817 个 PR 堆出来，重点在渲染与工程结构。Solari 是 Bevy 的实时路径追踪渲染器，这一版更快、更准、覆盖更多 Bevy 渲染特性，并通过 Metal 上了 macOS，同时接入了 DLSS。BSN 场景系统做了语法重写，更易读易组合，子实体全部生成后会触发可观测的 Ready 事件，方便挂初始化逻辑。Feathers UI 工具包补齐了颜色输入、可滚动列表、下拉选择与懒加载菜单等控件。ECS 侧引入实体级变更 tick：写入时要同时写列与实体两级，代价变高，但对那些被频繁查询、很少修改的实体，官方实测 GPU 网格提取快了 132 倍。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：Bevy（English）

原文发布：2026-10-08

本期推送：2026-10-27

Bevy 0.20

Posted on October 8, 2026 by Bevy Contributors

The Zorah scene rendered in Bevy Solari

Thanks to 227 contributors, 817 pull requests, community reviewers, and our generous donors, we're happy to announce the Bevy 0.20 release on crates.io!

For those who don't know, Bevy is a refreshingly simple data-driven game engine built in Rust. You can check out our Quick Start Guide to try it today. It's free and open source forever! You can grab the full source code on GitHub. Check out Bevy Assets for a collection of community-developed plugins, games, and learning resources.

To update an existing Bevy App or Plugin to Bevy 0.20, check out our 0.19 to 0.20 Migration Guide.

Since our last release a few months ago we've added a ton of new features, bug fixes, and quality of life tweaks, but here are some of the highlights:

  • Solari and DLSS: Solari, Bevy's realtime pathtraced renderer, is now faster, more accurate, supports more Bevy rendering features, and runs on macOS via Metal!
  • BSN Syntax Improvements: BSN, Bevy's new scene system, had some syntax changes that made it much easier to read and compose
  • Ready Event: BSN scene entities now trigger an observable 
    Ready
     event when all of their children have been spawned.
  • More UI Widgets: Bevy Feathers, Bevy's opinionated editor-centric UI toolkit, now has Color Input, Scrollable List View, Dropdown Selection, and Lazy Menu widgets. The Number Input widget is now scrubbable / draggable, and we've added Headless Tab Widgets.
  • WESL Shaders: Bevy has officially adopted the WESL shader language (a standardized extension of WGSL). WESL is already an improvement over Bevy's old custom WGSL dialect, and we've been working with the WESL team to plan out the future of shader development in Bevy.
  • Sprite Materials and Extended 2D Materials: It is now possible to create custom shader materials for Sprites, and 2D mesh materials can now be extended like they can in 3D.
  • Pan Orbit Camera: Bevy now has a "pan orbit camera", making it possible to navigate scenes in a CAD-like way.

    • Solari and DLSS #

    Authors:@JMS55, @mate-h, @stuartparmenterPRs:#24667, #24767, #25082, #25123, #25244, #25423, #25513, #25518, #25703, #25704, #25787, #25814

    Solari, Bevy's realtime pathtraced renderer, has seen major improvements to pretty much every aspect of the plugin!

    Read JMS55's blog for the technical details, or continue reading below for the high level overview.

    Improved Image Quality #

    Thanks to improvements in our ReSTIR implementation, rendering is now mostly unbiased, leading to much more accurate lighting.

    Additionally, thanks to some other changes, moving objects no longer have shadows that lag behind, and reflections now look significantly less shimmery in motion, especially for non-metallic materials.

    Improved Performance #

    DLSS-RR has gotten very good in recent updates, and for many scenes, ReSTIR costs a decent chunk of performance, and does not significantly improve image quality.

    As a result, we've decided to make ReSTIR optional, and turn it off by default.

    If you were using Solari in Bevy 0.19, check if the loss of ReSTIR affects your scene, and if so re-enable 

    SolariLighting::restir
    .

    With ReSTIR off, expect reduced shadow quality and missing shadows in motion in scenes with many lights. We are exploring cheaper ways of improving light sampling, without ReSTIR, to improve this in the future.

    In addition, Solari's scene management code is now retained (similar to retained render world optimizations in previous versions of Bevy), and overall much more optimized, leading to significantly reduced CPU costs.

    You may also want to take a look at the new fields in 

    SolariLighting
    . While we aim to set reasonable defaults that will work well across a wide variety of games, there are now many knobs (world cache size, per-pixel light sample count, temporal accumulation, and path tracing bounce count) that can be tweaked to improve performance or quality for your specific scene, project and hardware.

    Improved Compatibility #

    Solari now supports lighting from 

    Atmosphere
    and 
    EnvironmentMapLight
    s on cameras, in addition to the existing support for 
    DirectionalLight
     and emissive meshes. We're hoping to add support for the remaining 
    PointLight
    , 
    SpotLight
    , and 
    RectLight
     types in the near future.

    Solari now also runs on macOS, but note that there is currently no built-in denoiser included in 

    bevy_solari
    for macOS. MetalFX Ray Reconstruction might be a possible solution in the future (contributions welcome!)

    DLSS Updates #

    Finally, our 

    dlss_wgpu
    crate has been updated to support the latest version of DLSS, bringing support for DLSS-RR 4.5, which significantly improves denoising quality in Solari.

    If you were using DLSS in Bevy 0.19, make sure to download and setup the newest version of the DLSS SDK, else you will run into compiler errors.

    BSN Syntax Improvements #

    Authors:@cartPRs:#25318, #25626

    BSN landed with a few idiosyncrasies that caused friction in practice. We made some changes to BSN's syntax this cycle in the interest of improving its ergonomics and clarity. After this, the syntax should largely be nailed down.

    Explicit scene syntax #

    All scene references now require 

    @
    prefixes:
    // Before
bsn! {
    scene_variable
    scene_function()
    @SceneComponent
    {scene_expression}
}

// After
bsn! {
    @scene_variable
    @scene_function()
    @SceneComponent
    @{scene_expression}
}

    In addition to making it easier to spot scene inclusions (and unifying the syntax across cases), this freed us up to make component values much easier to work with!

    No more 
    template_value
    wrappers! #

    You can now remove all of those pesky 

    template_value
    wrappers from your component values:
    // Before
bsn! {
    template_value(component_variable)
    template_value(component_function())
}

// After
bsn! {
    component_variable
    component_function()
}

    Enums "just work" #

    Enums no longer require 

    VariantDefaults
    or 
    FromTemplate
    , provided they implement 
    Default
    and 
    Clone
    :
    // Before
#[derive(Component, Default, Clone, VariantDefaults)]
enum Foo {
    A { x: u32, y: u32 },
    #[default]
    B,
}

bsn! {
    Foo::B
}

// After
#[derive(Component, Default, Clone)]
enum Foo {
    A { x: u32, y: u32 },
    #[default]
    B,
}

bsn! {
    Foo::B
}

    If you were using an enum that didn't support 

    VariantDefaults
    , you can now remove the 
    template_value
    wrapper:
    // Before
bsn! {
    template_value(Foo::A)
}
// After
bsn! {
    Foo::A
}

    The removal of 

    VariantDefaults
    does mean that enums must now have every field specified:
    // Before (y field is initialized to its default value)
bsn! {
    Foo::A { x: 1 }
}

// After (y field must be manually specified)
bsn! {
    Foo::A { x: 1, y: 0 }
}

    We believe this tradeoff is worth it, as it increases BSN's compatibility with arbitrary Rust enums. Rust doesn't support "enum variant defaults" anyway!

    Chained method support #

    The "builder pattern" (and chained methods generally) previously required a 

    template_value
    wrapper. This can now be removed:
    // Before
bsn! {
    template_value(Transform::from_xyz(-2.5, 4.5, 9.0).looking_at(Vec3::ZERO, Vec3::Y))
}
// After
bsn! {
    Transform::from_xyz(-2.5, 4.5, 9.0).looking_at(Vec3::ZERO, Vec3::Y)
}

    Additionally, you can now remove the 

    template_value
    wrapper in cases like this:
    // Before
bsn! {
    template_value(node.clone())
}
// After
bsn! {
    node.clone()
}

    In general, you should now be able to remove all 

    template_value
    instances from your BSN declarations!

    Improved list syntax #

    BSN previously used commas to separate entities, with optional 

    ()
    around entities to make the boundaries clearer. This resulted in a lot of syntax noise, line noise, and over-indentation:
    bsn! {
    Node 
    Children [
        (
            #OkButton
            @button("Ok")
        ),
        (
            #CancelButton
            @button("Cancel")
        ),
    ]
}

    To avoid this, many developers opted for this syntax instead, which made it very hard to visually distinguish entities:

    bsn! {
    Node 
    Children [
        #OkButton
        @button("Ok"),
        #CancelButton
        @button("Cancel"),
    ]
}

    BSN now uses 

    --
    to separate entities in a list:
    bsn! {
    Node 
    Children [
        #OkButton
        @button("Ok")
        --
        #CancelButton
        @button("Cancel")
    ]
}

    This gives us the best of all worlds: entities are visually distinct, and there is no over-indentation, line noise, or syntax noise (the stats when compared to other competitors in the "markup format" space are very competitive!). Both 

    ()
    and 
    ,
    have been deprecated in this context.

    Using 

    []
    and 
    ()
    for 
    bsn_list!
     (and 
    bsn!
    ) is now discouraged / warned against (ex: 
    bsn_list! []
    ), as it can result in poor rustfmt autoformatting. Instead, use 
    bsn_list! {}
    , which is the only syntax that 
    rustfmt
    won't touch. Don't worry, we plan to build a BSN auto-formatter!
    bsn_list! {
    #Ok @button("Ok")
    --
    #Cancel @button("Cancel")
}

    Ready
    Event #

    Authors:@cartPRs:#25296

    We landed BSN, Bevy's next generation scene system, in our last release. It was missing a key piece though: the ability to easily run logic when a scene is fully "ready" and spawned (ex: all dependencies have loaded, the full hierarchy is present, and all of the initial components are inserted in the scene). This is a critical piece for building cohesive, standalone, composable scenes. It is also necessary to properly layer Bevy logic on top of other scene representations (like glTF).

    The closest we had was the 

    Add
    event for a given component, which runs "top down" (meaning children are not available). We needed a "bottom up" equivalent to enable building logic that relies on the complete loaded and spawned scene.

    The solution is pretty straightforward: trigger a new 

    Ready
    event for each entity in a spawned scene after the full spawn logic has run for that entity (including its descendants).

    This enables the following:

    #[derive(SceneComponent, Default, Clone)]
struct Widget;

impl Widget {
    fn scene() -> impl Scene {
        bsn! {
            Node { width: px(100), height: px(100) }
            on(|ready: On| {
                info!("The full scene, including 'widget.bsn' contents, is available here")
            })
            Children [
                Text("hello")
                --
                :"widget.bsn"
            ]
        }
    }
}

world.spawn(bsn! { @Widget })

    More Feathers Widgets #

    Authors:@viridia, @gagnus, @tmstoreyPRs:#25446, #25079, #24092, #24847, #24784, #24636, #24701

    Feathers, Bevy's opinionated editor-centric UI toolkit, now has more widgets for you to play with:

    Color Input #

    Bevy now has a compact color input selector that displays a color picker widget popup when clicked. This includes a color wheel selector, RGB, and HSL selectors, and a recently used colors grid.

    List View / Scrollbar #

    A scrollable, selectable list view.

    Dropdown Selection #

    A selection field that when clicked, displays a dropdown containing a list of options to select.

    Spawns a menu popup when the menu is opened and despawns it when it is closed. This is in contrast to the normal Menu widget, which just hides the menu.

    Number Input Widget Scrubbing / Dragging #

    The 

    FeathersNumberInput
    widget has been expanded to support both normal text input and scrubbing / dragging. There is a configurable "hard limit" (minimum and maximum value via any input method) and "soft limit" (minimum and maximum value via dragging), in addition to control over floating point precision and step sizes.

    Headless Tab Widgets #

    Authors:@jbuehler23PRs:#25515

    bevy_ui_widgets
    now has headless (bring-your-own-visuals) tab behavior: a 
    TabList
     container and 
    Tab
     headers.

    Selection is managed "externally". 

    SelectedTab
    on the list holds the selected tab; interaction emits 
    ValueChange>
     as a request, applied by the app or by the optional 
    tablist_self_update
     observer.

    Tabs support keyboard shortcuts and integrate with Bevy's focus, interaction, and accessibility systems.

    bsn! {
    TabList
    SelectedTab(Some(first_tab))
    on(tablist_self_update)
    Children [
        Tab Children [ Text("General") ]
        --
        Tab Children [ Text("Rendering") ]
    ]
}

    See the 

    headless_tabs
    example for controlled and self-updating tab lists in both orientations.

    WESL Shaders #

    Authors:@tychedelia, @BenjaminBrienenPRs:#25088

    Bevy's shaders are now written in WESL and the old "Custom Bevy Extended WGSL" language support has been removed.

    WESL is a language standard that extends WGSL to add important usability features like modules, imports, conditional compilation, and more. You can see what that looks like (and render pretty shader toys!) live in your browser in the WESL Playground.

    Bevy has historically handled these things in our own custom WGSL dialect, but we believe it is better for the wider shader ecosystem (and for us) to adopt a common standard where we can pool resources on language improvements, module ecosystems, and IDE tooling. We've been working closely with the WESL team to evolve the standard in a way that fits well into the Bevy picture.

    A critical part of that tooling is language server protocol support, in the form of wgsl-analyzer. That means syntax highlighting, go-to-definition, inlay hints, code folding, formatting and more, once installed for your IDE of choice.

    Custom shaders in the old Bevy WGSL dialect need to be translated to WESL and renamed from 

    .wgsl
    to 
    .wesl
    . Plain WGSL files with no preprocessor directives will keep working.

    Before: Custom Bevy Extended WGSL #

    #import bevy_pbr::forward_io::VertexOutput
#import "shaders/util.wgsl"::hsv_to_rgb
#ifdef VERTEX_COLORS
var tint: vec4;
#endif
@group(2) @binding(#{MATERIAL_BIND_GROUP}) var color: vec4;

    After: WESL #

    import bevy_pbr::render::forward_io::VertexOutput;
import super::util::hsv_to_rgb;
@if(VERTEX_COLORS)
var tint: vec4;
@group(2) @binding(constants::MATERIAL_BIND_GROUP) var color: vec4;

    Mesh Shaders #

    Authors:@ChristopherBiscardiPRs:#25627

    Mesh shaders are now integrated with Bevy's pipeline cache and are available for advanced users to take advantage of. Mesh shaders can be used to render:

  • Meshlets generated using tools like meshoptimizer
  • Procedural grass with dynamic level-of-detail, as seen here
  • Voxels, like nvidium
  • Particles
  • and more

    • Mesh shaders, at a high level, replace the classic vertex shader with a compute shader. This allows generating geometry directly on the GPU and passing those generated primitives directly to the fragment shader without using multiple pipelines or intermediary buffers (to pass data from a compute shader to a render pipeline).

    A 

    MeshPipeline
    contains:
  • an optional task shader (also known as amplification shader)
  • a mesh shader
  • a fragment shader

    • The new 

    MeshPipelineDescriptor
    can be used to define a 
    MeshPipeline
    . That 
    MeshPipeline
     is then used as a 
    RenderPipeline
    , which allows the re-use of Bevy's lower level rendering APIs such as 
    RenderContext::begin_tracked_render_pass
     to take advantage of the new 
    draw_mesh_tasks
     APIs.
    let mut pass = render_context.begin_tracked_render_pass(RenderPassDescriptor {
    label: Some("custom_mesh_shader_pass"),
    color_attachments: &[Some(target.get_color_attachment())],
    depth_stencil_attachment: Some(depth.get_attachment(StoreOp::Store)),
    ..default()
});

pass.set_render_pipeline(mesh_pipeline);
pass.set_bind_group(0, &bind_group, &[view_uniform_offset.offset]);

// draw_mesh_tasks dispatches the task shader if there is one,
// or dispatches the mesh shader if there is no task shader.
pass.draw_mesh_tasks(1, 1, 1);

    It is notable that mesh shaders are an advanced graphics approach with platform-specific performance considerations, and that this is the initial base support for the feature. Higher level user APIs, and easy integration with Bevy's 

    StandardMaterial
    , are left to future work.

    Mesh shaders are not supported on web platforms.

    Check out the new 

    mesh_shader_intro
    example for more usage examples.

    Sprite Materials #

    Authors:@cookie1170PRs:#25415

    Until now, Bevy's sprite renderer has been lacking a major feature: the ability to extend it with custom shaders! With this release, it's now possible to create custom materials for sprites by implementing the 

    MaterialExtension2d
    trait, inserting the 
    SpriteMaterial
     component and adding the 
    SpriteMaterialPlugin
     to your app.

    The shader can use functions exported from 

    bevy_sprite_render::sprite_mesh::functions
    , including:
    // Samples the sprite's final color, including the tint and alpha discard, at a given UV.
fn sample_final_color(uv: vec2, instance_index: u32) -> vec4;

// Samples the sprite's texture without tint and alpha discard at a given UV.
fn sample_sprite_texture(uv: vec2, instance_index: u32) -> vec4;

// Applies tint and alpha discard to the sprite's color.
fn get_final_color(sprite_color: vec4, instance_index: u32) -> vec4;

    Check out the 

    sprite_material
    example to see it in action!

    2D Extended Materials #

    Authors:@cookie1170PRs:#25183

    Bevy now provides a 2D analog to 3D's 

    ExtendedMaterial
    , which can be used to extend an existing material by implementing the 
    MaterialExtension2d
     trait:
    #[derive(AsBindGroup, Reflect, Clone)]
struct MyMaterial {
    #[uniform(20)]
    value: Vec4,
}

impl MaterialExtension2d for MyMaterial {
    fn fragment_shader() -> Option {
        Some("my_material.wesl".into())
    }
}

    This material can now be used in an 

    ExtendedMaterial2d
    struct:
    let handle = materials.add(ExtendedMaterial2d {
    base: ColorMaterial::from_color(Color::WHITE),
    extension: MyMaterial {
        value: Vec4::ZERO,
    },
});
commands.spawn((
    Mesh2d,
    MeshMaterial2d(handle),
));

    Sprite Render Backend Unification #

    Authors:@IceSentryPRs:#25432

    The sprite render backend was replaced by a new backend that reuses a lot of the infrastructure made for 3D. This resulted in improved performance in many cases and also makes future maintenance and improvements easier.

    Pan Orbit Camera #

    Authors:@aevyrie, @taishi-samaPRs:#25434

    We have upstreamed the awesome 

    bevy_editor_cam
    made by @aevyrie as the new 
    PanOrbitCamera
     in our 
    bevy_camera_controller
     crate!

    Usage #

    Add 

    MeshPickingPlugin
    and 
    DefaultPanOrbitCameraPlugins
    :
    app.add_plugins((
    MeshPickingPlugin,
    DefaultPanOrbitCameraPlugins,
))

    Then add the 

    PanOrbitCamera
    component on any 3D camera.
    commands.spawn((
    Camera3d::default(),
    PanOrbitCamera::default(),
))

    Full functionality is shown in the 

    camera/pan_orbit_camera_cad
    example.

    Weak System Ordering with 
    chain_weak
    #

    Authors:@JMS55PRs:#25128

    Ordering large groups of systems with 

    .chain()
    is convenient, but it can be overly strict. If system set 
    X
    is chained before system set 
    Y
    , every system in 
    X
    must finish before any system in 
    Y
    can start, even when the systems involved never touch the same data. This often leaves worker threads idle while they wait for a handful of stragglers at the end of a system set, a pattern that shows up frequently in the render world.

    The new 

    chain_weak()
    , 
    before_weak()
    , and 
    after_weak()
     functions provide a looser alternative. Like their regular counterparts, they request an ordering between successive elements, however that ordering is only kept between systems whose data accesses actually conflict. Systems that don't conflict are left unordered and may run in any order, including in parallel.
    schedule.configure_sets(
    (
        ExtractCommands,
        PrepareMeshes,
        CreateViews,
        Specialize,
        PrepareViews,
        Queue,
        PhaseSort,
        Prepare,
        Render,
        Cleanup,
        PostCleanup,
    )
        .chain_weak(),
);

    When two weakly-ordered systems actually conflict on their data access, a normal ordering is kept between them, so the earlier one still runs first. Two systems that conflict only through a non-conflicting system between them in the chain stay ordered as well. Non-conflicting systems, however, are left free to run in any order and overlap for increased parallelism!

    Two kinds of system are treated as always conflicting, so their ordering is always kept: an earlier system that produces deferred effects such as 

    Commands
    (so the later system observes them, with an 
    ApplyDeferred
     sync point inserted as usual), and exclusive systems (which cannot overlap anything regardless).

    Because the scheduler can only see accesses it tracks, dependencies expressed through interior mutability on read-only accesses, global state, or other untracked methods are not respected. Use 

    chain_weak
    only when your systems don't rely on such hidden ordering, otherwise stick with 
    chain
    .

    Contextual Theming #

    Authors:@viridiaPRs:#24969

    Feathers now supports "contextual theming", meaning that the theme variables can change depending on the parent entity. So widgets that are inside of a dialog box or subpanel can have different colors than widgets that are on a regular panel or window background.

    The design follows that of popular web toolkits like MUI, Radix, or Chakra. There's a new component, 

    ThemeContext
    , which lets you select which color scheme the widget's descendants should use; currently the available schemes are 
    Base
    , 
    Higher
    , 
    Highest
    , and 
    Floating
    , which correspond to the design plans for the Bevy scene editor.

    The theme context is used in conjunction with a new kind of design token, named 

    SemanticToken
    . The lookup process for a color now requires two stages: the 
    ThemeToken
     is converted into a 
    SemanticToken
    , and then the combination of 
    SemanticToken
    and 
    ThemeContext
     is used to look up a color.

    In addition to allowing context-specific color choices, this also makes it easier to design new themes! Instead of having to tediously choose colors for a hundred different theme tokens, the set of semantic tokens is much smaller, and the relationship between token and color is much more intuitive.

    Val::Em
    and 
    Val::Rem
    #

    Authors:@gagnusPRs:#25231

    Bevy UI now supports 

    em
    and 
    rem
     as sizing units. 
    em
    is the current font size (represented by an 
    EmSize
     component), 
    rem
    is a global "root" font size (represented by the existing 
    RemSize
     resource).

    EmSize
    is derived from 
    TextFont
     when one is on the same entity; propagating it down the hierarchy is left to your app.

    This is especially useful if you might want to vary your text size after authoring your UIs, for example as an accessibility feature or just to improve your UI on different devices.

    bsn! {
    Node { width: em(10) }
    Text("Hello")
    TextFont { font_size: FontSize::Rem(1.5) }
}

    The default font-size is now 

    rem(1)
    rather than 
    px(20)
    . This is a no-op if you're not changing 
    RemSize
     but it means your text will scale by default when you do.

    Per-Column Change Ticks #

    Authors:@pcwalton, @SkiFire13PRs:#25157, #25429

    Components can now opt-in to "column summary change ticks":

    #[derive(Component)]
#[component(summary_tick)]
struct MyComponent {
    /* fields here */
}

    When enabled, this will store a "column change tick" in addition to a "per-entity change tick", which allows cheaply skipping the whole column of entities when querying for changes, rather than needing to check every entity's component to see if it has changed.

    This makes mutations more expensive, as they need to write both the column change tick and the entity change tick, but for entities whose changes are queried often, but change infrequently, this tradeoff can easily be worth it! We've seen change ticks result in a 132x speedup in our GPU mesh extraction code!

    FixedNode
    #

    Authors:@ickshonpePRs:#24323

    FixedNode
    is a new marker component for Bevy UI.

    A UI node entity with the 

    FixedNode
    component is positioned relative to the target camera's viewport rather than its parent element. 
    FixedNode
    s don't inherit their parent's layout, clipping or transform context. They behave like a "root node".

    Elliptical Border Radius #

    Authors:@ickshonpePRs:#24779

    Bevy UI can now draw nodes with elliptical border geometry.

    The fields of 

    BorderRadius
    are now 
    CornerRadius
    s to enable different radius to be set for each axis.
    let a = BorderRadius::all(CornerRadius::circular(vh(10.)));
let b = BorderRadius::all(vh(10.)); // a == b
let c = BorderRadius::top_right(CornerRadius::new(px(10.), px(20.)));

    Schedule Randomization #

    Authors:@andriyDevPRs:#25094

    Before a schedule runs (and therefore, your systems), it first computes the system run order based on their ordering constraints (

    .before()
    , 
    .after()

item.title: 每帧 300 次还是单帧 24000 次：多人战斗里 Lua 耗高的两类根因该怎么分开查 ｜ 多人战斗中Lua持续高耗时，是瞬时峰值还是高频调用在作祟
item.description:
一句话：持续低帧率看长期占用路径，偶发卡顿看与卡顿帧对齐的瞬时峰值，两者优化手段完全不同。

要点：

  • 50V50 实测：一条 Lua 调用路径从每帧 100 多次涨到 300 次以上，另有路径在个别帧出现约 24000 次调用，前者影响持续帧率、后者决定偶发卡顿
  • 高频调用若跨 Lua 与 C#/Unity API 边界，要评估合并调用与集中处理，而不是只盯调用次数；寻路、路径更新这类逻辑要检查能否改为按需更新
  • 温度功耗后半段反而下降时，要对照主线程核心频率与同期 FPS 再判断降频，单核频率波动也可能只是正常调频或线程调度

为什么值得看：这两类问题的优化手段完全不同（减少重复更新 vs 合并跨界调用），先分类再动手能省掉大量无效优化；文中的排查顺序也可以直接搬成团队的性能回归检查清单。

中文摘要：这是一组来自真实项目的性能排查问答。第一个问题：50V50 多人战斗帧率持续偏低，CPU 耗时集中在 Lua，堆栈里既有持续高频调用，也有个别帧的集中调用，该先查哪个？结论是结合耗时与对帧率的影响定优先级——持续低帧率优先看长期占用最多的调用路径（某路径从每帧 100 多次涨到 300 次以上），偶发卡顿才看与卡顿帧对齐的瞬时峰值（某路径单帧约 24000 次）。同时要检查 Lua 与 C#/Unity API 的跨界调用，评估合并或集中处理，并确认寻路、路径更新这类逻辑能否改为按需执行。第二个问题：测试后半段温度与功耗反而下降，是否意味着 CPU 降频？作者建议对照主线程核心频率与同期 FPS，再看各模块耗时，不要仅凭曲线下判断。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：UWA 博客（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-27

多人战斗中Lua持续高耗时，是瞬时峰值还是高频调用在作祟

  • 作者：admin
  • /
  • 时间：5天前
  • /
  • 浏览：293 次
  • /
  • 分类：厚积薄发

    • 1）多人战斗中Lua持续高耗时，应优先排查什么
    2）战斗后期温度和功耗下降，判断CPU是否降频

    这是第497篇UWA技术知识分享的推送，精选了UWA社区的热门话题，涵盖了UWA问答、社区帖子等技术知识点，助力大家更全面地掌握和学习。

    UWA社区主页：community.uwa4d.com
    UWA QQ群：793972859

    本次推送的实战案例来自于使用UWA服务的项目的真实且典型的问题。UWA将关键线索、定位路径与处理建议整理成了可复用的案例笔记，便于大家快速对照、排查自身项目中的同类问题。

    实战案例

    Q：在50V50的多人战斗测试中，帧率持续偏低，CPU耗时主要集中在Lua逻辑。进一步查看函数堆栈，发现部分函数存在持续高频调用，也有个别函数在单帧出现大量调用。面对这种情况，应该优先排查瞬时调用峰值，还是持续高频调用？

    A：应结合函数的实际CPU耗时及其对帧率的影响确定排查优先级，而不能仅凭调用次数判断。对于持续低帧率，应优先关注长期占用较多CPU时间的调用路径；对于偶发卡顿，则应重点检查与卡顿帧对应的瞬时调用峰值。

    从函数调用情况来看，主要存在两类现象：

  • 持续高频调用：某条Lua调用路径从每帧100多次增加至300次以上，且相关节点耗时占比较高，需要检查是否存在不必要的重复更新；

  • 瞬时调用峰值：另一条Lua调用路径在个别帧出现约24,000次调用，需要结合对应帧的实际耗时，判断是否造成卡顿。

    建议重点排查以下两个方面：
    1. 检查函数耗时与调用频率
    沿调用堆栈定位主要耗时节点，结合调用次数判断问题是来自重复执行，还是单次执行耗时较高。例如部队寻路、路径更新等逻辑，检查是否需要每帧执行，能否改为按需更新。对于瞬时峰值，则应结合具体操作确认集中调用是否合理；

    • 2. 检查Lua跨层调用
    如果高频调用涉及Lua与C#或Unity API之间的交互，需要关注重复调用产生的开销，评估是否能够合并调用或集中处理部分逻辑。优化后，在相同测试条件下对比Lua函数耗时、调用次数及FPS，确认持续开销是否下降，同时检查是否仍存在明显的单帧卡顿。

    需要注意，Development包及较多Lua函数打点可能引入额外开销，建议在相同采集条件下验证优化效果。

    实战案例

    Q：在长时间多人战斗测试中，CPU温度明显高于GPU，设备功耗也处于较高水平。但随着战斗进行，后半段的温度和功耗反而下降，部分CPU核心频率也出现波动。这是否意味着CPU发生了降频，应该如何判断？

    A：温度和功耗下降既可能是业务负载减少，也可能与温控降频有关，不能仅凭曲线变化判断，需要结合CPU频率、各模块耗时和具体业务逻辑进行分析判断。

    测试中，部分设备CPU温度比GPU高出十几度，设备功耗约为5W，后半段则出现温度、功耗下降及部分CPU核心频率波动的现象。

    建议从以下三个方面排查：
    1. 对照CPU频率与FPS

    重点关注承担游戏主线程任务的CPU核心，检查其频率是否持续下降，以及同期FPS是否出现明显变化。需要注意，单个核心的频率波动不一定代表温控降频，也可能与正常调频或线程调度有关；

    2. 对比相近负载下的模块耗时
    CPU降频可能影响多个CPU侧模块的执行效率。在UI更新频率、粒子特效规模等业务条件相近的情况下，可以对比UI、粒子系统等模块的CPU耗时。如果多个模块的耗时明显增加，则需要结合设备热状态及线程调度情况，进一步判断是否存在温控或功耗限制；

    3. 排查战斗过程中的业务负载变化
    温度和功耗下降也可能是实际计算量减少所致，需要确认前后战斗状态是否发生变化。例如，部分战斗玩法存在伤兵机制，随着战斗推进，部分单位不再参与战斗，寻路、AI决策等逻辑的计算量随之减少，CPU负载也可能降低。

    建议对照温度下降前后的参战单位数量及相关函数调用次数，确认是否存在明显的业务负载变化。

    综合来看，温度和功耗下降不能直接认定为CPU降频，应结合CPU频率、FPS及相近负载下的模块耗时，区分硬件性能受限与业务计算量减少的影响，必要时通过相同业务负载下的对照测试进一步验证。

item.title: 肌肉激活不该靠手调：RLMuscle 让 RL 控制器驱动 1D 代理加 3D 体积仿真，迭代步数少 11.7 倍 ｜ RLMuscle: Muscle-Driven Character Animation via Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
一句话：1D 肌肉模型当快速代理留在控制回路，最终形变交给 3D 体积仿真，两级共享同一本构关系。

要点：

  • 把 1D 肌肉模型留在 RL 控制回路里当快速代理，最终形变交给 3D 体积仿真；两级共享同一套本构关系，所以触发运动与产生形变的是同一组激活值
  • 加入实测肌电（EMG）先验，把冗余的激活解拉向真实人体募集模式；并给出基于粗四面体笼的 XPBD 几何多重网格求解器
  • 达到同一约束容差：53 帧 / 49.1 ms，对比无多重网格的 621 帧 / 418.9 ms（步数少 11.7 倍、快 8.5 倍），峰值翻转四面体数量约少 3.7 倍

为什么值得看：这是把「物理正确的形变」塞进可交互帧预算的可行切分：学习负责政策、仿真负责形变，而不是让网络直接吐顶点。对做角色管线的人来说，等于把肌肉激活从美术手调变成可训练、可复现的量。

中文摘要：肌肉收缩带来的体表形变对角色动画的真实感至关重要，但主流 3D 动画管线里肌肉激活仍靠美术手动指定，既费时又不保证物理合理。RLMuscle 让强化学习控制器自己找每块肌肉的激活序列来跟踪参考动作：把 1D 肌肉模型留在 RL 控制回路里当快速代理，最终形变交给 3D 体积仿真，两级共享同一套本构关系，因此形变由驱动运动的那组激活直接产生。为消除冗余解，作者加入实测肌电先验，把解拉向真实的人体募集模式。数值上还提出基于粗四面体笼、重心坐标延拓的 XPBD 几何多重网格：达同一约束容差只需 53 帧 / 49.1 ms，而无多重网格要 621 帧 / 418.9 ms，峰值翻转四面体也少约 3.7 倍。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-27

RLMuscle: Muscle-Driven Character Animation
via Reinforcement Learning

Abstract

Body deformation caused by muscle contraction plays a vital role in the visual realism of character animation, yet in most 3D animation pipelines artists have to manually specify muscle activations, which is time-consuming and gives no guarantee of physical realism. To address this, we propose a new method in which a reinforcement learning (RL) controller discovers per-muscle activations that track reference motions without manual tuning. Existing RL muscle controllers stop at 1D muscles; we go one step further, keeping the 1D model inside the RL control loop as a fast surrogate, and using a 3D volumetric simulation to produce the final deformation. Because both stages share the very same constitutive law, the muscle deformation is produced by the same activations that generated the motion. We further add a measured electromyography (EMG) prior that steers the redundant activation solution toward real human muscle recruitment. To achieve stable, efficient, and realistic simulation, we propose a novel geometric multigrid for Extended Position-Based Dynamics (XPBD) that is built on a coarse tetrahedral cage with barycentric-coordinate prolongation and closes a V-cycle on tetrahedral meshes. Within this GPU-parallelized solver, we inject the same Hill-type force–length law as an energy-based fiber constraint that turns per-fiber activation into realistic muscle contraction and bulging. We demonstrate volumetric muscle simulation on a 194-muscle human body with a diverse set of motions (walk, kick, swim, overhead-squat, etc.), simulating the full-body model at 18 ms per frame on a single RTX 4090. Our work takes a step toward character animation that is not only visually convincing but also biomechanically grounded. The website with code and videos is at https://chunleili.github.io/project-page-rlmuscle/.

Index Terms:

Muscle simulation, XPBD, reinforcement learning, physics-based animation, character animation.

I Introduction

In animation, film, games, and virtual reality (VR), realistic muscle behavior is essential for believable character animation. Yet production pipelines still rely on hand-authored muscle activations, produced by one of two major authoring methods. The first is a tension line: the artist binds a line onto the skeleton, and the muscle associated with that line is activated once the line contracts below a set length threshold, so activation is triggered geometrically by bone motion. The second is keyframing: the artist directly animates each muscle’s activation value over time as a keyframed curve. Both encode activations chosen for visual plausibility, not physical plausibility. Consequently, there is no guarantee that hand-crafted tension can produce physically valid motions, because artists effectively decouple muscle deformation from motion dynamics. This expertise-driven workflow is not only labor-intensive; it also cannot answer the question at the heart of physics-based animation: what muscle activations actually produce a given motion? This is the muscle inverse problem: recovering the hidden control signals from observed motion. A principled solution would replace hand-tuning with physically consistent activations derived from the target motion, so that the resulting muscle deformation reflects the underlying dynamics rather than a visually plausible guess.

On the other hand, recent works on muscle simulation driven by reinforcement learning (RL) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] are mainly limited to a simplified 1D Hill-type muscle model, which falls short of the 3D volumetric muscle deformation needed for visual realism. The muscle inverse problem is challenging because the map from activation to joint motion is highly nonlinear, and the control space is high-dimensional (hundreds of muscles), which leads to intractability of analytical inversion, and extremely low sample efficiency in RL training.

We solve the muscle inverse problem by forward dynamics, i.e. searching for the activations that, once simulated, reproduce a target motion. This poses two challenges:

  • 1.

    Control. The map from muscle activation to joint motion is highly underdetermined and nonlinear, so analytical inversion is intractable, and naive RL exploration in this space is sample-inefficient.

  • 2.

    Physics. The numerical solver must handle volumetric muscle that is nonlinear, anisotropic, and nearly incompressible while remaining both stable and efficient.

    • We present the first system that addresses both challenges. Given a reference motion (motion capture or keyframed animation) and rest-pose 3D muscle/skeleton assets as input, it outputs a skeletal–muscular animation driven by physically consistent activations. Our work makes three technical contributions.

    Technical contribution 1: a muscle-control pipeline that decouples 1D control from 3D simulation under a unified constitutive law for fibers, solving the muscle inverse problem and freeing artists from hand-tuning (addressing Control). Existing RL muscle controllers [1, 3, 4, 5, 2] actuate 1D Hill-type muscles only, so they recover joint motion but not the 3D volumetric deformation that visual realism demands; conversely, optimization-based methods [6] that place the volumetric solver inside the control loop are unstable and did not converge in our tests. We propose to use the 1D model as a surrogate in RL and to produce the deformation from the 3D model. To bridge the gap between the two, we introduce a new fiber constraint based on the Hill–Millard constitutive curve, which is used in both the 1D and the 3D model. Following MASS [1], a policy network and a muscle network are co-trained in a single PPO [7] loop against a motion-mimicking reward [8] on the 1D surrogate. The recovered activations then drive the 3D volumetric muscles through the same Hill-type constitutive law [9] used by the surrogate, in a single forward pass with the 3D solver kept out of the control loop, so the volumetric deformation is consistent with the dynamics that produced the motion, reproducing realistic muscle bulging, stiffening, and contraction rather than a visually plausible guess.

    Technical contribution 2: a physiological electromyography (EMG) prior that steers the redundant activation solution toward measured human muscle recruitment (addressing Control). The activation-to-torque map is redundant, and existing muscle networks [1, 3, 4, 5, 2] reduce that redundancy from torque and effort alone, with nothing tying the result to a real recruitment pattern, so their activations drift away from measured human EMG. We propose to inject a measured surface EMG envelope [10] into the muscle-network loss, matched per synergist group and folded onto a common gait cycle, which pulls the recovered activations back toward the measured envelope (§IV-B).

    Technical contribution 3: a Petrov–Galerkin geometric multigrid for volumetric XPBD, integrated into a GPU-parallel framework that runs the full-body volumetric muscle model at 18 ms per frame on a single RTX 4090 (addressing Physics). Previous position-based hierarchies, such as HPBD [11], are formulated for cloth rather than tetrahedral meshes and never close a complete V-cycle, so they act only as a low-resolution driver; algebraic constructions [12] instead assemble a global matrix and thereby give up XPBD’s local, per-constraint solve. We propose to coarsen a tetrahedral cage geometrically, prolongate by barycentric coordinates, and close a full V-cycle with a Petrov–Galerkin restriction, which keeps the high-stiffness solve stable and efficient. The framework further contributes muscle–bone collision handling based on a signed distance field (SDF).

    II Related Work

    Position-Based Dynamics. PBD [13] is a popular framework for real-time deformable object simulation. It is widely used in applications such as PhysX [14] and Houdini Vellum [15]. Extended PBD (XPBD) [16] reformulates PBD as a dual-space energy minimization framework and introduces a compliance term to transform the infinite-stiffness to a finite-stiffness problem, which improves the convergence. Bender et al. [17] cast Finite Element Method (FEM) strain energy as position-based constraints, which makes it possible to apply various FEM-based constitutive laws in PBD. We refer readers to the survey [18] for more details. We use XPBD as our simulation engine and propose a novel muscle fiber constraint tied to the physiological properties of muscle.

    Multigrid. Multigrid [19] is a classical numerical method for accelerating and stabilizing simulation, running an iterative solver on grids of different resolutions to eliminate low-frequency errors. Unlike grid-based fluid solvers, which have a natural hierarchical structure, soft bodies provide no such structure, so building a hierarchy on them is challenging. Hierarchical PBD (HPBD) [11] introduces a hierarchical solver for PBD simulated cloth, whose coarsening is based on edge collapsing. For volumetric solids, by contrast, the hierarchy is built by coarsening the simulation mesh itself, and how easily this can be done depends on the element type: coarsening is straightforward and efficient on hexahedral meshes [20], but the tetrahedral meshes prevalent in computer graphics are harder to coarsen. Several strategies address this: some build a multilevel XPBD through gradual rigidifying [21], while barycentric-coordinate prolongation [22] constructs a hierarchy directly on tetrahedral meshes and has proved successful in FEM. Our previous work, Multi-Grid Position-Based Dynamics (MGPBD) [12], utilized algebraic multigrid to build the hierarchy. However, algebraic multigrid requires assembling a global matrix, which sacrifices the flexibility and lightweight nature of XPBD’s local, per-constraint solve; moreover, building the hierarchy purely from the numerical matrix lacks geometric and physical intuition. In this work we propose a novel barycentric-coordinate-based geometric multigrid for XPBD, which accelerates the convergence of the stiff volume and incompressibility constraints and yields more stable and efficient volumetric simulation than single-level XPBD.

    Volumetric muscle simulation. Muscle is a special type of soft tissue, characterized by anisotropic fiber forces and strong incompressibility. Kim et al. [23, 24, 25] proposed energy potentials for FEM that yield an inversion-free muscle material matching the constitutive law of real muscle. Angles et al. [26] used position-based elastic rods with volumetric scale to model muscle bundles.

    Muscle-actuated Hill muscle control by RL. In recent years, many researchers have used 1D Hill-type muscles to physically drive the dynamics of human motion (activation → muscle force → bone motion, i.e. forward dynamics). The Hill-type model approximates each muscle as a polyline anchored to local positions on the bones, and reinforcement learning is commonly employed to train a neural network that finds the activations producing the desired motion. OpenSim [27] provides 1D musculotendon simulation, and Myosuite [2] wraps it in an RL framework for muscle-actuated control. The most prominent of these is MASS (Muscle-Actuated Skeletal System) by Lee et al. [1], a two-level imitation-learning architecture that actuates 346 muscles; we adopt its dual-network design (§III-B). A line of follow-ups inherits the same control formulation: MuscleVAE [3], MAGNET [4], and MuscleMimic [5], alongside torque-actuated trackers such as DeepMimic [28, 8] with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [7]. These methods all drive only 1D line-segment Hill muscles; building on this 1D Hill-type RL control, we add a 3D volumetric muscle simulation driven by the same Hill law, turning the biomechanics into visually compelling muscle deformation.

    Inverse muscle activation for volumetric muscle. Some works also address the inverse muscle activation problem with 3D volumetric deformation, similar to ours, but they recover the activations by static optimization rather than inside a forward-dynamic control loop. Han et al. [29] solve a per-pose torque balance as a quadratic program (QP) and train an ML-deformer [30] to reproduce muscle deformation from joint state and activation, but such a static solve cannot guarantee that the recovered activations actually drive the target motion (activation → muscle force → bone motion). Lee et al. [6] embed Hill-type muscles in Projective Dynamics and obtain activations from a per-frame QP, which runs the volumetric solver inside the trajectory-optimization control loop, but in our tests it was very unstable and never converged. We instead learn the activations inside the RL control loop on a 1D Hill-type surrogate, so they are exactly the forces that drive the motion (§III-B), making the deformation genuinely physically actuated rather than fitted or pre-scripted.

    III Method

    Our system couples a 1D Hill-type muscle model (Nₘ=284) with an RL controller, then uses a volumetric muscle model (194 muscles) with the same Hill-type constitutive law to simulate the deformation. We first outline the pipeline (§III-A) and the RL co-training that solves the inverse problem (§III-B), then detail the 1D Hill dynamics (§III-C), the 3D volumetric simulation (§III-D), and the motion retargeting and muscle mapping that bridge the 1D and 3D models (§III-E).

    III-AOverview

    Figure 2 summarizes the system. The input is a 1D musculoskeletal asset together with a reference motion clip in Biovision Hierarchy (BVH) format. A reinforcement-learning imitation-learning stage solves the muscle inverse problem on this 1D asset (284 muscles), jointly producing the muscle-driven bone motion and the corresponding 1D muscle activation trajectory. A motion-retargeting step transfers the bone motion onto a 3D skeleton, while a muscle-mapping step lifts the per-musculotendon 1D activations to 3D activations. Both streams and 3D assets (bone and muscle geometries) are then fed to the XPBD-based 3D simulation engine (§III-D), which produces the volumetric muscle deformation used for the final 3D rendering. The 1D track therefore acts as a fast surrogate that solves the hard inverse problem once; the 3D track is a single forward simulation at inference. The RL co-training that solves the inverse problem (Fig. 3, Alg. 1) is detailed in §III-B.

    III-BReinforcement Learning Control

    The RL stage solves control challenges: it discovers the muscle activations (Nₘ=284) that make the simulated character track a reference motion. We split control across a policy networkπ_φ and a muscle networkμ_θ[1] and co-train them inside a single PPO loop against the motion-tracking reward (Fig. 3, Alg. 1) rather than learning them sequentially, so each rollout supplies a gradient for both and they adapt to each other. A third, training-only value networkV_ψ serves as PPO’s critic but never participates in control.

    III-B1 Two-Network Co-Training

    We train the controller for muscle-driven motion tracking with PPO, summarized in Alg. 1. Letting the policy explore the Nₘ=284 muscle activations directly is sample-inefficient, so the policy instead acts in the compact space of per-joint PD-target offsets: Stable proportional–derivative (PD) control [31] turns its action into a desired joint torque τᵈᵉˢ ∈ ℝ^N_θ (N_θ=50 degrees of freedom, DOF), the muscle network maps that torque to the activations a^Mₜ ∈ [0,1]^Nₘ (M for muscles), and the Hill model realizes the muscle torque that drives MuJoCo [32]. Both networks learn from the same rollout, PPO updating π_φ,V_ψ and a mean squared error (MSE) loss updating μ_θ. The observation is sₜ=[ bₜ, vₜ, φₜ ], where bₜ ∈ ℝ⁶⁶ stacks the center-of-mass position of each of the 22 non-root bodies in the root frame, vₜ ∈ ℝ⁶⁹ the world-frame center-of-mass velocities of all 23 bodies, and φₜ ∈ [0,1) is the phase of the reference clip (\dim(sₜ)=136).

    III-B2 Policy Network

    Motion-mimicking reward. Following DeepMimic [8] we use an exponential-kernel reward composed of pose, velocity, and end-effector terms, augmented with whole-body center of mass (COM) and pelvis-orientation terms for balance-critical motions; the pose error is the SO(3) geodesic between current and target joint frames:

    pⱼ=\log (Rⱼ^⊤ R^*ⱼ)^∨∈ℝ³,(1)
    rₚₒₛₑ=\exp (-kₚ∑_j∈J ∥pⱼ∥²),(2)

    rₜ=rₑₑ·(wₚ rₚₒₛₑ+wᵥ rᵥₑₗ+w_c r_com+wᵤ rᵤₚ),

    		(3)

    where rₜ is the tracking reward; Rⱼ,R^*ⱼ∈SO(3) are the current/target rotation matrices of joint j; \log(·)^∨ is the matrix log map returning the axis–angle vector; J is the set of tracked joints; and asterisks mark reference-motion targets. The remaining terms share the same kernel \exp(-k \lVert·\rVert²) applied to their own error: joint velocity for rᵥₑₗ, the positions xₖ of the five end-effector links for rₑₑ, the whole-body center of mass c for r_com, and the pelvis up axis u=Rₚₑₗᵥᵢₛe_y for rᵤₚ, which gives a yaw-free torso-tilt error (full expressions in the supplementary). End-effector errors are taken in the COM-relative frame so root drift does not corrupt limb-placement credit, and rₑₑ enters multiplicatively so gross limb misplacement suppresses local joint credit. The exponential kernel confines each term to [0,1] and saturates smoothly as the tracking error grows. Balance-critical motions (squat, single-leg kick) shift the task weights (wₚ,wᵥ,w_c,wᵤ) toward the COM and pelvis-up terms and add the root pose to J; without these terms the policy matches the pose but loses balance and falls. Kernel widths, per-task weights and the Mixamo [33] clips are listed in the supplementary.

    III-B3 Muscle Network

    The muscle network μ_θ maps the desired joint torque τᵈᵉˢ to per-muscle activations a^M ∈ [0,1]^Nₘ, solving the muscle inverse problem. This map is redundant: the Nₘ muscles far outnumber the N_θ DOFs, so infinitely many activation patterns realize the same torque. Classical biomechanics resolves the redundancy per frame with a quadratic program (QP); we instead use a simple supervised network to solve it. Layer sizes and training hyperparameters are given in the supplementary material.

    Muscle-network loss. The muscle network μ_θ is trained online with three losses (Eq. 4): a torque-realization term L_torque that inverts the activation-to-torque map τᵐᵘˢᶜ(a^M)=L a^M+b (§III-C), a minimum-effort regularizer L_reg that breaks the activation redundancy, and a physiological EMG prior L_emg. The first two are standard in muscle-actuated control; L_emg is our contribution: existing muscle networks [1, 3, 4, 5, 2] are trained on torque and effort alone, so their activations have no reason to match how a human recruits muscle (§IV-B), whereas L_emg steers the redundant solution toward a measured human EMG envelope. The three combine as

    L_μ=\underbracemean [(\tfrac1κ(τᵐᵘˢᶜ(a^M)-τᵈᵉˢ))²]_L_torque+w_reg \underbracemean[(a^M)²]_L_reg(4)
    +λ \underbraceL_emg_EMG prior,

    with torque scale κ=100, w_reg=0.01, and EMG weight λ (L_emg is defined in Eq. 6; setting λ=0 recovers the tracking-only loss for motions without a measured envelope). L_reg is the ∑a² minimum-effort criterion of classical static optimization [34], which on its own drives the activations away from physiological EMG measurements.

    III-B4 EMG Prior

    So far, we have obtained activations that generate physically plausible motion through muscle forces, but these activations are still physiologically implausible. We therefore steer the redundant solution toward real surface electromyography (sEMG) from Moreira et al. [10]. Two mismatches stand between that recording and our model (Fig. 4). The first is a muscle mismatch: the recording is coarse-grained, using only four right-leg electrodes, whereas our model is fine-grained. The second is a temporal misalignment: the recording is not aligned with the reference motion, so the two cannot be compared sample by sample.
