We apply two treatments, detailed in turn below: 1) we match each electrode not to a single fiber but to a whole synergist group; 2) we fold both signals onto a common gait cycle and compare only their shape and timing, not their magnitude.

    Synergist-group mean. Let ℂ be the EMG channels (the four right-leg surface electrodes of Moreira et al. [10]). A surface electrode integrates over a muscle region and the redundant solver distributes load within a synergist group, so channel c is matched not to one fiber but to the cross-section-weighted mean activation of its synergist group G_c:

    ā_c=∑_m∈G_cω_c,m a^Mₘ, ω_c,m=(f_0,m)/(∑_m^′∈G_cf_0,m^′),

    		(5)

    where f_0,m=σ₀A^Mₘ is the maximal isometric force of muscle m (Eq. 8), obtained from its physiological cross-sectional area A^Mₘ and the maximal isometric stress σ₀, the peak stress a fully activated fiber can sustain. Since σ₀ is uniform across muscles (value in the supplementary), the weight reduces to a ratio of cross-sectional areas, so the stronger muscles of a group dominate its mean. Matching the group mean rather than a single fiber also guards against a dead-unit pathology (supplementary).

    Gait-cycle alignment. Each rollout sample carries a gait phase φ=fmod(t, T)/T∈[0,1) recovered from its simulation time t, with T the gait-cycle period, and is placed on the 0 - 100% cycle as ((φ-φₕₛ)\bmod1)·100 to align it to right heel strike [35], where φₕₛ=0.254 is the heel-strike offset calibrated by forward kinematics on the reference foot. The prior is a phase-indexed MSE that pulls each group activation toward the peak-normalized human envelope ê_c(φ):

    L_emg=(1)/(|ℂ|)∑_c∈ℂw_emg,c (ā_c-s ê_c(φ))²,

    		(6)

    where s scales the unit-peak envelope into the activation range and w_emg,c weights each channel (the weight λ against torque realization is set in Eq. 4). The prior enters only the muscle-network loss; the policy’s motion objective (Eq. 3) is untouched, so it re-selects which activation realizes a motion without changing the motion itself. We use λ=1, s=0.3, and w_emg,c=1 for all channels; ê_c is the 13-subject Moreira cohort mean on a 101-bin gait grid. It is enabled wherever a measured envelope exists (the walk) and switched off (λ=0) otherwise; its effect on physiological plausibility is evaluated in §IV-B.

    III-C1D Hill-type Muscle Surrogate

    For motion to be truly actuated by muscle forces, the musculoskeletal system should closely match human anatomy. However, we empirically find that 3D volumetric muscles are overly flexible during RL training due to their excessive number of degrees of freedom, leading to unstable learning. Lee et al. [6] run the volumetric solver directly inside their optimization loop, which was also our initial idea. However, in our experiments, this approach was unstable and failed to converge. Therefore, we instead train against a 1D Hill-type muscle model [1, 3, 4, 5] as a surrogate, and then lift it to a 3D volumetric muscle model in the next section. The Hill-type model plays a dual role in our system: (i) as the 1D musculotendon surrogate that drives RL training, its scalar tension routed through MuJoCo tendon paths to the skeleton (Alg. 1); and (ii) as the constitutive law for the 3D XPBD volumetric muscle of §III-D, injected there as an energy-based fiber constraint (Eq. 19). We give the shared 1D formulation here and the 3D lift in §III-D. The 1D musculoskeletal asset (Fig. 5) is a rigid-body skeleton with spherical and revolute joints, actuated by 1D Hill-type muscles routed as polyline tendon paths between bone attachment sites.

    The Hill-type model (Fig. 6) places a tendon spring in series with a muscle belly, itself an active contractile element parallel to a passive spring. Each fiber generates a normalized scalar force:

    fₕᵢₗₗ=\underbrace\color[rgb]0.1211,0.4648,0.707a f^L(ℓ̃^M) f^V(ℓ̇^M)_\color[rgb]0.1211,0.4648,0.707active+\underbrace\color[rgb]0.1719,0.6289,0.1719f^PE(ℓ̃^M)_\color[rgb]0.1719,0.6289,0.1719passive+\underbrace\color[rgb]0.7734,0.3516,0.0664fᵀ(ℓ̃ᵀ)_\color[rgb]0.7734,0.3516,0.0664tendon,

    		(7)

    where a∈[0,1] is the muscle activation and ℓ̃^M the fiber length normalized by the optimal fiber length, so fₕᵢₗₗ is a dimensionless multiplier equal to 1 at that length (the 3D counterpart of ℓ̃^M, the along-fiber stretch λ_f, is defined in §III-D). We take the force–length curves f^L and f^PE from Millard et al. [9] and evaluate them through a look-up table to accelerate RL training; their piecewise-Bézier form and parameters are given in the supplementary. For simplicity we further assume 1) an infinitely stiff tendon and 2) no velocity-dependent force f^V, since only conservative forces admit an energy potential (§III-D4). We obtain the 1D muscle force by multiplying fₕᵢₗₗ by the peak isometric force f₀, which depends on the muscle (e.g., leg muscles are stronger than arm muscles). f₀=σ₀A^M (physiological cross-sectional area A^M). The resulting 1D Hill-type muscle force is

    F(a)=f₀(a f^L(ℓ̃^M)+f^PE(ℓ̃^M)).

    		(8)

    Muscle force to joint torque. Summing the segments of the anchor polyline gives the path length, hence the normalized fiber length ℓ̃^M that Eq. 7 evaluates; mapping the anchor forces through their point Jacobians makes the total torque affine in activation, τᵐᵘˢᶜ(a^M)=L a^M+b, with L the per-unit-activation moment arms and b the passive torque (root DOFs excluded; both derived in the supplementary). This closed-form, differentiable map is the Hill forward through which μ_θ is trained (§III-B) and the torque that drives MuJoCo.

    III-D3D Volumetric Muscle Simulation

    To achieve a stable, controllable, and realistic volumetric muscle simulation, three key challenges must be addressed: 1) anisotropic fiber force, 2) volume conservation, and 3) muscle–bone coupling. The first two drive the realism: the fiber force contracts the muscle along the fibers, while volume conservation makes it bulge in the orthogonal directions. Enforcing volume conservation is in turn limited by solver convergence: under the high stiffness muscle requires, an under-converged solve leaves visible artifacts and inverted tetrahedra. Muscle–bone coupling is governed by attachments: attachments that are too stiff distort the muscle, while those that are too soft fail to transmit force. We address them in turn. We embed the Hill-type curve into the constitutive law, so that per-fiber activation directly shortens the muscle along its fibers. We propose a GMG (Geometric Multigrid) solver for fast and stable simulation (§III-D2). Finally, we partition each muscle by masks into tendon and belly regions, attaching the tendons hard and the belly soft. We simulate the volumetric muscle with XPBD [16], giving first the solver update and the geometric multigrid that accelerates it, then the individual constraints.

    III-D1 XPBD Update

    The volumetric muscle deformation is driven by a set of position-based constraints: volume and shape preservation (§III-D3), anisotropic fiber contraction (§III-D4), attachment (§III-D5), and collision (§III-D6). Each is solved with the standard XPBD update:

    Δλ=(-C-α̃ λ)/(∑ᵢwᵢ\lVert∇C\rVert²+α̃),(9)
    Δxᵢ=wᵢ ∇C Δλ.(10)

    Here C is one of the constraint functions and ∇C its gradient with respect to the participating vertex positions. λ is the constraint’s accumulated Lagrange multiplier (reset to zero at the start of each time step) and Δλ is its per-iteration increment. α̃=1/(k Δt²) is the compliance, i.e. the inverse of the constraint stiffness k scaled by the squared time step Δt; a stiffer constraint thus has a smaller α̃. wᵢ is the inverse mass of vertex i, and Δxᵢ is the position correction applied to that vertex. Once all constraints have been projected, velocities are recovered from the position change over the step, v^f←(x^f-x^fₚᵣₑᵥ)/Δt. The individual constraints are defined next; each constraint’s gradient is derived in the supplementary.

    III-D2 Geometric Multigrid

    The geometric multigrid is a core contribution of this work: it is what makes our stiff, high-resolution volumetric muscle solve both stable and fast. Previous position-based hierarchies, such as HPBD [11], have two limitations: 1) they are formulated for cloth rather than tetrahedral meshes; 2) they do not close a complete V-cycle, so they act more like a low-resolution driver for the high-resolution mesh. Therefore, we develop a new algorithm for geometric multigrid XPBD that supports tetrahedral meshes with a Petrov–Galerkin restriction. We construct the two-level hierarchy by geometric coarsening: we first inflate the fine surface triangular mesh slightly, remesh it to a coarser triangle mesh, and then tetrahedralize it (Fig. 7). Our core insight is that the coarse tetrahedron acts as a “cage” that controls the motion of the fine vertices. The prolongator P is established by barycentric coordinates,

    x^f=x₀^f+∑ᵢ₌₁⁴wᵢ Δxᶜᵢ,(11)

    where w₁,…,w₄ are the barycentric coordinates of the fine vertex with respect to the coarse tetrahedron, with w₄=1-∑ᵢ₌₁³wᵢ. x₀^f is the fine position before the multigrid update. Each set of four weights for a tetrahedron defines a row of P. As in HPBD [11], we prolongate the coarse correction Δxᶜ instead of the direct coarse solution xᶜ.

    We define restriction as the least-squares state that best reproduces the fine state x^f within the cage subspace,

    xᶜ=*arg min_xᶜ \lVertP xᶜ-x^f\rVert₂²,

    		(12)

    whose normal equations give the Petrov–Galerkin restriction

    xᶜ=(P^⊤P)⁻¹P^⊤ (R) x^f.

    		(13)

    Since P has full column rank, R is the left pseudo-inverse of P, so restriction exactly recovers any coarse-level vector after prolongation, i.e., RP=I. A desirable property of this Petrov–Galerkin restriction is that it has RP=I, which is why we choose it over the Galerkin restriction R=P^⊤.

    Our restriction and prolongation processes are matrix-free and do not require explicit construction of the large sparse matrices P and R. Because every fine vertex is embedded in the cage of a single muscle, P, and hence P^⊤P, is block-diagonal across muscles, so Eq. (13) decouples into one small dense solve per muscle. We therefore precompute and store the per-muscle pseudo-inverse blocks (P^⊤P)⁻¹P^⊤ once, reducing restriction to a block-diagonal matrix–vector product at run time. The per-step volumetric simulation is summarized in Figure 8. Note that the multigrid can be easily switched off by skipping the restriction, coarse-solving, and prolongation steps, which reduces it to the classic XPBD algorithm.

    III-D3 Volume and Shape Preservation Constraints

    Incompressibility is enforced primarily by a Stable Neo-Hookean (SNH) material [25], cast as a coupled pair of XPBD constraints following Macklin and Müller [36], alongside an explicit volume constraint and an ARAP shape term:

    SNH Deviatoric: C_dev=\lVertF\rVert_F-√3,(14)
    SNH Hydrostatic: C_hyd=\detF-α, α=1+μ/λ,(15)
    Volume: Cᵥₒₗ=V-V₀,(16)
    ARAP: Cₐᵣₐₚ=\lVertF-R\rVert_F,(17)

    where F is the deformation gradient and R its rotation part, V and V₀ the current and rest volume, μ and λ the shear and bulk moduli, and α a rest-stability offset that makes the undeformed configuration an exact rest state of the energy. In SNH the hydrostatic term enforces incompressibility while the deviatoric term carries the shear response; the ARAP (As-Rigid-As-Possible) term further resists shear and preserves shape. For that term we found an SVD-based formulation with non-negative clamping [37] more robust than the polar-decomposition one.

    III-D4 Anisotropic Fiber Constraints

    We inject the 1D Hill law into the 3D medium as an energy-based fiber constraint. Whereas Lee et al. [6] realize the active fiber force through a first Piola–Kirchhoff stress, we formulate it at the position level for XPBD. The normalized fiber length of Eq. 7 is lifted from the 1D path measurement (§III-C) to the stretch of the deformation gradient F along the muscle’s rest fiber direction:

    λ_f=\lVertF d\rVert ≡ ℓ̃^M,

    		(18)

    where d is the unit fiber direction in the rest configuration. This 3D stretch is identically the 1D normalized fiber length: both are the current fiber length divided by its optimal (rest) length, so we keep ℓ̃^M for the 1D Hill curves and write λ_f for the same quantity in the 3D continuum. XPBD stores each elastic potential as the quadratic form Ψ=\tfrac12k C² with compliance α̃=1/(k V₀ Δt²), so setting \tfrac12C_fiber²=Ψ_fiber encodes the Hill strain energy directly in the constraint:

    Ψ_fiber=σ₀ ∫_λ_f,\min^λ_f fₕᵢₗₗ(s) ds, C_fiber=√2 Ψ_fiber,

    		(19)

    where fₕᵢₗₗ is given by Eq. 7, from which we drop f^V, fᵀ, and f^PE in the 3D medium. Because fₕᵢₗₗ is a piecewise quintic polynomial, the energy integral has a closed-form degree-10 polynomial per segment, avoiding numerical quadrature. Injecting the same Hill law that trains the policy makes the volumetric contraction obey exactly the constitutive relation the activations were solved against, and because only the along-fiber component is constrained, activation shortens the belly along d while volume conservation drives the orthogonal bulge. An anisotropic ARAP alternative is compared in §IV-D3; both constraints, their gradients, and the fiber stiffness are given in the supplementary.

    III-D5 Attachment Constraints

    The muscle is coupled to the skeleton by attachment constraints that drive attachment vertices toward their targets on the bone:

    C_attach=\lVertxᵢ-xᵢ^*\rVert-L₀,

    		(20)

    where xᵢ is the position of an attached vertex, xᵢ^* its target on the bone, and L₀ the rest length between the vertex and its target. The bone–muscle coupling is one-way, the rigid bone driving the deformable muscle, with targets found by a nearest-point search on the bone surface at the rest pose. Neighboring muscles are additionally tied to one another by inter-muscle springs, built once at the rest pose between nearby surface vertices of adjacent muscles; these keep the musculature bundled and are two-way, unlike the bone attachments. We use two kinds of attachment: pins, which are hard and impose the position directly, and springs, which are soft and allow some deformation. A user-painted mask assigns pins to the tendon regions near the origin and insertion and springs to the belly. The two are respectively Dirichlet and Robin boundary conditions.

    Their balance is a trade-off: too many pins drive up tetrahedron inversions and leave the surface unsmooth, while too few let the muscle lag behind and detach from the bone, most visibly on the thin, slender muscles that are dominated by these boundary conditions rather than by elasticity (§III-D2).

    III-D6 Collision Handling

    We handle muscle–bone collisions with an SDF [38]. Each bone is rigid, so its SDF φ_b is precomputed once at the rest pose and queried in the bone’s local frame, needing no per-substep tessellation or nearest-primitive search. A muscle surface vertex xₚ found to penetrate (φ_b<0) is resolved by a unilateral constraint projected alongside the other XPBD constraints,

    C_col=φ_b(xₚ), ∇C_col=∇φ_b(xₚ),

    		(21)

    which pushes the vertex back onto the bone surface along the SDF gradient and is released once it leaves the bone. We omit explicit muscle–muscle collision: neighboring muscles are already held apart by inter-muscle springs, and since the musculature is primarily bone-driven the residual inter-muscle penetration is minor. The broad/narrow-phase details and this trade-off are given in the supplementary.

    III-EMotion Retargeting and Muscle Mapping

    The RL stage operates on a 1D musculoskeletal asset, whereas the volumetric simulation runs on a 3D character with its own skeletal proportions and tetrahedral muscle meshes. Two transfer steps bridge the two representations (Fig. 2). Motion Retargeting: The 1D skeleton spans N_θ=50 actuated DOFs over 22 joints, the floating root aside (14 spherical joints at 3 DOF and 8 revolute joints at 1 DOF, i.e. 14×3+8×1=50). We first perform a joint-level retargeting to transfer the 1D skeleton motion onto the 3D skeleton, where 20 key points are selected and then full-body inverse kinematics is solved to recover the 3D joint angles. Muscle Mapping: Usually the 3D model and the 1D model do not have a one-to-one correspondence, so we similarly need to map the 284 1D Hill muscles onto the 194 3D volumetric muscles. The two assets differ in muscle count because they originate from different musculoskeletal models. We map them by anatomical semantic similarity and spatial correspondence, i.e., matching by anatomical name first and, for any muscle left unmatched, falling back to the nearest one. This step is optional if the two assets are already in one-to-one correspondence.

    IV Results

    We evaluate our system in four parts: a full-body demonstration on four motions (§IV-A), validation of the discovered activations against human sEMG (§IV-B), comparisons against production and neural volumetric muscle systems (§IV-C), and an ablation of each component (§IV-D). All RL policies are trained on the 1D Hill surrogate and the 3D volumetric simulation is run as a single forward pass at inference (§III-A).

    RL co-training is implemented in PyTorch, and the articulated body simulation used for training in MuJoCo [32], with 64 parallel environments per motion; the 3D simulation is implemented in Warp [39], is fully GPU accelerated, and runs on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X CPU. We adopt USD (Universal Scene Description) as the interchange format for all assets (skeletons, muscle tetrahedral meshes, fibers, and simulation caches), and render the final scenes in Houdini [15]. Training and simulation parameters are given in the supplementary.

    IV-AFull-Body Demonstration

    Figure 9 shows our full pipeline applied to four reference-motion clips that span a range of dynamic regimes: a periodic, ground-contact walk; a balance-critical kick that loads a single support leg; a free-floating swim driven by a surrogate fluid model [40]; and a squat that demands whole-body coordination under load. For each clip, the RL stage discovers per-muscle activations that track the reference on the 1D asset, and these activations drive the 194-muscle volumetric body through a single forward XPBD simulation. Each motion trains in under 2 hours, and the walk can be repeated indefinitely if the reference motion is cyclic. Table I reports the runtime and memory cost of this full-body volumetric simulation on a single RTX 4090. Swimming has no ground contact to react against, so rather than run a full fluid solver we give each body segment an ellipsoidal drag proxy [40] for the policy to push against.

    Figure 10 plots the tracking reward over the course of RL training for all four motions. Every curve rises steadily and plateaus near its maximum, confirming that the co-trained policy and muscle networks (Alg. 1) jointly converge to a high-quality tracking solution despite the underdetermined, non-negative, and nonlinear activation-to-torque map. Figure 11 quantifies the motion quality of a deterministic rollout of the trained walk (300 control steps at 30 Hz). Panel (a) is the joint-angle tracking error, the SO(3) geodesic distance penalized by rₚₒₛₑ in Eq. 3, averaging 10.5^∘ over the 18 tracked joints. Panel (b) is the COM-aligned position error of the five end effectors behind rₑₑ in Eq. 3, averaging 49 mm. Panel (c) is the relative torque residual, a scale-free counterpart of L_torque in Eq. 4, at 17.8% on average. Panel (d) is the mean activation over all muscles, the same minimum-effort quantity as L_reg in Eq. 4 but without the square, at 0.061. Together these show that the generated motion tracks the reference closely, yet does not follow it exactly: the activations have to keep the motion physically feasible, which is precisely what we expect.

    IV-BValidation Against EMG

    We now test the effect of the EMG prior on physiological plausibility, comparing the recovered activations against the Moreira sEMG [10] following the synergist-group and gait-alignment protocol of §III-B4 (Fig. 12).

    Without the prior, the policy leaves the human ±1 std band over most of the gait cycle (Fig. 12, left; mean in-band 20%, mean correlation -0.04), confirming that the redundancy is resolved non-physiologically. Adding it to muscle-network training steers that redundancy toward the measured solution while leaving the policy’s motion objective untouched: the recovered activations now track real sEMG (Fig. 12, right; mean in-band 91%, mean correlation 0.97, all on/off timings aligned) and still drive a stable, faithful gait, at negligible cost and without degrading the visual fidelity of the volumetric deformation. Activation–EMG mismatch in tracking-only controllers is widely reported [5, 2, 1]; our prior offers a simple remedy.

    IV-CComparison with Baselines

    We compare against two representative volumetric muscle systems: Houdini’s Otis solver [41], the production standard, and the recent neural musculoskeletal skin-deformation model of Han et al. [29] (Epic). Otis hand-authors activations from tension lines and simulates the motion with Vertex Block Descent [42]; Han et al. recover activations by a per-pose quasistatic equilibrium solve and deform an ML skinning model [30] trained on XPBD. Ours are learned inside the RL control loop and are exactly the forces that drive the motion (§III-B). We compare all three on the same reference pose. We could not include Lee et al. [6]. Their optimization-based controller re-runs the volumetric solver inside the control loop. This has caused repeated non-convergence, which then makes the control learning fail constantly. We therefore exclude it from the baseline methods.

    Figure 13 colors our muscle surface (left) by its per-vertex distance to the Otis reference (right) on the same full-body pose. Over most of the body the deviation stays within a few millimeters (blue–green), with larger deviations (yellow–red) at localized regions such as the thighs and shoulders, showing that our physically actuated muscles reproduce production-quality volumetric geometry. The two differ sharply in cost: our GPU solver runs at 18 ms/frame (Table I), whereas Otis, parallelized on the CPU through OpenCL, takes 20.8 s/frame on the same AMD Ryzen 9 5950X workstation. Figure 14 repeats this comparison against Han et al. [29]: the deviation stays small (blue) over most of the torso and grows (yellow–red) at the forearms and mid-abdomen, where the two pipelines differ most in musculature. In both cases the surfaces are close, and the essential difference is provenance: our deformation is produced by the forward-dynamic forces that generate the motion.

    IV-DAblation Study

    We ablate each major component of the volumetric pipeline (geometric multigrid, collision handling, and the Hill-type fiber constraint) to isolate its contribution.

    IV-D1 Effect of Multigrid

    We evaluate our multigrid solver in two complementary settings: a squashed-bunny benchmark, and a full-body volumetric muscle model.

    Squashed-bunny benchmark. The bunny (850K fine tetrahedra over a 5K coarse cage) is compressed and released to bounce back under identical parameters with and without multigrid (MG). Figure 15 shows MG converges faster with better deformation quality, its main cost being the coarse-level solve. Table II confirms this: MG reaches a fixed tolerance (constraint C<=0.1, 2-norm for vector C) in 53 frames and 49.1 ms vs. 621 frames and 418.9 ms without (11.7× fewer steps, 8.5× faster), and at 81 frames reaches C=0.082 where the fine-only solver stalls at C=0.979. Its small per-frame overhead (0.84 vs. 0.59 ms) is far outweighed by the fewer steps needed.

    Full-body muscle. Figure 16 shows these benefits carry over to the full-body volumetric muscle model. MG is what makes our high-stiffness volumetric simulation both stable and efficient. Figure 16 (bottom) quantifies this on the same example as Figure 13: MG holds both the constraint residual and the inverted-tetrahedron count far lower throughout the deformation, roughly a 3.7× reduction in peak inversions.

    IV-D2 Effect of Collision

    We ablate the collision handling of §III-D6 by disabling the muscle–bone collision constraints and re-running the same activation trajectory. Figure 17 compares the two: with collision handling the muscle bellies slide cleanly over the bones, whereas without it they sink in, concentrated around the knee and lower leg where the muscles wrap most tightly around the skeleton. Enabling collision handling essentially eliminates these interpenetrations.

    IV-D3 Effect of the Fiber Constraint

    We isolate the fiber constraint on a biceps brachii held by a single proximal tendon anchor, leaving the belly free to contract as activation ramps from 0 to 1. Four constraints are compared under an identical setup: (i) no fiber force, (ii) a plain stretch constraint C=\lVertFd\rVert, (iii) our Hill–Millard energy constraint (Eq. 19), and (iv) an anisotropic ARAP alternative [23, 24], built on Kim et al.’s anisotropic invariants and driving the along-fiber stretch toward an activation-set target through a symmetric quadratic well; its invariants, constraint, gradients, and a constitutive comparison against ours are given in the supplementary. Figure 18 reports the biceps’ shortening and girth change at full activation: about 21% shortening for Hill–Millard, 18% for the plain constraint, and 13% for anisotropic ARAP. Hill–Millard reproduces the exact 1D force–length law.

    V Limitations and Future Work

    Ideally, we would incorporate the 3D volumetric muscle simulation into the RL training loop. We tried this integrated pipeline first, but it proved slow, unstable, and uncontrollable for RL training. The difficulty originates from the two-way bone–muscle coupling: spring-based attachments are the naive strategy, but their stiffness has no physiological basis and is hard to tune, since how many springs to use and how stiff they should be are entirely unknown. We therefore use the 1D Hill model as a training surrogate and a separate 3D simulation for evaluation. We hope to achieve “3D-in-the-loop” training in future work, which requires two things: a stable and efficient rigid–deformable coupled simulation method, and a physiologically grounded coupling strategy. In addition, while our multigrid performs well on bulky muscles, it is less satisfactory on long, slender muscles, such as some of the muscles near the distal end of the forearm. We attribute this to two factors. First, our geometric coarsening struggles to produce a good coarse mesh for such thin, elongated geometry. Second, because these slender muscles are light and small in volume, their motion is governed more by the boundary conditions (the pin/attachment constraints) than by elastic response, whereas our multigrid is designed to accelerate the elasticity solve. We therefore exclude these slender muscles from the multigrid and solve them at the fine level only.

    VI Conclusion

    We have presented a system that recovers physically consistent muscle activations from a reference motion and turns them into volumetric muscle deformation. Reinforcement learning first explores the muscle activations on a fast 1D Hill-type surrogate, co-training a policy and a muscle network in a single PPO loop and steering the redundant activation solution toward measured human recruitment through an EMG prior. A GPU-parallel XPBD solver then simulates the volumetric muscles under the same Hill-type constitutive law, injected as an energy-based fiber constraint, with a geometric multigrid keeping the stiff solve stable and efficient.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：1D 肌肉模型当快速代理留在控制回路，最终形变交给 3D 体积仿真，两级共享同一本构关系。

要点：

  • 把 1D 肌肉模型留在 RL 控制回路里当快速代理，最终形变交给 3D 体积仿真；两级共享同一套本构关系，所以触发运动与产生形变的是同一组激活值
  • 加入实测肌电（EMG）先验，把冗余的激活解拉向真实人体募集模式；并给出基于粗四面体笼的 XPBD 几何多重网格求解器
  • 达到同一约束容差：53 帧 / 49.1 ms，对比无多重网格的 621 帧 / 418.9 ms（步数少 11.7 倍、快 8.5 倍），峰值翻转四面体数量约少 3.7 倍

为什么值得看：这是把「物理正确的形变」塞进可交互帧预算的可行切分：学习负责政策、仿真负责形变，而不是让网络直接吐顶点。对做角色管线的人来说，等于把肌肉激活从美术手调变成可训练、可复现的量。

中文摘要：肌肉收缩带来的体表形变对角色动画的真实感至关重要，但主流 3D 动画管线里肌肉激活仍靠美术手动指定，既费时又不保证物理合理。RLMuscle 让强化学习控制器自己找每块肌肉的激活序列来跟踪参考动作：把 1D 肌肉模型留在 RL 控制回路里当快速代理，最终形变交给 3D 体积仿真，两级共享同一套本构关系，因此形变由驱动运动的那组激活直接产生。为消除冗余解，作者加入实测肌电先验，把解拉向真实的人体募集模式。数值上还提出基于粗四面体笼、重心坐标延拓的 XPBD 几何多重网格：达同一约束容差只需 53 帧 / 49.1 ms，而无多重网格要 621 帧 / 418.9 ms，峰值翻转四面体也少约 3.7 倍。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-27

RLMuscle: Muscle-Driven Character Animation
via Reinforcement Learning

Abstract

Body deformation caused by muscle contraction plays a vital role in the visual realism of character animation, yet in most 3D animation pipelines artists have to manually specify muscle activations, which is time-consuming and gives no guarantee of physical realism. To address this, we propose a new method in which a reinforcement learning (RL) controller discovers per-muscle activations that track reference motions without manual tuning. Existing RL muscle controllers stop at 1D muscles; we go one step further, keeping the 1D model inside the RL control loop as a fast surrogate, and using a 3D volumetric simulation to produce the final deformation. Because both stages share the very same constitutive law, the muscle deformation is produced by the same activations that generated the motion. We further add a measured electromyography (EMG) prior that steers the redundant activation solution toward real human muscle recruitment. To achieve stable, efficient, and realistic simulation, we propose a novel geometric multigrid for Extended Position-Based Dynamics (XPBD) that is built on a coarse tetrahedral cage with barycentric-coordinate prolongation and closes a V-cycle on tetrahedral meshes. Within this GPU-parallelized solver, we inject the same Hill-type force–length law as an energy-based fiber constraint that turns per-fiber activation into realistic muscle contraction and bulging. We demonstrate volumetric muscle simulation on a 194-muscle human body with a diverse set of motions (walk, kick, swim, overhead-squat, etc.), simulating the full-body model at 18 ms per frame on a single RTX 4090. Our work takes a step toward character animation that is not only visually convincing but also biomechanically grounded. The website with code and videos is at https://chunleili.github.io/project-page-rlmuscle/.

Index Terms:

Muscle simulation, XPBD, reinforcement learning, physics-based animation, character animation.

I Introduction

In animation, film, games, and virtual reality (VR), realistic muscle behavior is essential for believable character animation. Yet production pipelines still rely on hand-authored muscle activations, produced by one of two major authoring methods. The first is a tension line: the artist binds a line onto the skeleton, and the muscle associated with that line is activated once the line contracts below a set length threshold, so activation is triggered geometrically by bone motion. The second is keyframing: the artist directly animates each muscle’s activation value over time as a keyframed curve. Both encode activations chosen for visual plausibility, not physical plausibility. Consequently, there is no guarantee that hand-crafted tension can produce physically valid motions, because artists effectively decouple muscle deformation from motion dynamics. This expertise-driven workflow is not only labor-intensive; it also cannot answer the question at the heart of physics-based animation: what muscle activations actually produce a given motion? This is the muscle inverse problem: recovering the hidden control signals from observed motion. A principled solution would replace hand-tuning with physically consistent activations derived from the target motion, so that the resulting muscle deformation reflects the underlying dynamics rather than a visually plausible guess.

On the other hand, recent works on muscle simulation driven by reinforcement learning (RL) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] are mainly limited to a simplified 1D Hill-type muscle model, which falls short of the 3D volumetric muscle deformation needed for visual realism. The muscle inverse problem is challenging because the map from activation to joint motion is highly nonlinear, and the control space is high-dimensional (hundreds of muscles), which leads to intractability of analytical inversion, and extremely low sample efficiency in RL training.

We solve the muscle inverse problem by forward dynamics, i.e. searching for the activations that, once simulated, reproduce a target motion. This poses two challenges:

  • 1.

    Control. The map from muscle activation to joint motion is highly underdetermined and nonlinear, so analytical inversion is intractable, and naive RL exploration in this space is sample-inefficient.

  • 2.

    Physics. The numerical solver must handle volumetric muscle that is nonlinear, anisotropic, and nearly incompressible while remaining both stable and efficient.

    • We present the first system that addresses both challenges. Given a reference motion (motion capture or keyframed animation) and rest-pose 3D muscle/skeleton assets as input, it outputs a skeletal–muscular animation driven by physically consistent activations. Our work makes three technical contributions.

    Technical contribution 1: a muscle-control pipeline that decouples 1D control from 3D simulation under a unified constitutive law for fibers, solving the muscle inverse problem and freeing artists from hand-tuning (addressing Control). Existing RL muscle controllers [1, 3, 4, 5, 2] actuate 1D Hill-type muscles only, so they recover joint motion but not the 3D volumetric deformation that visual realism demands; conversely, optimization-based methods [6] that place the volumetric solver inside the control loop are unstable and did not converge in our tests. We propose to use the 1D model as a surrogate in RL and to produce the deformation from the 3D model. To bridge the gap between the two, we introduce a new fiber constraint based on the Hill–Millard constitutive curve, which is used in both the 1D and the 3D model. Following MASS [1], a policy network and a muscle network are co-trained in a single PPO [7] loop against a motion-mimicking reward [8] on the 1D surrogate. The recovered activations then drive the 3D volumetric muscles through the same Hill-type constitutive law [9] used by the surrogate, in a single forward pass with the 3D solver kept out of the control loop, so the volumetric deformation is consistent with the dynamics that produced the motion, reproducing realistic muscle bulging, stiffening, and contraction rather than a visually plausible guess.

    Technical contribution 2: a physiological electromyography (EMG) prior that steers the redundant activation solution toward measured human muscle recruitment (addressing Control). The activation-to-torque map is redundant, and existing muscle networks [1, 3, 4, 5, 2] reduce that redundancy from torque and effort alone, with nothing tying the result to a real recruitment pattern, so their activations drift away from measured human EMG. We propose to inject a measured surface EMG envelope [10] into the muscle-network loss, matched per synergist group and folded onto a common gait cycle, which pulls the recovered activations back toward the measured envelope (§IV-B).

    Technical contribution 3: a Petrov–Galerkin geometric multigrid for volumetric XPBD, integrated into a GPU-parallel framework that runs the full-body volumetric muscle model at 18 ms per frame on a single RTX 4090 (addressing Physics). Previous position-based hierarchies, such as HPBD [11], are formulated for cloth rather than tetrahedral meshes and never close a complete V-cycle, so they act only as a low-resolution driver; algebraic constructions [12] instead assemble a global matrix and thereby give up XPBD’s local, per-constraint solve. We propose to coarsen a tetrahedral cage geometrically, prolongate by barycentric coordinates, and close a full V-cycle with a Petrov–Galerkin restriction, which keeps the high-stiffness solve stable and efficient. The framework further contributes muscle–bone collision handling based on a signed distance field (SDF).

    II Related Work

    Position-Based Dynamics. PBD [13] is a popular framework for real-time deformable object simulation. It is widely used in applications such as PhysX [14] and Houdini Vellum [15]. Extended PBD (XPBD) [16] reformulates PBD as a dual-space energy minimization framework and introduces a compliance term to transform the infinite-stiffness to a finite-stiffness problem, which improves the convergence. Bender et al. [17] cast Finite Element Method (FEM) strain energy as position-based constraints, which makes it possible to apply various FEM-based constitutive laws in PBD. We refer readers to the survey [18] for more details. We use XPBD as our simulation engine and propose a novel muscle fiber constraint tied to the physiological properties of muscle.

    Multigrid. Multigrid [19] is a classical numerical method for accelerating and stabilizing simulation, running an iterative solver on grids of different resolutions to eliminate low-frequency errors. Unlike grid-based fluid solvers, which have a natural hierarchical structure, soft bodies provide no such structure, so building a hierarchy on them is challenging. Hierarchical PBD (HPBD) [11] introduces a hierarchical solver for PBD simulated cloth, whose coarsening is based on edge collapsing. For volumetric solids, by contrast, the hierarchy is built by coarsening the simulation mesh itself, and how easily this can be done depends on the element type: coarsening is straightforward and efficient on hexahedral meshes [20], but the tetrahedral meshes prevalent in computer graphics are harder to coarsen. Several strategies address this: some build a multilevel XPBD through gradual rigidifying [21], while barycentric-coordinate prolongation [22] constructs a hierarchy directly on tetrahedral meshes and has proved successful in FEM. Our previous work, Multi-Grid Position-Based Dynamics (MGPBD) [12], utilized algebraic multigrid to build the hierarchy. However, algebraic multigrid requires assembling a global matrix, which sacrifices the flexibility and lightweight nature of XPBD’s local, per-constraint solve; moreover, building the hierarchy purely from the numerical matrix lacks geometric and physical intuition. In this work we propose a novel barycentric-coordinate-based geometric multigrid for XPBD, which accelerates the convergence of the stiff volume and incompressibility constraints and yields more stable and efficient volumetric simulation than single-level XPBD.

    Volumetric muscle simulation. Muscle is a special type of soft tissue, characterized by anisotropic fiber forces and strong incompressibility. Kim et al. [23, 24, 25] proposed energy potentials for FEM that yield an inversion-free muscle material matching the constitutive law of real muscle. Angles et al. [26] used position-based elastic rods with volumetric scale to model muscle bundles.

    Muscle-actuated Hill muscle control by RL. In recent years, many researchers have used 1D Hill-type muscles to physically drive the dynamics of human motion (activation → muscle force → bone motion, i.e. forward dynamics). The Hill-type model approximates each muscle as a polyline anchored to local positions on the bones, and reinforcement learning is commonly employed to train a neural network that finds the activations producing the desired motion. OpenSim [27] provides 1D musculotendon simulation, and Myosuite [2] wraps it in an RL framework for muscle-actuated control. The most prominent of these is MASS (Muscle-Actuated Skeletal System) by Lee et al. [1], a two-level imitation-learning architecture that actuates 346 muscles; we adopt its dual-network design (§III-B). A line of follow-ups inherits the same control formulation: MuscleVAE [3], MAGNET [4], and MuscleMimic [5], alongside torque-actuated trackers such as DeepMimic [28, 8] with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [7]. These methods all drive only 1D line-segment Hill muscles; building on this 1D Hill-type RL control, we add a 3D volumetric muscle simulation driven by the same Hill law, turning the biomechanics into visually compelling muscle deformation.

    Inverse muscle activation for volumetric muscle. Some works also address the inverse muscle activation problem with 3D volumetric deformation, similar to ours, but they recover the activations by static optimization rather than inside a forward-dynamic control loop. Han et al. [29] solve a per-pose torque balance as a quadratic program (QP) and train an ML-deformer [30] to reproduce muscle deformation from joint state and activation, but such a static solve cannot guarantee that the recovered activations actually drive the target motion (activation → muscle force → bone motion). Lee et al. [6] embed Hill-type muscles in Projective Dynamics and obtain activations from a per-frame QP, which runs the volumetric solver inside the trajectory-optimization control loop, but in our tests it was very unstable and never converged. We instead learn the activations inside the RL control loop on a 1D Hill-type surrogate, so they are exactly the forces that drive the motion (§III-B), making the deformation genuinely physically actuated rather than fitted or pre-scripted.

    III Method

    Our system couples a 1D Hill-type muscle model (Nₘ=284) with an RL controller, then uses a volumetric muscle model (194 muscles) with the same Hill-type constitutive law to simulate the deformation. We first outline the pipeline (§III-A) and the RL co-training that solves the inverse problem (§III-B), then detail the 1D Hill dynamics (§III-C), the 3D volumetric simulation (§III-D), and the motion retargeting and muscle mapping that bridge the 1D and 3D models (§III-E).

    III-AOverview

    Figure 2 summarizes the system. The input is a 1D musculoskeletal asset together with a reference motion clip in Biovision Hierarchy (BVH) format. A reinforcement-learning imitation-learning stage solves the muscle inverse problem on this 1D asset (284 muscles), jointly producing the muscle-driven bone motion and the corresponding 1D muscle activation trajectory. A motion-retargeting step transfers the bone motion onto a 3D skeleton, while a muscle-mapping step lifts the per-musculotendon 1D activations to 3D activations. Both streams and 3D assets (bone and muscle geometries) are then fed to the XPBD-based 3D simulation engine (§III-D), which produces the volumetric muscle deformation used for the final 3D rendering. The 1D track therefore acts as a fast surrogate that solves the hard inverse problem once; the 3D track is a single forward simulation at inference. The RL co-training that solves the inverse problem (Fig. 3, Alg. 1) is detailed in §III-B.

    III-BReinforcement Learning Control

    The RL stage solves control challenges: it discovers the muscle activations (Nₘ=284) that make the simulated character track a reference motion. We split control across a policy networkπ_φ and a muscle networkμ_θ[1] and co-train them inside a single PPO loop against the motion-tracking reward (Fig. 3, Alg. 1) rather than learning them sequentially, so each rollout supplies a gradient for both and they adapt to each other. A third, training-only value networkV_ψ serves as PPO’s critic but never participates in control.

    III-B1 Two-Network Co-Training

    We train the controller for muscle-driven motion tracking with PPO, summarized in Alg. 1. Letting the policy explore the Nₘ=284 muscle activations directly is sample-inefficient, so the policy instead acts in the compact space of per-joint PD-target offsets: Stable proportional–derivative (PD) control [31] turns its action into a desired joint torque τᵈᵉˢ ∈ ℝ^N_θ (N_θ=50 degrees of freedom, DOF), the muscle network maps that torque to the activations a^Mₜ ∈ [0,1]^Nₘ (M for muscles), and the Hill model realizes the muscle torque that drives MuJoCo [32]. Both networks learn from the same rollout, PPO updating π_φ,V_ψ and a mean squared error (MSE) loss updating μ_θ. The observation is sₜ=[ bₜ, vₜ, φₜ ], where bₜ ∈ ℝ⁶⁶ stacks the center-of-mass position of each of the 22 non-root bodies in the root frame, vₜ ∈ ℝ⁶⁹ the world-frame center-of-mass velocities of all 23 bodies, and φₜ ∈ [0,1) is the phase of the reference clip (\dim(sₜ)=136).

    III-B2 Policy Network

    Motion-mimicking reward. Following DeepMimic [8] we use an exponential-kernel reward composed of pose, velocity, and end-effector terms, augmented with whole-body center of mass (COM) and pelvis-orientation terms for balance-critical motions; the pose error is the SO(3) geodesic between current and target joint frames:

    pⱼ=\log (Rⱼ^⊤ R^*ⱼ)^∨∈ℝ³,(1)
    rₚₒₛₑ=\exp (-kₚ∑_j∈J ∥pⱼ∥²),(2)

    rₜ=rₑₑ·(wₚ rₚₒₛₑ+wᵥ rᵥₑₗ+w_c r_com+wᵤ rᵤₚ),

    		(3)

    where rₜ is the tracking reward; Rⱼ,R^*ⱼ∈SO(3) are the current/target rotation matrices of joint j; \log(·)^∨ is the matrix log map returning the axis–angle vector; J is the set of tracked joints; and asterisks mark reference-motion targets. The remaining terms share the same kernel \exp(-k \lVert·\rVert²) applied to their own error: joint velocity for rᵥₑₗ, the positions xₖ of the five end-effector links for rₑₑ, the whole-body center of mass c for r_com, and the pelvis up axis u=Rₚₑₗᵥᵢₛe_y for rᵤₚ, which gives a yaw-free torso-tilt error (full expressions in the supplementary). End-effector errors are taken in the COM-relative frame so root drift does not corrupt limb-placement credit, and rₑₑ enters multiplicatively so gross limb misplacement suppresses local joint credit. The exponential kernel confines each term to [0,1] and saturates smoothly as the tracking error grows. Balance-critical motions (squat, single-leg kick) shift the task weights (wₚ,wᵥ,w_c,wᵤ) toward the COM and pelvis-up terms and add the root pose to J; without these terms the policy matches the pose but loses balance and falls. Kernel widths, per-task weights and the Mixamo [33] clips are listed in the supplementary.

    III-B3 Muscle Network

    The muscle network μ_θ maps the desired joint torque τᵈᵉˢ to per-muscle activations a^M ∈ [0,1]^Nₘ, solving the muscle inverse problem. This map is redundant: the Nₘ muscles far outnumber the N_θ DOFs, so infinitely many activation patterns realize the same torque. Classical biomechanics resolves the redundancy per frame with a quadratic program (QP); we instead use a simple supervised network to solve it. Layer sizes and training hyperparameters are given in the supplementary material.

    Muscle-network loss. The muscle network μ_θ is trained online with three losses (Eq. 4): a torque-realization term L_torque that inverts the activation-to-torque map τᵐᵘˢᶜ(a^M)=L a^M+b (§III-C), a minimum-effort regularizer L_reg that breaks the activation redundancy, and a physiological EMG prior L_emg. The first two are standard in muscle-actuated control; L_emg is our contribution: existing muscle networks [1, 3, 4, 5, 2] are trained on torque and effort alone, so their activations have no reason to match how a human recruits muscle (§IV-B), whereas L_emg steers the redundant solution toward a measured human EMG envelope. The three combine as

    L_μ=\underbracemean [(\tfrac1κ(τᵐᵘˢᶜ(a^M)-τᵈᵉˢ))²]_L_torque+w_reg \underbracemean[(a^M)²]_L_reg(4)
    +λ \underbraceL_emg_EMG prior,

    with torque scale κ=100, w_reg=0.01, and EMG weight λ (L_emg is defined in Eq. 6; setting λ=0 recovers the tracking-only loss for motions without a measured envelope). L_reg is the ∑a² minimum-effort criterion of classical static optimization [34], which on its own drives the activations away from physiological EMG measurements.

    III-B4 EMG Prior

    So far, we have obtained activations that generate physically plausible motion through muscle forces, but these activations are still physiologically implausible. We therefore steer the redundant solution toward real surface electromyography (sEMG) from Moreira et al. [10]. Two mismatches stand between that recording and our model (Fig. 4). The first is a muscle mismatch: the recording is coarse-grained, using only four right-leg electrodes, whereas our model is fine-grained. The second is a temporal misalignment: the recording is not aligned with the reference motion, so the two cannot be compared sample by sample. We apply two treatments, detailed in turn below: 1) we match each electrode not to a single fiber but to a whole synergist group; 2) we fold both signals onto a common gait cycle and compare only their shape and timing, not their magnitude.

    Synergist-group mean. Let ℂ be the EMG channels (the four right-leg surface electrodes of Moreira et al. [10]). A surface electrode integrates over a muscle region and the redundant solver distributes load within a synergist group, so channel c is matched not to one fiber but to the cross-section-weighted mean activation of its synergist group G_c:

    ā_c=∑_m∈G_cω_c,m a^Mₘ, ω_c,m=(f_0,m)/(∑_m^′∈G_cf_0,m^′),

    		(5)

    where f_0,m=σ₀A^Mₘ is the maximal isometric force of muscle m (Eq. 8), obtained from its physiological cross-sectional area A^Mₘ and the maximal isometric stress σ₀, the peak stress a fully activated fiber can sustain. Since σ₀ is uniform across muscles (value in the supplementary), the weight reduces to a ratio of cross-sectional areas, so the stronger muscles of a group dominate its mean. Matching the group mean rather than a single fiber also guards against a dead-unit pathology (supplementary).

    Gait-cycle alignment. Each rollout sample carries a gait phase φ=fmod(t, T)/T∈[0,1) recovered from its simulation time t, with T the gait-cycle period, and is placed on the 0 - 100% cycle as ((φ-φₕₛ)\bmod1)·100 to align it to right heel strike [35], where φₕₛ=0.254 is the heel-strike offset calibrated by forward kinematics on the reference foot. The prior is a phase-indexed MSE that pulls each group activation toward the peak-normalized human envelope ê_c(φ):

    L_emg=(1)/(|ℂ|)∑_c∈ℂw_emg,c (ā_c-s ê_c(φ))²,

    		(6)

    where s scales the unit-peak envelope into the activation range and w_emg,c weights each channel (the weight λ against torque realization is set in Eq. 4). The prior enters only the muscle-network loss; the policy’s motion objective (Eq. 3) is untouched, so it re-selects which activation realizes a motion without changing the motion itself. We use λ=1, s=0.3, and w_emg,c=1 for all channels; ê_c is the 13-subject Moreira cohort mean on a 101-bin gait grid. It is enabled wherever a measured envelope exists (the walk) and switched off (λ=0) otherwise; its effect on physiological plausibility is evaluated in §IV-B.

    III-C1D Hill-type Muscle Surrogate

    For motion to be truly actuated by muscle forces, the musculoskeletal system should closely match human anatomy. However, we empirically find that 3D volumetric muscles are overly flexible during RL training due to their excessive number of degrees of freedom, leading to unstable learning. Lee et al. [6] run the volumetric solver directly inside their optimization loop, which was also our initial idea. However, in our experiments, this approach was unstable and failed to converge. Therefore, we instead train against a 1D Hill-type muscle model [1, 3, 4, 5] as a surrogate, and then lift it to a 3D volumetric muscle model in the next section. The Hill-type model plays a dual role in our system: (i) as the 1D musculotendon surrogate that drives RL training, its scalar tension routed through MuJoCo tendon paths to the skeleton (Alg. 1); and (ii) as the constitutive law for the 3D XPBD volumetric muscle of §III-D, injected there as an energy-based fiber constraint (Eq. 19). We give the shared 1D formulation here and the 3D lift in §III-D. The 1D musculoskeletal asset (Fig. 5) is a rigid-body skeleton with spherical and revolute joints, actuated by 1D Hill-type muscles routed as polyline tendon paths between bone attachment sites.

    The Hill-type model (Fig. 6) places a tendon spring in series with a muscle belly, itself an active contractile element parallel to a passive spring. Each fiber generates a normalized scalar force:

    fₕᵢₗₗ=\underbrace\color[rgb]0.1211,0.4648,0.707a f^L(ℓ̃^M) f^V(ℓ̇^M)_\color[rgb]0.1211,0.4648,0.707active+\underbrace\color[rgb]0.1719,0.6289,0.1719f^PE(ℓ̃^M)_\color[rgb]0.1719,0.6289,0.1719passive+\underbrace\color[rgb]0.7734,0.3516,0.0664fᵀ(ℓ̃ᵀ)_\color[rgb]0.7734,0.3516,0.0664tendon,

    		(7)

    where a∈[0,1] is the muscle activation and ℓ̃^M the fiber length normalized by the optimal fiber length, so fₕᵢₗₗ is a dimensionless multiplier equal to 1 at that length (the 3D counterpart of ℓ̃^M, the along-fiber stretch λ_f, is defined in §III-D). We take the force–length curves f^L and f^PE from Millard et al. [9] and evaluate them through a look-up table to accelerate RL training; their piecewise-Bézier form and parameters are given in the supplementary. For simplicity we further assume 1) an infinitely stiff tendon and 2) no velocity-dependent force f^V, since only conservative forces admit an energy potential (§III-D4). We obtain the 1D muscle force by multiplying fₕᵢₗₗ by the peak isometric force f₀, which depends on the muscle (e.g., leg muscles are stronger than arm muscles). f₀=σ₀A^M (physiological cross-sectional area A^M). The resulting 1D Hill-type muscle force is

    F(a)=f₀(a f^L(ℓ̃^M)+f^PE(ℓ̃^M)).

    		(8)

    Muscle force to joint torque. Summing the segments of the anchor polyline gives the path length, hence the normalized fiber length ℓ̃^M that Eq. 7 evaluates; mapping the anchor forces through their point Jacobians makes the total torque affine in activation, τᵐᵘˢᶜ(a^M)=L a^M+b, with L the per-unit-activation moment arms and b the passive torque (root DOFs excluded; both derived in the supplementary). This closed-form, differentiable map is the Hill forward through which μ_θ is trained (§III-B) and the torque that drives MuJoCo.

    III-D3D Volumetric Muscle Simulation

    To achieve a stable, controllable, and realistic volumetric muscle simulation, three key challenges must be addressed: 1) anisotropic fiber force, 2) volume conservation, and 3) muscle–bone coupling. The first two drive the realism: the fiber force contracts the muscle along the fibers, while volume conservation makes it bulge in the orthogonal directions. Enforcing volume conservation is in turn limited by solver convergence: under the high stiffness muscle requires, an under-converged solve leaves visible artifacts and inverted tetrahedra. Muscle–bone coupling is governed by attachments: attachments that are too stiff distort the muscle, while those that are too soft fail to transmit force. We address them in turn. We embed the Hill-type curve into the constitutive law, so that per-fiber activation directly shortens the muscle along its fibers. We propose a GMG (Geometric Multigrid) solver for fast and stable simulation (§III-D2). Finally, we partition each muscle by masks into tendon and belly regions, attaching the tendons hard and the belly soft. We simulate the volumetric muscle with XPBD [16], giving first the solver update and the geometric multigrid that accelerates it, then the individual constraints.

    III-D1 XPBD Update

    The volumetric muscle deformation is driven by a set of position-based constraints: volume and shape preservation (§III-D3), anisotropic fiber contraction (§III-D4), attachment (§III-D5), and collision (§III-D6). Each is solved with the standard XPBD update:

    Δλ=(-C-α̃ λ)/(∑ᵢwᵢ\lVert∇C\rVert²+α̃),(9)
    Δxᵢ=wᵢ ∇C Δλ.(10)

    Here C is one of the constraint functions and ∇C its gradient with respect to the participating vertex positions. λ is the constraint’s accumulated Lagrange multiplier (reset to zero at the start of each time step) and Δλ is its per-iteration increment. α̃=1/(k Δt²) is the compliance, i.e. the inverse of the constraint stiffness k scaled by the squared time step Δt; a stiffer constraint thus has a smaller α̃. wᵢ is the inverse mass of vertex i, and Δxᵢ is the position correction applied to that vertex. Once all constraints have been projected, velocities are recovered from the position change over the step, v^f←(x^f-x^fₚᵣₑᵥ)/Δt. The individual constraints are defined next; each constraint’s gradient is derived in the supplementary.

    III-D2 Geometric Multigrid

    The geometric multigrid is a core contribution of this work: it is what makes our stiff, high-resolution volumetric muscle solve both stable and fast. Previous position-based hierarchies, such as HPBD [11], have two limitations: 1) they are formulated for cloth rather than tetrahedral meshes; 2) they do not close a complete V-cycle, so they act more like a low-resolution driver for the high-resolution mesh. Therefore, we develop a new algorithm for geometric multigrid XPBD that supports tetrahedral meshes with a Petrov–Galerkin restriction. We construct the two-level hierarchy by geometric coarsening: we first inflate the fine surface triangular mesh slightly, remesh it to a coarser triangle mesh, and then tetrahedralize it (Fig. 7). Our core insight is that the coarse tetrahedron acts as a “cage” that controls the motion of the fine vertices. The prolongator P is established by barycentric coordinates,

    x^f=x₀^f+∑ᵢ₌₁⁴wᵢ Δxᶜᵢ,(11)

    where w₁,…,w₄ are the barycentric coordinates of the fine vertex with respect to the coarse tetrahedron, with w₄=1-∑ᵢ₌₁³wᵢ. x₀^f is the fine position before the multigrid update. Each set of four weights for a tetrahedron defines a row of P. As in HPBD [11], we prolongate the coarse correction Δxᶜ instead of the direct coarse solution xᶜ.

    We define restriction as the least-squares state that best reproduces the fine state x^f within the cage subspace,

    xᶜ=*arg min_xᶜ \lVertP xᶜ-x^f\rVert₂²,

    		(12)

    whose normal equations give the Petrov–Galerkin restriction

    xᶜ=(P^⊤P)⁻¹P^⊤ (R) x^f.

    		(13)

    Since P has full column rank, R is the left pseudo-inverse of P, so restriction exactly recovers any coarse-level vector after prolongation, i.e., RP=I. A desirable property of this Petrov–Galerkin restriction is that it has RP=I, which is why we choose it over the Galerkin restriction R=P^⊤.

    Our restriction and prolongation processes are matrix-free and do not require explicit construction of the large sparse matrices P and R. Because every fine vertex is embedded in the cage of a single muscle, P, and hence P^⊤P, is block-diagonal across muscles, so Eq. (13) decouples into one small dense solve per muscle. We therefore precompute and store the per-muscle pseudo-inverse blocks (P^⊤P)⁻¹P^⊤ once, reducing restriction to a block-diagonal matrix–vector product at run time. The per-step volumetric simulation is summarized in Figure 8. Note that the multigrid can be easily switched off by skipping the restriction, coarse-solving, and prolongation steps, which reduces it to the classic XPBD algorithm.

    III-D3 Volume and Shape Preservation Constraints

    Incompressibility is enforced primarily by a Stable Neo-Hookean (SNH) material [25], cast as a coupled pair of XPBD constraints following Macklin and Müller [36], alongside an explicit volume constraint and an ARAP shape term:

    SNH Deviatoric: C_dev=\lVertF\rVert_F-√3,(14)
    SNH Hydrostatic: C_hyd=\detF-α, α=1+μ/λ,(15)
    Volume: Cᵥₒₗ=V-V₀,(16)
    ARAP: Cₐᵣₐₚ=\lVertF-R\rVert_F,(17)

    where F is the deformation gradient and R its rotation part, V and V₀ the current and rest volume, μ and λ the shear and bulk moduli, and α a rest-stability offset that makes the undeformed configuration an exact rest state of the energy. In SNH the hydrostatic term enforces incompressibility while the deviatoric term carries the shear response; the ARAP (As-Rigid-As-Possible) term further resists shear and preserves shape. For that term we found an SVD-based formulation with non-negative clamping [37] more robust than the polar-decomposition one.

    III-D4 Anisotropic Fiber Constraints

    We inject the 1D Hill law into the 3D medium as an energy-based fiber constraint. Whereas Lee et al. [6] realize the active fiber force through a first Piola–Kirchhoff stress, we formulate it at the position level for XPBD. The normalized fiber length of Eq. 7 is lifted from the 1D path measurement (§III-C) to the stretch of the deformation gradient F along the muscle’s rest fiber direction:

    λ_f=\lVertF d\rVert ≡ ℓ̃^M,

    		(18)

    where d is the unit fiber direction in the rest configuration. This 3D stretch is identically the 1D normalized fiber length: both are the current fiber length divided by its optimal (rest) length, so we keep ℓ̃^M for the 1D Hill curves and write λ_f for the same quantity in the 3D continuum. XPBD stores each elastic potential as the quadratic form Ψ=\tfrac12k C² with compliance α̃=1/(k V₀ Δt²), so setting \tfrac12C_fiber²=Ψ_fiber encodes the Hill strain energy directly in the constraint:

    Ψ_fiber=σ₀ ∫_λ_f,\min^λ_f fₕᵢₗₗ(s) ds, C_fiber=√2 Ψ_fiber,

    		(19)

    where fₕᵢₗₗ is given by Eq. 7, from which we drop f^V, fᵀ, and f^PE in the 3D medium. Because fₕᵢₗₗ is a piecewise quintic polynomial, the energy integral has a closed-form degree-10 polynomial per segment, avoiding numerical quadrature. Injecting the same Hill law that trains the policy makes the volumetric contraction obey exactly the constitutive relation the activations were solved against, and because only the along-fiber component is constrained, activation shortens the belly along d while volume conservation drives the orthogonal bulge. An anisotropic ARAP alternative is compared in §IV-D3; both constraints, their gradients, and the fiber stiffness are given in the supplementary.

    III-D5 Attachment Constraints

    The muscle is coupled to the skeleton by attachment constraints that drive attachment vertices toward their targets on the bone:

    C_attach=\lVertxᵢ-xᵢ^*\rVert-L₀,

    		(20)

    where xᵢ is the position of an attached vertex, xᵢ^* its target on the bone, and L₀ the rest length between the vertex and its target. The bone–muscle coupling is one-way, the rigid bone driving the deformable muscle, with targets found by a nearest-point search on the bone surface at the rest pose. Neighboring muscles are additionally tied to one another by inter-muscle springs, built once at the rest pose between nearby surface vertices of adjacent muscles; these keep the musculature bundled and are two-way, unlike the bone attachments. We use two kinds of attachment: pins, which are hard and impose the position directly, and springs, which are soft and allow some deformation. A user-painted mask assigns pins to the tendon regions near the origin and insertion and springs to the belly. The two are respectively Dirichlet and Robin boundary conditions.

    Their balance is a trade-off: too many pins drive up tetrahedron inversions and leave the surface unsmooth, while too few let the muscle lag behind and detach from the bone, most visibly on the thin, slender muscles that are dominated by these boundary conditions rather than by elasticity (§III-D2).

    III-D6 Collision Handling

    We handle muscle–bone collisions with an SDF [38]. Each bone is rigid, so its SDF φ_b is precomputed once at the rest pose and queried in the bone’s local frame, needing no per-substep tessellation or nearest-primitive search. A muscle surface vertex xₚ found to penetrate (φ_b<0) is resolved by a unilateral constraint projected alongside the other XPBD constraints,

    C_col=φ_b(xₚ), ∇C_col=∇φ_b(xₚ),

    		(21)

    which pushes the vertex back onto the bone surface along the SDF gradient and is released once it leaves the bone. We omit explicit muscle–muscle collision: neighboring muscles are already held apart by inter-muscle springs, and since the musculature is primarily bone-driven the residual inter-muscle penetration is minor. The broad/narrow-phase details and this trade-off are given in the supplementary.

    III-EMotion Retargeting and Muscle Mapping

    The RL stage operates on a 1D musculoskeletal asset, whereas the volumetric simulation runs on a 3D character with its own skeletal proportions and tetrahedral muscle meshes. Two transfer steps bridge the two representations (Fig. 2). Motion Retargeting: The 1D skeleton spans N_θ=50 actuated DOFs over 22 joints, the floating root aside (14 spherical joints at 3 DOF and 8 revolute joints at 1 DOF, i.e. 14×3+8×1=50). We first perform a joint-level retargeting to transfer the 1D skeleton motion onto the 3D skeleton, where 20 key points are selected and then full-body inverse kinematics is solved to recover the 3D joint angles. Muscle Mapping: Usually the 3D model and the 1D model do not have a one-to-one correspondence, so we similarly need to map the 284 1D Hill muscles onto the 194 3D volumetric muscles. The two assets differ in muscle count because they originate from different musculoskeletal models. We map them by anatomical semantic similarity and spatial correspondence, i.e., matching by anatomical name first and, for any muscle left unmatched, falling back to the nearest one. This step is optional if the two assets are already in one-to-one correspondence.

    IV Results

    We evaluate our system in four parts: a full-body demonstration on four motions (§IV-A), validation of the discovered activations against human sEMG (§IV-B), comparisons against production and neural volumetric muscle systems (§IV-C), and an ablation of each component (§IV-D). All RL policies are trained on the 1D Hill surrogate and the 3D volumetric simulation is run as a single forward pass at inference (§III-A).

    RL co-training is implemented in PyTorch, and the articulated body simulation used for training in MuJoCo [32], with 64 parallel environments per motion; the 3D simulation is implemented in Warp [39], is fully GPU accelerated, and runs on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X CPU. We adopt USD (Universal Scene Description) as the interchange format for all assets (skeletons, muscle tetrahedral meshes, fibers, and simulation caches), and render the final scenes in Houdini [15]. Training and simulation parameters are given in the supplementary.

    IV-AFull-Body Demonstration

    Figure 9 shows our full pipeline applied to four reference-motion clips that span a range of dynamic regimes: a periodic, ground-contact walk; a balance-critical kick that loads a single support leg; a free-floating swim driven by a surrogate fluid model [40]; and a squat that demands whole-body coordination under load. For each clip, the RL stage discovers per-muscle activations that track the reference on the 1D asset, and these activations drive the 194-muscle volumetric body through a single forward XPBD simulation. Each motion trains in under 2 hours, and the walk can be repeated indefinitely if the reference motion is cyclic. Table I reports the runtime and memory cost of this full-body volumetric simulation on a single RTX 4090. Swimming has no ground contact to react against, so rather than run a full fluid solver we give each body segment an ellipsoidal drag proxy [40] for the policy to push against.

    Figure 10 plots the tracking reward over the course of RL training for all four motions. Every curve rises steadily and plateaus near its maximum, confirming that the co-trained policy and muscle networks (Alg. 1) jointly converge to a high-quality tracking solution despite the underdetermined, non-negative, and nonlinear activation-to-torque map. Figure 11 quantifies the motion quality of a deterministic rollout of the trained walk (300 control steps at 30 Hz). Panel (a) is the joint-angle tracking error, the SO(3) geodesic distance penalized by rₚₒₛₑ in Eq. 3, averaging 10.5^∘ over the 18 tracked joints. Panel (b) is the COM-aligned position error of the five end effectors behind rₑₑ in Eq. 3, averaging 49 mm. Panel (c) is the relative torque residual, a scale-free counterpart of L_torque in Eq. 4, at 17.8% on average. Panel (d) is the mean activation over all muscles, the same minimum-effort quantity as L_reg in Eq. 4 but without the square, at 0.061. Together these show that the generated motion tracks the reference closely, yet does not follow it exactly: the activations have to keep the motion physically feasible, which is precisely what we expect.

    IV-BValidation Against EMG

    We now test the effect of the EMG prior on physiological plausibility, comparing the recovered activations against the Moreira sEMG [10] following the synergist-group and gait-alignment protocol of §III-B4 (Fig. 12).

    Without the prior, the policy leaves the human ±1 std band over most of the gait cycle (Fig. 12, left; mean in-band 20%, mean correlation -0.04), confirming that the redundancy is resolved non-physiologically. Adding it to muscle-network training steers that redundancy toward the measured solution while leaving the policy’s motion objective untouched: the recovered activations now track real sEMG (Fig. 12, right; mean in-band 91%, mean correlation 0.97, all on/off timings aligned) and still drive a stable, faithful gait, at negligible cost and without degrading the visual fidelity of the volumetric deformation. Activation–EMG mismatch in tracking-only controllers is widely reported [5, 2, 1]; our prior offers a simple remedy.

    IV-CComparison with Baselines

    We compare against two representative volumetric muscle systems: Houdini’s Otis solver [41], the production standard, and the recent neural musculoskeletal skin-deformation model of Han et al. [29] (Epic). Otis hand-authors activations from tension lines and simulates the motion with Vertex Block Descent [42]; Han et al. recover activations by a per-pose quasistatic equilibrium solve and deform an ML skinning model [30] trained on XPBD. Ours are learned inside the RL control loop and are exactly the forces that drive the motion (§III-B). We compare all three on the same reference pose. We could not include Lee et al. [6]. Their optimization-based controller re-runs the volumetric solver inside the control loop. This has caused repeated non-convergence, which then makes the control learning fail constantly. We therefore exclude it from the baseline methods.

    Figure 13 colors our muscle surface (left) by its per-vertex distance to the Otis reference (right) on the same full-body pose. Over most of the body the deviation stays within a few millimeters (blue–green), with larger deviations (yellow–red) at localized regions such as the thighs and shoulders, showing that our physically actuated muscles reproduce production-quality volumetric geometry. The two differ sharply in cost: our GPU solver runs at 18 ms/frame (Table I), whereas Otis, parallelized on the CPU through OpenCL, takes 20.8 s/frame on the same AMD Ryzen 9 5950X workstation. Figure 14 repeats this comparison against Han et al. [29]: the deviation stays small (blue) over most of the torso and grows (yellow–red) at the forearms and mid-abdomen, where the two pipelines differ most in musculature. In both cases the surfaces are close, and the essential difference is provenance: our deformation is produced by the forward-dynamic forces that generate the motion.

    IV-DAblation Study

    We ablate each major component of the volumetric pipeline (geometric multigrid, collision handling, and the Hill-type fiber constraint) to isolate its contribution.

    IV-D1 Effect of Multigrid

    We evaluate our multigrid solver in two complementary settings: a squashed-bunny benchmark, and a full-body volumetric muscle model.

    Squashed-bunny benchmark. The bunny (850K fine tetrahedra over a 5K coarse cage) is compressed and released to bounce back under identical parameters with and without multigrid (MG). Figure 15 shows MG converges faster with better deformation quality, its main cost being the coarse-level solve. Table II confirms this: MG reaches a fixed tolerance (constraint C<=0.1, 2-norm for vector C) in 53 frames and 49.1 ms vs. 621 frames and 418.9 ms without (11.7× fewer steps, 8.5× faster), and at 81 frames reaches C=0.082 where the fine-only solver stalls at C=0.979. Its small per-frame overhead (0.84 vs. 0.59 ms) is far outweighed by the fewer steps needed.

    Full-body muscle. Figure 16 shows these benefits carry over to the full-body volumetric muscle model. MG is what makes our high-stiffness volumetric simulation both stable and efficient. Figure 16 (bottom) quantifies this on the same example as Figure 13: MG holds both the constraint residual and the inverted-tetrahedron count far lower throughout the deformation, roughly a 3.7× reduction in peak inversions.

    IV-D2 Effect of Collision

    We ablate the collision handling of §III-D6 by disabling the muscle–bone collision constraints and re-running the same activation trajectory. Figure 17 compares the two: with collision handling the muscle bellies slide cleanly over the bones, whereas without it they sink in, concentrated around the knee and lower leg where the muscles wrap most tightly around the skeleton. Enabling collision handling essentially eliminates these interpenetrations.

    IV-D3 Effect of the Fiber Constraint

    We isolate the fiber constraint on a biceps brachii held by a single proximal tendon anchor, leaving the belly free to contract as activation ramps from 0 to 1. Four constraints are compared under an identical setup: (i) no fiber force, (ii) a plain stretch constraint C=\lVertFd\rVert, (iii) our Hill–Millard energy constraint (Eq. 19), and (iv) an anisotropic ARAP alternative [23, 24], built on Kim et al.’s anisotropic invariants and driving the along-fiber stretch toward an activation-set target through a symmetric quadratic well; its invariants, constraint, gradients, and a constitutive comparison against ours are given in the supplementary. Figure 18 reports the biceps’ shortening and girth change at full activation: about 21% shortening for Hill–Millard, 18% for the plain constraint, and 13% for anisotropic ARAP. Hill–Millard reproduces the exact 1D force–length law.

    V Limitations and Future Work

    Ideally, we would incorporate the 3D volumetric muscle simulation into the RL training loop. We tried this integrated pipeline first, but it proved slow, unstable, and uncontrollable for RL training. The difficulty originates from the two-way bone–muscle coupling: spring-based attachments are the naive strategy, but their stiffness has no physiological basis and is hard to tune, since how many springs to use and how stiff they should be are entirely unknown. We therefore use the 1D Hill model as a training surrogate and a separate 3D simulation for evaluation. We hope to achieve “3D-in-the-loop” training in future work, which requires two things: a stable and efficient rigid–deformable coupled simulation method, and a physiologically grounded coupling strategy. In addition, while our multigrid performs well on bulky muscles, it is less satisfactory on long, slender muscles, such as some of the muscles near the distal end of the forearm. We attribute this to two factors. First, our geometric coarsening struggles to produce a good coarse mesh for such thin, elongated geometry. Second, because these slender muscles are light and small in volume, their motion is governed more by the boundary conditions (the pin/attachment constraints) than by elastic response, whereas our multigrid is designed to accelerate the elasticity solve. We therefore exclude these slender muscles from the multigrid and solve them at the fine level only.

    VI Conclusion

    We have presented a system that recovers physically consistent muscle activations from a reference motion and turns them into volumetric muscle deformation. Reinforcement learning first explores the muscle activations on a fast 1D Hill-type surrogate, co-training a policy and a muscle network in a single PPO loop and steering the redundant activation solution toward measured human recruitment through an EMG prior. A GPU-parallel XPBD solver then simulates the volumetric muscles under the same Hill-type constitutive law, injected as an energy-based fiber constraint, with a geometric multigrid keeping the stiff solve stable and efficient.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 能渲染不等于能用：FunCAD 让 agent 把需求翻成物理测试，机构设计从「看着像」变成「真能动」 ｜ Can It Actually Work? Synthesizing Functional CAD Mechanisms
item.description:
一句话：把抽象需求翻成针对具体候选的物理测试，用仿真反馈指导修改，46 个机构族做验收。

要点：

  • FunCAD-Harness 把抽象需求翻译成针对具体候选的物理测试，再用仿真反馈指导设计修订，而不是只看渲染结果
  • FunCADBench 覆盖 46 个机构族，包含相互依赖的多步操作；不同机构可能用完全不同的零件、控制与操作序列实现同一功能
  • 前沿 LLM agent 在视觉检查下「看着没问题」的设计，被物理测试暴露出细微机械失效；按功能组织测试后整任务成功率显著高于只给仿真工具

为什么值得看：「AI 造资产」的验收标准必须落在物理测试而不是渲染图。这套 harness 等于给引擎侧资产管线补了一道可执行验收：功能需求 → 测试用例 → 仿真反馈 → 修订，这个回路同样适用于自动化关卡与机关设计。

中文摘要：LLM agent 能生成看起来合理的 CAD 装配体，但这些设计往往完不成预期物理功能。作者把问题定义为功能化 CAD 设计：agent 要理解欠明确的请求，构造机构并在物理仿真中反复修订直到满足功能要求。难点在验证——同一个功能可以由完全不同的零件、控制与操作序列实现，因此测试必须是候选相关的。FunCAD-Harness 就是把抽象需求翻译成这种候选特定物理测试的框架，用仿真反馈驱动修订；配套的 FunCADBench 覆盖 46 个机构族，包含相互依赖的多步操作。实验显示，前沿 LLM agent 的设计在视觉检查下看似无误，却被物理测试抓出细微机械失效；按功能组织测试后，整任务成功率明显优于只提供仿真工具的做法。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-27

Can It Actually Work?
Synthesizing Functional CAD Mechanisms

Abstract

While LLM agents can generate visually plausible CAD assemblies, these designs often fail to fulfill their intended physical functions. We study functional CAD design, a setting where agents interpret underspecified requests to construct and iteratively revise mechanisms that satisfy functional requirements in physical simulation. Verifying these requirements is nontrivial: different candidate mechanisms may realize the same function through entirely different components, controls, and operating sequences. To bridge this gap, we propose FunCAD-Harness, a framework that translates abstract requirements into candidate-specific physical tests and uses simulation feedback to guide design revisions. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce FunCADBench, a benchmark spanning 46 mechanism families with interdependent and multi-step operations. Experiments across frontier LLM agents show that FunCAD-Harness exposes subtle mechanical failures invisible to visual inspection, substantially improving functional success rates over standard simulation-augmented baselines. Ultimately, our work marks a step toward CAD agents capable of translating human intent into working mechanisms.

thegenlab.ai/funcad/

1 Introduction

A longstanding ambition for generative AI is to turn human intentions into machines that can be built and made to work. Recent progress in LLM agents brings this ambition closer, enabling them to write modeling programs and operate CAD software to construct sophisticated mechanical designs for fabrication by 3D printing or CNC machining. Yet a visually plausible CAD model does not ensure that the resulting machine will fulfill the user’s request, because its function depends on how its parts interact physically during operation. Even an assembly with valid parts and plausible articulation can fail to transmit a load, maintain contact, or return to a state that permits the next operation. A gripper, for example, may grasp an object successfully but leave it poorly positioned after release, preventing the next grasp.
