一句话：把抽象需求翻成针对具体候选的物理测试，用仿真反馈指导修改，46 个机构族做验收。

要点：

  • FunCAD-Harness 把抽象需求翻译成针对具体候选的物理测试，再用仿真反馈指导设计修订，而不是只看渲染结果
  • FunCADBench 覆盖 46 个机构族，包含相互依赖的多步操作；不同机构可能用完全不同的零件、控制与操作序列实现同一功能
  • 前沿 LLM agent 在视觉检查下「看着没问题」的设计，被物理测试暴露出细微机械失效；按功能组织测试后整任务成功率显著高于只给仿真工具

为什么值得看：「AI 造资产」的验收标准必须落在物理测试而不是渲染图。这套 harness 等于给引擎侧资产管线补了一道可执行验收：功能需求 → 测试用例 → 仿真反馈 → 修订，这个回路同样适用于自动化关卡与机关设计。

中文摘要：LLM agent 能生成看起来合理的 CAD 装配体，但这些设计往往完不成预期物理功能。作者把问题定义为功能化 CAD 设计：agent 要理解欠明确的请求，构造机构并在物理仿真中反复修订直到满足功能要求。难点在验证——同一个功能可以由完全不同的零件、控制与操作序列实现，因此测试必须是候选相关的。FunCAD-Harness 就是把抽象需求翻译成这种候选特定物理测试的框架，用仿真反馈驱动修订；配套的 FunCADBench 覆盖 46 个机构族，包含相互依赖的多步操作。实验显示，前沿 LLM agent 的设计在视觉检查下看似无误，却被物理测试抓出细微机械失效；按功能组织测试后，整任务成功率明显优于只提供仿真工具的做法。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-27

Can It Actually Work?
Synthesizing Functional CAD Mechanisms

Abstract

While LLM agents can generate visually plausible CAD assemblies, these designs often fail to fulfill their intended physical functions. We study functional CAD design, a setting where agents interpret underspecified requests to construct and iteratively revise mechanisms that satisfy functional requirements in physical simulation. Verifying these requirements is nontrivial: different candidate mechanisms may realize the same function through entirely different components, controls, and operating sequences. To bridge this gap, we propose FunCAD-Harness, a framework that translates abstract requirements into candidate-specific physical tests and uses simulation feedback to guide design revisions. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce FunCADBench, a benchmark spanning 46 mechanism families with interdependent and multi-step operations. Experiments across frontier LLM agents show that FunCAD-Harness exposes subtle mechanical failures invisible to visual inspection, substantially improving functional success rates over standard simulation-augmented baselines. Ultimately, our work marks a step toward CAD agents capable of translating human intent into working mechanisms.

thegenlab.ai/funcad/

1 Introduction

A longstanding ambition for generative AI is to turn human intentions into machines that can be built and made to work. Recent progress in LLM agents brings this ambition closer, enabling them to write modeling programs and operate CAD software to construct sophisticated mechanical designs for fabrication by 3D printing or CNC machining. Yet a visually plausible CAD model does not ensure that the resulting machine will fulfill the user’s request, because its function depends on how its parts interact physically during operation. Even an assembly with valid parts and plausible articulation can fail to transmit a load, maintain contact, or return to a state that permits the next operation. A gripper, for example, may grasp an object successfully but leave it poorly positioned after release, preventing the next grasp. Because fabricating and assembling each candidate is costly, physical simulation offers a practical way to examine these interactions under specified inputs and loads and use the resulting feedback to revise the design.

Verifying a design through physical simulation, however, requires tests that reflect both the user’s intended function and the way the candidate mechanism realizes it. Users often describe what they want a machine to accomplish without specifying all the behaviors needed to achieve it. Even when these requirements are made explicit, they do not uniquely determine an experiment, because the same function can be realized by mechanisms that operate differently. For an alarm that must trigger autonomously at a requested time, a gravity-powered design requires raising a weight, whereas a mainspring-powered design requires winding. A test designed around one mechanism can therefore be inappropriate for the other, even though the intended function is unchanged.

We study whether LLM agents can carry this process from an underspecified request to a CAD mechanism that satisfies its functional requirements in simulation, a problem we term functional CAD design. To examine how far current agents can go on this task, we introduce FunCADBench, a benchmark spanning 46 mechanism families. Its tasks range from clamps and transmissions to mechanical counters, alarm clocks, and coin-sorting devices, whose functions depend on different combinations of geometry, force transmission, and changing contact states. Each task specifies a fixed request and an abstract functional test template while leaving the mechanical realization open. Success requires the resulting assembly to perform the complete requested behavior and satisfy the applicable geometric and physical constraints. Since repeated physical simulation can be costly for complex mechanisms, we develop a customized simulation environment to support efficient benchmark evaluation.

For this specific task, we develop FunCAD-Harness, which translates user requests into task requirements and abstract physical test templates. It then determines test conditions appropriate to the candidate mechanism and uses structured simulation feedback to guide design revision. Fig. 1 illustrates this workflow through an open-ended cup-access design and its printed prototype.

With FunCAD-Harness, we evaluate frontier models and baseline workflows on FunCADBench and find that structured physical testing and diagnostic feedback improve task success. The model comparisons also show that strong visual 3D modeling capabilities do not necessarily translate into superior functional design. To better understand how agents approach this task, we analyze their tool use and observe that they rely primarily on CAD programs and simulation, with little use of rendered images. Testing the role of visual access directly, a separate experiment shows that substantial task success remains possible when it is removed from the constructor.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    We formulate functional CAD design, in which agents translate underspecified requests into mechanisms that fulfill their intended functions in simulation, and introduce FunCADBench, spanning 46 mechanism families, with a simulation environment for efficient physical evaluation.

  • •

    We develop FunCAD-Harness, which derives requirements and abstract test templates from user requests, constructs physical tests suited to candidate mechanisms, and uses structured simulation feedback to guide iterative design and revision.

  • •

    We systematically evaluate frontier agents and baseline workflows, demonstrating the benefits of physical testing and diagnostic feedback. Our analyses further reveal performance–cost tradeoffs and recurring challenges in functional mechanical design.

    • 2 Related Work

    Mechanical design and AI for engineering. Mechanical design connects intended functions to the structure and motion of mechanisms [(Reuleaux, 2013)]. Computational approaches optimize mechanisms and structural topology [(Coros et al., 2013; Bendsøe et al., 2004)], while learned models predict performance and generate candidate designs [(Umetani & Bickel, 2018; Regenwetter et al., 2022)]. Co-design accounts for dependencies between morphology, motion, and control [(Ha et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2022)], and between hardware and software under resource and compatibility constraints [(Carlone & Pinciroli, 2019)]. LLMs connect natural-language specifications to design generation, analysis, and optimization tools [(Makatura et al., 2023)]. Executable evaluation supports both benchmarking, as in EngDesign’s cross-domain design tasks [(Guo et al., 2025)], and search, as in VLMgineer’s simulation-guided evolutionary co-design of robot-mounted tool geometry and action waypoints [(Gao et al., 2026)]. Closest to our setting, BesiegeField studies compositional machine design from textual functional demands, assembling standardized components in a game-based simulator and using simulation rewards and state feedback to revise the assembly [(Zhang et al., 2026)]. Our CAD setting expands the design space beyond predefined blocks: agents jointly synthesize part geometry, assembly structure, and operating inputs to realize the requested functions, producing CAD models that provide a basis for eventual fabrication.

    Programmatic CAD and physically grounded assets. Programmatic CAD and graphics representations make modeling operations and part composition editable [(Ritchie et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025)], with compilation, rendered views, and CAD-engine diagnostics providing feedback on geometric fidelity and modeling validity [(Alrashedy et al., 2025; Gong et al., 2026)]. Assembly benchmarks extend evaluation to functionality, manufacturability, and assemblability through executable geometry checks and drawing-based VLM judgments under supplied assembly graphs and engineering constraints [(Dong et al., 2026)]. Articulated-asset generation further tests how parts interact, using agent-authored checks of contact, clearance, containment, and pose-dependent relations [(Zhou et al., 2026)], or independent review and physical simulation of collisions, stability, and manipulation feasibility for coupled motions [(Cai et al., 2026)]. Whereas these approaches assess the realization and functional usability of specified objects, FunCADBench evaluates alternative mechanism architectures against a functional request’s complete operating requirements, including load transmission and dependent or repeated operations.

    Agent workflows, harnesses, and executable evaluation. Agent interfaces and runtimes organize tool use, context, and execution feedback [(Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025)], while automated search optimizes workflows and full harness programs against supplied evaluators [(Zhang et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026)]. Executable checks also guide artifact construction within a workflow, from stage gates for robot-learning environments, interfaces, rewards, and training configurations [(Li et al., 2026)] to geometric checks and finite-element stress and safety-factor feedback for structural CAD under prescribed loads, supports, and design-space constraints [(Berger et al., 2026)]. To accommodate generated implementations, software testing can adapt test inputs against a trusted reference and retain counterexamples for regression testing [(Kato, 2026)], or bind fixed functional tests to implementation-specific identifiers [(Liu et al., 2025)]. FunCAD-Harness extends candidate-specific test binding to operating mechanisms whose geometry, assembly, and inputs vary across designs. Registered requirements and abstract test templates remain fixed, while actuation, loads, and observations are bound to each candidate for simulation and source-geometry checks. This evaluates complete mechanism operation rather than structural response to a prescribed load case, and supplies feedback for structural revision.

    3 FunCADBench: Benchmark for Functional CAD Design

    3.1 Functional CAD design

    Mechanical design involves production cost, manufacturing processes, and regulatory requirements as well as mechanical behavior [(Pahl et al., 2007; Nisbett & Budynas, 2020)]. We focus on interpreting high-level user requests and determining whether a CAD mechanism fulfills the intended functions under appropriate physical conditions [(Zhang et al., 2026)]. Formally speaking, each task of functional CAD design is specified by a natural-language request describing a mechanism’s intended use. The request establishes its functional requirements, which describe the behaviors to achieve, and fixed constraints, which must be preserved throughout design. The agent produces a candidate design together with declared physical assumptions. Different mechanical implementations are acceptable as long as they satisfy these requirements; for example, a clamp may use different actuation mechanisms, but it must still close, hold an object, and release it.

    3.2 Task Families and Taxonomy

    To evaluate frontier LLM agents on this task across different mechanical demands, we introduce FunCADBench, a benchmark spanning 46 mechanism families (representative mechanisms are shown in Fig. 2). These range from elementary assemblies to coupled transmissions and devices with sequential or repeated operation. Fig. 3 shows mechanisms that LLM agents built for all 46 families in our experiments. Many of these families are drawn from familiar artifacts, such as clamps, whose intended uses can be described without specifying their internal mechanics. Several families pose open-ended mechanism design tasks that leave key architectural choices to the constructor. For example, the four-station indexing table (Task 40) must convert continuous input rotation into intermittent motion with dwell, without prescribing the indexing mechanism. We choose these families to cover different combinations of challenges along these axes–motion primitives, topology, complexity, contact, and geometric difficulty–each drawing on different agent capabilities (Table 1).

    3.3 Physical Evaluation and Success Criteria

    Functional requirements specify what an assembly must accomplish, while its mechanical realization determines how those functions can be tested. Similar to the separation between test logic and implementation-specific parameters in ProjectEval [(Liu et al., 2025)], we define abstract test templates for the required behaviors and bind them to each candidate mechanism, while keeping the requests and templates fixed across candidates for registered benchmark tasks. This binding identifies the candidate’s operating interfaces (e.g., bicycle handlebars) and observation signals, and specifies the inputs, loads, physical attributes, and environmental conditions needed to execute the template. These choices reflect how the mechanism operates while preserving the task’s required functions and fixed constraints. Parameters left open by the task may be selected or revised within its permitted scope (Appendix A.4). Given these parameters, we run physical simulation and record feedback signals, including forces, positions, and contact or collision events, for the relevant mechanical modules. The assembly succeeds under the task’s simulation protocol if it passes all required functional checks and all applicable source-geometry checks (e.g., collision checks) under its declared operating conditions.

    3.4 Simulation Environment

    Physical evaluation and repeated design revision require tests that can run within an agent’s working budget. Our simulation environment uses Project Chrono [(Tasora et al., 2016)] for rigid-body dynamics and Bullet [(Coumans, 2015)] for collision detection. Since resolving detailed mechanical interactions can be costly, the environment also supports equivalent models. Gear couplings, for example, represent transmission between rotating components without resolving individual tooth contacts [(Coros et al., 2013; Tasora et al., 2016)].

    When configuring a physical test, the agents choose between native simulation and a declared equivalent model for each interaction, recording its parameters and assumptions. If an equivalent model is used, it specifies force or torque laws for the corresponding source components, leaving the native solver to compute the resulting motion without prescribing output trajectories. Connections remain tied to finite regions of the source geometry and are released if those regions separate. The resulting motion provides the basis for functional checks, while separate audits examine the original CAD geometry at sampled poses. Appendix D describes the interaction models, audit scope, and execution procedure.

    4 Agentic Harness for Functional CAD Design

    A mechanism’s design determines how its functions can be tested, and the test results in turn inform how the design should change. FunCAD-Harness organizes this interaction into a closed loop for developing and revising CAD mechanisms (Fig. 5). Building on agentic CAD generation [(Zhou et al., 2026)] and simulation-based machine design [(Zhang et al., 2026)], the harness pairs a constructor responsible for mechanism design with a test-binding agent responsible for preparing physical tests.

    4.1 Functional requirements and test templates

    The constructor starts from a text prompt specifying the functional requirements, which describe what the mechanism must accomplish while leaving its mechanical realization open. A request for an alarm clock, for example, may require it to trigger autonomously at a specified time without prescribing a particular escapement design. Each test template specifies the operations, observations, and success criteria for verifying the requested behavior, leaving mechanism-dependent details to candidate-specific binding. For the 46 registered FunCADBench tasks, both prompts and test templates remain fixed across candidate designs.

    For requests outside the registered benchmark, the constructor first identifies the required functions, fixed constraints, and open operating parameters from the prompt, then proposes a test template. The test-binding agent checks its coverage and executability, and the constructor revises it accordingly. This additional template-authoring step is separate from the candidate-specific binding used to evaluate registered benchmark tasks.

    4.2 CAD construction and physical testing

    With the requirements and test templates in place, the constructor develops the CAD geometry, connections, operating inputs, and physical assumptions. The test-binding agent then binds each template to the candidate’s operating inputs and observable states without changing its geometry or declared mechanics. For the winch in Fig. 5, this involves identifying the handle, release control, and load attachment and configuring tests of lifting, holding, release, and re-locking. The parameters needed to execute these tests come from the task, geometry, design documentation, or task-authorized constructor choices. Their sources and any permitted adjustments are retained as described in Appendix A.4.

    Once the physical experiments have been specified through binding, the harness executes them without changing the CAD design between tests and checks the original geometry at sampled motion poses (Section 3.3). The execution program determines the outcomes from the recorded signals and applicable geometry checks.

    4.3 Revision from physical feedback

    These outcomes return to the constructor as per-function results, accompanied by physical signals, failed checks, geometry violations, and execution errors. Using this feedback, the constructor diagnoses failures and revises the geometry, connections, permitted operating parameters, or simulation representations. Since a revision may affect several functions, the test-binding agent updates the candidate-specific bindings for all required functions, and the harness reruns the full set of tests on the revised assembly.

    5 Experiments and Results

    5.1 Functional Design Performance

    We evaluate GPT-6 Astra, Kimi K3, Fable 5.1, and Grok 4.6 with FunCAD-Harness on all 46 tasks (details in Table 7), allowing one independent attempt per family within a three-hour active-time budget. Each model drives its own ReAct loop [(Yao et al., 2023)] for CAD construction, testing, and revision, with internal tests and revisions included in the generation process.

    After each batch of generation runs, we evaluate the resulting assemblies in a separate batch using GPT-6 Astra with a one-million-token context allowance and medium reasoning. The final-evaluation model, context allowance, and reasoning setting remain the same across all generation models and comparison settings, including Grok + history. The evaluation agent configures candidate-specific physical tests under the task’s required functions and fixed constraints, and the execution program determines their outcomes. Appendix E.1 provides the model settings and time-accounting details.

    Across the four models, agents solve 34 of the 46 tasks (Fig. 6). All four succeed on most low-complexity tasks, but their performance diverges on more demanding mechanisms. Every task solved exclusively by Fable has medium or high complexity, although even this strongest model solves only five of the 15 high-complexity tasks. We also compare success across the benchmark’s demand axes by weighting each task according to its requirement grade on the corresponding axis. All four models have their lowest weighted success rate on the contact axis, which covers engagement, release, friction, and changes in contact state.

    We also evaluate Grok with up to eight attempts per task and access to records from earlier attempts. This setting solves 36 tasks, including six unsolved by any model in the default setting, at a lower median cumulative constructor API cost than Astra’s default runs.

    5.2 Harness Comparisons

    To assess the contribution of structured physical testing, we compare FunCAD-Harness with three alternative workflows (Table 2). In the requirements-only and simulation-tools baselines, agents choose their own tests and may implement their own simulations. The binary-feedback variant retains the full harness workflow but returns only pass/fail simulation outcomes. We also test whether visual access contributes to construction and revision by repeating the Astra and Grok full-harness experiments with visual access removed only from the constructor. The other agents retain their standard visual access. All settings undergo independent final evaluation under the same protocol.

    Simulation access and whole-task success. Providing simulation tools improves success over requirements alone, and the full harness raises it further, from 8 to 22 tasks for Astra and from 10 to 19 for Grok. These gains span motion transmission and locking through mechanical contact. Both models additionally solve the rack-and-pinion gate, four-bar wiper, and hand-cranked whisk (Tasks 2–4), as well as the self-locking knife and spring-latch lock (Tasks 5 and 33).

    Access to simulation does not, however, ensure that the tests cover the complete requested behavior. In the simulation-tools setting, Astra tests a clock’s escapement for ten simulated minutes and its striker separately, but leaves the sequence of setting, triggering, and stopping the alarm while preserving timekeeping unverified. The delivered hour wheel also interferes with the alarm lever (Fig. 7b).

    Retaining functional checks through revision. Functional checks can also be lost during repair. In the simulation-tools setting, Grok replaces a numerically invalid loaded test of a ratchet screwdriver (Task 13) with a short stepping test, leaving the drive and return-stroke requirements unchecked. A separate full-harness run retains these checks, revealing that all four stroke checks pass but both checks for backward slip of the output fail.

    Diagnostic feedback and workflow completion. When a test fails, diagnostic feedback helps the constructor identify what needs to change. The full harness reports failed requirements, measured discrepancies, and physical-validity violations that can distinguish failure causes and guide repairs. Removing these diagnostics reduces recorded success from 22 to zero tasks for Astra and from 19 to eight for Grok. Astra’s binary-feedback runs include early delivery of partial results, so its zero successes include unfinished evaluation as well as failed checks. The benefit of diagnostic feedback extends to continued testing as well as design revision.

    5.3 Design and Revision Behavior

    Repairing failures in repeated operation. Fable’s gripper (Task 41) passes a short development test, but formal repeated-use testing reveals that the workpiece tips after release, causing the next grasp to miss it. The second grasp records 0 N against a 10 N minimum. Fable responds by widening the contact pads and support rest and reducing the permitted input-force limit from 50 to 35 N. The revised design leaves the workpiece positioned for reuse, and its second grasp reaches 14.40 N under the unchanged 5 N external load. Both grasp–release cycles and the geometry audit pass (Fig. 11).

    Restoring function can still leave geometric interference to resolve. In Grok’s spring-return door latch (Task 33), the latch initially rests on the strike-plate edge after closure, failing both re-locking checks while passing the other 13 functional checks. Grok reshapes the entry bevel and adds a catching shoulder, restoring engagement after both closures and passing all 15 functional checks. It then adds local relief to the faceplate to resolve the remaining latch–faceplate interference. The final revision passes both the functional checks and the audit of the original CAD geometry under unchanged test parameters (Fig. 8).

    Verification strategies and visual access. We analyze tool use on 41 task families with recorded harness-tool execution times for all four models (Appendix E.6, Fig. 9). Fable and Grok devote larger shares of their calls to reading requirements, documentation, and source code. Astra devotes more to simulation, geometric checks, and analysis of test results and traces, with a higher share of simulation calls than Fable on 40 of the 41 matched tasks. Despite these differences in call distribution, simulation-related operations account for 75–85% of recorded harness-tool execution time on average across tasks for every model.

    Agents obtain geometric and physical information primarily through CAD programs and simulation, with little use of rendered images. Without visual access, Astra’s constructor still succeeds on 20 of the 46 tasks, compared with 22 with visual access (Table 2). Grok shows a similar pattern, completing 18 tasks without visual access compared with 19 with it. Substantial functional design success therefore remains possible without visual inspection during construction and revision. Appendix F.5 provides the protocol and task-level results.

    5.4 Tool Use and Execution Time

    We analyze tool use on 41 tasks with timing records available for all four models (Fig. 9). Fable and Grok devote larger shares of their calls to reading requirements, documentation, and source code, whereas Astra devotes more to simulation, geometric checks, and feedback analysis. These differences in call frequency do not translate into equally different execution-time profiles. For every model, simulation and cost probes account for approximately 75–85% of recorded tool execution time, even when they make up a small share of calls. Their cost highlights the importance of efficient simulation for repeated design revision. Across models, visual inspection remains infrequent, consistent with agents obtaining geometric and physical information primarily through CAD programs and numerical feedback.

    5.5 Real-world Fabrication

    We 3D-printed and assembled prototypes to complement the simulation-based evaluation with qualitative examples of fabrication and assembly. Figure 10 shows selected prototypes, and supplementary videos document their operation. Additional examples appear in Figure 16 in Appendix G.

    6 Discussions

    From simulation to fabrication. Turning a simulated mechanism into a working machine requires accounting for uncertainty in both physics models and fabrication. Contact and friction approximations, manufacturing tolerances, assembly misalignment, and material variation can change whether parts slide, engage, or jam. Experiments with selected prototypes could calibrate uncertain parameters and identify missing effects, following approaches that calibrate simulators from real-world robot trajectories [(Chebotar et al., 2019)]. Testing over plausible parameter ranges would then assess robustness to fabrication and operating conditions. The same prototype measurements could also help adapt world models, which offer fast predictions of rigid, articulated, and deformable interactions [(Huang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025)]. Such adaptation could capture effects that are difficult to model explicitly and make repeated design tests more affordable.

    Coverage of functional tests. Improving simulation fidelity does not by itself ensure that the tests cover the intended behavior. Functional CAD design shares this challenge with project-level software generation in ProjectEval [(Liu et al., 2025)], where a high-level request must be translated into an artifact whose components work together. In both settings, ambiguous requirements and incomplete test suites can leave functions unchecked, while component tests may miss interactions. For mechanical systems, these interactions also depend on loads, initial states, and operation sequences, which determine contacts and the states available to later operations. Future harnesses could cover more of these conditions by combining requirement review and reusable engineering tests with automated searches for failure cases within the intended operating range [(Formica et al., 2024)]. The resulting tests could guide revisions and check that later designs preserve previously verified behavior.

    Multimodal interface fluency and physical reasoning. Despite its impressive visual 3D reconstruction capabilities [(Sun et al., 2026)], Astra does not dominate functional CAD design. Fable solves more tasks, while Grok with additional attempts and retained history exceeds the best default result at a lower median cumulative constructor API cost than Astra. This contrast raises the possibility that visual modeling performance partly reflects multimodal interface fluency rather than a corresponding advantage in physical reasoning. Our agents obtain geometric and physical information primarily through CAD programs and simulation, and Astra retains substantial task success when its constructor has no visual access. Given that targeted post-training can develop proficiency in computer-use and CAD workflows [(Ramrakhya et al., 2025; Gong et al., 2026)], training on these design–test–repair trajectories could improve functional design capabilities. Harnesses that help agents reuse prior designs and feedback could further improve the cost–performance tradeoff.

    7 Concluding Remarks

    Turning a high-level request into a functional CAD mechanism requires connecting the intended behavior to physical tests that reflect how the design operates. Through FunCADBench and its 46 mechanism families, we study this connection and develop FunCAD-Harness to use the resulting feedback for design revision. Our experiments show that organizing physical testing around the requested functions substantially improves whole-task success over providing simulation tools alone, helping agents repair failures in coupled and repeated operations. These findings highlight the importance of integrating functional verification into generation as LLM agents move from constructing 3D geometry toward designing mechanisms for practical use.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix

    Appendix A Prompts and Model-Visible Materials

    A.1 Task prompts and constructor instructions

    Each of the 46 registered task prompts combines family-specific functional requirements with shared CAD-delivery instructions. The requirements specify the intended use, required functions, permitted operations, and fixed constraints, while leaving the choice of geometry and assembly structure to the constructor. Attempts on the same registered family use the same task text; additional harness instructions describe the available tools and provide run-specific information, including the execution budget. Experiment-specific task adjustment (operating/performance parameters) are recorded separately from the original registered text. Fig. 5 presents an abbreviated description of the Task 42 winch task, whose functional requirements include lifting with reduction, holding against reverse load, and release followed by re-locking.

    The box below summarizes the principal instructions provided to the constructor during the experiments, retaining their design, delivery, and verification requirements while omitting file organization and execution details.

    These instructions separate mechanical construction from formal test binding: the constructor delivers the mechanism and its operating instructions, the test-binding agent binds the formal tests, and the program determines their outcomes from execution evidence.

    A.2 Harness Tool Descriptions and Returned Information

    The harness provides tools for building, previewing, checking, and simulating candidate mechanisms. Formal evaluation combines source preparation, independent test binding, physical execution, and source-geometry auditing.

    Source preparation loads the delivered geometry and physical scene for evaluation. After independent binding, interface checks verify that the required inputs and observations are connected to the prepared model; passing these checks does not establish functional success. Physical execution produces the signals used to evaluate functional criteria, complemented by audits of the original geometry at the initial configuration and sampled motion poses.

    The following excerpt shows the structured result of the second formal evaluation of the Task 3 wiper. The excerpt retains all five functional checks and the geometry-audit outcome, while omitting assertion expressions and ancillary metadata.

    In each observed_operands pair, the first value is the measured statistic and the second is its comparison bound. Cycle counts and accumulated rotation must meet or exceed their lower bounds, while joint separation and return error must not exceed their upper bounds. Lengths and angles are reported in metres and radians, respectively. All five functional checks and the source-geometry audit passed, and the harness marked the candidate as complete under the tested conditions.

    A.3 Test-Binding Instructions

    The final evaluation agent instantiates the task template for the submitted mechanism by identifying its operating inputs, loads, and observable physical states. The constructor’s operating instructions inform this process, but the correspondence is checked against the candidate’s actual geometry and mechanics. For example, testing a toolbox requires identifying the moving lid, its hinge, and a measurement of its opening angle; component names alone do not establish these relationships.

    The test-binding agent configures the candidate-specific experiment, while the program determines its outcome from execution evidence.

    Example of candidate-specific binding.

    The following excerpt shows the final evaluation agent’s binding for the second revision of the Task 3 wiper. Comments marked FILLED identify entries supplied when constructing the executable binding, including numerical parameters and component references. The provenance of these entries is recorded separately. Loading code and additional observation routines are omitted.

    The operation and observation names, such as input and wiper.angle_rad, belong to the fixed template interface. The test-binding agent connects these interfaces to the candidate’s actual crank, rocker, and reference frame. The numerical protocol implements the constructor’s recorded parameter request, with the provenance of each value retained alongside the binding. Here, period_s denotes the observation allowance per required cycle, not the commanded input-shaft period. With three required cycles, the total observation duration is 5.5 seconds.

    A.4 Permitted Operating and Performance Adjustments

    The task distinguishes required functions and explicit constraints from operating or performance parameters that the constructor may adjust. For example, a clamp task may permit changes to applied load or operating duration while still requiring closing, holding, and release. The constructor selects these values within the task’s permitted scope. The test-binding agent incorporates them into the test protocol and records their original values, revised values, and the reason for each change; programmatic validity checks remain in force. Completion is assessed under the final tested conditions, which are reported with the adjustment history.

    Example of a constructor-requested adjustment.

    After the first formal Task 3 evaluation failed its motion checks, the constructor requested an adjustment to the operating protocol. The following example combines the recorded parameter request with its accompanying decision rationale. Only the changed parameters are shown, and the rationale is condensed for presentation.

    The final evaluation agent implemented both requested changes in the updated binding. The remaining protocol parameters and source CAD geometry were unchanged. The second formal evaluation passed all five functional checks and the source-geometry audit, as illustrated in Appendix A.2. This example documents an operating-parameter adjustment and its subsequent evaluation; it does not isolate the effect of either parameter change individually.

    A.5 Template Authoring and Review for Open-Ended Requests

    Registered tasks reuse fixed functional templates, whereas open-ended requests require templates to be constructed for the requested functions. The constructor proposes the template, and an final evaluation agent checks it before candidate-specific binding.

    The constructor may revise the template, but template review and formal instance binding remain independent responsibilities. A candidate is not considered complete while any required function remains unverified.

    A.6 Materials for the Comparison Settings

    The four settings in Table 3 vary the support provided for simulation, functional evaluation, and diagnosis. Requirements only does not prohibit self-written simulations. Simulation tools supplies execution support but does not independently organize or enforce coverage of every required function. Full harness and binary feedback share the requirement-level workflow, differing in the diagnostic simulation feedback returned to the constructor.

    Requirements-only setting.

    This setting follows ordinary user interaction with an agent: the user describes the desired mechanism and its functions in a natural-language request, and the agent generates a corresponding CAD assembly. The agent chooses how to construct the mechanism and verify its functionality, without requirement-level testbeds or diagnostic feedback from FunCAD-Harness.

    Appendix B Mechanism Families and Task Taxonomy

    B.1 Mechanism Catalog

    FunCADBench comprises the 46 mechanism families listed in Table 4, numbered consecutively from 1 to 46. Each family is defined by its required functions and fixed constraints, while allowing different geometries, transmission arrangements, and permitted operating choices. Different designs that satisfy the requirements of a family are treated as alternative realizations rather than additional families. The table summarizes each family’s functional requirements and the operations and observations used to evaluate them. The specific components, inputs, measurements, and operating parameters are established through independent binding to each candidate design.

    B.2 Taxonomy Dimensions and Representative Mechanisms

    We characterize the mechanical demands of the tasks along five complementary dimensions: motion primitives, topology, complexity, contact, and geometric difficulty. These dimensions are not mutually exclusive categories: a mechanism family typically involves several dimensions, and task variants may place different demands on each.

    Motion primitives.

    This dimension describes how a mechanism converts and transmits motion, including input–output direction, phase relationships, and repeated or intermittent operation. In the four-bar wiper (3), continuous crank rotation must produce repeated wiper oscillation, so evaluation must capture the input–output relationship over complete motion cycles.

    Topology.

    This dimension describes connections, branches, and closed kinematic chains, together with the compatibility of the constraints they impose. In the scissor lift (14), revolute and prismatic connections form closed loops that constrain platform motion; the connections must therefore be individually valid and collectively kinematically compatible.

    Complexity.

    This dimension describes interactions among components and subsystems, state transitions, required operating sequences, and part count. The mechanical alarm clock (9) couples energy supply, timekeeping, and alarm operation through winding, running, and triggering, requiring coordination across subsystems and states.

    Contact.

    This dimension describes how engagement, sliding, locking, friction, and changes in contact state enable or prevent a behavior. In the self-locking utility knife (5), pressing the release changes the contact state to permit sliding, after which engagement at another detent restores locking.

    Geometric difficulty.

    This dimension describes the feature construction, alignment, clearance control, and assembly access needed to realize the intended mechanical relationships. The reversible dual-pawl ratchet wrench (34) illustrates these demands through its pawl–tooth geometry, pivot fit, and local clearances, whose shapes and relative placement must support the intended engagement.

    The five dimensions interact: adding components may introduce new contacts, while changing the topology may simplify geometry but complicate operation. The taxonomy therefore describes the mechanical diversity of the benchmark, while performance on an individual family generally reflects the combined effects of several capabilities.

    Appendix C Functional Specifications and Diagnostic Cases

    We use Fable’s design trajectory for the synchronized parallel gripper (Task 41) to illustrate how functional requirements guide construction, execution, and revision, and how the resulting evidence establishes completion. Appendix C.6 adds two repair cases that connect functional feedback to local geometric changes and renewed verification.

    C.1 From Input Requirements to Executable Tests

    Table 5 connects three levels of specification for the cases below. The input requirement states the intended behavior. The functional test template decomposes that behavior into operations, observations, and acceptance checks, with interfaces and parameters to be bound to a candidate. The candidate-specific simulation test supplies the actual controls, environment, measurements, and declared parameter values. Registered tasks reuse the template across candidates; open-ended requests require a new template and independent review, as described in Appendix A.

    The mapping is not one requirement per simulation run: several checks can share a continuous trial, preserving the states needed for later operations. For example, the second grasp uses the block left by the first release, and re-locking is checked after closing inputs have been removed. The trials also undergo source-geometry auditing at sampled poses, which is separate from the functional checks summarized above (Appendix D). These protocols test the required behaviors for particular designs; a different mechanism may need a different input location, operating policy, or observation mapping.

    C.2 Worked Example: Designing and Refining a Parallel Gripper

item.title: 学风格别把形状家族一起学进去：Open-Form 用 Geometry LoRA 加 Style LoRA 把结构与风格拆开 ｜ Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer
item.description:
一句话：难点不是学风格，而是在学风格时不把观察到的形状家族一起学进去。

要点：

  • 目标形态用结构草图表示，Geometry LoRA 负责结构贴合、Style LoRA 负责风格实现，把两件事显式解耦
  • 要让迁移「开放」，Geometry LoRA 必须是通用的：用部件删除与合并两种基础编辑，构造覆盖陌生几何的大量合成结构草图
  • 把从拉丁字母学到的几何设计语言迁移到希腊字形乃至人体姿态；人类偏好研究中对各基线在结构与风格两个维度均占优

为什么值得看：风格化资产流水线的通病是「风格一上就把可编辑结构毁掉」。把结构与风格拆到两个 LoRA，等于给资产管线留了可回退、可分别调节的参数面，也让同一套风格能跨形状家族复用。

中文摘要：几何风格通常只能从某个形状家族学到、再用回同一家族。这篇提出「开放形态」几何风格迁移：从风格化拉丁字母学到的设计语言，可以迁移到希腊字形，甚至人体姿态这种完全不同的结构。作者指出真正的难点不是学风格，而是学风格时不把承载它的形状家族一起学进去。方法用结构草图表示目标形态，并用 Geometry LoRA 与 Style LoRA 分别承担结构贴合与风格实现；关键要求是 Geometry LoRA 必须通用，因此提出几何增广策略：通过部件删除与合并两种基础编辑，构造大量覆盖陌生结构的合成草图。实验与消融验证了解耦与增广两件事都不可少，人类偏好研究中该方法在结构与风格维度上均优于各基线。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-27

Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer

Abstract

A geometric style learned from one family of shapes is typically applied to new shapes from the same family. We consider a more challenging setting: learning the geometric design language of a stylized Latin alphabet and applying it to new forms, from Greek glyphs to entirely different structures such as human poses. We introduce Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed. This setting is deceptively challenging: the difficulty is not merely learning a style, but learning the style without learning the shape family in which it was observed. We represent target forms by structural sketches and disentangle structural adherence from style realization using a Geometry LoRA and a style-specific LoRA. Critically, open-form transfer requires the Geometry LoRA to be universal. To achieve this, we devise a geometry-enrichment strategy that constructs a large and purposefully diverse collection of synthetic structural sketches spanning a broad range of unfamiliar geometries. Our experiments and ablations demonstrate the importance of both disentanglement and this universal geometry prior, enabling geometric styles learned from glyphs, pictograms, and other shape families to be transferred to substantially different, unseen forms.

††footnotetext: ∗Corresponding author

1 Introduction

Style transfer is a long-standing and intriguing problem in visual computing: given examples that contain both content and style, the goal is to capture the essence of the style, separate it from the particular content on which it is observed, and apply it to new content. The separation of style from content has been studied for decades [8, 7], and has more recently become central to neural style transfer and generative modeling [13, 27, 15]. At the heart of the problem lies the ability to distinguish what is represented from how it is expressed.

In this work, we focus on geometric style, where style governs how an underlying structure is geometrically realized. A canonical example is a font: different glyphs have different structures, yet their geometric realizations follow a coherent design language that makes them immediately recognizable as belonging to the same font. More generally, such geometric styles cannot be inferred from a single example; it is revealed through a collection of different shapes that share the same design language. Early work has considered related notions of separating style from content and transferring geometric style across shapes [25, 9].

Existing approaches [22, 29, 26] typically learn and apply such styles within a shared domain: a style observed on letters is transferred to other letters, and a style observed on human figures is applied to other human figures. We remove this restriction and consider transferring a geometric style to an open space of forms. As illustrated in Figure Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, a style learned from a Latin alphabet may be applied to Greek glyphs, or more radically, to human poses; conversely, a geometric style learned from pictograms may be applied to glyphs. We call this new setting Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed. We focus on forms whose underlying structure can be represented by a sparse structural sketch, which serves as the geometry to be styled.

The open-form setting, illustrated in Figure 2, is deceptively challenging. The difficulty is not simply learning a style, but learning the style without learning the shape family in which that style was observed. Existing font-generation methods can transfer styles to unseen glyphs [29, 26, 32, 18], and some explicitly separate character content from style. However, their structural component is learned and evaluated largely within the glyph domain, often within a single writing system. This distinction becomes critical when the target form leaves the source domain. A straightforward LoRA trained on a limited styled shape family learns an entangled style with the geometries observed at training (Sec. 4.2), causing it to drift toward familiar source-domain shapes when presented with substantially different target geometries.

Our approach addresses this entanglement by separating structural adherence from style realization. A Geometry LoRA is responsible for faithfully following the target structural sketch serving as a geometric-adherence prior, while a Style LoRA learns how that geometry should be realized in the desired style. Accordingly, the Geometry LoRA must be universal: generalize across the vast universe of styles, responding to structure rather than shape identity or residual stylistic cues. Acquiring such a universal geometry prior is itself non-trivial: a corpus of ordinary glyphs provides a limited and familiar geometry vocabulary, allowing the model to recognize known shapes rather than truly follow the input structure. We therefore introduce a geometry-enrichment strategy (GEE Sec. 3.2) that systematically leverages SVG font data to construct a large collection of unfamiliar synthetic geometries, untangled from their source style. This strategy proves vital for successfully learning a universal geometry LoRA.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce Open-Form Geometric Stylization, where a geometric style learned from one shape domain is applied to universally arbitrary forms.

  • •

    We show that open-form stylization requires separating structural adherence from style realization.

  • •

    Finally, we introduce a geometry-enrichment strategy for constructing the broad and diverse structural training distribution needed to acquire this universal prior.

    • We evaluate these ideas through controlled ablations and increasingly challenging transfers, from held-out glyphs and cross-alphabet transfer to unrelated forms such as human poses, demonstrating that a geometric style can be extended well beyond the family of shapes on which it was observed.

    2 Background and Related Work

    Our work builds on three lines of research: the separation of style and content, font and glyph style transfer, and structurally conditioned generation. Below we review each line, clarify how our notion of geometric style relates to them, and how they relate to our approach.

    2.1 Style and Content

    Our work is closely connected to the seminal work of Tenenbaum and Freeman [25] on separating style and content. Using bilinear models, they showed that a common style can be inferred from multiple observations and applied to new content. Particularly relevant to our setting is their treatment of fonts, where style is shared across different letters and can be used to synthesize previously unseen characters. This provides an early and elegant formulation of style as a factor that can be learned across a family of shapes and separated from their individual geometry. Our work builds on this perspective, but considers an open-form setting in which the new content need not belong to the same family: a geometric style learned from one alphabet may be applied to another alphabet, or even to a different class of structures such as human poses.

    More broadly, style transfer has a long history in computer vision and graphics, with much of the literature focusing on style as visual appearance. Early example-based methods [8, 7] synthesized and transferred texture by sampling local neighborhoods or patches from example images. [13] later introduced neural style transfer, demonstrating that content and artistic style can be represented separately within a deep network and recombined to render new content in the appearance of a reference image. Recent diffusion-based methods such as StyleAligned [15], B-LoRA [10], InstantStyle [28], and ZipLoRA [24] substantially extend the quality and flexibility of reference-based style transfer. Across these works, style is predominantly expressed through visual appearance, including texture, color, material, brushwork, and shading.

    Our notion of geometric style is different. Here, style determines how an underlying structure is geometrically realized: how curves are formed, junctions are connected, strokes vary in thickness, gaps are introduced, and structural elements terminate or interact. Such a style is naturally revealed by a set of related shapes rather than by a single reference image. Glyphs provide a particularly clean instance of this setting: individual characters differ in structure, while together they reveal a consistent geometric design language. Related notions of transferring geometric style across shapes were also explored in early work by [9]. More recently, geometric stylization has also been explored for 3D shapes  [5].

    Closely related, Abstraction in Style (AiS) [19] also separates geometry from appearance using two specialized LoRA adapters. However, AiS learns style-specific geometric abstraction, whereas our Geometry LoRA is universal, enabling a learned geometric style to generalize to unseen structural sketches across shape families.

    2.2 Font and Glyph Style Transfer

    Modern font-generation methods provide the closest setting to our work, as they explicitly transfer a common style across glyphs with different structures. FontDiffuser [29] formulates one-shot diffusion-based font generation, using multi-scale content aggregation to preserve character structure and contrastive learning to capture style. It generalizes to unseen characters and also demonstrates cross-lingual generation. MX-Font [22] addresses few-shot font generation using multiple localized experts that disentangle content and style while capturing different local style characteristics. It also demonstrates cross-lingual generalization to unseen writing systems. VecFusion [26] approaches font generation in the vector domain, explicitly modeling glyph topology, paths, and Bézier control points, and supports applications including glyph completion and few-shot style transfer. Skeleton-Guided Diffusion [32] is particularly related to our structural representation, using character skeletons to guide diffusion and preserve structure during font generation. StrokeStyles [1] decomposes font glyphs into meaningful stroke structures and uses this representation for consistent geometric stylization across characters.

    FLUX-Font [18] is particularly close to our work architecturally. It adapts a pre-trained diffusion transformer using separate LoRA modules [17] for glyph content and style, explicitly separating the two factors rather than learning them through a single adapter. Our method shares this general motivation, but separates structural adherence from style realization hierarchically: a universal Geometry LoRA is first trained to follow arbitrary structural sketches, and each Style LoRA is subsequently learned with this geometry prior active and fixed.

    Despite their differences, these methods share an important restriction: their structural representations and learned priors are designed for the glyph domain. Their goal is to generalize from observed characters to other characters, possibly across writing systems, but the target remains a glyph. Open-form transfer removes this restriction. The target structural sketch may describe a character, a pictogram, a human pose, or another unrelated form. Consequently, separating content from style within the font domain is not sufficient; the geometry-following component must itself generalize beyond the shape family in which the style was observed.

    2.3 Structural Conditioning

    Spatially conditioned diffusion models provide a complementary line of related work. ControlNet [31] and T2I-Adapter [20] condition pre-trained text-to-image models on spatial signals such as edges, depth, segmentation, poses, and sketches, while Sketch-Guided Diffusion [27] focuses specifically on generation controlled by free-form sketches. These methods demonstrate that strong spatial adherence can be learned over broad image distributions.

    Our problem, however, is not spatial conditioning alone. The structural sketch specifies a form whose geometric realization must change according to a style learned from a separate set of examples. The challenge is therefore to preserve the target structure while preventing the learned style from carrying with it the shape distribution on which that style was observed. We use structural conditioning as a means toward this goal, learning a universal geometry prior that remains fixed while different geometric styles are acquired. At inference, we treat structure and style as independent conditions and adopt the dual-conditioning guidance of InstructPix2Pix [3], allowing their strengths to be controlled separately.

    3 Method

    Given a collection of shapes sharing a geometric style, our goal is to learn that style and apply it to a new target form specified by a structural sketch. We use the term sketch-glyph for a pair consisting of a structural sketch and its styled realization. The term originates naturally from fonts, where a sketch specifies the structure of a character and the glyph realizes it in a particular font. In this work, we extend this notion to pictograms, symbols, and other structured forms that are not letters. Given a small collection of sketch-glyph pairs sharing a style, we aim to realize arbitrary new structural sketches in that style, as illustrated in Fig. 2.

    Figure 3 provides an overview of the method. Our key design is to separate the two responsibilities involved in this task. A Universal Geometry LoRA (UGL) provides a general ability to faithfully follow the input structural sketch, while a Style LoRA learns how the conditioned geometry should be realized in the target style. The two adapters are learned hierarchically rather than independently. UGL is trained once (Fig. 3ii); each Style LoRA is subsequently trained on top of the frozen UGL (Fig. 3iii).

    For this separation to support open-form transfer, UGL itself must generalize far beyond any particular shape family. We therefore train it on a large and purposefully diverse collection of synthetic geometries constructed by our Geometry Enrichment Engine (GEE) (Fig. 3i).

    At inference (Fig. 3iv), UGL and the selected Style LoRA are applied jointly. Their contributions can be controlled independently through separate geometry and style guidance scales, allowing us to balance adherence to the target structure against the strength of its stylistic realization. The following sections describe UGL, GEE, and Style LoRA training in detail.

    3.1 Universal Geometry LoRA (UGL)

    The purpose of UGL is to fine-tune a text-to-image diffusion model to follow open-form geometries (i.e. sketches). Starting from a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion transformer (DiT), we fit LoRA parameters on the DiT’s weights using sketch-glyph data pairs constructed by GEE. The rich, diverse synthetic data produced by the GEE allows us to select a high LoRA rank without overfitting, giving the UGL significant learning capacity. After this one-time training, we freeze UGL and share it across all Style LoRAs, providing a common geometry prior beyond each style’s specific training examples.

    3.2 Geometry Enrichment Engine (GEE)

    Fonts are a natural starting point for data augmentation: they are available in a large variety of styles, and more importantly, their SVG native representation enables truly geometric augmentations compared to raster form. However, using real font glyphs directly presents two limitations. First, available fonts cover a relatively narrow set of languages and therefore a limited vocabulary of structures, which may hinder generalization to unseen scripts and, even more, to out-of-domain forms such as symbols or pictograms. Second, the geometry of a glyph is itself tied to the style of its source font, so the conditioning structure may carry unwanted stylistic cues. To address both issues, we introduce GEE: a data-generation procedure that expands the range of training geometries while reducing their dependence on font style. To increase structural diversity, GEE takes advantage of the native SVG parameterization of fonts and constructs novel geometric forms by applying random sequences of geometric edits. We refer to each such sequence as a geometric recipe. A recipe may, for example, repeatedly remove or merge SVG parts, producing coherent but unfamiliar structures (Fig. 4(a)). Recipes also allow the GEE to address the second problem. A recipe applied to one font can be re-applied to matching letters from another font, producing paired data with similar structure but different styles (Fig. 4(b)). During UGL training, we form mixed pairs by taking the conditioning sketch from one font and the target from another font to which the same recipe was applied (Fig. 4(c)). The sketch and target therefore remain aligned in structure while differing in style, encouraging UGL to learn the supplied geometry independently of its stylistic realization.

    We next describe the editing primitives that drive the geometry enrichment process, first motivating their design and then outlining each one (full details in Appendix C).

    Structural editing primitives.

    A glyph’s structure is determined by how its strokes relate: which strokes meet and where they branch or terminate. Smooth transformations such as warping, shearing, or scaling can change a glyph’s appearance, but they do not create new structural relations between its strokes. To generate genuinely new structures, we therefore need operations that modify these relations. We propose two elementary edits: component removal and merging. This builds on a broader principle: deleting and recombining existing parts can generate meaningful structural variation [11], and related cut-based augmentations have been shown to improve recognition performance [6, 30]. Repeating these edits produces novel structural relations beyond those found in existing alphabets.

    To make both edits transferable across fonts, we edit the glyph’s structure rather than its contour, which is more sensitive to stylistic variation. We therefore represent each glyph as a graph, with strokes as edges and intersections and endpoints as nodes. A recipe is then expressed as a sequence of graph edits, with component removal and merging each applied one to three times. The edit type and its structural parameters are sampled when the recipe is created, specifying which component to remove or where components should connect. Because the edits are defined structurally, the same recipe can be replayed across fonts to produce the same underlying structure in multiple styles. Structural correspondence across styles is further explained in Appendix C.

    Graph extraction.

    We represent each glyph as a graph that captures its dominant stroke structure (Fig. 5). Starting from the glyph (a), we compute its medial axis together with the local inscribed-disk radius, which provides an estimate of stroke thickness (b). We prune short branches caused by serifs and other stylistic details, leaving the main stroke structure (c). Pixel chains are then collapsed into edges, with junctions and stroke endpoints represented as nod es (d). Finally, we classify each edge by its structural role: an edge between two junctions is a bar, while an edge from a junction to an endpoint is a leg (e).

    Component removal.

    Fig. 6 illustrates the process. Our strategy is to perform the edit in the medial-axis representation and then reconstruct the glyph back in the SVG domain. Outline points unrelated to the removed component are preserved exactly. Only the region surrounding the cut is reconstructed, where additional processing is needed to obtain a clean, style-consistent boundary. Using the graph extracted in the previous step, we locate the component to remove from its structure, which lets us find the same component across styles (a). As seen in Fig. 6(b), simply removing the red branch can leave bulges where it connects to the remaining blue branches. We therefore trim these regions and reconnect the remaining blue branches. We then separate the pixels belonging to the removed region from those that should remain (c). This produces a pixel removal mask, which we convert to a smooth vector representation (d).Additional reconstruction steps are described in the appendix. The final removal result is shown in (e).

    Merging.

    Fig. 7 illustrates the process. We begin with two glyphs from the same style: a guest (a) and a host (b), and aim to combine them into a single coherent glyph. As in component removal, we perform the edit in the medial-axis representation and reconstruct the result in the SVG domain. Using the graphs extracted in the previous step, we identify where the guest should connect to the host based on their structural attributes. The process starts by randomly generating a candidate merging recipe, combining a set of simple augmentations, such as mirroring, rotation, and scaling, with a pair of connection points selected from the guest and host graphs, shown as red points in (c,d). To assess the result produced by the recipe, we apply the augmentations and connect the glyphs at the selected points. We approve only recipes that produce a clean, coherent shape (e). A merging recipe is retained only if it succeeds across a minimum number of styles. Additional implementation details are provided in the appendix. The final merging result is shown in (f).

    3.3 Style LoRA

    We train a separate Style LoRA on sketch-glyph pairs for each target style, as shown in Fig. 3(iii). The backbone and UGL parameters remain fixed, while UGL continues to guide the geometry throughout training. Only the Style LoRA is optimized, allowing it to focus on how that geometry is realized in the target style. Here we use a low-rank adapter, far smaller than UGL: its limited capacity helps keep the style update from re-learning geometry or competing with the shared geometry prior. Following previous work [12, 23], we associate each style with a unique rare token. This token and a short appearance description provide the textual conditioning during both Style LoRA training and inference.

    Geometry reinforcement.

    The few style examples also share a limited family of geometries, so the Style LoRA may still tie the learned style to those geometries despite UGL’s structural guidance. To preserve open-form transfer, we mix geometry-enriched sketch-glyph pairs into its training batches, shown by the connection from GEE to Style LoRA training in Fig. 3. These pairs expose the model to geometries outside the target style’s examples throughout adaptation, reinforcing its ability to follow new structures while learning the style.

    3.4 Inference

    After training, we apply UGL and the selected Style LoRA jointly to the base diffusion model to map structural sketches to styled outputs (Fig. 3iv). To control geometry adherence and style strength separately, we adopt dual classifier-free guidance following InstructPix2Pix [3]. During training, the structural sketch, the style caption, or both are dropped to their null conditions, so a single network learns all four conditioning combinations. During sampling, we combine three forward passes using two CFG coefficients to obtain separate geometry and style guidance strengths, balancing adherence to the input sketch geometry vs. the target style. Appendix B provides the guidance formulation and implementation details.

    This joint application supports transfer to new forms without further training: a pictogram style can depict new human poses, while a sculptural style can turn free-form strokes into tubular shapes (Fig. Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer). The same sketch can also be rendered in different learned styles (Fig. 2). Section 4 evaluates these capabilities through qualitative and quantitative comparisons and ablations of the method’s main components.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate our method across fonts, pictograms, and object-centric styles, using sketches of increasing structural novelty:

  • •

    In-domain, held-out test examples from the same source domain as the style training data

  • •

    Near-domain, semantically related but structurally unseen examples, such as non-Latin glyphs for fonts and everyday human poses for pictograms

  • •

    Out-of-domain, structures from unrelated shape families, such as non-glyph sketches for font styles or non-human sketches for pictogram styles.

    • We compare against prior methods and perform targeted ablations to assess both open-set transfer quality and the contributions of our main design choices.

    4.1 Training and Evaluation Data

    The training data for the universal geometry LoRA (UGL) is produced by the geometry enrichment engine (GEE) from 80 base glyphs (Latin letters, Latin Extended letters, and digits) shared across 16 fonts. Applying 6,000 random recipes yields 42,705 sketch–glyph pairs, on which UGL is trained once (Appendix D). Each style is represented by a small exemplar set with manually drawn structural sketches. We hold out six examples per style for evaluation and train the Style LoRA on the remainder, yielding roughly 20–70 sketch–exemplar pairs per style. During Style LoRA training, 10% of each batch is replayed from the UGL training pairs using their original style-free captions, helping preserve the learned geometry prior while adapting to style. For evaluation, we use a benchmark of 50 curated sketches per style category (fonts and pictograms). To analyze how well our method and the baselines generalize, the sketches span the in-, near-, and out-of-domain tiers defined above. We evaluate across twelve styles, and for each style all methods receive the same sketches and style references.

    4.2 Open-form Geometric Generalization

    We tailored our main technical contributions, the universal geometry LoRA (UGL) and the geometry enrichment engine (GEE), to open-form generalization and the challenges of fine-tuning large models.

    In this section, we demonstrate the necessity of both components; later in Table 12 we also present a quantitative evaluation that supports each claim.

    We begin with the most direct alternative: avoid the UGL by fine-tuning a single low-rank adapter on the few sketch-glyph pairs available for a given style. While this formulation preserves both the target geometry and the learned style on held-out examples from the same style family, it does not generalize to out-of-domain structures. Instead, the model takes a shortcut by producing results resembling the closest training example, best seen in the bottom rows of Fig. 8 (w/o UGL), where the model outputs styled examples similar to English alphabet letters rather than the desired geometry. Row w/o UGL in Table 12 quantifies this behavior.

    A natural hypothesis for this phenomenon is that each geometry is observed only through a single realization in the target style, providing too little variation to disentangle the geometry and style.

    An intuitive solution is to train a geometry adapter on ordinary glyphs drawn from a broad corpus of fonts, using the same training settings as UGL but without employing GEE, and then train the same Style LoRAs on top of it. Unfortunately, the failure persisted, now in an even more revealing form. The UGL is even more biased towards common geometries from the train set, e.g. alphabet letters, as again seen in the bottom row of the w/o GEE section of Fig 8. These results are again supported by data in Table 12.

    What is instead needed is a training distribution with fewer geometric correlations, preventing the model from capturing a specific shape identity. This is solved by our second technical contribution (GEE Sec. 3.2). The GEE’s immense augmentation strategy forces the geometry model to rely on the supplied structure rather than recognizing a known geometry. With this enriched corpus, completing our full method, the out-of-domain score rises to 0.94 (Ours in Table 12), with a geometry factor of 0.97 and style within 3% of the ceiling, and the characteristic substitutions largely disappear.

    4.3 Qualitative Evaluation

    We compare against FontDiffuser [29], MX-Font [22], Gemini 3.1 (Nano-Banana 2) [14], and gpt-image-1-mini [21]. All methods receive the same target sketch and style references, except FontDiffuser, which uses a single reference. We include the general-purpose models for completeness, as they require no per-style training. Additional comparisons, including the adapter-based methods B-LoRA and ZipLoRA as well as AiS, are provided in Appendix A.

    In the in-domain tier, we evaluate held-out sketches (Fig. 9). Our method closely matches the ground truth while preserving the requested geometry and fine stylistic details. Gemini and GPT often capture the overall style but drift toward familiar poses or glyphs and lose fine font details. FontDiffuser often deviates from the input structure, while MX-Font follows it more closely but transfers the target style less faithfully.

    In the near-domain tier (Fig. 11), we transfer styles to related but unseen forms: non-Latin glyphs. Baselines often distort these unfamiliar inputs toward known forms or lose structural or stylistic details, while our method follows the supplied geometry and preserves the target style. The zoomed examples highlight reference motifs retained in the outputs, demonstrating transfer beyond the forms seen during style adaptation.

    The out-of-domain tier (Fig. 10) provides a stronger test by applying pictogram and object-centric styles to structures from unrelated shape families. Across these sketches, our method retains the characteristic shapes and appearance of each style while following the new structure, demonstrating open-form transfer beyond the source domain.

    4.4 Quantitative Results

    We evaluate whether our method follows the structural sketch while realizing the target style, and how well both hold as the target geometry moves away from the style’s source domain. On the in-domain tier, where paired ground truth is available, we report LPIPS for perceptual similarity to the ground truth and SSIM for agreement in local image structure. For the near- and out-of-domain tiers, where paired ground truth is unavailable, we use VLM-as-a-judge [4]. The judge separately scores structural adherence to the sketch and stylistic fidelity to the references; we report their product, normalized by the score of real examples from the corresponding style (judge setup and prompt in Appendix F).

    Comparison and ablation.

    Table 12 reports judge scores by style family (Fonts, Non-Fonts) and by distance from the training domain (Near, Out), followed by LPIPS and SSIM. Our full method achieves the best results across all reported measures. In the upper block, the font generators closely follow the sketch but lack style fidelity, whereas the general-purpose models better capture the target style but drift from the input structure, as reflected in their lower Out scores. The lower block ablates our method. w/o UGL removes the UGL and trains the Style LoRA directly on the base model. Non-hierarchical trains the Style LoRA without the UGL and adds the UGL only at inference. w/o GEE trains the UGL, and applies geometry reinforcement, on original glyphs only, without GEE. w/o Reinforcement uses the GEE-trained UGL but omits geometry reinforcement during style training. Their performance shows that the importance of our design choices becomes more pronounced as the target geometry moves farther from the training domain. In particular, removing geometry reinforcement lowers the Near score from 0.975 to 0.966, but causes a substantially larger drop in the Out score, from 0.941 to 0.872. This suggests that preserving geometric adherence during style adaptation is particularly important for unfamiliar forms.

    User study.

    We complement these measures with user preferences collected from 32 participants, who compare our result against each baseline in terms of style, structure, and overall preference (Appendix G). Fig. 12 shows the same trend as Table 12: our results are preferred over every baseline on all three criteria, with the largest margins in style and overall preference.

    5 Conclusions, Limitations and Future Work

    We introduced Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where a geometric style learned from one family of shapes is applied to structures well beyond that family. We showed that learning geometric style requires separating how a shape is realized from the particular geometry on which that style is observed. However, disentanglement is necessary but not sufficient. To transfer a geometric language to unseen forms, the geometry component must itself be universal.

    These findings suggest an asymmetric view of geometry and style. Geometry should be learned broadly, across a large and diverse space of structures, and can be learned once as a reusable capability. Style, in contrast, can be learned from a much narrower collection of examples and specialized independently. Our Universal Geometry LoRA and Style LoRA instantiate this separation, while GEE provides the geometric diversity needed to make the former universal.

    As with many fine-tuned generative models, some challenges remain. Complex structures can expose a tradeoff between geometric and stylistic fidelity, while strong or recurring stylistic elements can occasionally interfere with the target structure or become overemphasized. Improving this separation, particularly for increasingly complex geometries and styles, is an interesting direction for future work. We believe this principle may extend beyond geometric style transfer, enabling learned visual languages to be applied outside the domains in which they were observed.
