    Appendix A Further Comparisons

    Sec. 4 compares against font-generation models and general-purpose image generators. Here we include additional comparisons with three recent methods that are particularly relevant to our setting. B-LoRA [10] and ZipLoRA [24], like ours, use low-rank adapters to separate what is depicted from how it is rendered, while Abstraction in Style (AiS) [19] explicitly models structural abstraction as part of stylization. Fig. 13 shows the B-LoRA and ZipLoRA results next to ours for the same sketch and style; AiS is discussed separately below.

    B-LoRA.

    B-LoRA leverages LoRA to implicitly separate the style and content of a single image by jointly learning the LoRA weights of two specific SDXL blocks, which can then be used as independent components. We use the official implementation and settings, which we verified by reproducing the authors’ published example. The content adapter is trained on the structural sketch and the style adapter on six training examples of the style, matching the other reference-based baselines. As Fig. 13 (left) shows, the style block carries only the palette and texture of the style: the geometric style is lost, and the structure of the sketch is replaced by hallucinated, unrelated content, because a thin line drawing provides little reconstruction signal.

    ZipLoRA.

    ZipLoRA merges independently trained style and subject LoRAs by learning per-column merger coefficients that minimize their interference. As no official implementation exists, we implement it on our own backbone, which isolates the merging strategy: the content adapter is our UGL and the style adapter is a Style LoRA trained without the UGL, as in the Non-hierarchical ablation (Sec. 12). Both adapters are frozen and only the coefficients are optimized, with the paper’s hyperparameters. With all coefficients at one, the two adapters are simply added, which is exactly the Non-hierarchical configuration of our ablation study; sampling uses its sketches, prompts, seeds and guidance. The learned coefficients scale down both adapters, averaging 0.39-0.48 for the UGL and 0.24-0.52 for the Style LoRA across the three styles. As Fig. 13 (right) shows, the result follows the sketch, but the conflict between structure and style remains, only in a milder form: style-specific details such as the pictogram tile and the wedge-shaped terminals of the display font are weakened. Training the Style LoRA with the UGL active, as we do, avoids the conflict altogether.

    Abstraction in Style (AiS). AiS is designed specifically for styles in which abstraction extends beyond color and texture to geometric and structural deformation. AiS explicitly separates structural abstraction from visual stylization in two stages: it first transforms the target into an intermediate abstraction proxy that reflects the structural tendencies of the reference style, and then renders this proxy into the final stylized output. Both stages are learned from a small set of visual exemplars through its Visual Analogy Transfer framework. This makes AiS particularly relevant to our setting, as it is one of the few recent methods that explicitly treats structural reinterpretation as part of style transfer.

    Fig. 14 compares AiS with our method on three styles: two pictogram sets and a sculptural style. We train AiS on the same style references and use the structural sketch as the abstraction target. AiS captures the visual appearance of each style, but on the pictogram styles its outputs do not reliably follow the sketch: across the scripts, strokes are rearranged, omitted, or fused, while the runner pose is only loosely preserved. On the sculptural style, whose exemplars are themselves single continuous strokes, AiS follows the sketch more closely, though it renders every glyph as one uniform tube. This reflects AiS’s design: its abstraction proxy follows structural tendencies learned from the references rather than the geometry of a specific target. Our method follows each sketch closely while preserving the same style traits, including the tile deformation and stroke bands of the orange set.

    Appendix B Dual Classifier-Free Guidance

    Our generator is conditioned on two inputs: a sketch image c_I of the target geometry and a text caption c_T that carries the style token. Conventional text-conditioned classifier-free guidance (CFG) [16] has a single scale: it amplifies the caption, while the sketch enters both branches as an ordinary, unamplified condition, so the strength of the geometric conditioning cannot be controlled. We therefore adopt the compositional guidance of InstructPix2Pix [3], which separates the two conditions into terms with independent scales.

    Null conditions.

    CFG requires the network to model the unconditional branches, so during training each sample is assigned to one of the four conditioning branches listed in Table 2: most samples keep both conditions, one in five drops the style caption, and a small share drops the sketch or both. The image null ∅_I is the complete absence of reference tokens, i.e. the model’s native text-to-image mode, rather than a blank or noise image, and the text null ∅_T is the empty prompt.

    Guidance.

    Let v_θ(zₜ,c_I,c_T) denote the predicted velocity at noise level t. Each sampling step evaluates the unconditional, geometry-conditioned, and fully conditioned branches of Table 2 (the style-only branch is not used at sampling) and combines them as

    ṽ_θ(zₜ,c_I,c_T) =v_θ(zₜ,∅_I,∅_T)(1)
    +s_I[v_θ(zₜ,c_I,∅_T)-v_θ(zₜ,∅_I,∅_T)]
    +s_T[v_θ(zₜ,c_I,c_T)-v_θ(zₜ,c_I,∅_T)].

    The first bracket moves the prediction toward the sketch and is scaled by the geometry scale s_I; the second adds the contribution of the style token on top of the sketch and is scaled by the style scale s_T. With s_I=s_T, the two brackets merge into one and the rule becomes single-scale CFG on the joint condition (c_I,c_T). Values of s_I above 1 amplify the geometric conditioning independently of the style scale. In practice we use s_I∈[4,6] and s_T∈[2,3] (Sec. 4).

    Reading the two levers.

    Fig. 15 jointly sweeps the two guidance scales for a held-out sketch of a “3”. The grid makes the roles of the two guidance signals and their characteristic failure modes clear.

    With no sketch guidance (s_I=0, top row), the sketch is effectively ignored: increasing s_T strengthens the style but does not recover the geometry of a “3”. At s_I=1, a coherent letterform emerges, but with incorrect geometry, and strong style guidance can further distort its shape.

    At the other extreme, strong sketch guidance (s_I=8, bottom row) reliably preserves the geometry but weakens the appearance signal. Increasing s_T restores the red tubular style, though gradients and translucency remain muted. The intermediate regime (s_I=6, third row) provides the best balance, recovering the correct “3” while preserving the inflated volume and warm gradient of the exemplars. We therefore choose our operating point in this regime.

    Appendix C Geometry Enrichment Engine: Details

    This appendix details the construction of the geometry-enriched training corpus used to train UGL (Sec. 3.2).

    Generating unfamiliar geometries.

    We begin with 80 base glyphs (Latin letters, Latin Extended letters, and digits) shared across 16 fonts and treat them as raw geometric material. We expand this initial vocabulary using two simple structural operations: component removal, which removes a structural part of a glyph, and merging, which combines components from two glyphs. The operations are applied iteratively, allowing newly generated shapes to participate in subsequent operations. As illustrated in Fig. 4 of Sec. 3.2, the resulting forms quickly depart from recognizable characters, producing a much broader distribution of coherent but unfamiliar geometries.

    We represent each sequence of structural operations as a geometric recipe. Importantly, a recipe is defined independently of a particular font and can therefore be applied to corresponding glyphs across multiple fonts. This produces related geometric constructions realized in different styles. Beyond increasing geometric diversity, this correspondence is what allows us to separate the structural information conveyed by a sketch from the style of its target realization.

    A GEE recipe is a sequence of component-removal and merging operations, with both operations applied one to three times. The output of one step is the input of the next. Both operations share a first step, graph extraction, described next.

    Graph extraction.

    Editing a glyph’s outline directly is fragile, since a removal or a join depends on local contour details that differ from style to style. Both operators therefore act on the glyph’s underlying stroke structure, which we extract as a graph; Fig. 5 of Sec. 3.2 illustrates the steps. Starting from the glyph (a), we compute its medial axis transform, which gives the centerline of every stroke together with the radius of the maximal inscribed disk at each point, a local estimate of stroke thickness (b). Treating the axis pixels as a graph, we prune the short branches caused by serifs and other stylistic contour details, retaining the dominant stroke structure (c). Chains of pixels between meeting points are then collapsed into single edges, junctions become nodes and stroke ends become tips (d). Finally, each edge is classified (e). An edge between two junctions is a bar, and an edge from a junction to a tip is a leg. Because these roles do not depend on the exact contour of a style, an operation on these graphs can be replayed across styles.

    Structural correspondence.

    A recipe names the component it edits, but only within the style on which it was defined. To apply the same edit consistently across styles, we must identify the corresponding component in each style. We represent the selected component using a compact descriptor consisting of its type (bar or leg), the orientation of the chord connecting its endpoints, its midpoint normalized by the glyph’s bounding box, and its arc length relative to glyph size. For each other style, we compare this descriptor with all removable components of the same type and select the component with the smallest weighted distance, provided that the distance is below a matching tolerance. If no component falls below this tolerance, the recipe is not applied to that style. A recipe is retained only if at least a minimum number of styles remain (we configured as 6).

    Component removal.

    Fig. 6 of Sec. 3.2 illustrates the process step by step. Given the extracted graph, we aim to remove exactly one structural component, such as a leg or bar, while keeping the rest of the outline unchanged and reconstructing the cut in the font’s own terminal style (a). The component to be removed is described by its structural attributes in the graph. In each style, we use these attributes to identify the corresponding component, so that the same component is removed consistently across styles. Removing only the skeleton associated with the component’s edge is not sufficient, since part of its medial axis may also belong to the junction. To avoid leaving an artificial bulge, we remove medial-axis points near the junction within a radius slightly smaller than its inscribed-disk radius (b). This creates a small gap, which we reconnect with a straight stroke that smoothly bridges the surviving branches. We remove pixels belonging to the deleted limb while preserving those shared with surviving strokes. We then fill small junction concavities using the convex hull of the surviving strokes (c). The removal is defined as a pixel mask, but the output must be vectorized. We therefore trace the removal region into a smooth contour and subtract it from the original glyph outline (d). Geometry outside the edited region is preserved exactly. The newly exposed cut boundary has no counterpart in the original glyph. To reconstruct it in a style-consistent way, we search other glyphs from the same font for a matching outline segment, after normalizing for position, scale, and rotation. We then fit this donor segment to the exposed boundary and insert it into the cut region. The result is a glyph with one structural component removed while preserving the original outline wherever possible (e).

    Merging.

    Fig. 7 of Sec. 3.2 illustrates the process. The connection between the two glyphs is described through structural attributes of their graphs. These attributes identify where the guest should attach to the host and allow the corresponding connection to be found across styles. We begin with two glyphs from the same style: a guestgₐ (a) and a hostg_b (b). Our goal is to attach the guest to the host so that they form a single coherent glyph. The merge has two stages. First, we augment the pair,

    ĝₐ=augment(gₐ), ĝ_b=augment(g_b),

    to generate multiple candidate configurations. The host may be mirrored, while the guest may be also rotated and scaled. These choices are randomly sampled when the recipe is created. In Fig. 7(c), for example, the host is unchanged while the guest is mirrored and rotated by 270^∘. We then merge the augmented pair,

    merge(ĝₐ,ĝ_b).

    On the guest, the connection is anchored at a stroke end facing the host, marked by the red dot in Fig. 7(c). On the host, we select the stroke end facing the guest; if none exists, we use the nearest skeleton point (Fig. 7(d)). The guest is then translated so that the two connection points align. We keep only merges that form a coherent single shape, with a localized overlap at the junction and no narrow gaps or small enclosed holes, as shown in Fig. 7(e). A merge recipe is retained only if it succeeds across a minimum number of styles, ensuring that the structural relation transfers consistently. Small fragments extending beyond the seam are removed to produce the final glyph, as shown in Fig. 7(f).

    Style-suppressed structural sketches.

    For each generated glyph, we extract a structural sketch from its medial axis. A raw medial axis, however, can retain local characteristics of the font from which it was extracted, allowing the conditioning sketch to inadvertently reveal style. We therefore simplify the extracted structure by pruning small branches associated with local stylistic details and approximating the remaining structure with a limited set of Bézier curves. During training, we additionally apply random modifications to these curves. Together, these operations preserve the dominant structure while making residual stylistic cues unreliable.

    We now describe the style-suppressing operations in more detail.

    Pruning. We first remove branches that are more likely to arise from outline decoration than from genuine stroke structure. Pruning is defined relative to the local stroke width rather than by an absolute length threshold. In an initial pass, branches shorter than 0.4 stroke widths are removed. This suppresses small decorative spurs without systematically eliminating genuinely short structural components. Serifs require separate treatment. At a serif terminal, the medial axis often splits into two short branches on opposite sides of the stroke. Removing either branch independently would shorten the stroke rather than remove only its decoration. We distinguish such serif pairs from genuine bifurcations using the line segment joining the two branch tips. If this segment lies entirely inside the glyph, the branches are treated as the two prongs of a serif. If it exits the glyph, as between the upper arms of a Y, the branches are treated as genuine structure and retained. A detected serif pair is replaced by a single branch between the two prongs, preserving the full stroke extent while discarding the terminal shape. In our fonts, serif branches span at most approximately one stroke width, whereas genuine structural limbs typically span two to five stroke widths. We therefore merge a pair only when both branches are shorter than 1.5 stroke widths. A final pruning pass removes branches shorter than 0.9 stroke widths, except where such a branch independently captures a substantial part of the glyph structure.

    Representational bottleneck. We next approximate the pruned medial axis with a limited number of cubic Bézier curves. This sparse representation acts as an explicit information bottleneck rather than merely a compact encoding. A limited number of smooth curves can preserve the coarse glyph geometry, including stroke paths, curvature, and connectivity, while lacking the capacity to reproduce fine stylistic irregularities inherited from the original outline. Curve fitting is performed adaptively. The axis is initially represented by a single cubic Bézier curve and is subdivided at the point of maximum fitting error only when needed. Capacity is therefore allocated preferentially to regions that require additional geometric detail. Across our data, a glyph is represented by approximately ten curves on average and by at most 12. If this capacity is exceeded, the least significant cues are discarded as intended. The subdivision tolerance is expressed relative to stroke thickness. Because the medial axis is defined by its distance to the glyph boundary, constraining the fitting error in this way keeps the approximation geometrically consistent with the glyph interior. The resulting representation is deliberately lossy while remaining faithful to the underlying stroke geometry.

    Although pruning and curve compression remove much of the stylistic information, they cannot guarantee complete invariance. A sufficiently expressive model may still exploit residual correlations between the conditioning sketch and the target style. We therefore introduce two training-time mechanisms in UGL to make such residual information unreliable.

    Perturbation during training. During training, each conditioning stroke is randomly perturbed while the corresponding target glyph remains unchanged. The model therefore does not observe a single exact skeleton as the unique conditioning representation of a target. Large-scale structure is preserved, while small local details become unreliable as predictive features. The curve representation allows us to perturb strokes structurally rather than at the pixel level. We deform the interior of each curve while keeping its endpoints fixed, preserving junctions and overall connectivity. Perturbation magnitude is scaled by curve length and correlated along the stroke, causing the stroke to bend smoothly as a whole rather than introducing high-frequency local noise. Each interior control point is displaced by a Gaussian whose standard deviation is a fraction of the curve’s chord length, capped at twice that deviation so that a curve cannot fold back on itself. We resample this fraction uniformly for every sample at every epoch, from [0.10,0.20] when training UGL and from [0.03,0.08] when training a Style LoRA (Table 3), so the model sees a range of sketch precision rather than one fixed noise level.

    Cross-style pairing.

    To further prevent the sketch from serving as a style condition, we exploit the cross-font correspondence provided by the geometric recipes. Rather than always pairing a target glyph with its own extracted sketch, we can condition it on a sketch extracted from another font generated by the same recipe. Although their precise medial axes may differ, the sketch and target share the same underlying construction while belonging to different styles. This cross-style pairing discourages UGL from using the conditioning sketch to infer the target style.

    Together, geometry enrichment, style suppression, and cross-style pairing produce a broad training distribution in which structural sketches primarily communicate geometry rather than shape identity or style. Training UGL on this corpus encourages it to follow the supplied structure, providing the universal geometry prior required for open-form transfer.

    Appendix D Training details

    Both adapters are LoRA modules [17] on the attention projections of the FLUX.2-klein-base-4B transformer [2] (80 linear layers); the backbone, the VAE and the Qwen3 text encoder stay frozen, the text encoder in 8-bit. UGL uses rank 192 with α=192; every Style LoRA uses rank 32 with α=32 and is trained with UGL attached as a frozen adapter, never merged. Both stages use AdamW-8bit (learning rate 10⁻⁴, constant after a linear warm-up, β=(0.9,0.999), weight decay 0.01, ε=10⁻⁶), an EMA of the adapter weights with decay 0.99, gradient checkpointing, and a flow-matching objective at 256×256 for both the target and the sketch condition. Adapter weights are stored in fp16. Table 3 lists the per-stage settings.

    Appendix E Additional Results

    Figure 16: Sculptural and decorative styles on pose and glyph sketches. Each row is one structural sketch (left): four pose sketches (top) and five glyph sketches (bottom); each column is one style, shown by three reference examples at the top.

    Appendix F VLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation

    We employ a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation framework to assess generated results in the open-set regimes, where no unique paired ground truth exists: for a target structure outside the style’s own shape family there is no single correct rendering to compare against, so paired metrics such as LPIPS and SSIM are undefined. The judge is asked instead whether the requested structure is depicted and whether it is realized in the demonstrated geometric design language.

    Each judged candidate is presented as a single composite image with labeled panels: a top row of K=6 style references, and a bottom row holding the target structural sketch and the candidate. References are drawn only from the style’s training rows, so the judge never sees the ground-truth target of the case it is grading. All panels are rendered at 256×256 on a common canvas, and nothing in the image or the prompt identifies the method that produced the candidate.

    We score each candidate absolutely rather than in pairs. This has two consequences we rely on: the resulting scalar does not depend on which baselines happen to be included in the comparison, and there is no left–right position bias to mitigate. To remove the remaining ordering effect, the six style references are shuffled per case with a fixed per-case permutation. The judge is instructed to return a single JSON object conforming to a strict response schema, which prevents the answer from drifting into prose and bounds the output length.

    The response to the example query illustrates the two axes being scored independently. Geometry is 4 rather than 5 because the judge locates two nameable departures from the sketch before scoring it: the rider is given the head the sketch leaves implicit, and the bicycle frame is redrawn cleaner than the tangle of strokes it was traced from. Style is 4 because the candidate carries the references’ badge, weight and figure convention onto a sport none of them shows, while stopping short of being mistaken for one of them. Both flags are false: the candidate reproduces no shown reference, and it is not the sketch passed through unstyled.

    F.1 Judge Configuration

    We use the same judge configuration for the entire evaluation: all reported numbers come from gemini-3.1-pro-preview with a structured response schema and medium media resolution. Each candidate is judged in a single pass. Scores are aggregated hierarchically, matching the rest of our protocol: samples within a case, cases within a style, then styles weighted equally.

    Appendix G User Study

    G.1 User Study Setup

    We complement the VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation with a human preference study. Unlike the judge, which scores each candidate absolutely, the study is pairwise: participants see two results for the same input and indicate which one is better. Relative judgments are easier for non-expert participants to make consistently than absolute ratings, and they directly answer the question of interest, namely whether our results are preferred over those of each baseline.

    Each question is presented as a single composite image with labeled panels: a top row with the style references and the structural sketch, and a bottom row with two results, A and B. One result is ours and the other is produced by a baseline, both generated for the same style and the same sketch. All panels, including the two results, are rendered at the same size on a common canvas, so that the native output resolution of a method is not revealed, and nothing in the image or the text identifies the method behind a result.

    The study contains 12 questions: three for each of the four baselines (MX-Font, FontDiffuser, Gemini, and GPT-Image), each on a different style, covering black-and-white fonts, decorative fonts, and pictogram styles. The sketches span held-out glyphs, non-Latin glyphs, human poses, and symbols. For each question, participants answer three multiple-choice items, on style, structure, and overall preference, each with the options Result A, Result B, and About the same.

    To control for ordering and position effects, we prepare four editions of the questionnaire. Each edition shuffles the order of the questions, never placing the same baseline in two consecutive questions, and randomizes which side shows our result. Within every edition our result appears as A in exactly half of the questions, and the side assignment is mirrored between editions, so that any preference for a side cancels out. Participants reach the study through a single link that assigns them to one of the editions at random. Responses are anonymous, and each participant answers one edition.

    The example illustrates why the two axes are asked separately. Both results depict a recognizable treble clef, so the structure item mainly asks whether the particular structure of the sketch is preserved, such as its proportions, the spiral around the stem, and the hooked tail. The style item asks something different: whether the result carries the distinctive traits of the references, such as the rounded, asymmetric blue tile, the bold white strokes with rounded ends, and the thin parallel lines that accompany the figures, rather than merely sharing their colors.

    Before the first question, participants are shown one worked example in the same layout, with the intended answers marked and a one-line explanation of each. Its two results are not method outputs: one is a letter of a reference font and the other is the same letter in a plain serif font, so the intended answers are unambiguous and do not bias participants toward any method.

    G.2 Aggregation

    For each baseline and each of the three items, we report the percentage of votes that prefer our result, prefer the baseline’s result, or rate the two as about the same, pooled over participants, editions, and the three questions of that baseline. Significance is assessed with a two-sided exact binomial test against 50% on the decisive votes, i.e., after discarding About the same answers. In total, 32 participants completed the study.

item.title: 过去压成状态、现在走注意力：PASPA 用块间持久状态做长时共语动作生成，FGD 降到 3.532 ｜ Past as State, Present as Attention: Persistent-State Blockwise Flow Matching for Long-Horizon Co-Speech Motion Generation
item.description:
一句话：历史该被压成紧凑状态而不是越长越好：块间持久状态 + 块内双向注意力，FGD 3.532。

要点：

  • 「Past as State, Present as Attention」：块间用持久状态压缩缓慢变化的风格，块内用双向自注意力建模快速变化的局部动态
  • 在 blockwise flow matching 框架里实例化，配合多块监督、prefill-decode 状态缓存与条件/历史的混合 CFG
  • 对照组显示把历史注意力从 Attn₈ 扩到 Attn_all 仍不如 PASPA；完整 Hybrid CFG 把 FGD 从 4.450 压到 3.532

为什么值得看：长序列生成里「保留多少原始历史」和「怎么用历史」是两件事。这条把「过去的风格该压成状态、当下的动态才需要注意力」讲得最直白，对长时动画、对话动作与 NPC 行为序列生成可以直接借用这套结构。

中文摘要：长时共语动作生成要求时序连贯且风格一致，现有做法要么只条件于最近若干帧当种子（会逐渐漂移），要么保留越来越长的显式历史（维护贵、数据少时学不动）。作者把问题归结为过去与现在的不对称：过去的动作携带缓慢变化的风格，应被紧凑总结；当前片段有快速变化的局部动态，需要细粒度建模。据此提出 PASPA：用块间持久状态总结历史，用块内双向自注意力建模当前片段，并实例化在 blockwise flow matching 框架里，配合多块监督、prefill-decode 状态缓存与混合无分类器引导。实验显示，单纯把历史注意力从 8 帧扩到全历史仍不如 PASPA，而完整的混合 CFG 把 FGD 从 4.450 降到 3.532。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-23

本期推送：2026-10-27

Past as State, Present as Attention:
Persistent-State Blockwise Flow Matching for
Long-Horizon Co-Speech Motion Generation

Abstract

Co-speech motion generation remains challenging over long horizons due to the need for temporal coherence and consistent style. Existing methods typically generate long motions segment by segment, either conditioning on a short seed of recent frames, which gradually drifts, or retaining ever-longer explicit histories, which are costly to maintain and hard to learn from limited data. We trace these limitations to a key asymmetry between past and present: past motion carries slowly varying style that should be compactly summarized, whereas the current segment exhibits fast-changing local dynamics that require fine-grained modeling. This asymmetry motivates a simple Past-As-State, Present-as-Attention principle for long-horizon co-speech motion generation. Following this principle, we propose PASPA, which summarizes past history with an inter-block persistent state and models the current segment with intra-block bidirectional self-attention. We instantiate PASPA within a blockwise flow matching framework, with multi-block supervision for effective training over variable histories, prefill-decode state caching for efficient rollout, and hybrid classifier-free guidance for enhanced history and speech conditioning. Extensive public-benchmark experiments show that PASPA achieves state-of-the-art FGD performance and preserves motion style across long-sequence generation.

1 Introduction

Humans naturally accompany speech with expressive body movements that convey emphasis, emotion, and communicative intent beyond words alone [53]. Co-speech motion generation aims to synthesize realistic full-body motions that are temporally aligned and semantically consistent with speech [56]. It is crucial to applications like digital humans [99], virtual assistants [86], and animated characters [24].

Early co-speech motion generation often relies on direct speech-to-motion mapping [87], but the inherent one-to-many nature of speech-to-motion correspondence has made generative modeling increasingly important [38]. Accordingly, diffusion models [26] and flow matching [50, 42], the prevailing generative paradigms, have been widely adopted in this field.111 We use diffusion and flow matching interchangeably in this paper due to their mathematical equivalence [4, 43]. While they improve short-horizon realism and controllability [90, 48], long-horizon co-speech motion generation remains challenging, as it requires preserving temporal coherence [75] and speaker style [3] (see Fig.1).

For long-horizon generation, most methods proceed segment by segment, making inter-block history propagation the central challenge. A common strategy is to use only a seed (i.e., the previous segment’s last few frames; Fig.2a) [44, 91, 90] as condition. With such limited history, temporal coherence and style gradually drift over time (see Fig.1a) [75]. Recent streaming methods exploit longer histories [75, 77, 8], but retain contexts like frames or tokens (see Fig.2b). Maintaining such explicit histories incurs growing memory and compute costs as horizons extend, especially with attention-based backbones [74]. More critically, learning to exploit ever longer explicit histories is difficult given the limited data in co-speech motion generation [44], often leading to unstable style preservation (see Fig.1b). These observations raise a fundamental question: is there a more effective way to represent and propagate the past than explicitly attending to raw historical sequences?

We answer this affirmatively: the past and present play distinct roles in motion generation and should be represented accordingly. Past history primarily carries slowly varying stylistic traits (e.g., gesture amplitude and spatial preference) [1, 3], which should be compactly summarized rather than stored verbatim. By contrast, local motion dynamics are fast-changing, making full-resolution modeling of the current block more suitable for capturing fine-grained motion details. This asymmetry motivates a simple Past-As-State, Present-as-Attention principle: the past should be compressed as a persistent state that is carried across segments, while the present should be modeled with full attention for expressive generation (see Fig.2c). Guided by this principle, we propose PASPA, which achieves temporally coherent and style-consistent long-horizon co-speech motion generation (see Fig.1c).

In PASPA, past history and the current block are handled by two complementary mechanisms. For past history, we design a block-level recurrent state mechanism built upon Gated DeltaNet [83, 81], which progressively summarizes preceding blocks into a persistent state and provides a selective-retention, temporal-decay inductive bias for slowly evolving motion style. For the current block, we use blockwise self-attention [74, 60] to enable full bidirectional interaction for fine-grained modeling. We integrate them into a hybrid PASPA module, which forms the core component of our model.

We build PASPA on a semi-autoregressive blockwise flow matching (BFM) framework inspired by recent block diffusion paradigms [6, 94], and develop tailored training and inference protocols. For training, we apply distinct noise levels to multiple blocks and supervise their denoising in parallel, yielding dense multi-block supervision and exposing each block to states summarizing variable-length histories. For inference, PASPA separates state prefilling from iterative decoding and reuses cached historical states for efficient rollout. To improve generation quality, we introduce a hybrid classifier-free guidance [27] that augments audio-conditioned guidance with history-drop guidance [66], enabling explicit control over historical dependence while preserving speech alignment.

Our main technical contributions are: (1) We identify a key asymmetry in the roles of past and present in co-speech motion generation, and formulate a simple past-as-state, present-as-attention principle for long-horizon modeling. (2) Following this principle, we propose PASPA, a persistent-state method built on blockwise flow matching, whose core module couples inter-block persistent state modeling with intra-block attention. (3) We develop tailored training and inference schemes, including multi-block supervision, prefill-decode decoupling with state caching, and hybrid classifier-free guidance.

2 Related Work

Co-Speech Motion Generation.

The task synthesizes speech-aligned body movements. Its one-to-many nature motivates generative paradigms such as diffusion models (DMs) [26, 67] and VQ-VAE-based generation [73] for realism and diversity [24, 2, 1, 98, 93]. Further enhancements for semantic controllability include hierarchical designs and language-based guidance [59, 49, 41, 9, 89]. VQ-VAE-based methods [85, 44, 51, 91, 92] generate motions through learned codebooks, but often suffer from limited diversity due to discrete code constraints. DM-based methods [11, 5, 13, 54, 90] better support diverse motion synthesis and have become a dominant paradigm in this field.

Diffusion Models and Flow Matching.

DMs [26] and Flow Matching (FM) [42, 50] have achieved strong results in image generation [14, 17]. Advances include novel architectures [58, 20, 78], conditional guidance [27, 37, 32], and accelerated sampling [65, 50]. They also extend to sequential domains (e.g., video) via autoregressive (AR) factorization for variable-length rollout [6, 10, 62]. Representative approaches include Block Diffusion [6, 94], which combines intra-block denoising with inter-block autoregression, and Diffusion Forcing [10], which assigns independent per-token noise levels to bridge next-token prediction [61] and full-sequence diffusion. Related advances mitigate exposure bias [29], enable real-time generation [47], and support flexible history conditioning [66]. This AR diffusion paradigm has also been adapted to motion generation [25, 96, 8, 77].

Long-Context Sequence Modeling.

Attention [74] dominates long-context modeling but scales quadratically with sequence length [70] and lacks inductive biases for data-limited regimes [18]. Alternatives like state space models [22, 16] and linear attention [34, 83, 82] replace pairwise attention with linear recurrent state updates, improving efficiency and introducing stronger temporal inductive bias. Specifically, Gated DeltaNet (GDN) [81] is highly relevant to us, as its gating and delta-rule updates yield a temporal-decay bias that we leverage to model continuous motion dynamics. Such long-context designs have also been adopted in motion generation (e.g., Motion Mamba [95]).

3 Methodology

3.1 Preliminary

Co-Speech Motion Generation.

This task synthesizes motion x∈ℝ^T×C and facial expression e∈ℝ^T×Cₑ from a speech waveform a∈ℝ^Tₐ. Following the SMPL-X [52, 57] parameterization, the motion sequence x consists of J=55 joint rotations and a 3D global translation. The joint rotations are converted from axis-angle to the 6D representation (rot6d) [97], yielding C=6J+3=333. Following FLAME [40], the expression e is represented by Cₑ=100 FLAME coefficients. For long-horizon generation, co-speech motion is commonly generated segment by segment [90, 91, 44]. Accordingly, the motion and expression sequences are partitioned into N blocks of length K, denoted by x=[x¹,…,x^N] and e=[e¹,…,e^N], where xⁿ∈ℝ^K×C and eⁿ∈ℝ^K×Cₑ denote the n-th motion and expression blocks, respectively. The waveform is segmented analogously into N blocks of length Kₐ (i.e., a=[a¹,…,a^N]), where aⁿ∈ℝ^Kₐ denotes the n-th speech segment.

Flow Matching.

Our method builds on FM [42, 50], a prevailing generative paradigm. It constructs a probability path by linearly interpolating between clean motion x₀ and noise z, governed by time t:

xₜ=(1-t)x₀+tz, z∼ℕ(0,I), t∈[0,1],

(1)

where ℕ denotes the Gaussian distribution. Typically, FM learns the path velocity and samples by solving the corresponding probability flow ordinary differential equation [42, 50] of this path.

3.2 Past-as-State, Present-as-Attention Module

In segment-by-segment motion generation [44, 90], past history and the current block serve different roles. Empirically, style cues remain correlated over long timescales, whereas local motion dynamics decay rapidly (see Fig.3). Motivated by this asymmetry, PASPA (see Fig.4) decouples their processing: an inter-block persistent state compactly summarizes past history, while an intra-block bidirectional attention models the current block via dense interaction.

3.2.1 Inter-Block Persistent State.

Why Persistent State for the Past?

Past history carries stable style and long-range tendencies. Such information is abstract and sparse: its effective content lies in a few persistent components, and token-level attention would waste capacity on transient fluctuations. Thus, the past should be selectively condensed into a persistent state, not indiscriminately preserved. We achieve this via Gated DeltaNet (GDN) [81], whose gating [82] and delta-rule [76, 63] updates suppress fluctuations and accumulate informative trends, yielding a strong inductive bias for history propagation in our data-limited setting.

Blockwise Gated DeltaNet (BGDN).

GDN is token-recurrent, but our generation proceeds block by block. We thus propose a blockwise GDN (BGDN, Fig.4a), driven by a tailored Block-Causal GDN kernel. Inside the BGDN module (Fig.4 (a.1)), we take the noisy current block as input and the encoded clean history as the context. Following GDN, we derive queries qᵢ∈ℝ^dₖ from the input, with keys kᵢ∈ℝ^dₖ, values vᵢ∈ℝ^dᵥ, and gates αᵢ,βᵢ∈(0,1) from the context, omitting GDN’s temporal mixing to prevent cross-block leakage. Within the kernel, these variables update a persistent state Sᵢ∈ℝ^dᵥ×dₖ and yield outputs o∈ℝ^dᵥ. o are then projected to produce final outputs.

Inside the kernel (Fig.4 (a.2)), we retain GDN’s standard state update to accumulate histories:

Sᵢ=Sᵢ₋₁(αᵢ(I-βᵢkᵢkᵢ^\intercal))+βᵢvᵢkᵢ^\intercal,

(2)

where αᵢ adaptively decays irrelevant fluctuations, and βᵢ governs the delta-rule update for selective information injection. However, applying GDN’s dynamic read mechanism to blockwise generation would cause intra-block future leakage. We therefore restrict reads to the frozen block-initial state:

GDN:oᵢ=Sᵢqᵢ, BGDN:oᵢ=S_[n]⁰qᵢ ∀(n-1)K

(3)

where S_[n]ʳ (0≤r≤K) denotes the state after processing the r-th token of block n. Instead of reading the continuously updated state Sᵢ, all queries within block n exclusively read from the block-start state S_[n]⁰ (also the previous block’s final state S_[n-1]^K). This formulation mathematically guarantees that each block only conditions on strict past history, ensuring the blockwise causality.

Efficient Implementation.

GDN admits an efficient chunkwise parallel form [81, 84] (detailed in AppendixB). Since we leave the state update of GDN unchanged, its parallel computation requires no modification. The read, however, must be adapted to enforce block-causality. Specifically, the computational chunk size is fixed to the generation block size K, and all tokens in block n exclusively share the block-start state S_[n]⁰ (i.e., the previous block’s final state S_[n-1]^K). This yields:

O_[n]^BGDN=Q_[n](S_[n]⁰)^\intercal∈ℝ^K×dᵥ, Q_[n]∈ℝ^K×dₖ, S_[n]⁰=S_[n-1]^K∈ℝ^dᵥ×dₖ.

(4)

This reduction to a dense matrix multiplication makes the read highly amenable to Tensor Core acceleration, for which we implement a custom Triton [72] kernel based on FLA [84].

3.2.2 Intra-Block Bidirectional Attention.

Why Bidirectional Attention for the Present?

The current block carries fast-changing dynamics, such as velocities and fine-grained articulations, which demand dense modeling of local motion details. Correspondingly, BGDN shares a common block-start state, leaving token-to-token interactions within the current block unmodeled. We assign this role to a dedicated bidirectional self-attention module [74] rather than a causal one: although frames within a block follow a micro-level temporal order, each token still benefits from both preceding and subsequent local context within the segment.

Blockwise Multi-Head Self-Attention (BMHSA).

Applying bidirectional self-attention [74] across the entire sequence naively would break the block-level semi-autoregression. We therefore propose BMHSA, which permits bidirectional interaction within each block while strictly forbidding any cross-block interaction. Given an input sequence X∈ℝ^NK×d, the output is computed as follows:

O=Softmax ((QKᵀ)/(√d)+Bᵇˡᵏ)VW_O, Bᵇˡᵏᵢⱼ=\begincases0&⌈i/K⌉=⌈j/K⌉ -∞&otherwise\endcases,

(5)

where i,j∈{1,…,NK} are token indexes, Bᵇˡᵏ∈{0,-∞}^NK×NK is the block-diagonal mask (see Fig.4b). We compute the query, key, and value matrices Q,K,V∈ℝ^NK×d as Q=XW_Q, K=XW_K, and V=XW_V, respectively, with rotary position embedding (RoPE) [68] applied to Q and K. Here, W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O∈ℝ^d×d are projection matrices, with W_O used for output projection. The formulation above is single-head, with the multi-head extension following [74].

Efficient Implementation.

Rather than materializing B, we reshape X from ℝ^NK×d to ℝ^N×K×d and apply standard bidirectional attention, treating the block index as batch (see Fig.4b). This yields the same output as Eq.5 while reducing the complexity from O((NK)²d) to O(NK²d).

3.2.3 Network Architecture.

We instantiate our PASPA layer following the DiT design [58] (see Fig.4) with two modifications. Structurally, we replace the self-attention sublayer with two sequential sublayers: BGDN and BMHSA. For adaptive modulation, we replace AdaLN with AdaRMSNorm [15], where the modulation parameters are predicted from the Fourier-embedded timestep t[69] and the speaker ID embedding. Our architecture follows GlobalDiff [90], but uses our PASPA layer. We first use a frozen audio-to-expression network to obtain expressions from WavLM features [12] and speaker ID. Motions are represented in global rotation space and split into torso (with translation) and hands branches. For each branch, the noisy stream embeds body-part motion with full noisy motion, audio features, and expressions as tokens for the stacked PASPA layers, while the history stream encodes clean past motion into each BGDN module (eₕ,eₜ in Fig.4). The branch outputs are merged to the full motion.

3.3 Blockwise Flow Matching

Inspired by recent block diffusion paradigms [6, 94], we formalize segment-by-segment motion generation as semi-autoregressive process with block-causal factorization p(x|a,e)=∏ₙ₌₁^Np(xⁿ|x^Sec.3.2.3). This process applies inter-block autoregression for long-horizon causality and intra-block bidirectional modeling for dense local dynamics.

Multi-Block Supervision.

To realize the semi-autoregressive factorization, we instantiate the FM interpolation in Eq.1 for each block, allowing every block to carry its own timestep tⁿ∈[0,1]:

x_tⁿⁿ=(1-tⁿ)x₀ⁿ+tⁿzⁿ, zⁿ∼ℕ(0,I), ∀n=1,…,N,

(6)

where x₀ⁿ is the n-th clean block.Following common practice in motion generation [90, 71], we train the network F_θ to directly predict each clean block x₀ⁿ, rather than the velocity in FM [42]. The block-causal F_θ performs dense parallel denoising over the entire sequence in a single forward pass:

x̂₀=[x̂₀¹,x̂₀²,…,x̂₀^N]^\intercal=F_θ([x_t¹¹,x_t²²,…,x_t^N^N]^\intercal,x₀,t,a), t=[t¹,t²,…,t^N]^\intercal,

(7)

where a is the aligned speech and x₀=[x₀¹,…,x₀^N]^\intercal is encoded as ground-truth history following teacher forcing [55, 64]. BGDN routes only x₀^Sec.3.2.1). Unlike per-block supervision [91, 90, 44], each iteration accumulates loss over all blocks, yielding N× denser supervision. More critically, heterogeneous block timesteps expose the model to diverse current-block noise levels at each history length, improving rollout robustness. Notably, we enforce t¹≤t²≤⋯≤t^N to mirror the inference-time noise profile, and replace the typical uniform timestep distribution with a logit-normal one [20]. Both are supported by ablations in Tab.3.

Loss Function.

We supervise the predicted x̂₀ in Eq.7 with the following overall objective222 With a slight abuse of notation, we use L to denote both the scalar loss term and the corresponding loss function.:

L=𝔼_x₀,a,z,t[1/N∑ₙ₌₁^N[e^-u(tⁿ)Lᵣₒₜⁿ+sg(e^-u(tⁿ))(Lⱼₒᵢₙₜⁿ+L_structⁿ)+u(tⁿ)]+L_bd],(8)
L_bd=1/N-1∑ₙ₌₁^N-1[Lᵣₒₜ (b̂ₙ,bₙ)+Lᵥₑₗ (b̂ₙ,bₙ)+L_acc (b̂ₙ,bₙ)].(9)

Here, Lᵣₒₜⁿ is the MSE loss on rot6d [97] and translations, while Lⱼₒᵢₙₜⁿ and L_structⁿ are forward kinematics (FK)-based losses on joint positions and skeletal structures adopted from GlobalDiff [90]. To adaptively mitigate optimization conflicts across blocks at varying noise levels, we train a small MLP u(·) to predict per-timestep weights [33] rather than manual tuning. We apply a stop-gradient (sg) to prevent the fluctuations of FK-based losses from destabilizing u(·). The boundary loss L_bd regularizes cross-block continuity via velocity and acceleration matching losses (i.e., Lᵥₑₗ,L_acc) on the transition windows b̂ₙ and bₙ of x̂₀ⁿ and x₀ⁿ, and is excluded from the adaptive weighting as each window spans two blocks at different timesteps. See AppendixC for definitions of Lᵣₒₜ,Lⱼₒᵢₙₜ,L_struct,Lᵥₑₗ,L_acc,b̂ₙ,bₙ.

3.4 Inference for Long-Horizon Rollout

Prefill-Decode Rollout with State Caching.

For long-horizon inference, PASPA employs a prefill-decode rollout (see Algorithm1). Prefill only encodes the clean segment to update the BGDN state, bypassing the denoising sublayers. Invoked after each block iteration (line 8), it integrates the freshly denoised block into the state. Decode (lines 4-7) treats S strictly as a read-only condition. It iteratively denoises the current block (line 7), evaluating F_θ under varying conditions for hybrid CFG (detailed below). Throughout the rollout, the fixed-size S is the sole persistent cache, initialized by prefilling seed x_seed and a_seed (or zeros) and reused across all N blocks. Unlike linearly growing token caches [74, 36], S guarantees an O(1) query complexity per step, regardless of history length.

Hybrid Classifier-Free Guidance.

Standard CFG [27] modulates only the condition cⁿ, leaving historical dependence uncontrolled. Motivated by [66], we introduce a learnable null state S_∅ for hybrid guidance via four predictions (Algorithm1, lines 5-6): unconditional (S_∅,∅), condition-only (S_∅,cⁿ), history-only (S,∅), and full (S,cⁿ). They are combined via a multilinear composition (Algorithm1, line 7) that incorporates marginal and second-order joint terms, empirically outperforming simpler alternatives (see Tab.11). To prevent distortions at noise extremes [37], scales w_cond(t) and wₕᵢₛₜ(t) are time-dependent, activating only during mid-noise intervals [0.1,0.6] (otherwise 1). To train Hybrid CFG, we independently drop cⁿ with probability 10% and sample S as unchanged, null S_∅, or interpolated αS+(1-α)S_∅ with probabilities 70%/10%/20%, where α is uniformly sampled from [0,1]. This interpolation enables continuous inference-time control of history strength.

4 Experiments

Setup.

We evaluate on BEAT2 [44] using its official splits, and on SHOW [85] following the evaluation protocol of DiffSHEG [11]. Following [54], BEAT2 comparisons use both the “Scott” subset (1 Speaker) and the full test set (All Speakers), while ablations use the 1 Speaker setting. PASPA is optimized via Muon [46, 31] with auxiliary AdamW [35] (training details in Sec.E.1). We report FGD [86] (the primary quality indicator) and Diversity (Div) [38] on both datasets, with BC [39] and face MSE [80] on BEAT2, and Beat Alignment (BA) on SHOW. Here, ↑/↓ indicate that higher/lower values are better. For readability, BEAT2 FGD and MSE are multiplied by 10 and 10⁸, respectively; SHOW metrics are reported without rescaling. In all tables, gray rows mark our final setting; bold and underlined denote the best and second-best results. See AppendicesD, E and F for details.

4.1 Main Results

Results on BEAT2.

Table1 compares PASPA with prior methods on BEAT2. In the 1 Speaker setting, PASPA achieves the best FGD (the primary quality metric) and MSE, indicating superior generation quality. It also obtains the second-best Div and competitive BC, reflecting favorable diversity and speech-motion alignment. In the All Speakers setting, PASPA achieves the best FGD and MSE, showing its stronger multi-speaker generalization. Compared with the FM-based GlobalDiff [90], PASPA improves all metrics, suggesting the advantage of persistent-state history modeling for FM-based co-speech motion generation. Figure5 also qualitatively shows that PASPA produces more natural gestures with better semantic alignment to speech than the baselines.

We further conduct a blind ranking study on BEAT2 with 18 participants, yielding 167 valid ranking groups. Participants rank four anonymized methods on 20-second clips across four criteria, with randomized method order and a ground-truth reference. The four criteria are motion realism, semantic consistency with speech, motion-speech synchronization, and motion diversity. PASPA achieves the highest top-1 win rate across all four criteria (see Fig.7), with 39.8% overall, further supporting these findings. See Secs.E.3 and F.3 for study details and the supplementary material for video demos.

Results on SHOW.

To complement our primary evaluation, we evaluate PASPA on SHOW using the same training recipe as on BEAT2 without dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning. As shown in Fig.7, PASPA achieves the lowest FGD, our primary generation-quality metric, at 0.00111, a 43.9% reduction from our FM-based baseline GlobalDiff, which achieves an FGD of 0.00198. PASPA yields slightly higher BA than GlobalDiff, while its Div remains second best. These results provide complementary evidence of PASPA’s effectiveness beyond BEAT2 in co-speech motion generation.

4.2 Ablations and Analysis

As outlined in Sec.3, PASPA’s architecture realizes the past–present asymmetry through inter-block persistent-state modeling and intra-block bidirectional attention. Weakly monotonic timesteps and adaptive weighting stabilize multi-block learning, while Hybrid CFG refines generation quality at inference time and prefill-decode separation accelerates generation. The following ablations and analyses examine these complementary roles and their effects on generation quality and efficiency.

Asymmetric Past-Present Modeling.

We validate the PASPA principle by varying the past and current modeling under a fixed training recipe in Tab.3. Removing history (history branch output set to zero) substantially degrades FGD, confirming the necessity of long-range context. Increasing token-attention history from Attn₈ to Attnₐₗₗ improves FGD, but still underperforms PASPA, showing that retaining more raw history does not guarantee effective history utilization. Moreover, replacing current-block attention with state-based recurrent modeling (i.e., State+State) yields worse FGD than even the no-history variant. This shows that the current block benefits from dense bidirectional interaction and that state-based current-block modeling hurts generation quality. These comparisons validate PASPA’s past-as-state, present-as-attention division, which yields the best FGD.

Blockwise Training Formulation.

We show the build-up ablation of our training recipe in Tab.3. Naively switching from single-block (Single) to multi-block (Multi) supervision degrades FGD despite denser supervision, due to unordered block timesteps and imbalanced losses across blocks and noise levels. Weakly monotonic timesteps (Mono) and adaptive loss weighting (AdaW; see Eq.8) address these two issues, significantly reducing FGD to 5.614. Beyond the two critical stabilizers, SG (i.e., sg(·) in Eq.8) reduces FGD to 5.216, and LogitN (i.e., logit-normal time sampling [20]) brings it to 4.450. We use the optimal LogitN parameters in Tab.3; see Tab.7 for the full sweep.

Classifier-Free Guidance.

Figure10 evaluates the CFG build-up, including training dropout and inference guidance. Condition dropout, acting as data augmentation, already reduces FGD from 4.450 to 3.937, and condition guidance further improves it to 3.883. However, history dropout without guidance slightly degrades FGD, emphasizing that it offers no inherent quality gain alone. Further adding history guidance without the second-order joint term also remains worse than condition CFG. Only the full Hybrid CFG substantially reduces FGD to 3.532, validating the explicit interaction between condition and history guidance. The activation interval is fixed to t∈[0.1,0.6]. Detailed CFG scale, composition, and activation-interval ablations are in Tabs.11, 8, 8 and 11. An end-to-end comparison with and without CFG under the main-experiment setting is in Tab.12.

Long-Rollout Analysis.

We quantify long-rollout quality preservation in Fig.10 (implementation in Sec.E.2). We construct controlled baselines: Short Seed uses the last 8 frames, while Token Attention attends to all past tokens. They represent finite-window and full-history conditioning, respectively, with other settings matched to PASPA. We use these controlled variants rather than complete methods to isolate history propagation from method-specific differences (e.g., architecture, losses). Although all methods start with reasonable FGD, Short Seed degrades most severely, Token Attention degrades less by retaining explicit history, and PASPA shows the weakest degradation, proving persistent states better preserve long-range tendencies. PASPA also achieves the highest diversity (Div) throughout rollout. Figure1 shows consistent qualitative trends, supporting PASPA’s long-rollout advantage. See Fig.12 for complementary long-rollout trends, additional metrics, and uncertainty estimates.

We further test efficiency without CFG on synthetic ultra-long rollouts in Fig.10, where PASPA w/o PD denotes PASPA without prefill-decode separation. PASPA matches Short Seed’s peak memory and stays far below Token Attention’s, as history is accumulated into a fixed-size state instead of growing explicit tokens. While latency increases with length for all methods, prefill-decode separation is decisive: it accelerates PASPA from the slowest to the fastest. See Sec.E.2 for details.

Hybrid CFG Inference Overhead.

Since Fig.10 benchmarks all methods without CFG, we measure the additional cost of enabling Hybrid CFG in Tab.4. Enabling Hybrid CFG increases latency (Lat.) by only 4.9–9.1% and peak memory (Mem.) by 0.01 GB across the evaluated lengths. We attribute this modest latency increase to batched guidance exploiting spare GPU capacity, as the small motion-generation workload does not saturate the GPU. Together with Tab.12, these results show that Hybrid CFG improves quality with modest latency overhead and nearly unchanged memory scaling.

5 Conclusion

We present PASPA for long-horizon co-speech motion generation based on the observation that past history and the current segment demand different treatments. PASPA realizes this via a hybrid design, summarizing past history into a persistent state while modeling the current segment with bidirectional attention. Built on blockwise flow matching, PASPA incorporates multi-block supervision for effective training and a prefill-decode protocol with hybrid classifier-free guidance for stable, expressive inference. Extensive public-benchmark evaluations show that PASPA achieves state-of-the-art FGD performance, preserving style and preventing temporal drift during extended motion generation.

Acknowledgments

This work was supported by the Alibaba Research Intern Program.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Empirical Motivation for the Asymmetry Between Past and Present

Diagnostic Setup.

As illustrated in Fig.3, we employ autocorrelation analysis to investigate whether stylistic features and frame-level local dynamics exhibit distinct temporal persistence in co-speech motion generation. The analysis is conducted on the training subset of BEAT2 [44].

For each sequence, we convert SMPL-X rotations [52, 57] to 3D joint positions by forward kinematics. To factor out orientation and scale variations, we respectively remove pelvic global yaw and normalize seven root-relative upper-body joints (neck, shoulders, elbows, wrists) by shoulder width. We use

Pₜ=[pₜⁿᵉᶜᵏ,pₜ^left-shoulder,pₜʳⁱᵍʰᵗ⁻ˢʰᵒᵘˡᵈᵉʳ,pₜ^left-elbow,pₜʳⁱᵍʰᵗ⁻ᵉˡᵇᵒʷ,pₜ^left-wrist,pₜʳⁱᵍʰᵗ⁻ʷʳⁱˢᵗ]∈ℝ^7×3

to denote the normalized upper-body pose at frame t, where each pₜ^(·)∈ℝ³ is a root-local 3D joint position. Both the style and local feature families are computed over the same trailing window Wₜ={t-W+1,…,t} with W=30 frames (i.e., 1 s).

The style feature sₜ∈ℝ⁵ consists of five sub-features, defined as follows:

sₜ=[sₜᵉˣᵗ,sₜˢᵖᵃⁿ,sₜʰᵉⁱᵍʰᵗ,sₜˡᵃᵗ,sₜᵒᶜᶜ],

(10)

whose five components are computed as follows:

  • •

    Extension measures the average distance from the elbows and wrists to the neck:

    sₜᵉˣᵗ=1/4W∑_r∈Wₜ∑_a∈Jₑₓₜ∥pᵣᵃ-pᵣⁿᵉᶜᵏ∥₂,

    		(11)

    with Jₑₓₜ={left-elbow,right-elbow,left-wrist,right-wrist}.

  • •

    Span measures the average distance between the two wrists:

    sₜˢᵖᵃⁿ=1/W∑_r∈Wₜ∥pᵣ^left-wrist-pᵣʳⁱᵍʰᵗ⁻ʷʳⁱˢᵗ∥₂.

    		(12)
  • •

    Height measures the average wrist height relative to the neck along the vertical axis:

    sₜʰᵉⁱᵍʰᵗ=1/2W∑_r∈Wₜ[(pᵣ^left-wrist-pᵣⁿᵉᶜᵏ)_y+(pᵣʳⁱᵍʰᵗ⁻ʷʳⁱˢᵗ-pᵣⁿᵉᶜᵏ)_y].

    		(13)
  • •

    Laterality measures the left-right asymmetry of hand extension:

    sₜˡᵃᵗ=1/W∑_r∈Wₜ(∥pᵣʳⁱᵍʰᵗ⁻ʷʳⁱˢᵗ-pᵣⁿᵉᶜᵏ∥₂-∥pᵣ^left-wrist-pᵣⁿᵉᶜᵏ∥₂).

    		(14)
  • •

    Occupancy measures the spatial extent explored by the wrists within the window:

    sₜᵒᶜᶜ=\log(tr[Cov({pᵣ^left-wrist,pᵣʳⁱᵍʰᵗ⁻ʷʳⁱˢᵗ}_r∈Wₜ)]+ε).

    		(15)

    • These components provide an interpretable diagnostic of stylistic speaker characteristics, whose temporal persistence can be compared with local motion dynamics.

    The local motion feature lₜ∈ℝ²¹ is defined as a window-level high-pass pose residual:

    lₜ=vec(Pₜ-1/W∑_r∈WₜPᵣ)∈ℝ²¹.

    		(16)

    Here, vec(·) flattens the 7×3 joint-position matrix into a 21D vector. This residual removes the local window mean and emphasizes fast-changing pose variations around the recent motion tendency. By construction, lₜ and sₜ forms complementary frequency components over the same window Wₜ, attributing any difference to the data rather than the operator.

    For the alternative features shown in the inset of Fig.3, with the local feature unchanged, we replace the hand-designed style feature sₜ with the windowed raw pose mean:

    sₜᵃˡᵗ=vec(1/W∑_r∈WₜPᵣ)∈ℝ²¹,

    		(17)

    which is used to examine robustness against the choice of our hand-crafted style descriptors.

    Feature Preprocessing.

    Before computing autocorrelation, we apply two preprocessing steps.

    First, to prevent speech energy from inflating the autocorrelation of features, we partial out its linear contribution from each feature dimension. Let yₜ∈ℝ^D denote any of sₜ, lₜ, or sₜᵃˡᵗ, and let ρₜ denote the frame-aligned log-RMS speech energy (i.e., the natural logarithm of the per-frame root mean square of the waveform). For each frame t, we build a lagged audio-energy vector:

    uₜʳᵐˢ=[ρ_t-L,…,ρₜ,…,ρ_t+L]^\intercal, L=15,

    		(18)

    which covers a temporal range of ±0.5 seconds at 30 FPS. For each feature dimension d, we fit a ridge regressor [28] from the lagged audio energy to the feature value:

    β̂_d=\arg\min_β∑_t∈I(y_t,d-(uₜʳᵐˢ)^\intercalβ)²+λ∥β∥₂²,

    		(19)

    where I denotes the valid frame indices with complete audio lags and we use λ=1. We replace each feature dimension with its residual to obtain features without linear speech-energy contribution:

    ỹ_t,d=y_t,d-(uₜʳᵐˢ)^\intercalβ̂_d.

    		(20)

    Second, each feature dimension is standardized to zero mean and unit variance using per-speaker statistics, so that no single dimension dominates the autocorrelation. For notational simplicity, we use yₜ to denote the preprocessed feature sequence in the following.

    Trace Autocorrelation.

    Given a preprocessed multivariate feature sequence yₜ∈ℝ^D, where yₜ can be either the style feature sₜ or the local feature lₜ, we measure its temporal persistence using trace autocorrelation (ACF). Let ȳ denote the temporal mean. For a temporal lag τ, the trace ACF is:

    r_y(τ)=(tr(1/T-τ∑ₜ₌₁^T-τ(yₜ-ȳ)(y_t+τ-ȳ)^\intercal))/(tr(1/T∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ(yₜ-ȳ)(yₜ-ȳ)^\intercal)).

    		(21)

    This yields a variance-weighted ACF over feature dimensions, without selecting a coordinate.

    After computing sequence-level ACFs, we aggregate these ACFs r_y(τ) in two stages:

  • •

    Within each speaker, we average the per-sequence ACFs weighted by \max(Tᵢ-τ,0), where Tᵢ is the length of sequence i, so that short sequences contribute less at large lags.

  • •

    Across speakers, we aggregate via the Fisher-z transform [21]:

    r̄_y(τ)=\tanh(1/S∑ₛ₌₁^Sarctanh(r_yˢ(τ))), τ>0,

    		(22)

    where r_yˢ(τ) is the within-speaker ACF of speaker s, and S is the number of speakers. Specifically, we set r̄_y(0)=1 by definition.

    • Finally, we estimate 95% confidence intervals by bootstrap resampling [19] over speakers (2000 resamples), which corresponds to the shaded regions shown in Fig.3. The same procedure is applied to both main and alternative features.

    Observations and Implications.

    Figure3 reveals a clear temporal-persistence asymmetry between the two feature types. The style ACF r̄ₛ(τ) remains substantially positive beyond 100 frames. Conversely, the local ACF r̄ₗ(τ) decays to near zero within a few tens of frames, indicating that frame-level pose dynamics are inherently short-term. The pattern persists when replacing hand-crafted style descriptors with the windowed raw pose mean (inset), confirming the asymmetry is data-intrinsic rather than descriptor-induced. This asymmetry motivates PASPA’s core design: past history mainly carries slowly varying stylistic tendencies that should be summarized into a persistent state, whereas the current block contains fast-changing local dynamics that benefit from dense intra-block attention.

    Appendix B Background: Chunkwise Parallel Form of Gated DeltaNet

    We denote the query, key, and value matrices as Q,K∈ℝ^T×dₖ and V∈ℝ^T×dᵥ, where T is the sequence length and dₖ,dᵥ denote the per-head query/key and value dimensions, respectively.

    The chunkwise parallel form partitions Q,K,V into N=T/K non-overlapping chunks of size K (assuming T is divisible by K). The n-th chunk (n∈{1,2,…,N}) of Q is written as Q_[n]:=q_(n-1)K+1:nK+1 and analogously for K_[n],V_[n]. We further denote the r-th token within chunk n as qʳ_[n]:=q_(n-1)K+r∈ℝ^dₖ, with kʳ_[n],vʳ_[n] defined analogously. The scalar gating αʳ_[n] and write-strength βʳ_[n] follow the same within-chunk indexing. Finally, we define the cumulative gating product γʳ_[n]:=∏ⱼ₌₁ʳαʲ_[n] for the first r tokens of chunk n, with γ⁰_[n]:=1 by convention.

    The chunkwise parallel form computes the state update and output read for an entire chunk via:

    S_[n+1]=\overrightarrowS_[n]+(Ũ_[n]-\overleftarrowW_[n]S^\intercal_[n])^\intercal\overrightarrowK_[n],(23)
    O_[n]=\underbrace\overleftarrowQ_[n]S^\intercal_[n]_inter-chunk term+\underbrace(Q_[n]K^\intercal_[n]⊙M)(Ũ_[n]-\overleftarrowW_[n]S^\intercal_[n])_intra-chunk term,(24)

    where M∈ℝ^K×K is the intra-chunk causal mask with Mᵢⱼ=1 if i≥j and 0 otherwise. The output O_[n]∈ℝ^K×dᵥ decomposes into two terms: an inter-chunk term that reads from the block-start state S_[n] carrying information from previous chunks, and an intra-chunk term capturing token-level interactions within the current chunk. We detailed the core notations of Eqs.23 and 24 below.

    Arrow Notation.

    The left and right arrows denote cumulative gating coefficients within a chunk:

    \overleftarrowqʳ_[n]=γʳ_[n]qʳ_[n], \overleftarrowwʳ_[n]=γʳ_[n]wʳ_[n], \overrightarrowkʳ_[n]=(γ^K_[n])/(γʳ_[n])kʳ_[n], \overrightarrowS_[n]=γ^K_[n]S_[n],

    		(25)

    with the first three equations extending to stacked matrix forms \overleftarrowQ_[n],\overleftarrowW_[n],\overrightarrowK_[n]∈ℝ^K×dₖ, whose r-th rows are \overleftarrowqʳ_[n],\overleftarrowwʳ_[n],\overrightarrowkʳ_[n], respectively. Intuitively, left arrows rescale each token by the cumulative gating from the start, while right arrows apply the remaining gating toward final position K.

    WY coefficients and the UT transform.

    The matrices Ũ_[n]∈ℝ^K×dᵥ and W_[n]∈ℝ^K×dₖ are the WY representation [7] coefficients for the cumulative generalized Householder product ∏ᵢ(I-βⁱ_[n]kⁱ_[n]k^i\intercal_[n]) that arises when unrolling Eq.2 across a chunk. The matrices Ũ_[n] and W_[n] admit closed-form expressions via the UT transform [30], as follows:

    T_[n]=[I+strictLower(diag(β_[n])(Γ_[n]⊙K_[n]K^\intercal_[n]))]⁻¹diag(β_[n]),(26)
    W_[n]=T_[n]K_[n], Ũ_[n]=T_[n]V_[n].(27)

    Here Γ_[n]∈ℝ^K×K is the decay-aware mask with (Γ_[n])ᵢⱼ=(γⁱ_[n])/(γʲ_[n]) for i≥j and 0 otherwise, and strictLower(·) extracts the strictly lower-triangular part of a matrix, zeroing out other parts.

    Remarks.

    Equations23 and 24) consist of dense matrix multiplications and element-wise operations, making the chunkwise form well-suited for tensor-core acceleration. Flash Linear Attention (FLA) [84] further provides Triton-accelerated implementations of such chunkwise kernels.

    Appendix C Detailed Formulations of Loss Functions

    In this section, we provide the exact mathematical definitions of the individual loss terms.

    C.1 Details of Sequence-Level Losses

    The rotation loss Lᵣₒₜⁿ is the per-frame Mean Squared Error (MSE) between predicted and ground-truth motion representations within block n:

    Lᵣₒₜⁿ=1/K∑ᵢ₌₁^K∥x̂₀^n,i-x₀^n,i∥₂²,

    		(28)

    where x̂₀^n,i and x₀^n,i denote the predicted and ground-truth 6D motion representations with the global translation at the i-th frame of block n, respectively.

    Following GlobalDiff [90], we apply forward kinematics (FK) to map the rotations [97] into 3D joint positions in the global space. We denote the predicted and ground truth FK joint positions at the i-th frame of block n as Ĵ₀^n,i and J₀^n,i, respectively, and define two FK-based losses on top of them.

    The joint loss Lⱼₒᵢₙₜⁿ directly supervises absolute joint positions:

    Lⱼₒᵢₙₜⁿ=1/K∑ᵢ₌₁^K∥Ĵ₀^n,i-J₀^n,i∥₂².

    		(29)

    The structural loss L_structⁿ instead supervises bone-level relations, enforcing consistency of pairwise bone-angle similarities to discourage unnatural bone stretching. Let 𝔼 denote the set of bones in the kinematic tree, where each bone e=(p(j),j) connects a child joint j to its parent p(j). The normalized predicted bone direction d̂^n,iₑ and ground truth bone direction d^n,iₑ are

    d̂^n,iₑ=(Ĵ^n,iⱼ-Ĵ^n,iₚ₍ⱼ₎)/(∥Ĵ^n,iⱼ-Ĵ^n,iₚ₍ⱼ₎∥₂+ε), d^n,iₑ=(J^n,iⱼ-J^n,iₚ₍ⱼ₎)/(∥J^n,iⱼ-J^n,iₚ₍ⱼ₎∥₂+ε).

    		(30)

    The predicted and ground truth pairwise bone-angle similarity matrix Â^n,i and A^n,i are

    Â^n,i_e,e^′=(d̂^n,iₑ)^⊤d̂^n,i_e^′, A^n,i_e,e^′=(d^n,iₑ)^⊤d^n,i_e^′.

    		(31)

    The structural loss is then defined as:

    Lⁿ_struct=(1)/(K|𝔼|²)∑ᵢ₌₁^K∑_e,e^′∈𝔼ρ (Â^n,i_e,e^′-A^n,i_e,e^′),

    		(32)

    where we use ρ(Δ)=|Δ| (the original GlobalDiff paper uses the squared form ρ(Δ)=Δ²).

    C.2 Details of Boundary Losses

    Boundary Windows.

    The transition window b̂ₙ at the boundary of the n-th predicted block x̂ⁿ₀ concatenates the last W predicted frames of block n with the first W predicted frames of block n+1:

    b̂ₙ:=(b̂ₙ⁽¹⁾,…,b̂ₙ^(2W)), where b̂ₙ⁽ʲ⁾=\begincasesx̂₀^n, K-W+j&j=1,…,W, x̂₀^n+1, j-W&j=W+1,…,2W.\endcases

    		(33)

    and K is the block size. The ground truth window bₙ is constructed analogously from the clean n-th block x₀ⁿ. In all of our experiments, we set W=4.

    Boundary Loss Formulations.

    Since adjacent blocks are denoised without temporal overlap during the training process, kinematic discontinuities may appear at the transition points. To address this, we impose the boundary loss on the concatenated 2W-frame boundary window (b̂ₙ,bₙ) in Eq.33.

    Specifically, the boundary rotation loss Lᵣₒₜ(b̂ₙ,bₙ) applies the MSE in Eq.28 to the 2W frames of the transition window. To explicitly guarantee temporal smoothness, we compute the first-order (velocity) and second-order (acceleration) finite differences on the FK-derived joint positions of the boundary window. The velocity matching loss Lᵥₑₗ and acceleration matching loss L_acc are:

    Lᵥₑₗ(b̂ₙ,bₙ)=1/2W-1∑ᵢ₌₁^2W-1∥(Ĵ_bₙⁱ⁺¹-Ĵ_bₙⁱ)-(J_bₙⁱ⁺¹-J_bₙⁱ)∥₂²,(34)
