We note that the injectivity of a vector field does not depend on the magnitude of the vectors and hence opt to normalize all vectors to unit norm.

    5.1 Empirical Evidence of Injectivity and Accuracy

    We begin by empirically validating the injectivity of the flows, as well as the accuracy of our advection algorithm, Algorithm 2. We flow a given point for a certain amount of time, and then flip the vector field and flow the resulting point “back in time” – we visualize this experiment in Figure 8 with red/yellow for forward/backward paths, validating injectivity as well as exhibiting the accuracy of the algorithm. For quantitative evaluation, we repeat this process for random source and sink vertices alongside a random initialization of Laplacian weights, sample 100,000 random points, and measure the error between the start point and the point flowed back via the two steps above. We report the aggregated Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Maximum Absolute Error (MXE) in Table 1. No error exceeds 10⁻⁸ on average and 10⁻⁵ at maximum. A few models with triangles that have very small area or are near-degenerate result in less accurate results, mainly because of inaccuracy in numerics of the harmonic equation/gradient operator leading to a slight drift in the calculation of the time it takes to cross an edge.

    5.2 Flows Defined from Different Types of Laplacians

    Theorem 1 guarantees an injective flow for any valid configuration of strictly positive Laplacian weights. In Figure 2 we show flows computed via the cotangent Laplacian [pinkall1993] (clamped to have only positive weights) and via the Mean Value Coordinates (MVC) [floater2003mean] Laplacian. These lead to smooth flows along the harmonic isolines. To show more elaborate flows, Figure 7 shows results for Laplacians with arbitrary entries, which result in more oscillating vector fields and trajectories (see also Figure 8). In all cases, the flows are injective.

    5.3 Discrete Time-Dependent Flows

    In the continuous case, flows are often defined by time-dependent vector fields u(p,t)[chen2018neural]. Following our aim to provide a discrete counterpart of continuous flows, we can produce a time-discrete analogue of the above, where we switch between different harmonic functions discretely, at different time intervals – Figure 9 shows trajectories of points where the harmonic function governing the flow is changed four times. The resulting flow is more elaborate and, as shown on the right, can yield trajectories that intersect, although the flow remains injective (the two points each traverse the intersection point at different moments in time).

    5.4 Gradient-Based Injective Field Optimization

    All steps of Algorithm 1 are differentiable, specifically with respect to the entries of the Laplacian; hence, by leveraging gradient-based optimization, we can effectively optimize the Laplacian edge weights [sun2024tuttenet, aigerman2024generative] thereby optimizing the vector field while maintaining its injectivity. We next show preliminary experiments validating the optimizeability of this representation. We implement the algorithm in PyTorch, which provides automatic differentiation. We use a simple optimization scheme, via the Adam [kingma2015] optimizer with a fixed step size of 0.1, run for 5000 iterations.

    Approximating non-injective vector fields.

    In Figure 10, we show a result of optimizing a randomly-initialized injective vector field to align with a given, non-injective vector field (obtained via [crane2010]), by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) between the per-face target vectors and the optimized injective field. This leads to an injective vector field that still closely mimics the broader directional trends of the target field, as shown in the blowups.

    Satisfying sparse vector constraints.

    We evaluate the ability of our optimization to satisfy sparse directional constraints across specific faces of a mesh. In Figure 11, black arrows denote ten user-defined constraint vectors. We minimize the MSE loss between the injective vector field and these vectors, exclusively on the constrained faces. We visualize the continuous trajectories passing through five of these constrained faces on the mesh. As shown in the insets of Figure 11(a), the initial vector field (red arrows) naturally deviates from the arbitrary constraints imposed by the target vectors, and is corrected by optimization to achieve near-perfect alignment, sometimes via rather contorted paths.

    6 Conclusion

    Theorem 1 draws a connection between harmonic functions and injective flows and proposes a Tutte-like method for computing them. We hope that in the coming years, this method will find applications within the geometry processing community similar to those of Tutte’s embedding, e.g., producing injective initializations for vector field optimization algorithms, serving as a fast method to construct an injective vector field, or optimizing injective fields.

    While our main contribution is theoretical, on a practical level, our method comes with several limitations, which we hope to solve in future work. First, the method is limited to specific topology and boundary conditions. We believe that extensions to some other specific boundary conditions on specific domains are possible. Furthermore, similarly to Tutte’s embedding, injective extensions to non-euclidean domains [aigerman2016hyperbolic] can lead to a more general and less constrained construction. We also note that we have only shown a few “proof-of-concept” experiments to validate the capability of optimizing the vector field to specific goals, as we focused mainly on the injectivity of the flow, and used PyTorch’s vanilla autodiff with Adam [kingma2015] that does not use adaptive step size nor line search. The current optimization framework is insufficient on its own to optimize for flows that can be used in downstream tasks. As our top future priority, we mark the goal of devising a framework that can output production-ready flows. This requires regularizing the vector fields, e.g., via as-Killing-as-possible [benchen2010killing] or a vector Dirichlet energy  [stein2020simple]. Lastly, our parameterization of injective flows via gradients of a family of harmonic functions does not cover the full space of injective vector fields. As several of our flows are composed (as in Figure 9), the space of injective flows is increased, and we set as important future work to show (both theoretically and practically) that with enough such compositions, any flow can be attained.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Proofs of Lemmas

    Proof of Lemma 1.

    Let e=(i,j) be a half-edge, let t=(i,j,k) be its triangle, and define the edge vector as r⃗=(vⱼ-vᵢ)/(\lVertvᵢ-vⱼ\rVert). In standard linear FEM fashion, consider z as defining an affine function over the triangle, z(p)=aᵀp+b for any point p∈t, uniquely defined as requiring that it interpolates the values zᵢ,zⱼ,zₖ on the vertices, i.e., z(v_α)=z_α,α∈{i,j,k}. We will prove that the sign of the directional derivative (∂z)/(∂r⃗) in the direction r⃗ is equal to both terms in the lemma. First, by restricting z to a one-dimensional function over the edge, we have (∂z)/(∂r⃗)=(zⱼ-zᵢ)/(\lVertvᵢ-vⱼ\rVert)\overset\eqrefeq:1form=(δₑ)/(\lVertvᵢ-vⱼ\rVert); therefore, sign((∂z)/(∂r⃗))=sign(δₑ). Second, a directional derivative is also equal to the inner product between the gradient and the direction, i.e., (∂z)/(∂r⃗)=<∇ₜz,r⃗>. Since applying the same rotation to both vectors does not change their inner product, we have (∂z)/(∂r⃗)==. Thus, we get sign((∂z)/(∂r⃗))=-sign(). Hence, sign(δₑ)=-sign()=Fₑ. ∎

    Proof of Lemma 2.

    We first convert the vertex flux to a more relaxed definition (refer also to Figure 6):

    Definition 3.

    Flux parity: for triangle (o,i,j), we say the triangle has even-parity flux with respect to the vertex o if F_o,i=F_j,o; otherwise, if F_o,i=-F_j,o, we say the triangle has odd-parity flux with respect to the vertex o.

    In other words, positive/negative vertex fluxes are even-parity fluxes, and a zero vertex flux is odd-parity (see Figure 6 for an illustration, where triangles are highlighted in red if they have even-parity flux with respect to the 1-ring’s center vertex). Hence, translating the conditions of Property 2 to parity, it is a necessary condition that two triangles have even-parity flux and the rest have odd-parity flux; the next lemma shows that in fact these two conditions are exactly equivalent, i.e., the parity condition ensures vertex injectivity:

    Lemma 4.

    i) The flux is an injective regular flux over a vertex o iff there are exactly two triangles t¹,t² of the vertex’s 1-ring that have even-parity vertex flux (with respect to o) and all the rest of the triangles have odd-parity vertex flux. ii) The flux is an injective vortex flux iff all triangles have odd-parity vertex flux (with respect to o).

    We prove this lemma later. Now, as illustrated in Figure 6, note that two consecutive edges (o,i),(o,i+1) of the 1-ring correspond to the oriented half-edges (o,i),(i+1,o) of the triangle (o,i,i+1). Hence, if there’s no sign change (F_(o,i)=F_(o,i+1)), then by the anti-symmetry of the 1-form we have F_(o,i)=-F_(i+1,o), i.e., the triangle has odd-parity flux into o. Similarly, if there is a sign change (F_(o,i)=-F_(o,i+1)), then by the anti-symmetry of the 1-form we have F_(o,i)=F_(i+1,o) and the triangle has even-parity flux into o.

    In sum: an index of 1 is defined as no sign changes in the 1-ring, in turn meaning all triangles in the 1-ring have odd-parity flux, which by Lemma 4 entails a vortex injective vertex, as defined in Subsection 3.3 (and vice versa: having all odd-parity flux triangles entails an index of 1).

    Similarly, an index of 0 is defined as exactly two sign changes, hence exactly two triangles of the 1-ring have even-parity flux, which per Lemma 4 entails a regular injective vertex, as defined in Subsection 3.3 (and vice versa: two even-parity triangles entail an index of 0).

    All other numbers of sign changes have negative index, and all correspond to the last remaining case, of a non-injective vertex. With this, we have proven Lemma 2. ∎

    Proof of Lemma 3.

    We begin by reducing the equation in Theorem 3.5 in [gortler2006] to our setting. The original equation stipulates that for a polygonal mesh of genus g with a given 1-form δ,

    ∑_v∈Vind(v) (vertex index)+∑_t∈Tind(t) (face index)=2-2g.

    		(11)

    Aside from the vertex index term (defined in Subsection 4.3), there is an additional face index term; however, it is irrelevant to us: this is computed for polygonal meshes, by walking over the (polygonal) face’s edges and counting how many sign changes occur; for our case this term is always zero since, by definition of δᵢ (Equation (8)), we have that for a triangle with edges e₁,e₂,e₃ it holds that δ₁+δ₂+δ₃=0, entailing exactly two sign changes, thereby leading to zero contribution. Plugging in the genus of the sphere (g=0) to the right-hand side of Equation (11), we get from their theorem that our 1-form δ satisfies

    ∑_v∈Vind(v)=2.

    		(12)

    We note that all vertices except the source and sink satisfy the discrete harmonic equation, and thus it is well-known (and easy to prove) that they satisfy a discrete maximum principle: a vertex o has a vertex vⱼ in its 1-ring with a higher value zₒzₖ. By the definition of δ, Equation (8), this entails δ_(o,j)>0, and δ_(o,k)<0. As such, there must be at least two sign changes transpiring across the edges of the 1-ring of o. Thus the index of all vertices is non-positive, except the source and sink. Since the indices sum to 2, this implies both the source and the sink must have the maximal index, i.e., 1. With that, the sum of the indices of all the other vertices must be exactly zero. Due to non-positivity, this entails that the index of each of those vertices is zero. ∎

    Proof of Lemma 4.

    (⇒) i) Assume the vertex flux is regular injective, i.e., per the definition in Section 3.3, Property 2, there is one triangle t⁺ with positive vertex flux, and one t⁻ with negative vertex flux, and all others with zero vertex flux. Then, by the definition of parity, both t⁺,t⁻ have even-parity vertex flux while the rest have odd-parity vertex flux, as desired. ii) Assume the vertex flux is vortex injective. Then all triangles have zero vertex flux, which has odd parity.

    (⇐) i) Assume that there are exactly two triangles t¹,t² with even-parity vertex flux, with the rest having odd-parity vertex flux. We need to show that the definition of regular injective vertex from Subsection 3.3, Property 2 is satisfied. Odd-parity flux triangles have zero vertex flux; hence, all that remains is to prove that one of t¹,t² has positive vertex flux, and one has negative vertex flux (as opposed to both positive or both negative). Without loss of generality, assume t¹ has positive vertex flux. Due to Equation (5), we have F_(o,i)=F_(i+1,o)=+1. Using the anti-symmetry between a half-edge and its twin (Equation (8)), we have F_i+1,o=-F_o,i+1, entailing F_o,i+1=-1. We consider two cases:

  • 1.

    If (o,i+1) is a half-edge of t², we are done: since t² has even-parity flux, its other edge satisfies F_(i+2,o)=F_(o,i+1)=-1, and thus both have negative edge flux, entailing the vertex flux is negative.

  • 2.

    If the half-edge belongs to a triangle other than t², it is a triangle with odd-parity flux, implying F_(i+2,o)=-F_(o,i+1)=-(-1)=+1. By induction, we can show that when iterating over all triangles until reaching t², for each triangle (o,j,j+1) we have F_(j,o)=1 and F_(o,j+1)=-1. Once we reach t², we are once again in the setting of case 1, and the proof is concluded.

    • ii) Assume all triangles have odd-parity vertex flux; then there are no sign changes, and each triangle must have zero vertex flux, i.e., entailing the vertex flux is vortex injective. ∎

item.title: agent 写的 XR 应用只有一半能跑：GenXR-Bench 在消费级头显上跑 112 个任务，最强配置 Pass@1 仅 50.9% ｜ GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development
item.description:
一句话：112 个 XR 任务、真机执行、脚本加自适应交互双测，10 个模型里最强配置 Pass@1 只有 50.9%。

要点：

  • 任务构成：24 个功能实现、21 个 bug 修复、67 个应用生成，共 112 个专家任务，测试同时使用脚本化与自适应交互，并配合程序化断言与视觉断言
  • 测试套件可信度：在消费级 XR 硬件上真实执行 124 个候选应用，与专家盲评判断的一致率达 96.5%
  • 结果：评估 10 个模型，最强配置整体 Pass@1 仅 50.9%，失败集中在异步传感器生命周期等运行时理解上

为什么值得看：XR 是「AI 造交互式 3D 应用」最苛刻的形态——连续用户运动、空间输入、环境感知三者同时生效。它的失败模式等于一张清单，告诉你引擎运行时该把哪些状态、生命周期和事件暴露给 agent，才不至于让它们只会写静态页面。

中文摘要：编码 agent 已经从单文件生成走到仓库级长任务，但在 XR 这种运行时依赖连续运动、空间输入与环境感知的应用上，还没有端到端的评测。GenXR-Bench 补上这一块：112 个专家任务分成功能实现、bug 修复与应用生成三类，held-out 测试既有脚本化交互也有自适应交互，同时用程序化断言和视觉断言检查功能与运行时行为。测试套件本身也做了验证——对 124 个跑在消费级 XR 硬件上的候选应用，其判定与专家盲评一致率 96.5%。对 10 个模型的实测显示最强配置整体 Pass@1 只有 50.9%，失败分析反复指向异步传感器生命周期这类运行时语义，而不是语法或 API 记忆。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-27

GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development

Abstract

Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities in authoring interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench’s testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.

1 Introduction

Coding agents have become increasingly capable of building interactive software. Recent benchmarks have expanded beyond algorithmic problems [(Jimenez et al., 2024)] to end-to-end interactive applications, evaluating how models handle dynamic user input in web and desktop environments [(Lu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025)]. Extended reality (XR) introduces a distinct set of challenges for code generation. Unlike 2D software governed by discrete event loops, XR applications operate within continuous 3D physical spaces. Functional correctness depends on the real-time coordination of head and hand kinematics, spatial coordinate transformations, environmental sensing, mixed-reality rendering, and physical ergonomics. Consequently, generating XR software requires reasoning about spatial mathematics, runtime sensor lifecycles, and embodied interaction semantics that are absent in flat-screen software engineering.

Despite these demands, evaluating coding agents in XR remains largely unexplored due to an execution and verification bottleneck. Existing coding benchmarks rely on programmatic unit tests [(Jimenez et al., 2024)] or browser action runners [(Lu et al., 2025)], which cannot verify spatial scene graphs or continuous 3D tracking inputs. Conversely, 3D code-generation benchmarks focus primarily on generating static shapes rather than reactive software [(Gao et al., 2026)], while prior XR benchmarks focus on hardware performance and runtime systems rather than evaluating generative code synthesis [(Huzaifa et al., 2021; Bierbaum et al., 2003; Popescu et al., 2025)]. Evaluating agent-generated XR software requires an automated and comprehensive testing suite capable of simulating physical environments, exercising embodied user actions, and verifying runtime behavior across diverse implementations.

We present GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench comprises 112 expert-curated tasks across two tiers: (1) SDK engineering tasks, consisting of 24 feature implementations and 21 bug repairs in core subsystems such as occlusion shaders, raycast reprojection, and gestural state machines; (2) Application generation tasks, consisting of 67 end-to-end experiences spanning education, healthcare, daily living, design, and entertainment, distilled from a taxonomy of 436 peer-reviewed XR systems papers. To support reproducible, headless execution without the proprietary GUI navigation and multi-gigabyte build toolchains of desktop game engines, all tasks are built on XR Blocks [(Li et al., 2025)], an open-source WebXR framework. To test candidate implementation at scale, we introduce GenXR-Test, the first set of testing tools that pair deterministic kinematic actors with adaptive VLM-controlled agents in simulated XR environments, evaluating runtime results through both scene-graph assertions and scoped visual checks.

To validate our authored evaluation suite, eight blinded XR experts evaluated 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Across 372 evaluation runs, our automated suite achieved 96.5% mean accuracy against human expert ground truth with a 4.0% flakiness rate, demonstrating that simulator-based evaluation reliably reflects physical device execution. We evaluate 10 model configurations on the full benchmark. The strongest configuration achieves an overall Pass@1 of 50.9%, with performance dropping to 29.2% on SDK feature tasks. Diagnostic analysis reveals recurring failure modes across models: 64.4% of failed runs exhibit coordinate-transformation errors, 44.9% encounter asynchronous sensor initialization races, and 34.5% fail to distinguish bimanual interaction semantics.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    GenXR-Bench: An open-source benchmark of 112 expert-authored tasks evaluating coding agents on XR software engineering, spanning SDK-level feature development, bug repair, and end-to-end application synthesis.

  • •

    GenXR-Test: XR tooling for automated evaluations using scripted kinematic actors, adaptive VLM agents, runtime state assertions, and scoped visual checks in simulated 3D environments.

  • •

    Hardware-Grounded Validation: A validation study across 372 physical XR device trials demonstrating that simulator-based evaluation achieves 96.5% agreement with expert human judgment with low flakiness (4.0%).

  • •

    Empirical Analysis of Coding Agents in XR: An evaluation of 10 model configurations identifying key bottlenecks in frontier models, including coordinate-frame handling, sensor lifecycles, and embodied interaction semantics.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Interactive Software Engineering Benchmarks

    Interactive software often requires its own set of runtime evaluations. Recent agent benchmarks treat interactivity as the benchmark itself, using operating systems and interactive worlds to evaluate agents in controlled application environments [(Xie et al., 2024; Rawles et al., 2025; Trivedi et al., 2024; Koh et al., 2024)], while embodied-agent benchmarks similarly test long action sequences in fixed 3D environments [(Kolve et al., 2017; Puig et al., 2018; Savva et al., 2019; Shridhar et al., 2020)]. Interactive software generation benchmarks often leverage these systems to evaluate generated software: website development benchmarks use agent-controlled browser actions to evaluate functionality [(Lu et al., 2025; Koh et al., 2024)]; ArtifactsBench [(Zhang et al., 2025)], Interaction2Code [(Xiao et al., 2025)], and InteractScience [(Chen et al., 2026b)] combine runtime interaction and rendering with multimodal evaluations using vision-language models as judges [(Zheng et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024)]; game-development benchmarks [(Chi et al., 2026; La et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a)] combine functional, visual, and behavioral evaluations with interaction testing. GenXR-Bench extends runtime evaluations to XR software by simulating embodied interactions and environmental sensing to become the first benchmark to formalize evaluations of physically grounded interactive applications beyond relying purely on LLM judges. A systematic comparison of GenXR-Bench against these existing benchmarks is shown in Table1.

    2.2 Generative 3D and XR Authoring

    Natural-language 3D authoring predates coding agents, with early systems such as WordsEye [(Coyne and Sproat, 2001)] and the framework proposed by [Chang et al. (2014)] translating text into virtual scenes. Recent approaches use language models to generate procedural content and interactive environments [(Sun et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024b; Yang et al., 2024c)]. As a result, code-based 3D generation benchmarks increasingly extend evaluation beyond simple primitives to perceptually and physically correct models [(Gao et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2025b)]. In XR, Text2VRScene [(Yin et al., 2024)] and VRCopilot [(Zhang et al., 2024)] allow users to use language to author new scenes and layouts. LLMR generates XR application features in real time [(De La Torre et al., 2024)]; DreamCodeVR generates object behaviors from speech within VR [(Giunchi et al., 2024)]; and LLMER produces structured specifications that control XR objects [(Chen et al., 2025)]. GenAssist explores iterative agentic rendering loops to refine XR applications guided by human ratings [(Srinidhi et al., 2026)]. XARP [(Caetano et al., 2026)] and XR Blocks [(Li et al., 2025)] introduce agent-native XR authoring toolkits for easy XR code generation. Closest to our work, [Du et al. (2026)] demonstrate that current LLMs can author XR applications that initialize without errors. GenXR-Bench continues this work, building upon the XR Blocks framework validated by [Du et al. (2026)] to systematically verify whether candidate implementations satisfy task-specific functional and interactive requirements across diverse XR development tasks.

    2.3 Automated XR Testing

    XR presents unique evaluation challenges because runtime behaviors depend continuously on the user’s kinematics, physical environment, and spatial interaction dynamics [(Bowman et al., 2001)]. Automated XR testing spans from replaying device input with state checkpoints [(Bierbaum et al., 2003)], categorizing WebXR [(Li et al., 2020)] and Unity [(Rzig et al., 2023)] bugs, and formalizing XR interface heuristics [(Nielsen and Molich, 1990; Gu et al., 2025a; Utting et al., 2012)]. The OpenXR Conformance Test Suite checks whether XR runtimes implement OpenXR interfaces consistently [(Khronos OpenXR Working Group, 2025)]. VR-ReST derives functional tests from requirements and scene-graph structure [(Corrêa Souza et al., 2018)]. Other work simulates user actions through camera-based exploration and scripted XR controllers [(Wang, 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Gu and Rojas, 2025; Zhu et al., 2025)]. XRintTest constructs an interaction-flow graph in existing Unity scenes [(Gu et al., 2026)]. Commercial solutions such as Meta XR Operator [(Meta, 2026)] integrate an LLM-driven tester into XR development to run natural-language tasks in Unity. Closest to our work are XR benchmarks that target end-to-end systems [(Huzaifa et al., 2021)], machine-learning workloads [(Kwon et al., 2023)], and performance criteria [(Popescu et al., 2025)]. We extend prior works by introducing GenXR-Test, which empowers task authors to define implementation-agnostic functional tests executed deterministically within a reproducible simulator environment.

    3 GenXR-Bench

    GenXR-Bench consists of 112 expert-curated XR software engineering tasks. Each task contains a natural-language specification, an editable project scaffold, and a held-out evaluation suite. The specification defines the required implementation and observable behavior. The scaffold provides the relevant code, tools, interfaces, documentation, and assets needed to complete the task. The evaluation suite contains human-authored tests written using GenXR-Test described in Section3.4.

    All tasks use XR Blocks 0.21.0[(Li et al., 2025)], a web framework for building cross-platform XR applications. Prior work has demonstrated that LLMs can generate complete XR Blocks applications from a single prompt [(Du et al., 2026)]. Using a common web framework reduces variation caused by engine-specific editors, deployment workflows, and device toolchains that often require complex GUI navigation. All agents were given access to XR Blocks DevTools, a suite of tools for debugging, running, and developing XR Blocks applications that simplifies multimodal development.

    3.1 Benchmark Composition

    GenXR-Bench covers three types of XR development tasks motivated by real-world use cases: feature implementation, bug repair, and application generation. Examples are shown in AppendixD.

    SDK feature implementation. Feature tasks require agents to implement a missing XR Blocks capability while retaining the surrounding SDK, interfaces, documentation, and relevant examples. Tasks cover capabilities such as hand interaction, sensing, spatial design, and rendering that form the primitive features for core XR development. These tasks are designed to evaluate an agent’s ability to implement and understand low-level XR functionality and focus on software engineering.

    SDK bug repair. Repair tasks begin with a snapshot of the XR Blocks SDK containing a reproduced behavioral issue. The specification describes the observable failure and required behavior without identifying the faulty implementation. Agents must locate and repair the defect while preserving related functionality.

    Application generation. Application tasks require agents to build a complete XR experience from a natural-language specification. Each specification outlines the intended experience, interaction flow, spatial behavior, and success conditions. Agents must combine SDK capabilities and design a working application that meets the specification.

    3.2 Benchmark Curation and Construction

    The benchmark tasks were curated and sourced by five XR experts, including professional XR engineers, XR researchers, and contributors to XR Blocks. All tasks were validated on XR hardware by reviewers to ensure that they accurately reflect real-world usage.

    SDK tasks. To source the SDK tasks, we interviewed core XR Blocks contributors and inspected all 552 pull requests and issues available as of August 24, 2026. Maintainer reports and pull requests were pooled into a candidate list of potential features and prior bugs, then filtered based on their relevance to XR engineering, evaluation feasibility, and scope. An author converted each selected candidate into a self-contained benchmark task. For feature tasks, the author removed the target implementation while retaining its public interface and context. For repair tasks, the author reproduced the selected defect in a pinned XR Blocks snapshot. SDK tasks contain both fail-to-pass tests for the target behavior and pass-to-pass tests for related behavior that test writers identified as potentially affected by candidate implementations. Authors were instructed to create adversarial solutions and conduct three rounds of test-suite refinement.

    Application tasks. We derived an application taxonomy from 436 XR systems papers published at top human-computer interaction and spatial computing venues. Using this taxonomy, gemini-3.5-flash generated 1,000 candidate application ideas. XR experts selected 67 candidates based on XR specificity, realism, implementation feasibility, and evaluation feasibility. Following [Luo et al. (2026)], we expanded the selected ideas into full specifications using gemini-3.6-flash, manually reviewed and edited by XR experts. AppendixB describes the full procedure.

    Authors then created an evaluation suite for each application task. Since there can be multiple valid implementations, we do not require a canonical reference solution. Authors refined each specification and evaluation suite using expert-reviewed valid and adversarial candidates, revising the task specification over up to 10 iterations. Tests were designed to assess the required interactive experience while accommodating differences between implementations.

    3.3 Benchmark Statistics

    GenXR-Bench contains 112 tasks consisting of 24 SDK feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 app generation tasks. XR experts rated 28 tasks as easy, 38 as medium, and 46 as hard based on subsystem breadth, interaction length, and expected implementation effort. Experts also assigned labels based on each task’s coverage of core XR capabilities, including interaction, user interfaces (UI), hand recognition, virtual object manipulation, depth sensing, object placement, perception, drawing, audio, and head tracking. A task could receive multiple capability labels depending on its scope. Figure3 summarizes the task types and capability coverage.

    3.4 GenXR-Test Evaluation Framework

    To build each evaluation suite, we introduce GenXR-Test, a set of testing tools for the creation of adaptive interaction tests. Each held-out evaluation suite combines actors that simulate user actions and environmental inputs with assertions that check the resulting application behavior. This allows tests to assess SDK implementations and generated applications under controlled runtime conditions. A custom simulator provides fully articulated hand inputs as well as various physical scenes and objects to simulate real-world XR environments. Figure4 illustrates an example evaluation test. More information on the implementation of our evaluation suite can be found in AppendixA.

    Evaluation Actors. Actors are testing functions that simulate head, hand, controller, gesture, object, environment, and time inputs. A scripted actor runs a predefined action sequence, such as performing a hand gesture, pressing a specified control, or following a path. Authors use scripted actors when the required action can be specified before execution, improving reproducibility and reducing variation in test execution. An adaptive actor is a VLM-powered agent that follows a narrowly scoped natural-language instruction when the required action cannot be reliably determined without knowledge of the candidate implementation, following prior work [(Lu et al., 2025)]. For example, it may locate and activate a generated control or find an object needed for a later assertion. Authors use adaptive actors when differences in layout or interaction flow make fixed action sequences unreliable.

    Evaluation Assertions. After an actor produces a runtime state, assertions determine whether the required functional behavior has occurred. Programmatic assertions inspect runtime properties such as object transforms, spatial relationships, interaction state, collisions, tracking state, sensor outputs, and emitted events. For example, a test might check that a virtual object follows the hand and disappears upon colliding with a wall. Authors use programmatic assertions whenever the required behavior can be checked deterministically, focusing on observable outcomes to reduce flakiness [(Luo et al., 2014)]. VLM-based assertions assess visual outcomes that are difficult to express directly as programmatic checks. Each assertion receives rendered images from the simulated user’s point of view and a narrowly scoped, human-authored criterion. These criteria describe an expected visual outcome rather than asking the VLM to judge the overall function of the experience, which limits judging failures. This design follows the findings of [Cho et al. (2026); Huang et al. (2024)] and is evaluated in Section4.

    Semantic Tags. Valid applications can use different identifiers and scene hierarchies for equivalent objects. Tasks in GenXR-Bench require evaluated coding agents to assign semantic tags to specified objects. Examples include controls, targets, and interactable objects. These tags allow actions and assertions to locate functionally equivalent objects without requiring a fixed implementation. Semantic roles are defined in the task specification and are limited to descriptions of the objects to be tagged, reducing the risk of exposing tests. Task authors are also explicitly instructed to limit the use of semantic tags to avoid forcing a single correct implementation.

    3.5 Evaluating Application Design

    An application can satisfy its functional requirements while remaining difficult or uncomfortable to use. We therefore report a separate design score for application-generation tasks, following prior work in website generation [(Lu et al., 2025)]. During test execution, we record videos of the evaluator running the candidate application and use a VLM as a judge to rate the application against ten XR design heuristics, each on a 1–5 Likert scale. The design score is intended to supplement functional evaluations. Details on the development of the XR heuristics and the alignment of the VLM judge with human evaluators are provided in AppendixC and AppendixE, respectively.

    3.6 Analysis of App Verifier Reliability

    We validate our evaluation suite through expert evaluations of 124 candidate applications across 62 app tasks in GenXR-Bench that did not require a specific physical object or setting. The candidates were generated with gemini-3.5-flash and gemini-3.7-flash. We purposefully select gemini-3.5-flash to add a greater diversity of generated app quality.

    Eight XR experts participated in the evaluation. Each candidate received independent binary judgments of functional correctness from two evaluators, each of whom assessed the full functionality of the application. In cases of disagreement, a third independent evaluator re-examined the candidate and made the final decision. Evaluators were blind to the candidate source and verifier results and interacted freely with the application. For each candidate app, at least one evaluation used XR hardware (Galaxy XR, Meta Quest 3) to ensure alignment with real use cases.

    We ran the automated evaluation suite three times for each candidate, producing 372 evaluation runs. As shown in Table2, the verifier aligns strongly with human evaluations (accuracy: 96.5%) and is reproducible (flakiness: 4.0%). These results indicate that the evaluation suite reliably reflects expert assessments of XR app functionality. Disagreements occurred primarily in applications where experts performed tasks through interaction behaviors that the automated tests did not accommodate, such as a ball spawning at the wrist rather than the fingertips. These cases present a limitation of the verifier when candidate implementations depart from expected spatial interaction conventions.

    4 Evaluations

    4.1 Evaluation Setup

    Evaluation environment. Following the procedures in the DeepSWE benchmark [(Huang et al., 2026)], we evaluated all model configurations using mini-swe-agent[(Yang et al., 2024a)] harness within the Harbor Framework [(Harbor Framework Team, 2026)]. Agents could access XR Blocks source code, documentation, examples, and relevant dependency documentation, while other network access was restricted. Adaptive actors and VLM-based assertions used gemini-3.8-flash.

    Model choices. We select a variety of different models to evaluate. From the Google Gemini family, we evaluate gemini-3.1-pro-preview, gemini-3.5-flash, gemini-3.6-flash, gemini-3.7-flash, and gemini-3.8-flash, all at the high thinking level. From the OpenAI GPT family, we evaluate gpt-5.6-luna and gpt-5.6-sol, both at the xhigh reasoning level. From the Anthropic Claude family, we evaluate claude-opus-5 at the medium reasoning level111 We evaluate claude-opus-5 at medium due to cost constraints.. For open-weight models, we evaluate deepseek-v4-pro-0813 and deepseek-v4.1-flash at the xhigh reasoning level.

    Metrics. For all evaluations, we use Pass@1, the percentage of tasks completed successfully in one attempt, to evaluate the functionality of proposed solutions. Tasks are only considered successful when all required tests pass. For application-generation tasks, we report the mean of the 10 heuristic ratings produced by the VLM judge described in Section3.5 as the Design Score. This metric supplements the evaluation of functional correctness through Pass@1.

    4.2 Discussion of Results

    We now discuss our findings from evaluating coding agents as described in Table3. Detailed results and findings are found in AppendixF.

    XR development remains challenging even for frontier models. Across GenXR-Bench, XR development remains challenging even for frontier models, with the best performing model only reaching a Pass@1 of 50.9 ( claude-opus-5). XR functionality and design performance diverged where claude-opus-5 achieves the highest application-generation Pass@1 at 47.8%, while gpt-5.6-sol achieves the highest mean Design Score at 4.03. Notably, while SDK repair scores were high, SDK implementation and application-generation scores remained low, indicating that behavioral repair and bug identification pose a far easier challenge than end-to-end XR app implementation. Models further from the frontier were far less capable, failing on foundational spatial-computing concepts or completely unable to create core application objects. These smaller models suffer heavily from web development coding hallucinations, poor metric understanding, and API hallucinations. Frontier models are more capable of avoiding these errors but still fail at higher-order spatial reasoning, including bimanual coordination (Figure12), room geometry visualizations (Figure13), and physical alignment (Figure14).

    Model-written tests are not indicative of success. Notably, models were relatively incapable of writing effective tests where the testing-to-editing ratio for each model was not indicative of overall success. Instead, models tend to overwrite unit tests that did not validate actual XR functionality and fail to have the foresight to predict real runtime conditions. Models that were more willing to evaluate code through runtime tests were also more successful. We report a detailed breakdown of agent tool usage in Table11.

    4.3 Failure Analysis and Directions for Improvement

    XR experts then manually analyzed task failure modes and grouped them into recurring categories. These failures indicate potential openings for improving the ability of agents to create spatial and embodied experiences. We provide a more detailed analysis in AppendixG.

    Asynchronous initialization and environmental updates. Startup race conditions occurred in 44.9% of failed runs. Implementations began gameplay updates or sensing-dependent calculations before the required assets or tracking state were available, causing runtime exceptions. Other implementations checked for detected surfaces only at startup and did not respond when the surfaces became available later. This behavior also limited the functionality of some applications that passed the tests. For instance, in the lascaux-torch task shown in Figure11, successful implementations made virtual walls to simulate a cave whereas an XR developer might have developed shaders to place cave paintings on physical walls. These findings suggest a need for better handling of initialization dependencies and continuous sensing input throughout execution.

    Coordinate transformations. Coordinate-frame errors occurred in 64.4% of failed runs. Implementations compared positions expressed relative to different parent objects without first transforming them to a common coordinate frame. This was especially apparent for objects parented by user transforms like the hand as is visible in Figure14 where models anchored buttons directly to hands’ root joint rather than placing them onto the palm surface. These failures highlight recurring difficulties in maintaining a consistent spatial model of the physical world, the user, and virtual content in XR development.

    Embodied interaction detection and usability. Current models still lack an embodied understanding of how humans exist and interact in XR and spatial computing settings. Agents often struggled with hand interactions and asymmetric hand gestures (34.5% of failures), accepting interactions from either hand interchangeably and failing to enforce separate tracking semantics. Other failures involved gesture recognition, as shown in Figure12, where candidate applications often failed to detect the framing pose. Agents often treated physical touch as a discrete click, relying on Boolean bounding-box intersections without tracking continuous penetration along surface normals. This often caused unstable contact detection during interactions. Finally, agents routinely failed to account for human ergonomics, placing interactive buttons out of comfortable reach, positioning menus behind the user, or rendering spatial UI at disproportionate scales, degrading ergonomic usability.

    5 Conclusion

    We present GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark to evaluate the functional and interactive correctness of agent-generated XR software. To create GenXR-Bench, five XR experts hand-wrote and curated 112 tasks spanning core XR engineering workflows within XR Blocks, using our novel automated XR testing framework, GenXR-Test. We find that frontier coding agents still struggle with XR development tasks, especially when tasks require continuous reasoning over embodied interactions and asynchronous XR runtime state. Our findings highlight the need to improve the embodied understanding of agents. We envision GenXR-Bench as a foundational testbed for advancing spatially situated software engineering across spatial AI, perception, and embodied interactions.

    6 AI Use Disclosure

    In this work, we used generative AI tools for dataset generation, benchmark authoring, data analysis, paper writing and editing. We did not use generative AI tools to develop conceptual frameworks. We developed GenXR-Bench alongside human evaluators, ensuring that domain experts guided all parts of this work and reviewed all AI-assisted work. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

    7 Ethics Statement

    This work investigates LLM-based code generation for XR applications to improve our understanding of how models reason about spatial computing and implement it in concrete applications. Our data collection was limited to real-world XR frameworks and was guided by contributors to ensure that all data is controlled and accessible. We take care to anonymize all potentially personally identifiable information. XR applications carry risks, including placing users at risk of physical harm by obscuring real-world hazards, so we limit our scope to safe, non-sensitive settings. All pretrained models used are publicly available and are used in accordance with their licenses. We believe our work contributes to the study of frontier coding capabilities.

    8 Reproducibility Statement

    We have made considerable efforts to ensure the reproducibility of our results. All prompts used for data generation or evaluation are published in our appendix. We include details of dataset construction, preprocessing, and evaluation metrics. Our benchmark will be released as open source upon publication. Furthermore, we implement the benchmark using the Harbor Framework [(Harbor Framework Team, 2026)] to support reproduction and access.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A GenXR-Bench Implementation

    GenXR-Bench is built on the XR Blocks framework [(Li et al., 2025)]. We pin all benchmark tasks to a stable version of XR Blocks 0.21.0, remove extraneous add-ons, and precache all runtime network downloads to support network-isolated execution in Harbor. The following XR Blocks features enable XR evaluations in simulated environments, which simplifies much of the complexity in other XR frameworks like Unity, Godot, or Unreal Engine that require in-depth understanding and usage of GUI features to run the engine. Instead, XR Blocks is implemented through common web frameworks like Three.js and WebXR. Thus, XR Blocks remains a strong environment to evaluate XR understanding and can be viewed as a viable native engine equivalent. The following XR Blocks capabilities enable simulated XR evaluations.

    Articulated hand simulations. To simulate XR interactions accurately, we use the articulated hand simulations provided by XR Blocks. The pose of each hand is represented by XYZ joint rotations and computed through forward kinematics over the XR hand skeleton. Tests can select common pose presets or specify joint rotations directly. Joint limits prevent actors from producing unrealistic hand poses. All poses are injected directly into the XR Blocks runtime to support standard gesture-recognition implementations and XR interaction logic in candidate applications.

    Simulated physical environments. XR Blocks’ simulator also supports multiple human-authored physical environments. These environments simulate physical room information by injecting it into plane, mesh, depth, and object-detection pathways at runtime. Each environment includes navigation meshes that enable realistic movement. GenXR-Bench uses two scenes: Living Room and Office. For tasks that require specific objects (e.g., a plate or coins), XR Blocks supports direct object injection into object-detection pipelines.

    Simulation time control. To support automated evaluations, we use the simulation-time controls provided by XR Blocks to expose explicit wait and frame-stepping operations. When execution is paused, tests can run VLM-based evaluators and manually advance the simulation and physics clocks. This control reduces dependence on host timing and hardware, enabling tests to examine intermediate states.

    Scene context formatting. XR Blocks’ context module provides a structured, agent-friendly scene observation that prunes scene graphs and adds natural-language labels to simplify test authoring and adaptive actor control. The resulting context includes hierarchical object trees, visible-object summaries, stable identifiers, and labeled set-of-marks screenshots. Adaptive actors receive the scene context to reduce token usage and improve action reliability. Figure5 shows an example.

    A.1 Runtime Verifier Implementation

    GenXR-Test for GenXR-Bench is part of the broader XR Blocks DevTools system for controlling and testing XR Blocks applications. Applications run in Chromium through Playwright [(Microsoft, 2025)]. Tests use either Vitest [(Vitest Team, 2021)] or a custom Vitest extension that enables the XR Blocks runtime simulations described below.

    DevTools testing sessions. Each testing session copies all files into an isolated application workspace and relinks dependencies. After Playwright starts the application server, the testing session injects runtime readers and action controllers. These components support direct assertions about runtime state and embodied actions beyond keyboard controls. Tests perform actions and observations through a session object. Each session is a deterministic interaction test that can be replayed with different dominant hands and physical scenes. Every session is recorded as a video for post hoc analysis or use by the VLM judge. Actions operate on semantic targets. When paired with semantic tags, these targets make interaction tests more reproducible, limit flakiness, and reduce the number of steps required by adaptive actors. Table4 lists all supported actions.

    Appendix B XR App Prompt Creation

    To source XR app ideas, we searched the Semantic Scholar Index [(Allen Institute for AI, 2015)] for peer-reviewed full papers on XR systems published between 2016 and 2026 at major human-computer interaction and spatial computing venues (IEEE VR, IEEE ISMAR, ACM CHI, ACM UIST, ACM VRST, IEEE TVCG, ACM IMWUT/UbiComp, ACM SUI, ACM MobileHCI, ACM IUI, Frontiers in Virtual Reality, ACM TOCHI, and IJHCS). This search produced 436 papers. Two XR experts, assisted by Gemini Notebook [(Google Labs, 2026)], grouped these works into five core categories and their relevant subdomains: entertainment, education, design, healthcare, and daily living (Table5).

    Using this taxonomy as a seed, evaluators used gemini-3.5-flash to generate 1,000 candidate application ideas (AppendixB). Another XR expert screened all candidates for XR specificity, realism, implementation feasibility, and evaluation feasibility to select the final 67 app ideas. These ideas were expanded with gemini-3.6-flash and then edited manually (AppendixB).

    Appendix C XR Heuristics

    Following the procedure in AppendixB, we collected 38 additional papers on formal evaluations of XR applications, for a total of 474 papers. Evaluators used each paper’s title and abstract to identify work that explicitly proposed or validated an evaluation tool. We excluded papers that used only generic off-the-shelf surveys (e.g., the System Usability Scale and NASA-TLX). We then downloaded all papers and analyzed them with Gemini Notebook to identify distinct evaluation variables that could be traced to a specific work. The identified heuristics were deduplicated, grouped, and mapped to Nielsen’s 10 usability heuristics to create XR-specific adaptations. We then rephrased the heuristics as declarative statements for scoring on a 1–5 Likert scale. We discarded candidate metrics that required specific hardware, were overly specific, or required human cognitive testing. Table6 shows the final set of XR heuristics.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：112 个 XR 任务、真机执行、脚本加自适应交互双测，10 个模型里最强配置 Pass@1 只有 50.9%。

要点：

  • 任务构成：24 个功能实现、21 个 bug 修复、67 个应用生成，共 112 个专家任务，测试同时使用脚本化与自适应交互，并配合程序化断言与视觉断言
  • 测试套件可信度：在消费级 XR 硬件上真实执行 124 个候选应用，与专家盲评判断的一致率达 96.5%
  • 结果：评估 10 个模型，最强配置整体 Pass@1 仅 50.9%，失败集中在异步传感器生命周期等运行时理解上

为什么值得看：XR 是「AI 造交互式 3D 应用」最苛刻的形态——连续用户运动、空间输入、环境感知三者同时生效。它的失败模式等于一张清单，告诉你引擎运行时该把哪些状态、生命周期和事件暴露给 agent，才不至于让它们只会写静态页面。

中文摘要：编码 agent 已经从单文件生成走到仓库级长任务，但在 XR 这种运行时依赖连续运动、空间输入与环境感知的应用上，还没有端到端的评测。GenXR-Bench 补上这一块：112 个专家任务分成功能实现、bug 修复与应用生成三类，held-out 测试既有脚本化交互也有自适应交互，同时用程序化断言和视觉断言检查功能与运行时行为。测试套件本身也做了验证——对 124 个跑在消费级 XR 硬件上的候选应用，其判定与专家盲评一致率 96.5%。对 10 个模型的实测显示最强配置整体 Pass@1 只有 50.9%，失败分析反复指向异步传感器生命周期这类运行时语义，而不是语法或 API 记忆。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-27

GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development

Abstract

Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities in authoring interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench’s testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.

1 Introduction

Coding agents have become increasingly capable of building interactive software. Recent benchmarks have expanded beyond algorithmic problems [(Jimenez et al., 2024)] to end-to-end interactive applications, evaluating how models handle dynamic user input in web and desktop environments [(Lu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025)]. Extended reality (XR) introduces a distinct set of challenges for code generation. Unlike 2D software governed by discrete event loops, XR applications operate within continuous 3D physical spaces. Functional correctness depends on the real-time coordination of head and hand kinematics, spatial coordinate transformations, environmental sensing, mixed-reality rendering, and physical ergonomics. Consequently, generating XR software requires reasoning about spatial mathematics, runtime sensor lifecycles, and embodied interaction semantics that are absent in flat-screen software engineering.

Despite these demands, evaluating coding agents in XR remains largely unexplored due to an execution and verification bottleneck. Existing coding benchmarks rely on programmatic unit tests [(Jimenez et al., 2024)] or browser action runners [(Lu et al., 2025)], which cannot verify spatial scene graphs or continuous 3D tracking inputs. Conversely, 3D code-generation benchmarks focus primarily on generating static shapes rather than reactive software [(Gao et al., 2026)], while prior XR benchmarks focus on hardware performance and runtime systems rather than evaluating generative code synthesis [(Huzaifa et al., 2021; Bierbaum et al., 2003; Popescu et al., 2025)]. Evaluating agent-generated XR software requires an automated and comprehensive testing suite capable of simulating physical environments, exercising embodied user actions, and verifying runtime behavior across diverse implementations.

We present GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench comprises 112 expert-curated tasks across two tiers: (1) SDK engineering tasks, consisting of 24 feature implementations and 21 bug repairs in core subsystems such as occlusion shaders, raycast reprojection, and gestural state machines; (2) Application generation tasks, consisting of 67 end-to-end experiences spanning education, healthcare, daily living, design, and entertainment, distilled from a taxonomy of 436 peer-reviewed XR systems papers. To support reproducible, headless execution without the proprietary GUI navigation and multi-gigabyte build toolchains of desktop game engines, all tasks are built on XR Blocks [(Li et al., 2025)], an open-source WebXR framework. To test candidate implementation at scale, we introduce GenXR-Test, the first set of testing tools that pair deterministic kinematic actors with adaptive VLM-controlled agents in simulated XR environments, evaluating runtime results through both scene-graph assertions and scoped visual checks.

To validate our authored evaluation suite, eight blinded XR experts evaluated 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Across 372 evaluation runs, our automated suite achieved 96.5% mean accuracy against human expert ground truth with a 4.0% flakiness rate, demonstrating that simulator-based evaluation reliably reflects physical device execution. We evaluate 10 model configurations on the full benchmark. The strongest configuration achieves an overall Pass@1 of 50.9%, with performance dropping to 29.2% on SDK feature tasks. Diagnostic analysis reveals recurring failure modes across models: 64.4% of failed runs exhibit coordinate-transformation errors, 44.9% encounter asynchronous sensor initialization races, and 34.5% fail to distinguish bimanual interaction semantics.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    GenXR-Bench: An open-source benchmark of 112 expert-authored tasks evaluating coding agents on XR software engineering, spanning SDK-level feature development, bug repair, and end-to-end application synthesis.

  • •

    GenXR-Test: XR tooling for automated evaluations using scripted kinematic actors, adaptive VLM agents, runtime state assertions, and scoped visual checks in simulated 3D environments.

  • •

    Hardware-Grounded Validation: A validation study across 372 physical XR device trials demonstrating that simulator-based evaluation achieves 96.5% agreement with expert human judgment with low flakiness (4.0%).

  • •

    Empirical Analysis of Coding Agents in XR: An evaluation of 10 model configurations identifying key bottlenecks in frontier models, including coordinate-frame handling, sensor lifecycles, and embodied interaction semantics.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Interactive Software Engineering Benchmarks

    Interactive software often requires its own set of runtime evaluations. Recent agent benchmarks treat interactivity as the benchmark itself, using operating systems and interactive worlds to evaluate agents in controlled application environments [(Xie et al., 2024; Rawles et al., 2025; Trivedi et al., 2024; Koh et al., 2024)], while embodied-agent benchmarks similarly test long action sequences in fixed 3D environments [(Kolve et al., 2017; Puig et al., 2018; Savva et al., 2019; Shridhar et al., 2020)]. Interactive software generation benchmarks often leverage these systems to evaluate generated software: website development benchmarks use agent-controlled browser actions to evaluate functionality [(Lu et al., 2025; Koh et al., 2024)]; ArtifactsBench [(Zhang et al., 2025)], Interaction2Code [(Xiao et al., 2025)], and InteractScience [(Chen et al., 2026b)] combine runtime interaction and rendering with multimodal evaluations using vision-language models as judges [(Zheng et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024)]; game-development benchmarks [(Chi et al., 2026; La et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a)] combine functional, visual, and behavioral evaluations with interaction testing. GenXR-Bench extends runtime evaluations to XR software by simulating embodied interactions and environmental sensing to become the first benchmark to formalize evaluations of physically grounded interactive applications beyond relying purely on LLM judges. A systematic comparison of GenXR-Bench against these existing benchmarks is shown in Table1.

    2.2 Generative 3D and XR Authoring

    Natural-language 3D authoring predates coding agents, with early systems such as WordsEye [(Coyne and Sproat, 2001)] and the framework proposed by [Chang et al. (2014)] translating text into virtual scenes. Recent approaches use language models to generate procedural content and interactive environments [(Sun et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024b; Yang et al., 2024c)]. As a result, code-based 3D generation benchmarks increasingly extend evaluation beyond simple primitives to perceptually and physically correct models [(Gao et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2025b)]. In XR, Text2VRScene [(Yin et al., 2024)] and VRCopilot [(Zhang et al., 2024)] allow users to use language to author new scenes and layouts. LLMR generates XR application features in real time [(De La Torre et al., 2024)]; DreamCodeVR generates object behaviors from speech within VR [(Giunchi et al., 2024)]; and LLMER produces structured specifications that control XR objects [(Chen et al., 2025)]. GenAssist explores iterative agentic rendering loops to refine XR applications guided by human ratings [(Srinidhi et al., 2026)]. XARP [(Caetano et al., 2026)] and XR Blocks [(Li et al., 2025)] introduce agent-native XR authoring toolkits for easy XR code generation. Closest to our work, [Du et al. (2026)] demonstrate that current LLMs can author XR applications that initialize without errors. GenXR-Bench continues this work, building upon the XR Blocks framework validated by [Du et al. (2026)] to systematically verify whether candidate implementations satisfy task-specific functional and interactive requirements across diverse XR development tasks.

    2.3 Automated XR Testing

    XR presents unique evaluation challenges because runtime behaviors depend continuously on the user’s kinematics, physical environment, and spatial interaction dynamics [(Bowman et al., 2001)]. Automated XR testing spans from replaying device input with state checkpoints [(Bierbaum et al., 2003)], categorizing WebXR [(Li et al., 2020)] and Unity [(Rzig et al., 2023)] bugs, and formalizing XR interface heuristics [(Nielsen and Molich, 1990; Gu et al., 2025a; Utting et al., 2012)]. The OpenXR Conformance Test Suite checks whether XR runtimes implement OpenXR interfaces consistently [(Khronos OpenXR Working Group, 2025)]. VR-ReST derives functional tests from requirements and scene-graph structure [(Corrêa Souza et al., 2018)]. Other work simulates user actions through camera-based exploration and scripted XR controllers [(Wang, 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Gu and Rojas, 2025; Zhu et al., 2025)]. XRintTest constructs an interaction-flow graph in existing Unity scenes [(Gu et al., 2026)]. Commercial solutions such as Meta XR Operator [(Meta, 2026)] integrate an LLM-driven tester into XR development to run natural-language tasks in Unity. Closest to our work are XR benchmarks that target end-to-end systems [(Huzaifa et al., 2021)], machine-learning workloads [(Kwon et al., 2023)], and performance criteria [(Popescu et al., 2025)]. We extend prior works by introducing GenXR-Test, which empowers task authors to define implementation-agnostic functional tests executed deterministically within a reproducible simulator environment.

    3 GenXR-Bench

    GenXR-Bench consists of 112 expert-curated XR software engineering tasks. Each task contains a natural-language specification, an editable project scaffold, and a held-out evaluation suite. The specification defines the required implementation and observable behavior. The scaffold provides the relevant code, tools, interfaces, documentation, and assets needed to complete the task. The evaluation suite contains human-authored tests written using GenXR-Test described in Section3.4.

    All tasks use XR Blocks 0.21.0[(Li et al., 2025)], a web framework for building cross-platform XR applications. Prior work has demonstrated that LLMs can generate complete XR Blocks applications from a single prompt [(Du et al., 2026)]. Using a common web framework reduces variation caused by engine-specific editors, deployment workflows, and device toolchains that often require complex GUI navigation. All agents were given access to XR Blocks DevTools, a suite of tools for debugging, running, and developing XR Blocks applications that simplifies multimodal development.

    3.1 Benchmark Composition

    GenXR-Bench covers three types of XR development tasks motivated by real-world use cases: feature implementation, bug repair, and application generation. Examples are shown in AppendixD.

    SDK feature implementation. Feature tasks require agents to implement a missing XR Blocks capability while retaining the surrounding SDK, interfaces, documentation, and relevant examples. Tasks cover capabilities such as hand interaction, sensing, spatial design, and rendering that form the primitive features for core XR development. These tasks are designed to evaluate an agent’s ability to implement and understand low-level XR functionality and focus on software engineering.

    SDK bug repair. Repair tasks begin with a snapshot of the XR Blocks SDK containing a reproduced behavioral issue. The specification describes the observable failure and required behavior without identifying the faulty implementation. Agents must locate and repair the defect while preserving related functionality.

    Application generation. Application tasks require agents to build a complete XR experience from a natural-language specification. Each specification outlines the intended experience, interaction flow, spatial behavior, and success conditions. Agents must combine SDK capabilities and design a working application that meets the specification.

    3.2 Benchmark Curation and Construction

    The benchmark tasks were curated and sourced by five XR experts, including professional XR engineers, XR researchers, and contributors to XR Blocks. All tasks were validated on XR hardware by reviewers to ensure that they accurately reflect real-world usage.

    SDK tasks. To source the SDK tasks, we interviewed core XR Blocks contributors and inspected all 552 pull requests and issues available as of August 24, 2026. Maintainer reports and pull requests were pooled into a candidate list of potential features and prior bugs, then filtered based on their relevance to XR engineering, evaluation feasibility, and scope. An author converted each selected candidate into a self-contained benchmark task. For feature tasks, the author removed the target implementation while retaining its public interface and context. For repair tasks, the author reproduced the selected defect in a pinned XR Blocks snapshot. SDK tasks contain both fail-to-pass tests for the target behavior and pass-to-pass tests for related behavior that test writers identified as potentially affected by candidate implementations. Authors were instructed to create adversarial solutions and conduct three rounds of test-suite refinement.

    Application tasks. We derived an application taxonomy from 436 XR systems papers published at top human-computer interaction and spatial computing venues. Using this taxonomy, gemini-3.5-flash generated 1,000 candidate application ideas. XR experts selected 67 candidates based on XR specificity, realism, implementation feasibility, and evaluation feasibility. Following [Luo et al. (2026)], we expanded the selected ideas into full specifications using gemini-3.6-flash, manually reviewed and edited by XR experts. AppendixB describes the full procedure.

    Authors then created an evaluation suite for each application task. Since there can be multiple valid implementations, we do not require a canonical reference solution. Authors refined each specification and evaluation suite using expert-reviewed valid and adversarial candidates, revising the task specification over up to 10 iterations. Tests were designed to assess the required interactive experience while accommodating differences between implementations.

    3.3 Benchmark Statistics

    GenXR-Bench contains 112 tasks consisting of 24 SDK feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 app generation tasks. XR experts rated 28 tasks as easy, 38 as medium, and 46 as hard based on subsystem breadth, interaction length, and expected implementation effort. Experts also assigned labels based on each task’s coverage of core XR capabilities, including interaction, user interfaces (UI), hand recognition, virtual object manipulation, depth sensing, object placement, perception, drawing, audio, and head tracking. A task could receive multiple capability labels depending on its scope. Figure3 summarizes the task types and capability coverage.

    3.4 GenXR-Test Evaluation Framework

    To build each evaluation suite, we introduce GenXR-Test, a set of testing tools for the creation of adaptive interaction tests. Each held-out evaluation suite combines actors that simulate user actions and environmental inputs with assertions that check the resulting application behavior. This allows tests to assess SDK implementations and generated applications under controlled runtime conditions. A custom simulator provides fully articulated hand inputs as well as various physical scenes and objects to simulate real-world XR environments. Figure4 illustrates an example evaluation test. More information on the implementation of our evaluation suite can be found in AppendixA.

    Evaluation Actors. Actors are testing functions that simulate head, hand, controller, gesture, object, environment, and time inputs. A scripted actor runs a predefined action sequence, such as performing a hand gesture, pressing a specified control, or following a path. Authors use scripted actors when the required action can be specified before execution, improving reproducibility and reducing variation in test execution. An adaptive actor is a VLM-powered agent that follows a narrowly scoped natural-language instruction when the required action cannot be reliably determined without knowledge of the candidate implementation, following prior work [(Lu et al., 2025)]. For example, it may locate and activate a generated control or find an object needed for a later assertion. Authors use adaptive actors when differences in layout or interaction flow make fixed action sequences unreliable.

    Evaluation Assertions. After an actor produces a runtime state, assertions determine whether the required functional behavior has occurred. Programmatic assertions inspect runtime properties such as object transforms, spatial relationships, interaction state, collisions, tracking state, sensor outputs, and emitted events. For example, a test might check that a virtual object follows the hand and disappears upon colliding with a wall. Authors use programmatic assertions whenever the required behavior can be checked deterministically, focusing on observable outcomes to reduce flakiness [(Luo et al., 2014)]. VLM-based assertions assess visual outcomes that are difficult to express directly as programmatic checks. Each assertion receives rendered images from the simulated user’s point of view and a narrowly scoped, human-authored criterion. These criteria describe an expected visual outcome rather than asking the VLM to judge the overall function of the experience, which limits judging failures. This design follows the findings of [Cho et al. (2026); Huang et al. (2024)] and is evaluated in Section4.

    Semantic Tags. Valid applications can use different identifiers and scene hierarchies for equivalent objects. Tasks in GenXR-Bench require evaluated coding agents to assign semantic tags to specified objects. Examples include controls, targets, and interactable objects. These tags allow actions and assertions to locate functionally equivalent objects without requiring a fixed implementation. Semantic roles are defined in the task specification and are limited to descriptions of the objects to be tagged, reducing the risk of exposing tests. Task authors are also explicitly instructed to limit the use of semantic tags to avoid forcing a single correct implementation.

    3.5 Evaluating Application Design

    An application can satisfy its functional requirements while remaining difficult or uncomfortable to use. We therefore report a separate design score for application-generation tasks, following prior work in website generation [(Lu et al., 2025)]. During test execution, we record videos of the evaluator running the candidate application and use a VLM as a judge to rate the application against ten XR design heuristics, each on a 1–5 Likert scale. The design score is intended to supplement functional evaluations. Details on the development of the XR heuristics and the alignment of the VLM judge with human evaluators are provided in AppendixC and AppendixE, respectively.

    3.6 Analysis of App Verifier Reliability

    We validate our evaluation suite through expert evaluations of 124 candidate applications across 62 app tasks in GenXR-Bench that did not require a specific physical object or setting. The candidates were generated with gemini-3.5-flash and gemini-3.7-flash. We purposefully select gemini-3.5-flash to add a greater diversity of generated app quality.

    Eight XR experts participated in the evaluation. Each candidate received independent binary judgments of functional correctness from two evaluators, each of whom assessed the full functionality of the application. In cases of disagreement, a third independent evaluator re-examined the candidate and made the final decision. Evaluators were blind to the candidate source and verifier results and interacted freely with the application. For each candidate app, at least one evaluation used XR hardware (Galaxy XR, Meta Quest 3) to ensure alignment with real use cases.

    We ran the automated evaluation suite three times for each candidate, producing 372 evaluation runs. As shown in Table2, the verifier aligns strongly with human evaluations (accuracy: 96.5%) and is reproducible (flakiness: 4.0%). These results indicate that the evaluation suite reliably reflects expert assessments of XR app functionality. Disagreements occurred primarily in applications where experts performed tasks through interaction behaviors that the automated tests did not accommodate, such as a ball spawning at the wrist rather than the fingertips. These cases present a limitation of the verifier when candidate implementations depart from expected spatial interaction conventions.

    4 Evaluations

    4.1 Evaluation Setup

    Evaluation environment. Following the procedures in the DeepSWE benchmark [(Huang et al., 2026)], we evaluated all model configurations using mini-swe-agent[(Yang et al., 2024a)] harness within the Harbor Framework [(Harbor Framework Team, 2026)]. Agents could access XR Blocks source code, documentation, examples, and relevant dependency documentation, while other network access was restricted. Adaptive actors and VLM-based assertions used gemini-3.8-flash.

    Model choices. We select a variety of different models to evaluate. From the Google Gemini family, we evaluate gemini-3.1-pro-preview, gemini-3.5-flash, gemini-3.6-flash, gemini-3.7-flash, and gemini-3.8-flash, all at the high thinking level. From the OpenAI GPT family, we evaluate gpt-5.6-luna and gpt-5.6-sol, both at the xhigh reasoning level. From the Anthropic Claude family, we evaluate claude-opus-5 at the medium reasoning level111 We evaluate claude-opus-5 at medium due to cost constraints.. For open-weight models, we evaluate deepseek-v4-pro-0813 and deepseek-v4.1-flash at the xhigh reasoning level.

    Metrics. For all evaluations, we use Pass@1, the percentage of tasks completed successfully in one attempt, to evaluate the functionality of proposed solutions. Tasks are only considered successful when all required tests pass. For application-generation tasks, we report the mean of the 10 heuristic ratings produced by the VLM judge described in Section3.5 as the Design Score. This metric supplements the evaluation of functional correctness through Pass@1.

    4.2 Discussion of Results

    We now discuss our findings from evaluating coding agents as described in Table3. Detailed results and findings are found in AppendixF.

    XR development remains challenging even for frontier models. Across GenXR-Bench, XR development remains challenging even for frontier models, with the best performing model only reaching a Pass@1 of 50.9 ( claude-opus-5). XR functionality and design performance diverged where claude-opus-5 achieves the highest application-generation Pass@1 at 47.8%, while gpt-5.6-sol achieves the highest mean Design Score at 4.03. Notably, while SDK repair scores were high, SDK implementation and application-generation scores remained low, indicating that behavioral repair and bug identification pose a far easier challenge than end-to-end XR app implementation. Models further from the frontier were far less capable, failing on foundational spatial-computing concepts or completely unable to create core application objects. These smaller models suffer heavily from web development coding hallucinations, poor metric understanding, and API hallucinations. Frontier models are more capable of avoiding these errors but still fail at higher-order spatial reasoning, including bimanual coordination (Figure12), room geometry visualizations (Figure13), and physical alignment (Figure14).

    Model-written tests are not indicative of success. Notably, models were relatively incapable of writing effective tests where the testing-to-editing ratio for each model was not indicative of overall success. Instead, models tend to overwrite unit tests that did not validate actual XR functionality and fail to have the foresight to predict real runtime conditions. Models that were more willing to evaluate code through runtime tests were also more successful. We report a detailed breakdown of agent tool usage in Table11.

    4.3 Failure Analysis and Directions for Improvement

    XR experts then manually analyzed task failure modes and grouped them into recurring categories. These failures indicate potential openings for improving the ability of agents to create spatial and embodied experiences. We provide a more detailed analysis in AppendixG.

    Asynchronous initialization and environmental updates. Startup race conditions occurred in 44.9% of failed runs. Implementations began gameplay updates or sensing-dependent calculations before the required assets or tracking state were available, causing runtime exceptions. Other implementations checked for detected surfaces only at startup and did not respond when the surfaces became available later. This behavior also limited the functionality of some applications that passed the tests. For instance, in the lascaux-torch task shown in Figure11, successful implementations made virtual walls to simulate a cave whereas an XR developer might have developed shaders to place cave paintings on physical walls.
