一句话：在 Unity 里执行与视频模型匹配的动作序列，用模拟器状态当参考，评七个维度、九个场景。

要点：

  • 在 Unity 物理仿真里执行与视频模型相同的动作序列，用模拟器导出的状态作参考，同时做感知层与物理因果层评估
  • 七个评估维度：动作可控性、场景与角色一致性、提示遵循、运动学、流体力学、物理因果、光照；共 9 个场景
  • 现有 SOTA 模型在标准感知指标看不见的维度（如运动学与物理因果）上普遍存在明显差距

为什么值得看：世界模型要当引擎用，验收就必须是状态级而不是像素级。用 Unity 当真值裁判这套做法，引擎团队自己也能照搬：同一段动作序列喂给模型与仿真器，比对状态而不是比对画面，直接做成回归测试。

中文摘要：交互式世界模型在机器人、游戏引擎与数字孪生上潜力巨大，但现有 benchmark 主要衡量感知相似度，而不是真实应用真正依赖的物理因果一致性。WMEval 把评测锚在 Unity 的物理仿真上：在仿真器与视频模型里执行互相匹配的动作序列，用模拟器导出的状态作为参考，从而既能做感知层评估，也能做物理因果层评估。它覆盖 9 个场景，从七个维度考察模型——动作可控性、场景与角色一致性、提示遵循、运动学、流体力学、物理因果与光照。对当前最强模型的实测显示，标准感知指标看不出问题的那些维度上，差距依然显著，而这些维度恰恰决定了模型能否真的当引擎用。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-24

本期推送：2026-10-27

WMEval: Evaluating Interactive World Models Grounded on Physical Simulations

Abstract

Interactive world models hold immense potential for high-stakes applications in robotics, game engines, and immersive digital twins, yet existing benchmarks primarily focus on perceptual similarity rather than the physical-causal coherence essential for real-world utility. We introduce WMEval, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates interactive world models against Unity-based physical simulations. By leveraging Unity as a high-fidelity ground-truth oracle, we shift evaluation beyond perceptual visual assessment toward the objective state-based verification required for downstream applications. Spanning 9 diverse scenes, WMEval assesses action controllability, scene and character consistency, prompt adherence, kinematics, fluid mechanics, physical causality, and lighting. By executing matched action sequences in both the simulator and the world model, WMEval enables evaluation at both the perceptual level and the physical-causal level, using simulator-derived states as reference. Experiments on state-of-the-art models reveal significant room for improvement in dimensions that remain hidden by standard perceptual metrics but are vital for real-world deployments. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/WMEval.

1 Introduction

Video generative models are increasingly positioned as interactive world-modeling engines [(Bruce et al., 2024; Google DeepMind, 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026)]: given observations and actions, they are expected to generate futures that are visually plausible and physically coherent [(Valevski et al., 2025; He et al., 2026)]. This shift moves video models beyond open visual prediction toward action-conditioned simulation [(Qin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026)]. However, evaluation remains challenging: current models struggle with controllability, scene consistency, and physical state evolution.

Existing evaluations only partially address this need. Video-generation benchmarks primarily measure visual quality, spatio-temporal consistency, or prompt alignment [(Huang et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025; Han et al., 2025)]. Recent interactive world-model benchmarks evaluate scene consistency and action control through perceptual similarity to references [(Ye et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2025)]. Broader world-modeling video benchmarks further test scientific-law adherence or physics-related generation violations [(Hu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025)]. However, for interactive applications such as robotics, autonomous driving, and gaming, an interactive world model must preserve consistency, controllability, and causal outcomes under interaction. Whether action-conditioned generations obey the same physical constraints as a reference engine therefore remains largely untested. Table 1 summarizes this gap. This calls for a standardized evaluation protocol specifying how action space should be configured, what references should be used, and how generations should be compared.

We introduce WMEval, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating interactive world models against physical simulation references. We build on Unity because it is a widely used real-time 3D development platform with mature tooling and a large asset ecosystem, making it practical to construct diverse scenes. Across 9 Unity scenes, WMEval pairs each scene with a set of deliberately designed action trajectories to stress test 6 different world modeling dimensions including action controllability, scene and character consistency, kinematics and mechanics, fluid mechanics, physical causality, as well as lighting and shading.

By grounding evaluation in a Unity-based physical simulator, WMEval executes matched action trajectories in both the simulator and the interactive world model. We use Unity not just as a visual target, but as a controllable reference engine that provides simulator-derived states, and causal event traces. This enables WMEval to evaluate generations beyond perceptual quality through reference quantities such as velocity, momentum, energy, motion trajectories, and material properties.

WMEval provides a metric suite that combines dimension-specific CV-based metrics for comparing generations with simulator-derived states, and holistic metrics for video-level similarity and prompt-scene consistency. We evaluate six state-of-the-art systems that are sufficiently capable and compatible with our standardized evaluation protocol. Results on WMEval reveal a substantial gap between current interactive world model systems and physical-simulator grounded references: models often preserve visual fidelity and action-responsive motion, but fail on simulator-consistent spatial relations, mechanical quantities, fluid invariants, lighting coherence, and multi-stage causal chains.

To summarize, in this work we make the following contributions:

  • •

    We propose WMEval, an interactive world-model benchmark that evaluates interactive world models through matched comparisons against physical-simulator references, using deliberately designed action trajectories across 9 diverse Unity scenes.

  • •

    We develop an evaluation suite that combines dimension-specific CV-based metrics, with holistic video-level and VLM-as-a-judge evaluations, covering video quality, prompt consistency, physical-law adherence, action controllability, and action-driven causality.

  • •

    We benchmark six state-of-the-art interactive world models and reveal world modeling failure cases that are not captured by video-quality or perceptual-similarity metrics alone.

    • 2 Related Work

    3D World Construction Models. One representative line of world-modeling work constructs explicit, navigable 3D world representations from text, images, or videos. Models such as HY-World 2.0 and Marble generate high-fidelity 3D environments by combining generative modeling with geometric representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting [(Team HY-World et al., 2026; World Labs, 2025)]. These methods prioritize 3D scene reconstruction, view-consistent rendering, and interactive exploration, rather than explicitly modeling action-conditioned environment dynamics.

    Interactive World Models. The other line of work uses action-conditioned video diffusion models to simulate interactive environments that evolve over time. In WMEval, we focus on image-to-video interactive world models that generate rollouts autoregressively under either action-control or camera-control interactions. We evaluate Project Genie [(Bruce et al., 2024)], LingBot-World [(Robbyant Team et al., 2026)], Matrix-Game 2.0 and 3.0 [(He et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026)], HY-WorldPlay [(Sun et al., 2026)], and Waypoint-1.5 [(Overworld, 2026)] because they represent a diverse set of latest interactive world-model systems with publicly accessible or experimentally usable interfaces.

    Interactive World-Model Benchmarks. Recent benchmarks have begun to evaluate video generators as world models. MIND evaluates memory consistency and action control in open-domain closed-loop generations [(Ye et al., 2026)], while WorldSimBench evaluates world simulators through perceptual assessment and action-level embodied tasks [(Qin et al., 2025)]. More recently, WBench provides broad multi-turn evaluation of interactive world models across interaction adherence, consistency, and physics-related dimensions [(Ying et al., 2026)]. Broader video-world-model benchmarks such as WorldModelBench and VideoScience-Bench test instruction following, physics adherence, or scientific-law reasoning in generated videos [(Li et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026)]. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in standardizing world-model inputs, interaction protocols, and evaluation protocols across models. WMEval fills this gap by providing simulator-based physical references, controlled action trajectories, and a comprehensive metrics suite.

    3 WMEval

    3.1 Benchmark Design

    Figure 1 summarizes the end-to-end WMEval evaluation protocol. The benchmark consists of three stages. First, for each scene and evaluation dimension, we define a semantic action trajectory over actor and camera controls. Second, this trajectory is executed in parallel by a Unity reference environment and the interactive world model under evaluation. Unity provides both rendered observations and simulator-derived physical quantities, while the world model exposes generated observations only. Third, WMEval compares the two rollouts using dimension-specific metrics and holistic video-level metrics. When simulator-grounded quantities are required, CV- or VLM-based evaluators recover the corresponding physical quantities from the world-model rollouts. We next introduce the Unity scenes, formalize how matched action-conditioned rollouts are generated, and describe the dimension-specific and holistic metrics used to evaluate them.

    3.1.1 Scenes

    We construct nine controlled Unity environments as reference testbeds for interactive world models. Each scene exposes controls, observations, and simulator-derived states through Unity ML-Agents [(Unity Technologies, 2026)], enabling paired execution of the same semantic action trajectory in the simulator and the world model. Together, the scenes target six evaluation dimensions: action controllability, scene and character consistency, kinematics and mechanics, fluid mechanics, physical causality, and lighting and shading. Detailed scene configurations, action spaces, and simulator states are provided in Appendix A.

    For action-conditioned dynamics, BallRoller uses a controllable sphere moving through ramps, obstacles, and passive objects to test action responsiveness and motion consistency. BeamDomino triggers a multi-stage rolling→impact→topple→cascade sequence, providing a controlled test of action-driven physical causality [(Li et al., 2026)]. BilliardGame uses three-ball carom billiards with deterministic physics to test collision dynamics and post-collision motion, while RacingCar evaluates vehicle motion under steering, throttle, and braking.

    For scene and appearance consistency, ChessBoard places a humanoid character among large reflective objects, providing a testbed for character and lighting consistency. MirrorRollingBall increases scene complexity with a reflective ball and up to 48 surrounding objects, stressing multi-object spatial consistency and tracking. SunRisesAndSets isolates lighting and shading through controlled camera motion and directional illumination, while WanderingGarden provides the most visually complex scene, with foliage, particles, NPC motion, and designated anchor objects for evaluating spatial and object consistency.

    Finally, LiquidContainer manipulates a sealed bottle through six-degree-of-freedom motion to induce controlled tilt and sloshing. Its stylized liquid dynamics provide a reproducible reference for sealed-container motion rather than a general-purpose fluid simulation.

    3.1.2 Evaluation Settings

    Action Space and Action Trajectories.

    Each scene e defines a semantic action space A⁽ᵉ⁾ with d_c⁽ᵉ⁾ continuous controls and, when needed, d_d⁽ᵉ⁾ discrete branches:

    A⁽ᵉ⁾=[-1,1]^d_c⁽ᵉ⁾×∏ₖ₌₁^d_d⁽ᵉ⁾{0,…,Kₖ⁽ᵉ⁾-1}.

    		(1)

    These controls represent scene-level semantics such as actor motion, steering, braking, camera motion, or object manipulation. For each evaluation dimension d, we define scene-specific trajectories

    Γ_d={(eᵢ,γᵢ⁽ᵈ⁾)}ᵢ₌₁^N_d, γᵢ⁽ᵈ⁾=(a⁽ⁱ⁾₁,…,a⁽ⁱ⁾_Tᵢ), a⁽ⁱ⁾ₜ∈A^(eᵢ).

    		(2)

    Each trajectory is designed to elicit a measurable target behavior. For example, controllability trajectories induce directional motion, mechanics trajectories trigger collisions, and causality trajectories trigger multi-stage event chains.

    Action Adaptation.

    Interactive world models expose heterogeneous native control interfaces. We therefore match actions at the level of semantic controls and physical time rather than low-level action tokens. For each model, a lightweight adapter maps the semantic trajectory to the closest supported native controls and aligns their duration according to the model’s frame rate or action stride. A model is evaluated only on dimensions for which its interface supports the required control semantics.

    Matched Rollouts.

    Given semantic action aᵢ₊₁, the Unity reference produces

    (ôᵢ₊₁,ŝᵢ₊₁,m̂ᵢ₊₁)=𝔼⁽ᵉ⁾(ŝᵢ,aᵢ₊₁),

    		(3)

    where ôᵢ₊₁ is the rendered observation, ŝᵢ₊₁ the simulator state, and m̂ᵢ₊₁ evaluation metadata such as object velocities, trajectories, lighting states, and event labels. The world model receives the controls and produces observations,

    oᵢ₊₁∼p_θ(oᵢ₊₁|o_≤i,a⁽ᵐ⁾_≤i+1),

    		(4)

    while its underlying state remains latent. This yields paired rollouts indexed by the same semantic action trajectory and physical timing. Simulator states {ŝᵢ,m̂ᵢ}ᵢ₌₁ᵀ then provide the reference quantities for the simulator-grounded metrics.

    Simulator Implementation.

    WMEval works on any simulator exposing the required reference rollouts and physical states can define benchmark cases. Once packaged, evaluation only requires generating from the seed frame under the prescribed actions. We provide a Unity-based reference package in the supplementary material.

    3.2 Metrics Design

    WMEval evaluates generated rollouts using dimension-specific and holistic metrics. Dimension-specific metrics compare candidate-side measurements against Unity-derived states and event traces to diagnose consistency, controllability, physical dynamics, lighting, and causal transitions. Holistic metrics evaluate video-level perceptual similarity and prompt-scene consistency. Detailed metric definitions, calibration, and implementation details are provided in Appendix B.

    Action Controllability.

    This dimension evaluates whether generated motion follows the intended action or camera-control input. Using RAFT optical flow [(Teed and Deng, 2020)], we separate state-level agreement with Unity-reference flow (Ground Truth RAFT) from alignment with the commanded motion (Synthetic RAFT).

    Physical Causality.

    This dimension evaluates whether matched actions preserve multi-stage causal state transitions. Following CausalStep [(Li et al., 2026)], we measure full- and partial-chain preservation and causal reasoning, applying the same judging pipeline to Unity references and world-model rollouts to quantify reference-side judge error. Detailed metrics are provided in Appendix B.6.

    Kinematics and Mechanics.

    This dimension evaluates whether matched controls produce simulator-consistent motion and mechanical outcomes. We report Final Displacement Error (FDE) and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) for trajectory agreement, together with ExactMatch and ErrorRate for quantities such as terminal momentum and kinetic energy.

    Fluid Mechanics.

    This dimension evaluates sealed-container slosh against a controlled parametric reference in which surface tilt and wobble depend on container acceleration. We measure motion-field agreement, tracked-region stability, orientation consistency, slosh-spectrum agreement, and LPIPS. The candidate-side measurements depend on SAM 2 tracking; its Unity-side calibration and the resulting scope of these metrics are detailed in Appendix B.4.1.

    Lighting and Shading.

    This dimension evaluates whether illumination and cast shadows remain geometrically and temporally coherent under controlled camera motion. We report scene retention (Scene Retention Rate, SRR), shadow presence (Shadow Detection Rate, SDR), light-direction coherence (Multi-Object Sun Disagreement, MOSD), temporal smoothness (Shadow Direction Jitter, SDJ), footprint stability (Shadow Area Stability, SAS), and shape stability (Shadow Shape Drift, SSD), using GroundingDINO, SAM 2, and Hu moments  [(Liu et al., 2025; Ravi et al., 2025; Hu, 1962)].

    Environment Object and Character Consistency.

    This dimension evaluates whether objects, spatial relations, and character identity persist under controlled camera motion. We report Depth AbsRel and DistMAE for geometry, ObjPerm for anchor-object persistence, and CharConsis for character identity, using GroundingDINO, SAM 2, and DINOv2 [(Oquab et al., 2024)].

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experiment Settings

    We evaluate six state-of-the-art interactive world models: Google Project Genie [(Bruce et al., 2024; Google DeepMind, 2025)], LingBot-World [(Robbyant Team et al., 2026)], Matrix-Game 2.0 [(He et al., 2025)], Matrix-Game 3.0 [(Wang et al., 2026)], HY-WorldPlay [(Sun et al., 2026)], and Waypoint-1.5 [(Overworld, 2026)]. Since these systems expose different interfaces, we evaluate each dimension on the subset of models that satisfies its interface requirements, e.g., third-person camera control for object consistency and action control for mechanics and causality. The open-source model runs were executed on a single host with 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Unless otherwise noted, we report mean ± standard deviation over five generations. For the model comparisons that support our main conclusions, we additionally test whether the conclusion remains unchanged over all \binom53=10 three-run subsets and apply metric-appropriate statistical tests.

    4.1.1 Measurement Reliability

    Evaluator and Generation Size Calibration.

    We calibrate learned evaluators against simulator-derived physical quantities and audit their validity on generated videos. Across evaluation dimensions, the resulting calibration errors are sufficiently small for the reported comparisons within each metric’s stated scope (Table 12). Full calibration and validity analyses are in Appendix C.1. Moreover, we ensure the main findings do not depend on a particular choice of five generations. The controllability ordering is unchanged across all \binom53=10 three-run subsets. When the evidence does not separate two models for example, Project Genie and LingBot-World on prompt consistency – we report them as comparable. Full analyses are in Appendix C.2.

    4.2 Results and Insights

    Across evaluation dimensions, three recurring gaps emerge in current world models. First, following an immediate control does not guarantee correct causal state evolution. Second, perceptually plausible generations can still violate physical quantities or multi-stage causal structure. Third, consistency along one axis, such as temporal smoothness or foreground appearance, does not imply consistency along others, such as spatial geometry or lighting. We analyze these failures below.

    4.2.1 Action and Causal State Evolution

    Controllability is necessary but insufficient for faithful state evolution.

    Physical causality first requires the model to respond to the intended control: if an action fails to trigger the correct motion, its downstream physical consequences cannot be correct. We therefore ask whether successful immediate action following is also sufficient for faithful state evolution. Table 2 shows that it is not. On MirrorRollingBall, Project Genie and LingBot-World nearly perfectly follow the general commanded direction (Synthetic-RAFT cosine 0.98 and 1.00), yet their subsequent state evolution still deviates substantially from the Unity reference (relative flow errors of 0.77 and 0.49, respectively). The same pattern appears on BeamDomino: both achieve a Synthetic-RAFT cosine of 0.99, while retaining state-level errors of 0.44 and 0.34. Details of per-scene controllability analyses are provided in Appendix E.4.

    Short-horizon causal understanding does not compose into full causal chains.

    Finally, BeamDomino tests whether an action propagates through the four-stage rolling→impact→topple→cascade chain, rather than merely producing recognizable individual events. For example, Project Genie generations remain close to Unity references on Isolated Causal Reasoning Accuracy (ICRA; 90% vs. 100%), meaning that it can usually answer causal questions about individual stages for instance, Why does the red ball begin to move in this video segment? Yet it preserves the complete causal chain in only 3/15 rollouts, compared with 13/15 for Unity. This failure is systematic across trajectory types: none of its ten glancing and direct_strike rollouts preserves the full chain. These results reveal a compositional gap: plausible individual causal transitions do not guarantee that their physical consequences propagate correctly through the full event chain. Further causal trajectory analyses are provided in Appendix E.2.

    Contact-dependent mechanics remain hard.

    We next ask whether the resulting trajectories preserve mechanical consequences under matched controls. Table 4 compares the relatively smooth vehicle motion in RacingCar with the collision-dependent dynamics of BilliardGame. On BilliardGame, both models track the ball closely (FDE 0.83 and 0.45 m), yet their robust mechanics error (26.8% and 23.3%) is about five times Unity’s 4.9%. On RacingCar, Project Genie executes the commanded turn (DTW 2.28 m) but overshoots the endpoint by 9.39 m, with a similar 25.7% mechanics error; Matrix-Game 2.0 instead advances the camera past a car that stays parked, so its FDE (29.65 m) equals that of a stationary car. Generating action-responsive motion is thus easier than reproducing its momentum and energy, with or without contact.

    4.2.2 Perceptual Quality and Physical Adherence

    Perceptual similarity can hide distinct interaction failures.

    Perceptual metrics are widely used as proxies for rollout fidelity: MIND reports LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR, while iWorld-Bench uses LPIPS, SSIM, and MSE for motion smoothness [(Ye et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026)]. Yet visual similarity does not reveal whether the interaction evolves correctly. On BeamDomino, Project Genie’s cLPIPS is nearly identical to LingBot-World’s (0.60 vs. 0.61), yet it preserves the full causal chain in only 3/15 rollouts versus 13/15 for Unity. On BallRoller, Project Genie has cLPIPS 0.56 versus 0.38 for LingBot-World, while its generated motion is misaligned with the commanded direction (Synthetic-RAFT cosine -0.33 vs. 1.00). Thus, perceptual similarity captures appearance-level divergence but can obscure failures in control execution and causal state propagation.

    On LiquidContainer, Table 6 evaluates whether the liquid moves like the reference, maintains a stable apparent size and surface orientation, matches its oscillation pattern, and remains perceptually similar. Compared to Project Genie, HY-WorldPlay achieves a much lower LPIPS (0.300 vs. 0.624), yet it exhibits more surface orientation deviations. It also renders the bottle at about half of the reference’s apparent size (median scale ratio 0.51, Table 14), allowing the well-matched background to dominate LPIPS. Thus, strong perceptual similarity does not imply physical adherence.

    Physical axes expose distinct failure modes across models.

    HY-WorldPlay keeps the liquid’s apparent size stable but tilts its surface unlike Unity, whereas Project Genie keeps the tilt closer but lets the liquid area and flow drift; on third-person RacingCar, Project Genie turns the car but overshoots, whereas Matrix-Game 2.0 moves the camera instead of the car. Additional results and analyses for fluid mechanics are provided in Appendix E.1.

    4.2.3 Local and Long-Horizon Consistency

    Large viewpoint changes expose spatial inconsistency.

    Table 7 evaluates whether environment background, objects, and characters remain stable as the camera departs from the initial view. The results show substantial spatial inconsistency across models. On Garden, Project Genie exhibits large depth error, ranging from 36.7% to 169.9%. On BilliardGame, its character consistency drops from 76.2% under perturbation to 29.8% under the full 360^∘ trajectory. MirrorRollingBall is more stable, retaining 99.9% character consistency under perturbation and 84.9% under 360^∘ rotation. The degradation is more pronounced for weaker models: Matrix-Game 3.0 drops from 91.2% to 16.0% character consistency on BilliardGame and from 14.8% to 4.7% on MirrorRollingBall, while Matrix-Game 2.0 falls from 95.0% to 14.7% and from 48.3% to 6.7%, respectively. These results suggest that maintaining persistent scene geometry and character identity over large camera motion remains challenging even when local views appear visually consistent.

    Stable-looking shadows do not imply a coherent global light source.

    Table 8 asks whether models keep the anchor scene in view, maintain stable individual shadows, and make shadows across objects agree on a common light direction. Project Genie and LingBot-World retain the anchor scene in 96.5% and 100% of frames, yet their inferred sun directions from different objects disagree by 65.8^∘ and 60.1^∘. Waypoint-1.5 makes the gap clearest: it retains the scene throughout the rollout and produces the smoothest, most shape-stable shadows, yet has the largest sun-direction disagreement (98.3^∘). Thus, locally plausible shadows need not correspond to a coherent scene-level light source.

    Foreground objects are easier to preserve than the surroundings.

    Table 9 shows the same local–global gap in prompt consistency. On third-person RacingCar, Project Genie, LingBot-World, and HY-WorldPlay score 1.00 on foreground objects but only 0.76, 0.72, and 0.71 on the environment. Thus, salient objects are preserved more reliably than the broader scene. Human evaluation shows a strong alignment with the VLM results with a Spearman coefficient ρ=0.90 (Table 11 from Appendix B.8.1), Project Genie and LingBot-World performances are statistically in-distinguishable (p=0.99).

    5 Conclusion

    We introduced WMEval, a comprehensive world model benchmark grounded in a physical simulator to evaluate interactive world models under matched action trajectories. Across nine Unity scenes and six state-of-the-art interactive world models, our results show that current models can often preserve coarse visual fidelity, foreground entities like the main character in third-person view, and action-responsive motion. However, current world models still fall short in many aspects: models struggle to preserve spatial relations under camera motion, maintain object and character identity over long horizons, reproduce mechanically valid trajectories and physical quantities, conserve fluid properties, render coherent lighting and shadows, and propagate multi-stage causal chains. These failures are often hidden by perceptual metrics, demonstrating that WMEval can effectively serve its intended role: exposing physical-causal gaps through standardized and simulator-grounded evaluation.

    Appendix A Unity Scenes

    WMEval comprises nine Unity scenes, each designed to isolate specific physical-causal dimensions (illustrated in Fig. 2). All scenes expose their state through the Unity ML-Agents Toolkit, enabling evaluation at both the perceptual and physical-causal level. Technical specifications are summarized in Table 10.

    A.1 BallRoller

    Scene description.

    BallRoller is a compact square arena with a flat blue-gray floor and low white boundary walls, viewed from a fixed side-table camera that looks diagonally into the play area. The player controls a smooth white sphere that rolls across the floor. Static obstacles—a yellow ramp, a magenta dome, a cyan cube—are placed throughout the arena, and a cluster of 15 colored physics balls is scattered on the floor. On contact, these passive balls are knocked away by the player sphere, producing multi-body rigid-body collisions.

    Action space.

    Two continuous actions: horizontal force along the X axis and horizontal force along the Z axis, each in [-1,+1], applied directly to the player ball’s rigidbody via AddForce.

    Observation space.

    A 48-dimensional vector: the player’s local position (3 floats) concatenated with the local positions of up to 15 passive physics balls (15×3=45 floats). Notably, velocities are not included, so a world model must infer dynamics from positional changes across time steps.

    Camera.

    A fixed-offset follow camera that computes a world-space offset from the player at initialization and rigidly translates with the player ball in every subsequent frame.

    Evaluation dimensions.

    BallRoller is used for action controllability (both Ground Truth RAFT and Synthetic RAFT), causal LPIPS (collision events between the player and passive balls), and prompt–scene consistency (VLM-as-judge). The omission of velocity from the observation vector is a deliberate design choice: it tests whether a world model can reason about latent velocities from position histories alone, a prerequisite for accurate multi-body collision prediction.

    A.2 BeamDomino

    Scene description.

    BeamDomino is a physics-driven causal-chain scene in which the player drives a heavy floor ball under continuous control to strike a supporting structure and trigger a downstream domino cascade. The scene decomposes into four canonical stages: rolling, impact, topple, and cascade, linking ball trajectory to multi-body contact, structural collapse, roof-ball release, and delayed domino propagation.

    Its two-tone domino design and staged geometry provide clear visual cues for fall direction and causal progression. The scene, therefore, tests whether a world model reproduces the correct causal state transitions rather than merely generating visually plausible motion.

    Small errors in impact location, momentum transfer, contact ordering, or pillar/sector selection can produce qualitatively different cascades. This sensitivity is what makes BeamDomino a targeted test of action-driven physical causality [(Li et al., 2026)].

    Trajectory shapes.

    Under the same nominal action prompt, small perturbations of the initial ball state produce three qualitatively different ground-truth cascades:

  • •

    canonical: the ball strikes a leg, the platform tilts past the fall threshold, the roof ball is released, and the dominoes topple.

  • •

    glancing: the ball clips a leg, but the platform survives; the dominoes are subsequently toppled by the ball directly.

  • •

    direct-strike: the ball bypasses the platform and hits the domino row first.

    • Benchmark trajectories include all three. The classifier and per-shape QA stage chains are detailed in Appendix D.5.

    Action space.

    Two continuous actions: force along Z (forward/backward) and force along X (left/right), each in [-1,+1]. The applied force magnitude is 80 N with a maximum ball speed of 20 m/s. This action channel is agent-specific it acts on the floor ball’s rigid body rather than camera-relative.

    World models without a faithful action-channel mapping for (Fₓ,F_z) on a non-camera body are not evaluated on this scene: a prompt-driven substitute for the ball action, e.g., LingBot-World (Cam)’s natural-language prompt, is not action-matched.

    Observation space.

    A 92-dimensional vector comprising: the floor ball’s position, linear velocity, and angular velocity (9); the roof ball’s position, linear velocity, and an airborne flag (7); per-domino tilt magnitude and fallen flag for each of the 20 dominoes (20×2=40); cascade summary statistics including the fraction of dominoes fallen and the elapsed cascade duration (2); camera position and Euler angles (6); three pillar states each with position, Euler angles, and a kinematic flag (3×7=21); and the roof slab state with position, Euler angles, and a kinematic flag (7).

    Camera.

    A fixed-offset follow camera positioned at (0,6,-12) relative to the floor ball, with smooth interpolation (Lerp factor 8/s) and continuous LookAt targeting the ball.

    Evaluation dimensions.

    BeamDomino is the primary scene for physical causality evaluation using the CausalStep framework [Li et al. (2026)], which grades whether the four canonical stages occur in correct causal order. It is also used for action controllability (RAFT) and causal LPIPS.

    The three-step causal chain is central to the design: prediction errors at any stage compound downstream, so a world model must faithfully propagate momentum through impact, structural collapse, and cascade to score well.

    A.3 BilliardGame

    Scene description.

    BilliardGame implements a three-ball carom billiards setup on a standard billiard table. Unlike the other scenes, this scene uses a custom deterministic fixed-point 3D physics engine (Calculable Mechanics v2) rather than Unity’s default PhysX solver, ensuring analytically reproducible ball–ball and ball–cushion collisions. The player positions up to three balls on the table and executes a cue shot with configurable angle, force, and English (off-center hit point on the cue ball face).

    Action space.

    A mixed action space with 10 continuous and 2 discrete dimensions. The continuous actions encode: the initial positions of three balls on the table surface (3×2=6 floats mapped from [-1,+1] to table half-dimensions), the cue angle ([0,2π]), shot strength ([0,maxForce]), and the 2D hit point on the cue ball face (clamped to the unit circle, encoding topspin/backspin/sidespin). The two discrete branches control shot execution (wait vs. execute) and simulation termination (normal vs. force-end).

    Observation space.

    A 13-dimensional vector: the local positions of three balls relative to the table frame (3×3=9), the normalized cue pivot angle (1), the current force setting (1), and the 2D normalized hit point (2).

    Camera.

    A fixed overhead view of the billiard table.

    Evaluation dimensions.

    BilliardGame is used for kinematics and mechanics evaluation (ball trajectory matching via DTW and FDE; momentum and energy conservation via exact-match percentage and error rate) and causal LPIPS. The 2D hit-point action directly controls post-collision trajectories through spin, making this scene particularly demanding: a world model must capture not only elastic collision angles but also the effect of torque-induced spin on subsequent ball paths.

    A.4 ChessBoard

    Scene description.

    ChessBoard features a giant black-and-white chessboard ground plane under a flat gray sky, surrounded by oversized glossy chess pieces (king, queen, rook, bishop, knight, pawn). A large reflective chrome sphere stands near the center of the board. The player controls a gray humanoid mannequin character in third-person view, navigating around the chess pieces with the ability to run and jump.

    Action space.

    Two continuous actions (horizontal movement along X and Z, each in [-1,+1]) plus two discrete branches: jump (0 or 1) and sprint (0 or 1).

    Observation space.

    An 8-dimensional vector: the character’s local position (3), local rotation as a quaternion (4), and a grounded flag (1). The minimal state representation forces reliance on the visual observation from the camera for spatial reasoning.

    Camera.

    A Cinemachine third-person follow camera that smoothly tracks the humanoid avatar.

    Evaluation dimensions.

    ChessBoard is used for scene and character consistency and prompt–scene consistency (VLM-as-judge). The visually distinctive environment—with its regular grid pattern, specular chess pieces, and the chrome sphere—provides unambiguous landmark features for testing whether a world model preserves scene geometry, object identity, and the reflective material properties of the sphere across extended rollouts. The combination of discrete jump actions and continuous movement on the structured chessboard grid creates sharp visual transitions (ground-to-airborne state changes) that test character animation consistency.

    A.5 MirrorRollingBall

    Scene description.

    MirrorRollingBall places a reflective chrome sphere (the player-controlled ball) on a flat open ground surrounded by a field of up to 48 large glossy yellow balls. Bright directional sunlight casts visible shadows beneath all objects. The scene is visually simpler than BallRoller but exposes substantially more state: full kinematic information (position and velocity) for all tracked objects.

    Action space.

    Two continuous actions: force along X and force along Z, each in [-1,+1], applied via AddForce to the player ball.

    Observation space.

    A 297-dimensional vector: the player ball’s position, linear velocity, and angular velocity (9), concatenated with the position and linear velocity of up to 48 yellow balls (48×6=288). Missing balls are zero-padded to maintain a fixed-length vector.

    Camera.

    A fixed-offset follow camera identical in design to BallRoller.

    Evaluation dimensions.

    MirrorRollingBall is used for scene and character consistency (depth AbsRel, pairwise distance MAE, and character identity preservation via DINOv2), prompt–scene consistency, and contributes to kinematics evaluation through ball-to-ball collision tracking. The scene supports configurable ball counts (10, 20, 30, or 48 yellow balls), enabling controlled evaluation of how consistency metrics degrade as scene complexity increases.

    A.6 LiquidContainer

    Scene description.

    LiquidContainer is a continuous-control fluid manipulation scene in which the player drives a sealed, partially filled glass bottle through six degrees of freedom. The bottle is rendered against a coastal HDRI and rests on a checker-and-cross calibration floor that anchors scale and orientation cues.

    The scene evaluates whether a world model preserves the visual appearance of a moving air-liquid interface under transparent-glass refraction, together with the first-order constraints its parametric reference enforces: projected-area stability under rigid-body motion, a gravity-aligned free surface at each tilt angle, and damped-oscillator slosh decay. The reference is a parametric slosh model rather than a fluid solver, and its scope is stated in Appendix B.4.

    Unlike discrete rigid-body scenes, failures here do not appear as single event-state errors. They appear as continuous physical violations: projected volume drift, incorrect surface tilt, unstable velocity fields, and off-frequency sloshing that persists after the triggering action.

    Action space.

    Six continuous actions: forward/back, right/left, up/down translation, and pitch, yaw, roll rotation, each in [-1,+1].

    Observation space.

    A 24-dimensional vector: world position (3), forward direction (3), up direction (3), linear velocity (3), angular velocity (3), Euler angles normalized to [-1,+1] (3), and the six current input values (6). The redundant orientation representation (direction vectors plus Euler angles) provides robust pose information.

    Camera.

    A static side-view camera (c2_static_side regime) that frames the bottle and calibration floor.

    Evaluation dimensions.

    LiquidContainer is the sole scene for fluid mechanics evaluation, scoped to sealed-container slosh (Appendix B.4). It tests five metric families: velocity field fidelity (cosine similarity), volume conservation (normalized mask-area standard deviation and per-second drift), surface orientation (RMS tilt residual of the air-liquid interface), slosh spectrum (meniscus power spectrum L₁), and segment-aligned LPIPS as a perceptual sanity check.

    Every visible element doubles as a calibration affordance: the checker floor provides spatial reference, the red cap marks the bottle’s orientation, and the sealed liquid surface must align with gravity at each tilt angle.

    A.7 RacingCar

item.title: 端到端自动做科研：SplatLab 复现 3DGS 基线、提假设、跑消融、写稿，每个数字都绑一次训练 ｜ SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research
item.description:
一句话：插件式变异 + 八岛 Elo 锦标赛 + 常驻证伪器，报告里每个数字必须绑定可回溯的训练运行。

要点：

  • 候选从已验证复现的主干上变异插件生成；跨 8 个岛做级联加权 Elo 锦标赛，按实测 GPU PSNR 打分并附语言反馈
  • 常驻证伪器从边缘场景、稀疏视角、超参扰动三面攻击幸存者，每次失败扣 δ=30 Elo，并在写稿前拥有否决权
  • 报告里每个数字都必须绑定到一次可回溯的训练运行；只要还有未关闭的论断，该运行就不能终止

为什么值得看：自动科研系统的真正价值不是会写稿，而是「报告数字可回溯」这条工程约束——它同样适用于任何自动调参、自动优化流水线：先让证据链闭合，再谈结论。

中文摘要：复现一篇 3DGS 论文往往要几周工程，才谈得上提出扩展。已有自动科研系统会读论文、写假设、写代码，但受限于固定模板、可执行性低、可追溯性差，且从未在一个活跃的视觉子领域里端到端演示过。SplatLab 就针对 3DGS：给定研究提示、目标论文链接或什么都不给，它能复现已发表基线、提出扩展、在 Mip-NeRF 360 与 LLFF 上训练与消融、写出稿件，并把每个报告的数字绑定到一次有日志的训练运行。其设计要点包括：候选通过变异已验证复现主干上的插件产生；跨 8 个岛做级联加权 Elo 锦标赛，按实测 GPU PSNR 评分并给语言反馈；常驻证伪器对幸存者做压力测试、失败扣 Elo，且在写稿前有否决权；数字与运行强绑定，未关闭论断时运行不得终止。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-27

SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research

Abstract

Reproducing a published 3DGS paper takes weeks of expert engineering before any extension can be proposed. Prior autonomous-research systems read papers, draft hypotheses, and write code, but suffer from limited template length, executability, and traceability. Specifically, none has been demonstrated end-to-end in a live computer-vision subfield with intense activity. SplatLab is an autonomous research system for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses these limitations. Given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, it reproduces a published baseline, proposes an extension, trains and ablates across Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, writes the manuscript, and binds every reported number to a logged training run. Five design choices distinguish it: (i) candidates mutate plugins from a verified-reproduction backbone matched to published baselines; (ii) a cascade-weighted Elo tournament across eight islands scores on measured GPU PSNR with verbal-gradient feedback; (iii) a standing falsifier subtracts Elo on failure, integrating stress-test survival into selection; (iv) every reported number is bound to a logged training run, and the run cannot terminate while any claim is unbacked; (v) a seven-category 3DGS taxonomy wraps EVOLVE-BLOCK markers in domain-aligned scaffolds transferable across 3DGS repositories. SplatLab produces manuscripts that beat their reproduced target by +0.18 to +3.78 dB PSNR, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, for which no prior 3DGS method exists. The research cycle compresses from months of graduate-student time to days of mostly autonomous compute. Code, all manuscripts, experiment ledgers, and the cross-run paper store can be found at http://seemandhar.github.io/splatlab.

1 Introduction

Automating scientific discovery is a long-standing research ambition, traceable through early symbolic systems such as the Automated Mathematician [46] and DENDRAL [6], the conceptual programme of AI-generating algorithms[7], and a contemporary line of work in which LLMs compose research ideas, write training code, run experiments, and produce manuscripts [25, 48, 35, 11, 24, 41, 9, 37]. The classical research workflow is bounded by an individual researcher’s time and reading bandwidth, neither of which scales with the publication rate of an active subfield. Automating parts of the cycle could return researcher time to ideation and analysis. Computer vision is a natural place to test this: a single subfield now produces thousands of follow-up papers in a few years, and reproducing one published method often takes engineering effort comparable to producing a new one.

We are not aware of an autonomous-research pipeline demonstrated end-to-end in a computer-vision subfield where reproducing a single prior paper takes weeks of expert engineering. Existing systems edit short LaTeX templates over brief training runs, rank free-text hypotheses without executing a training loop, or build experimentation on top of LLM-written reimplementations that have not been externally verified against the target paper [25, 48, 11, 24, 35, 41, 9, 53, 20, 17, 22, 45]. PaperBench measures this verification gap: across 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight and Oral papers, the strongest evaluated agent reaches 21.0% average replication [38]. Without a verified reimplementation, an improvement claim has no fixed external reference: reported metrics may not trace to a measurement on disk, long-running agents drift from their objective as context fills, and comparisons are sometimes made against unspecified baselines. Table 2 summarises four common gaps: domain framework, verified baseline, full-loop refinement, and claim-to-log binding.

Progress on this problem appears to require a domain-specialised research stack constructed on top of verified reproductions, rather than only improvements in generalist coding ability. Generalist agentic frameworks [31, 13, 47, 50, 43] were designed for software engineering, where every task starts from a fresh codebase, not for the iterative refinement atop a verified baseline that scientific research typically requires. Four design choices follow: choose a single live subfield, build a verified-reproduction backbone for it, expose a structured modification space to the ideator, and bind every reported number to a logged GPU run.

We instantiate this for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [19], an active subfield of neural rendering since 2023. Reproducing a 3DGS paper on top of gsplat[52] requires correct densification scheduling, opacity reset, spherical-harmonic activation, and view-dependent appearance, none of which is supplied by the prompt a generalist code agent receives; on a 30-paper 3DGS reproduction benchmark, current frontier models succeed on roughly 5% of inputs [16]. The verified-reproduction backbone has two parts: Nerfify[16] converts NeRF papers into Nerfstudio plugins matching expert-written code; Splatify[15] extends the construction to 3DGS through a context-free grammar over a modular template with nine composable extension hooks. Every candidate that reaches our experimentation phase mutates a Splatify plugin already verified to train, and match its target.

We present SplatLab, an execution-grounded research system demonstrated in 3D Gaussian Splatting that produces research manuscripts with verified experiments from a one-line prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, with every reported number traced to a logged GPU run. SplatLab orchestrates 36 agents across seven phases (research, ideation, implementation, experimentation, analysis, writing, peer review) without a fixed DAG. Five design decisions distinguish SplatLab from prior autonomous-research and program-search systems; each is detailed in Section 3. (i) Grounded Elo on real GPU PSNR. Idea ranking uses cascade-weighted, grounding-conditional Elo scored on measured PSNR rather than the model-judged proposal scores of AI Co-Scientist [11], with ReEvo-style verbal gradients [51] fed back to the ideator. (ii) In-loop falsifier coupled to selection. A standing adversarial falsifier extending AIGS [24] runs in-loop; each failed attack deducts Elo, making stress-test survival a selection signal rather than a post-hoc check. (iii) Claim-backed verification. Every number that reaches a draft is bound to a logged experiment, and the run cannot terminate while any claim lacks a backing measurement, a binding absent from prior pipelines [25, 48]. (iv) Verified-reproduction backbone. Every candidate mutates a Splatify plugin already verified against its target, providing a fixed reference for every reported gain. (v) Domain-aligned modification space. Seven 3DGS novelty categories wrap EVOLVE-BLOCK markers and the splatify island tournament [15] in category-aligned scaffolds; a cross-codebase auto-mapper places them in arbitrary 3DGS repositories so the diff space coincides with the field’s modification space.

On Mip-NeRF 360 [3] and LLFF [27], SplatLab produces manuscripts that each beat their reproduced target by +0.18 to +3.78 dB PSNR, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, a domain not addressed by prior 3DGS work. The research cycle (read, reproduce, extend, train, ablate, write) compresses from months of graduate-student time to days of mostly autonomous compute, enabling design-space sweeps not feasible at single-researcher pace. SplatLab, all agents, and the code can be found at http://seemandhar.github.io/splatlab.

2 Related Work

End-to-end automated research pipelines.

SplatLab sits closest to systems that take a goal and emit a manuscript. The AI Scientist and v2 produce ML papers via fixed templates and agentic tree search [25, 48]. Agent Laboratory, MLR-Copilot, AI-Researcher, NovelSeek/InternAgent, Dolphin, and CodeScientist organize the literature-to-paper loop with role-specialized agents [35, 22, 41, 29, 53, 17]; CycleResearcher post-trains an LLM on a research-review-refine cycle, and AgentRxiv adds a shared preprint pool across runs [45, 34]. AIGS adds a post-hoc FalsificationAgent, data-to-paper traces claims back to data, Curie embeds rigor through agent control modules, and PaperBench grades replication against author rubrics [24, 14, 20, 38]. All operate over agent-written reimplementations whose match to the target is itself unverified; SplatLab requires every candidate to mutate a plugin already verified to compile, train, and reach the target’s headline. None condition on a (B,L) pair, none fuse falsification with cascade-weighted Elo, and none allow reviewer-spawned re-experimentation rather than only prose edits.

Autonomous discovery without manuscript output.

A second line of work runs the scientific loop but stops short of a paper. Google’s AI co-scientist uses a multi-agent Elo tournament over 203 biomedical goals with wet-lab validation in drug repurposing and antimicrobial resistance [11]. The Virtual Lab designed 92 SARS-CoV-2 nanobodies validated experimentally [39]; Coscientist and ChemCrow connect GPT-4 to wet-lab and computational chemistry tools [5, 26]. ResearchAgent and Si et al. study LLM ideation in isolation, with the latter finding LLM ideas judged more novel but slightly less feasible than expert ideas in a 100+ NLP-researcher study [1, 36]. Wei et al. survey the landscape [44]; we sit at their Level-3 “full agentic discovery” but instantiate it for graphics rather than wet-lab biology. Closest to our tournament is the AI co-scientist’s Elo loop, but it ranks free-text hypotheses rather than compiled training runs against a (B,L) substrate, and updates ratings uniformly rather than scaling by evaluation depth.

Evolutionary program search and multi-agent infrastructure.

SplatLab’s island tournament with EVOLVE-BLOCK markers builds on LLM-driven program evolution. FunSearch pairs an LLM with a systematic evaluator on an island-based loop [33]; AlphaEvolve generalizes this to entire codebases via a Gemini ensemble [30]. EoH co-evolves natural-language “thoughts” and code, ReEvo introduces verbal gradients (LLM reflections on why one heuristic beat another, fed back into mutation), Promptbreeder evolves prompts self-referentially, and Mind Evolution scales inference-time compute through genetic search [23, 51, 10, 21]. We adopt verbal gradients from ReEvo but route them into the ideator rather than a heuristic mutator, and replace per-individual fitness with cascade-weighted, grounding-conditional Elo so cheap dry-run wins do not dominate ratings of full-train candidates against the verified substrate. MetaGPT, ChatDev, AutoGen, and SWE-agent supply the orchestration primitives we reuse [13, 31, 47, 50], while LLM-as-a-judge, MARG, and AgentReview inform our reviewer-driven re-experimentation but treat review as terminal rather than a gate that can demand new substrate experiments [54, 8, 18].

3 Method

SplatLab is a system for verified evolutionary research over a reproducible substrate. The substrate is a 3DGS reproduction backbone (splatify[15]/nerfify[16]) whose plugins match their published targets; every extension SplatLab proposes mutates a plugin already verified to match its target. This scaffolding separates SplatLab from prior systems that pursue unconstrained autonomous discovery over unverified agent-written code, whose drafts are neither traceable to logs nor reproducible by retraining. The claim is narrower and stronger: SplatLab performs autonomous iterative discovery within a live, technically demanding subfield, with every iteration anchored to a measured baseline and bound to a logged training run.

Formally, given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, SplatLab returns P=(Pₜₑₓ, P_pdf, L, ℂ)=W(x; D), where Pₜₑₓ is the LaTeX source, P_pdf the compiled PDF, L binds every number in Pₜₑₓ to a training run on disk, and ℂ is the codebase that produced those numbers. The fixed context D=(ℝ,B,H,G) supplies the 3DGS literature corpus ℝ, the splatify backbone B, the nine EVOLVE-BLOCK hooks H, and the target conference template G. SplatLab produces both ℂ and L in the same run against the verified B; its writing stage can re-enter implementation to spawn new training runs.

Fig. 2 decomposes W into six stages, each acting on the same verified substrate: Grounding instruments a measured bottleneck on the matched plugin; Ideation pre-ranks candidate fixes by idea-level Elo; Implementation compiles survivors into EVOLVE-BLOCK mutations of the plugin; Refinement runs a cascade-weighted Elo tournament across eight islands with standing falsification, scored on real ns-train PSNR; Audit verifies that every reported number traces back to a measurement on the verified substrate; Synthesis writes the manuscript through reviewer-driven loops that may re-enter Stages 3–4. Stages run under a three-level hierarchy (Professor, PhD coordinators, Undergrad leaf agents; 36 total) with no fixed DAG: the master may revisit any earlier stage on a falsifier veto, audit failure, or reviewer-spawned ablation.

3.1 SplatLab

Stage 1: Grounding.

Stage 1 anchors the run in the substrate. Two parallel investigations produce the thesis spineΓ, the only artefact Stages 2–6 condition on. The first reads the literature: a Researcher queries arXiv, Semantic Scholar, and Google Scholar and pulls from a persistent cross-run paper store via RAG, with retrievals written back before Stage 1 closes so the corpus grows monotonically across runs. Retrieved PDFs are parsed by MinerU [42] and a Limitation Brainstormer cross-references each paper’s stated limitations against critiques in later work, emitting L-IDs: deduplicated limitation strings such as L-127: opacity reset destabilises late refinement, each with its supporting citation set. The second reads the substrate: a Bottleneck Analyst trains the verified splatify plugin on representative Mip-NeRF 360 scenes and profiles per-tile loss, PSNR trajectory, memory, and gradient norms; patterns become B-IDs: measurement-anchored strings such as B-04: PSNR plateau at 25.65 dB on garden, each tagged with the EVOLVE-BLOCK category it implicates. Γ contains the splatify reproduction vector V, the L-IDs, and the B-IDs.

Stage 2: Grounded ideation.

Stage 2 turns Γ into a ranked set of candidates worth running on the substrate, all without running any training. A candidate is a tuple (\textttmechanism,c,l,b,Δ̂), where c∈{1,…,7, \textttopen} indexes one of seven 3DGS novelty categories, l is the L-ID it claims to address, b the B-ID it claims to attack, and Δ̂ a predicted delta on the headline metric. An Ideator generates candidates conditioned on Γ over five iterations; between rounds, a Web Scout fires fresh literature searches keyed on the previous round’s L-IDs and B-IDs, so prior art widens monotonically rather than re-sampling from a fixed window [36]. Each candidate clears four checks: Precedent (the L-ID/B-ID citation set supports the claim), Novelty (neither a restatement of prior work nor a parameter-only tweak lacking a new signal, state, or mechanism, as screened by the Tweak Trap), Saturation (fewer than T logged negatives in the category-mechanism cell), and Orthogonality (not a near-duplicate of another admitted candidate); rejection routes back to the Web Scout as a Meta-Pivot signal. Survivors enter a bracket tournament with initial Elo 1200, judged by an LLM-as-Judge along four axes: novelty against the L-ID citation set, specificity to the B-ID, implementability within the category, and predicted-delta plausibility. Top-quartile uses multi-turn debate; lower tiers use single-turn pairwise comparisons. The output passes into Stage 3 where each candidate becomes a real plugin mutation, and into the GPU-grounded tournament in Stage 4.

Stage 3: Verified-plugin implementation.

Stage 3 mutates the substrate. Each surviving idea becomes a code change to a splatify/nerfify plugin [15, 16] that already compiles, trains, and matches the target’s published headline; the verified-plugin contract attributes downstream gains to the proposed mechanism rather than to silent reimplementation drift. A Hook Mapper resolves the abstract category c into a concrete subset of the nine EVOLVE-BLOCK hooks (densification, regularisation, loss, rendering, pruning, initialisation, scheduling, opacity, harmonics) and places EVOLVE-BLOCK markers around the corresponding regions, following [30] but over a verified plugin rather than agent-written code; for c=\textttopen, a cross-codebase auto-mapper locates insertion points that span existing hooks, compose them, or introduce new ones. EVOLVE-BLOCKs are paired code comments that delimit regions agents can modify while preserving the surrounding verified implementation. An Implementer generates the code under three constraints: a Citation Graph retrieves L-ID/B-ID-anchored papers and their published implementations as reference code; a Graph of Thoughts[4] controller structures reasoning into generation, aggregation, and refinement nodes so a failed branch can be revisited rather than restarted; and a context-free Grammar of splatify restricts output to legal hook-level rewrites. Mutations are emitted as structured diffs [30] rather than full rewrites. The diff is applied, the plugin compiled, and a 100-iteration smoke test trains on a single Mip-NeRF 360 scene; a candidate that compiles, finishes the smoke test stably, and instantiates the requested hooks clears the contract. Failures return to the Implementer with the build log as a verbal-gradient signal, capped at a repair budget before logging to the cross-run store as a build-failure negative.

Stage 4: Cascade-weighted tournament.

Stage 4 makes the substrate the judge. Each candidate is trained and scored on real PSNR; ratings are conditioned on the grounding pair (B,L) (benchmark ID, loss ID), so strength is tracked per evaluation context rather than as a scalar leaderboard.

Each candidate flows through four stages of increasing rigour: smoke (100-iteration sanity check), probe (full-iteration on one scene), multi-scene (full-iteration on a stratified subset), and the full benchmark, which only the champion enters. Stage s updates Elo with weight wₛ∈{0.2,0.5,1.0} from smoke through multi-scene, so a smoke win cannot drown out a multi-scene loss; without this gating, a three-generation eight-island run on Mip-NeRF 360 would exceed multiple GPU-months. For a match between candidates i and j at stage s,

Rᵢ^(B,L)←Rᵢ^(B,L)+K·wₛ·(Sᵢ-Eᵢ^(B,L)), Eᵢ^(B,L)=(1)/(1+10^(Rⱼ^(B,L)-Rᵢ^(B,L))/400),

(1)

with K=32, initial rating 1200, and Sᵢ∈{0,0.5,1} from the headline-metric comparison. Each update is paired with an LLM rationale naming the regime, metric delta, and likely causal mechanism; rationales accumulate in a Lessons File fed back to the Ideator as a verbal gradient [51]. Smoke failures route to a Debugger for up to three patches before logging to the Fail Train.

Survivors are distributed across eight islands and mutated by five operators selected by a multi-armed bandit over per-operator success rates: Refine (local rewrites), Crossover (two-parent mixing), Single-Parent (one-parent mutation), Tweak (hyperparameter perturbation), and Rewrite (full-block regeneration). Per-island Elo distributions form a Pareto front over (B,L); promotion requires Pareto improvement, not scalar dominance. A standing falsifier attacks every survivor along three axes: edge scenes (OOD trajectories, extreme exposure), sparse-view reduction, and hyperparameter perturbation within published ranges. Each failed attack subtracts δ=30 Elo, making stress-test survival a selection signal rather than a post-hoc check; the falsifier holds veto power before manuscript writing. Once a champion emerges, the remaining GPU budget splits between chain (sequential variants extending the winner) and orthogonal (independent branches recombining components from non-champion islands), shifting from chain-heavy to orthogonal-heavy as the champion’s per-iteration gain saturates.

Stage 5: Integrity audit.

Stage 5 binds the draft back to the substrate. Six audits run between the Stage 4 champion and the draft; any failure aborts the run as a research log. Provenance: a content-hash chain links every reported number to its (experiment ID, commit, config) triple. Faithfulness: the Stage 3 rationale is checked against the diff actually applied, catching drift that PaperOrchestra [37] cannot reach by construction. Novelty: the mechanism is re-resolved against Semantic Scholar with a query expanded by post-hoc results, catching prior work the Stage 2 Validator missed. Compute match: the headline metric is recomputed under the baseline’s compute envelope; gains that fail are reclassified as compute-confounded. Cross-codebase port: the winning hook is ported via the Stage 3 auto-mapper to a second 3DGS codebase indexed by splatify; gains that fail are flagged as codebase-specific. Claim check: every numerical or theoretical claim is resolved against the experiment ledger; load-bearing mismatches terminate the run, closing the hallucination failure mode that AI Scientist [25] drafts leave open.

Stage 6: Manuscript synthesis.

Stage 6 turns substrate-grounded results into a manuscript that, when challenged, re-enters the substrate. The (B,L) pair routes the run: a new discovery or beating SOTA triggers Mode B (manuscript synthesis), otherwise Mode A (research log only). Five writers run in parallel: Summary Writer (abstract, introduction), Body Writer (method, experiments; consumes the Stage 4 Lessons File), Related Work (citation floor enforced via the Stage 1 Researcher), Figure Generator (result plots from the ledger), and PaperBanana [55] (conceptual diagrams). A VLM Figure Checker audits axis labels, legend completeness, and number-vs-caption agreement; an Ablation Designer reads the EVOLVE-BLOCK diff and emits leave-one-out ablations, a Failure Analyst surfaces residual-error heatmaps, and a Visual Comparator tiles qualitative renders against the reproduced baseline. Three reviewer agents argue under an Editor (Methodology, Domain, Devil’s Advocate); the panel extends AgentReview [18] by demanding new training runs, not only prose edits. New experiments can re-enter Stage 4 with the comment as a verbal-gradient seed. The loop terminates when no reviewer raises a New-Experiment concern.

4 Experiments

We evaluate two aspects of SplatLab: the research process, through run outcomes, component ablations, failure analysis, and compute costs; and its outputs, through method performance, idea and manuscript quality, and human and multi-agent peer review. Detailed run outcomes and failure cases are reported in the appendix.

Experimental Setup.

We run SplatLab multiple times: a mix of prompted runs (x is a target-paper SOTA), single prompt and autonomous runs (x=∅, the system selects its own target from the literature); per-run mode and target are listed in supp. None of the runs required manual code edits after dispatch. Each run’s splatify plugin or original source code is verified against its target’s published headline or, against the paper reported numbers, before SplatLab begins (Table 1). Standard benchmarks are Mip-NeRF 360 [3] (nine unbounded scenes, including flowers and treehill) and LLFF [27]; every 8th image is held out for testing following [2], with all training runs at 30k iterations on NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. We test inter-domain discovery on three out-of-distribution scenes captured for this work and not previously addressed by 3DGS: nebula (astrophotographic), bubble, and diamond. We report PSNR (dB)↑, SSIM↑, and LPIPS↓.

Our experiments are designed to demonstrate not equalized search budgets, but system capability under end-to-end operation (with long-run autonomy a critical challenge that we overcome). Besides scaling, our benefits accrue through the combination of verified reproduction, structured mutation space and grounded evaluation. Reproduction details, the LLM stack, per-run compute budgets, and per-scene breakdowns are in the supplementary.

Run outcomes.

Across 16 runs, SplatLab trained 198 experiment branches, yielding five verified positives, five marginal results with appropriately qualified claims, five non-PSNR contributions, and one recorded failure. The Appendix details selection rejections, training failures, and outcomes by target regime.

Compute cost.

Runs used a 24–48-hour wall-clock budget, averaging 113M API tokens across approximately 1,000–1,500 LLM calls. GPU consumption ranged from 2–36 GPU-hours per run, with estimated LLM API costs of $150–250. Detailed accounting appears in the Appendix.

Generated Methods vs. SOTA.

We evaluate SplatLab on multiple targets in two regimes. Three are out-of-distribution scenes (Nebula, Bubble, Diamond) with vanilla 3DGS [19] as the baseline; the remaining eight target published 3DGS methods on Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, where the discovered variant must beat a tuned, peer-reviewed reference under the original paper’s iteration count, scene set, and compute budget. Table 1 pairs each baseline with the SplatLab-discovered method on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS; Figure 3 shows the regime-matched qualitative comparison. The discovered method exceeds its baseline on PSNR in every pairing, with gains from +0.18 to +3.78 dB, the largest on the astrophotographic nebula scene, a regime where 3DGS has not previously been applied.

Multi-seed Robustness.

To evaluate seed sensitivity, we reran GNS-AA with five seeds. GNS achieved 25.95±0.07 dB, while GNS-AA achieved 26.18±0.05 dB, yielding +0.23±0.09 dB compared with the originally reported +0.18 dB. Other generated studies also use three or four seeds. Improvements within the estimated noise floor are reported as marginal rather than verified gains.

SplatLab vs. Prior Discovery Systems.

Table 2 positions SplatLab against the eight closest autonomous-research and discovery systems on the capability axes of Section 3. SplatLab is the only system that satisfies all five rows anchoring our contributions: a verified-reproduction backbone for a live subfield, grounding-conditional idea re-ranking, a standing falsifier coupled to selection, claim-backed verification, and a reviewer panel that can spawn new training runs rather than only prose edits. Full results including wall clock and token comparison in the supplementary.

Idea and Manuscript Quality.

We evaluate SplatLab at two stages of its pipeline: ideation (Table 3) and final manuscript (Table 4). At ideation, twenty Stage 2 candidates are scored against ten PhD-student ideas and ten recently accepted workshop / conferences ideas under the blind-expert protocol of [36]. At manuscript, three baseline pipelines each produce a draft from five human-verified prompts reverse-engineered from SplatLab runs; drafts are scored against the published 3DGS paper for each prompt under the LLM-as-a-Judge paired protocol of [37], verified by graphics-area human reviewers. SplatLab outperforms prior systems by large margins at both stages and scores close to human ground truth at the manuscript level.

LLM and Human Peer Review.

We review the top five SplatLab-generated papers against five 3DGS papers accepted at CVPR or NeurIPS 2025 under the NeurIPS rubric (Soundness, Presentation, Novelty on 1–4; overall on 1–6, 3.5 = borderline). Each paper is scored independently by a multi-agent reviewer similar to ScholarPeer [12], with separate agents per review axis and a chair agent for aggregation, and by a graphics-area human reviewer blind to authorship. The multi-agent reviewer slightly favors SplatLab on every axis (3.6 vs. 3.5 overall), consistent with the residual LLM-judge bias toward AI-generated content [54]. The human reviewer reads the comparison differently: published papers score higher on Soundness and Presentation (3.6 and 3.8 vs. 3.2 and 3.0) but lower on Novelty (3.1 vs. 3.5), with the published set landing at clear accept (4.1) and SplatLab at borderline (3.5). The split matches what the rest of the paper argues: verified plugins and the integrity audit close the soundness gap on numbers, but human authors still write better papers, while the machine-pace design-space sweep surfaces mechanisms human-paced research has not yet reached.

Real Workshop Acceptance.

Three SplatLab-generated manuscripts were accepted as posters at a CVPR 2026 workshop: AttDis & Friends, NeedleSwap, and AuditSplat. Figure 4 shows page snapshots from the three accepted manuscripts.

Component Validation and Ablations.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：插件式变异 + 八岛 Elo 锦标赛 + 常驻证伪器，报告里每个数字必须绑定可回溯的训练运行。

要点：

  • 候选从已验证复现的主干上变异插件生成；跨 8 个岛做级联加权 Elo 锦标赛，按实测 GPU PSNR 打分并附语言反馈
  • 常驻证伪器从边缘场景、稀疏视角、超参扰动三面攻击幸存者，每次失败扣 δ=30 Elo，并在写稿前拥有否决权
  • 报告里每个数字都必须绑定到一次可回溯的训练运行；只要还有未关闭的论断，该运行就不能终止

为什么值得看：自动科研系统的真正价值不是会写稿，而是「报告数字可回溯」这条工程约束——它同样适用于任何自动调参、自动优化流水线：先让证据链闭合，再谈结论。

中文摘要：复现一篇 3DGS 论文往往要几周工程，才谈得上提出扩展。已有自动科研系统会读论文、写假设、写代码，但受限于固定模板、可执行性低、可追溯性差，且从未在一个活跃的视觉子领域里端到端演示过。SplatLab 就针对 3DGS：给定研究提示、目标论文链接或什么都不给，它能复现已发表基线、提出扩展、在 Mip-NeRF 360 与 LLFF 上训练与消融、写出稿件，并把每个报告的数字绑定到一次有日志的训练运行。其设计要点包括：候选通过变异已验证复现主干上的插件产生；跨 8 个岛做级联加权 Elo 锦标赛，按实测 GPU PSNR 评分并给语言反馈；常驻证伪器对幸存者做压力测试、失败扣 Elo，且在写稿前有否决权；数字与运行强绑定，未关闭论断时运行不得终止。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-27

SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research

Abstract

Reproducing a published 3DGS paper takes weeks of expert engineering before any extension can be proposed. Prior autonomous-research systems read papers, draft hypotheses, and write code, but suffer from limited template length, executability, and traceability. Specifically, none has been demonstrated end-to-end in a live computer-vision subfield with intense activity. SplatLab is an autonomous research system for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses these limitations. Given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, it reproduces a published baseline, proposes an extension, trains and ablates across Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, writes the manuscript, and binds every reported number to a logged training run. Five design choices distinguish it: (i) candidates mutate plugins from a verified-reproduction backbone matched to published baselines; (ii) a cascade-weighted Elo tournament across eight islands scores on measured GPU PSNR with verbal-gradient feedback; (iii) a standing falsifier subtracts Elo on failure, integrating stress-test survival into selection; (iv) every reported number is bound to a logged training run, and the run cannot terminate while any claim is unbacked; (v) a seven-category 3DGS taxonomy wraps EVOLVE-BLOCK markers in domain-aligned scaffolds transferable across 3DGS repositories. SplatLab produces manuscripts that beat their reproduced target by +0.18 to +3.78 dB PSNR, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, for which no prior 3DGS method exists. The research cycle compresses from months of graduate-student time to days of mostly autonomous compute. Code, all manuscripts, experiment ledgers, and the cross-run paper store can be found at http://seemandhar.github.io/splatlab.

1 Introduction

Automating scientific discovery is a long-standing research ambition, traceable through early symbolic systems such as the Automated Mathematician [46] and DENDRAL [6], the conceptual programme of AI-generating algorithms[7], and a contemporary line of work in which LLMs compose research ideas, write training code, run experiments, and produce manuscripts [25, 48, 35, 11, 24, 41, 9, 37]. The classical research workflow is bounded by an individual researcher’s time and reading bandwidth, neither of which scales with the publication rate of an active subfield. Automating parts of the cycle could return researcher time to ideation and analysis. Computer vision is a natural place to test this: a single subfield now produces thousands of follow-up papers in a few years, and reproducing one published method often takes engineering effort comparable to producing a new one.

We are not aware of an autonomous-research pipeline demonstrated end-to-end in a computer-vision subfield where reproducing a single prior paper takes weeks of expert engineering. Existing systems edit short LaTeX templates over brief training runs, rank free-text hypotheses without executing a training loop, or build experimentation on top of LLM-written reimplementations that have not been externally verified against the target paper [25, 48, 11, 24, 35, 41, 9, 53, 20, 17, 22, 45]. PaperBench measures this verification gap: across 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight and Oral papers, the strongest evaluated agent reaches 21.0% average replication [38]. Without a verified reimplementation, an improvement claim has no fixed external reference: reported metrics may not trace to a measurement on disk, long-running agents drift from their objective as context fills, and comparisons are sometimes made against unspecified baselines. Table 2 summarises four common gaps: domain framework, verified baseline, full-loop refinement, and claim-to-log binding.

Progress on this problem appears to require a domain-specialised research stack constructed on top of verified reproductions, rather than only improvements in generalist coding ability. Generalist agentic frameworks [31, 13, 47, 50, 43] were designed for software engineering, where every task starts from a fresh codebase, not for the iterative refinement atop a verified baseline that scientific research typically requires. Four design choices follow: choose a single live subfield, build a verified-reproduction backbone for it, expose a structured modification space to the ideator, and bind every reported number to a logged GPU run.

We instantiate this for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [19], an active subfield of neural rendering since 2023. Reproducing a 3DGS paper on top of gsplat[52] requires correct densification scheduling, opacity reset, spherical-harmonic activation, and view-dependent appearance, none of which is supplied by the prompt a generalist code agent receives; on a 30-paper 3DGS reproduction benchmark, current frontier models succeed on roughly 5% of inputs [16]. The verified-reproduction backbone has two parts: Nerfify[16] converts NeRF papers into Nerfstudio plugins matching expert-written code; Splatify[15] extends the construction to 3DGS through a context-free grammar over a modular template with nine composable extension hooks. Every candidate that reaches our experimentation phase mutates a Splatify plugin already verified to train, and match its target.

We present SplatLab, an execution-grounded research system demonstrated in 3D Gaussian Splatting that produces research manuscripts with verified experiments from a one-line prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, with every reported number traced to a logged GPU run. SplatLab orchestrates 36 agents across seven phases (research, ideation, implementation, experimentation, analysis, writing, peer review) without a fixed DAG. Five design decisions distinguish SplatLab from prior autonomous-research and program-search systems; each is detailed in Section 3. (i) Grounded Elo on real GPU PSNR. Idea ranking uses cascade-weighted, grounding-conditional Elo scored on measured PSNR rather than the model-judged proposal scores of AI Co-Scientist [11], with ReEvo-style verbal gradients [51] fed back to the ideator. (ii) In-loop falsifier coupled to selection. A standing adversarial falsifier extending AIGS [24] runs in-loop; each failed attack deducts Elo, making stress-test survival a selection signal rather than a post-hoc check. (iii) Claim-backed verification. Every number that reaches a draft is bound to a logged experiment, and the run cannot terminate while any claim lacks a backing measurement, a binding absent from prior pipelines [25, 48]. (iv) Verified-reproduction backbone. Every candidate mutates a Splatify plugin already verified against its target, providing a fixed reference for every reported gain. (v) Domain-aligned modification space. Seven 3DGS novelty categories wrap EVOLVE-BLOCK markers and the splatify island tournament [15] in category-aligned scaffolds; a cross-codebase auto-mapper places them in arbitrary 3DGS repositories so the diff space coincides with the field’s modification space.

On Mip-NeRF 360 [3] and LLFF [27], SplatLab produces manuscripts that each beat their reproduced target by +0.18 to +3.78 dB PSNR, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, a domain not addressed by prior 3DGS work. The research cycle (read, reproduce, extend, train, ablate, write) compresses from months of graduate-student time to days of mostly autonomous compute, enabling design-space sweeps not feasible at single-researcher pace. SplatLab, all agents, and the code can be found at http://seemandhar.github.io/splatlab.

2 Related Work

End-to-end automated research pipelines.

SplatLab sits closest to systems that take a goal and emit a manuscript. The AI Scientist and v2 produce ML papers via fixed templates and agentic tree search [25, 48]. Agent Laboratory, MLR-Copilot, AI-Researcher, NovelSeek/InternAgent, Dolphin, and CodeScientist organize the literature-to-paper loop with role-specialized agents [35, 22, 41, 29, 53, 17]; CycleResearcher post-trains an LLM on a research-review-refine cycle, and AgentRxiv adds a shared preprint pool across runs [45, 34]. AIGS adds a post-hoc FalsificationAgent, data-to-paper traces claims back to data, Curie embeds rigor through agent control modules, and PaperBench grades replication against author rubrics [24, 14, 20, 38]. All operate over agent-written reimplementations whose match to the target is itself unverified; SplatLab requires every candidate to mutate a plugin already verified to compile, train, and reach the target’s headline. None condition on a (B,L) pair, none fuse falsification with cascade-weighted Elo, and none allow reviewer-spawned re-experimentation rather than only prose edits.

Autonomous discovery without manuscript output.

A second line of work runs the scientific loop but stops short of a paper. Google’s AI co-scientist uses a multi-agent Elo tournament over 203 biomedical goals with wet-lab validation in drug repurposing and antimicrobial resistance [11]. The Virtual Lab designed 92 SARS-CoV-2 nanobodies validated experimentally [39]; Coscientist and ChemCrow connect GPT-4 to wet-lab and computational chemistry tools [5, 26].
