ResearchAgent and Si et al. study LLM ideation in isolation, with the latter finding LLM ideas judged more novel but slightly less feasible than expert ideas in a 100+ NLP-researcher study [1, 36]. Wei et al. survey the landscape [44]; we sit at their Level-3 “full agentic discovery” but instantiate it for graphics rather than wet-lab biology. Closest to our tournament is the AI co-scientist’s Elo loop, but it ranks free-text hypotheses rather than compiled training runs against a (B,L) substrate, and updates ratings uniformly rather than scaling by evaluation depth.

Evolutionary program search and multi-agent infrastructure.

SplatLab’s island tournament with EVOLVE-BLOCK markers builds on LLM-driven program evolution. FunSearch pairs an LLM with a systematic evaluator on an island-based loop [33]; AlphaEvolve generalizes this to entire codebases via a Gemini ensemble [30]. EoH co-evolves natural-language “thoughts” and code, ReEvo introduces verbal gradients (LLM reflections on why one heuristic beat another, fed back into mutation), Promptbreeder evolves prompts self-referentially, and Mind Evolution scales inference-time compute through genetic search [23, 51, 10, 21]. We adopt verbal gradients from ReEvo but route them into the ideator rather than a heuristic mutator, and replace per-individual fitness with cascade-weighted, grounding-conditional Elo so cheap dry-run wins do not dominate ratings of full-train candidates against the verified substrate. MetaGPT, ChatDev, AutoGen, and SWE-agent supply the orchestration primitives we reuse [13, 31, 47, 50], while LLM-as-a-judge, MARG, and AgentReview inform our reviewer-driven re-experimentation but treat review as terminal rather than a gate that can demand new substrate experiments [54, 8, 18].

3 Method

SplatLab is a system for verified evolutionary research over a reproducible substrate. The substrate is a 3DGS reproduction backbone (splatify[15]/nerfify[16]) whose plugins match their published targets; every extension SplatLab proposes mutates a plugin already verified to match its target. This scaffolding separates SplatLab from prior systems that pursue unconstrained autonomous discovery over unverified agent-written code, whose drafts are neither traceable to logs nor reproducible by retraining. The claim is narrower and stronger: SplatLab performs autonomous iterative discovery within a live, technically demanding subfield, with every iteration anchored to a measured baseline and bound to a logged training run.

Formally, given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, SplatLab returns P=(Pₜₑₓ, P_pdf, L, ℂ)=W(x; D), where Pₜₑₓ is the LaTeX source, P_pdf the compiled PDF, L binds every number in Pₜₑₓ to a training run on disk, and ℂ is the codebase that produced those numbers. The fixed context D=(ℝ,B,H,G) supplies the 3DGS literature corpus ℝ, the splatify backbone B, the nine EVOLVE-BLOCK hooks H, and the target conference template G. SplatLab produces both ℂ and L in the same run against the verified B; its writing stage can re-enter implementation to spawn new training runs.

Fig. 2 decomposes W into six stages, each acting on the same verified substrate: Grounding instruments a measured bottleneck on the matched plugin; Ideation pre-ranks candidate fixes by idea-level Elo; Implementation compiles survivors into EVOLVE-BLOCK mutations of the plugin; Refinement runs a cascade-weighted Elo tournament across eight islands with standing falsification, scored on real ns-train PSNR; Audit verifies that every reported number traces back to a measurement on the verified substrate; Synthesis writes the manuscript through reviewer-driven loops that may re-enter Stages 3–4. Stages run under a three-level hierarchy (Professor, PhD coordinators, Undergrad leaf agents; 36 total) with no fixed DAG: the master may revisit any earlier stage on a falsifier veto, audit failure, or reviewer-spawned ablation.

3.1 SplatLab

Stage 1: Grounding.

Stage 1 anchors the run in the substrate. Two parallel investigations produce the thesis spineΓ, the only artefact Stages 2–6 condition on. The first reads the literature: a Researcher queries arXiv, Semantic Scholar, and Google Scholar and pulls from a persistent cross-run paper store via RAG, with retrievals written back before Stage 1 closes so the corpus grows monotonically across runs. Retrieved PDFs are parsed by MinerU [42] and a Limitation Brainstormer cross-references each paper’s stated limitations against critiques in later work, emitting L-IDs: deduplicated limitation strings such as L-127: opacity reset destabilises late refinement, each with its supporting citation set. The second reads the substrate: a Bottleneck Analyst trains the verified splatify plugin on representative Mip-NeRF 360 scenes and profiles per-tile loss, PSNR trajectory, memory, and gradient norms; patterns become B-IDs: measurement-anchored strings such as B-04: PSNR plateau at 25.65 dB on garden, each tagged with the EVOLVE-BLOCK category it implicates. Γ contains the splatify reproduction vector V, the L-IDs, and the B-IDs.

Stage 2: Grounded ideation.

Stage 2 turns Γ into a ranked set of candidates worth running on the substrate, all without running any training. A candidate is a tuple (\textttmechanism,c,l,b,Δ̂), where c∈{1,…,7, \textttopen} indexes one of seven 3DGS novelty categories, l is the L-ID it claims to address, b the B-ID it claims to attack, and Δ̂ a predicted delta on the headline metric. An Ideator generates candidates conditioned on Γ over five iterations; between rounds, a Web Scout fires fresh literature searches keyed on the previous round’s L-IDs and B-IDs, so prior art widens monotonically rather than re-sampling from a fixed window [36]. Each candidate clears four checks: Precedent (the L-ID/B-ID citation set supports the claim), Novelty (neither a restatement of prior work nor a parameter-only tweak lacking a new signal, state, or mechanism, as screened by the Tweak Trap), Saturation (fewer than T logged negatives in the category-mechanism cell), and Orthogonality (not a near-duplicate of another admitted candidate); rejection routes back to the Web Scout as a Meta-Pivot signal. Survivors enter a bracket tournament with initial Elo 1200, judged by an LLM-as-Judge along four axes: novelty against the L-ID citation set, specificity to the B-ID, implementability within the category, and predicted-delta plausibility. Top-quartile uses multi-turn debate; lower tiers use single-turn pairwise comparisons. The output passes into Stage 3 where each candidate becomes a real plugin mutation, and into the GPU-grounded tournament in Stage 4.

Stage 3: Verified-plugin implementation.

Stage 3 mutates the substrate. Each surviving idea becomes a code change to a splatify/nerfify plugin [15, 16] that already compiles, trains, and matches the target’s published headline; the verified-plugin contract attributes downstream gains to the proposed mechanism rather than to silent reimplementation drift. A Hook Mapper resolves the abstract category c into a concrete subset of the nine EVOLVE-BLOCK hooks (densification, regularisation, loss, rendering, pruning, initialisation, scheduling, opacity, harmonics) and places EVOLVE-BLOCK markers around the corresponding regions, following [30] but over a verified plugin rather than agent-written code; for c=\textttopen, a cross-codebase auto-mapper locates insertion points that span existing hooks, compose them, or introduce new ones. EVOLVE-BLOCKs are paired code comments that delimit regions agents can modify while preserving the surrounding verified implementation. An Implementer generates the code under three constraints: a Citation Graph retrieves L-ID/B-ID-anchored papers and their published implementations as reference code; a Graph of Thoughts[4] controller structures reasoning into generation, aggregation, and refinement nodes so a failed branch can be revisited rather than restarted; and a context-free Grammar of splatify restricts output to legal hook-level rewrites. Mutations are emitted as structured diffs [30] rather than full rewrites. The diff is applied, the plugin compiled, and a 100-iteration smoke test trains on a single Mip-NeRF 360 scene; a candidate that compiles, finishes the smoke test stably, and instantiates the requested hooks clears the contract. Failures return to the Implementer with the build log as a verbal-gradient signal, capped at a repair budget before logging to the cross-run store as a build-failure negative.

Stage 4: Cascade-weighted tournament.

Stage 4 makes the substrate the judge. Each candidate is trained and scored on real PSNR; ratings are conditioned on the grounding pair (B,L) (benchmark ID, loss ID), so strength is tracked per evaluation context rather than as a scalar leaderboard.

Each candidate flows through four stages of increasing rigour: smoke (100-iteration sanity check), probe (full-iteration on one scene), multi-scene (full-iteration on a stratified subset), and the full benchmark, which only the champion enters. Stage s updates Elo with weight wₛ∈{0.2,0.5,1.0} from smoke through multi-scene, so a smoke win cannot drown out a multi-scene loss; without this gating, a three-generation eight-island run on Mip-NeRF 360 would exceed multiple GPU-months. For a match between candidates i and j at stage s,

Rᵢ^(B,L)←Rᵢ^(B,L)+K·wₛ·(Sᵢ-Eᵢ^(B,L)), Eᵢ^(B,L)=(1)/(1+10^(Rⱼ^(B,L)-Rᵢ^(B,L))/400),

(1)

with K=32, initial rating 1200, and Sᵢ∈{0,0.5,1} from the headline-metric comparison. Each update is paired with an LLM rationale naming the regime, metric delta, and likely causal mechanism; rationales accumulate in a Lessons File fed back to the Ideator as a verbal gradient [51]. Smoke failures route to a Debugger for up to three patches before logging to the Fail Train.

Survivors are distributed across eight islands and mutated by five operators selected by a multi-armed bandit over per-operator success rates: Refine (local rewrites), Crossover (two-parent mixing), Single-Parent (one-parent mutation), Tweak (hyperparameter perturbation), and Rewrite (full-block regeneration). Per-island Elo distributions form a Pareto front over (B,L); promotion requires Pareto improvement, not scalar dominance. A standing falsifier attacks every survivor along three axes: edge scenes (OOD trajectories, extreme exposure), sparse-view reduction, and hyperparameter perturbation within published ranges. Each failed attack subtracts δ=30 Elo, making stress-test survival a selection signal rather than a post-hoc check; the falsifier holds veto power before manuscript writing. Once a champion emerges, the remaining GPU budget splits between chain (sequential variants extending the winner) and orthogonal (independent branches recombining components from non-champion islands), shifting from chain-heavy to orthogonal-heavy as the champion’s per-iteration gain saturates.

Stage 5: Integrity audit.

Stage 5 binds the draft back to the substrate. Six audits run between the Stage 4 champion and the draft; any failure aborts the run as a research log. Provenance: a content-hash chain links every reported number to its (experiment ID, commit, config) triple. Faithfulness: the Stage 3 rationale is checked against the diff actually applied, catching drift that PaperOrchestra [37] cannot reach by construction. Novelty: the mechanism is re-resolved against Semantic Scholar with a query expanded by post-hoc results, catching prior work the Stage 2 Validator missed. Compute match: the headline metric is recomputed under the baseline’s compute envelope; gains that fail are reclassified as compute-confounded. Cross-codebase port: the winning hook is ported via the Stage 3 auto-mapper to a second 3DGS codebase indexed by splatify; gains that fail are flagged as codebase-specific. Claim check: every numerical or theoretical claim is resolved against the experiment ledger; load-bearing mismatches terminate the run, closing the hallucination failure mode that AI Scientist [25] drafts leave open.

Stage 6: Manuscript synthesis.

Stage 6 turns substrate-grounded results into a manuscript that, when challenged, re-enters the substrate. The (B,L) pair routes the run: a new discovery or beating SOTA triggers Mode B (manuscript synthesis), otherwise Mode A (research log only). Five writers run in parallel: Summary Writer (abstract, introduction), Body Writer (method, experiments; consumes the Stage 4 Lessons File), Related Work (citation floor enforced via the Stage 1 Researcher), Figure Generator (result plots from the ledger), and PaperBanana [55] (conceptual diagrams). A VLM Figure Checker audits axis labels, legend completeness, and number-vs-caption agreement; an Ablation Designer reads the EVOLVE-BLOCK diff and emits leave-one-out ablations, a Failure Analyst surfaces residual-error heatmaps, and a Visual Comparator tiles qualitative renders against the reproduced baseline. Three reviewer agents argue under an Editor (Methodology, Domain, Devil’s Advocate); the panel extends AgentReview [18] by demanding new training runs, not only prose edits. New experiments can re-enter Stage 4 with the comment as a verbal-gradient seed. The loop terminates when no reviewer raises a New-Experiment concern.

4 Experiments

We evaluate two aspects of SplatLab: the research process, through run outcomes, component ablations, failure analysis, and compute costs; and its outputs, through method performance, idea and manuscript quality, and human and multi-agent peer review. Detailed run outcomes and failure cases are reported in the appendix.

Experimental Setup.

We run SplatLab multiple times: a mix of prompted runs (x is a target-paper SOTA), single prompt and autonomous runs (x=∅, the system selects its own target from the literature); per-run mode and target are listed in supp. None of the runs required manual code edits after dispatch. Each run’s splatify plugin or original source code is verified against its target’s published headline or, against the paper reported numbers, before SplatLab begins (Table 1). Standard benchmarks are Mip-NeRF 360 [3] (nine unbounded scenes, including flowers and treehill) and LLFF [27]; every 8th image is held out for testing following [2], with all training runs at 30k iterations on NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. We test inter-domain discovery on three out-of-distribution scenes captured for this work and not previously addressed by 3DGS: nebula (astrophotographic), bubble, and diamond. We report PSNR (dB)↑, SSIM↑, and LPIPS↓.

Our experiments are designed to demonstrate not equalized search budgets, but system capability under end-to-end operation (with long-run autonomy a critical challenge that we overcome). Besides scaling, our benefits accrue through the combination of verified reproduction, structured mutation space and grounded evaluation. Reproduction details, the LLM stack, per-run compute budgets, and per-scene breakdowns are in the supplementary.

Run outcomes.

Across 16 runs, SplatLab trained 198 experiment branches, yielding five verified positives, five marginal results with appropriately qualified claims, five non-PSNR contributions, and one recorded failure. The Appendix details selection rejections, training failures, and outcomes by target regime.

Compute cost.

Runs used a 24–48-hour wall-clock budget, averaging 113M API tokens across approximately 1,000–1,500 LLM calls. GPU consumption ranged from 2–36 GPU-hours per run, with estimated LLM API costs of $150–250. Detailed accounting appears in the Appendix.

Generated Methods vs. SOTA.

We evaluate SplatLab on multiple targets in two regimes. Three are out-of-distribution scenes (Nebula, Bubble, Diamond) with vanilla 3DGS [19] as the baseline; the remaining eight target published 3DGS methods on Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, where the discovered variant must beat a tuned, peer-reviewed reference under the original paper’s iteration count, scene set, and compute budget. Table 1 pairs each baseline with the SplatLab-discovered method on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS; Figure 3 shows the regime-matched qualitative comparison. The discovered method exceeds its baseline on PSNR in every pairing, with gains from +0.18 to +3.78 dB, the largest on the astrophotographic nebula scene, a regime where 3DGS has not previously been applied.

Multi-seed Robustness.

To evaluate seed sensitivity, we reran GNS-AA with five seeds. GNS achieved 25.95±0.07 dB, while GNS-AA achieved 26.18±0.05 dB, yielding +0.23±0.09 dB compared with the originally reported +0.18 dB. Other generated studies also use three or four seeds. Improvements within the estimated noise floor are reported as marginal rather than verified gains.

SplatLab vs. Prior Discovery Systems.

Table 2 positions SplatLab against the eight closest autonomous-research and discovery systems on the capability axes of Section 3. SplatLab is the only system that satisfies all five rows anchoring our contributions: a verified-reproduction backbone for a live subfield, grounding-conditional idea re-ranking, a standing falsifier coupled to selection, claim-backed verification, and a reviewer panel that can spawn new training runs rather than only prose edits. Full results including wall clock and token comparison in the supplementary.

Idea and Manuscript Quality.

We evaluate SplatLab at two stages of its pipeline: ideation (Table 3) and final manuscript (Table 4). At ideation, twenty Stage 2 candidates are scored against ten PhD-student ideas and ten recently accepted workshop / conferences ideas under the blind-expert protocol of [36]. At manuscript, three baseline pipelines each produce a draft from five human-verified prompts reverse-engineered from SplatLab runs; drafts are scored against the published 3DGS paper for each prompt under the LLM-as-a-Judge paired protocol of [37], verified by graphics-area human reviewers. SplatLab outperforms prior systems by large margins at both stages and scores close to human ground truth at the manuscript level.

LLM and Human Peer Review.

We review the top five SplatLab-generated papers against five 3DGS papers accepted at CVPR or NeurIPS 2025 under the NeurIPS rubric (Soundness, Presentation, Novelty on 1–4; overall on 1–6, 3.5 = borderline). Each paper is scored independently by a multi-agent reviewer similar to ScholarPeer [12], with separate agents per review axis and a chair agent for aggregation, and by a graphics-area human reviewer blind to authorship. The multi-agent reviewer slightly favors SplatLab on every axis (3.6 vs. 3.5 overall), consistent with the residual LLM-judge bias toward AI-generated content [54]. The human reviewer reads the comparison differently: published papers score higher on Soundness and Presentation (3.6 and 3.8 vs. 3.2 and 3.0) but lower on Novelty (3.1 vs. 3.5), with the published set landing at clear accept (4.1) and SplatLab at borderline (3.5). The split matches what the rest of the paper argues: verified plugins and the integrity audit close the soundness gap on numbers, but human authors still write better papers, while the machine-pace design-space sweep surfaces mechanisms human-paced research has not yet reached.

Real Workshop Acceptance.

Three SplatLab-generated manuscripts were accepted as posters at a CVPR 2026 workshop: AttDis & Friends, NeedleSwap, and AuditSplat. Figure 4 shows page snapshots from the three accepted manuscripts.

Component Validation and Ablations.

item.title: agent 造得比玩得好：AutoTavern 20 天重建炉石战棋，PPO 打到天梯前二十平均 1.60 名 ｜ Build, Don't Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players
item.description:
一句话：20 天重建完整模拟器并训练出超过服务器前十的 AI，说明 agent 在「造」上远强于「玩」。

要点：

  • 专职 LLM 研究 agent 共享类型化研究记忆，每个论断要过验证闸门，再用真实对局闭环，同时改进模拟器、对手、策略与自身研究流程
  • 20 天产出 TavernGym（首个内容完整的实况复刻）与 23 个版本 TavernAgent，用 PPO 对着校准到真实对局的对手训练
  • 天梯评分从 6000 涨到约 15000：最近 20 局平均名次 1.60、80% 第一，各项统计均优于服务器前十（2.34 / 59%）；TavernBench 上答对 91%、决策 0.03 秒

为什么值得看：结论值得反复读：LLM agent 在「造系统」上远强于「操作游戏」，把 agent 放在工程位而不是玩家位，收益高一个量级。对引擎团队来说，这更像一份「用 agent 重建并校准一个复杂模拟器」的流程样本。

中文摘要：作者把「LLM agent 能不能从原始数据一路做到能和人对抗的系统」放进炉石战棋这个硬场景：八人自动战斗、随机商店与战斗、隐藏信息、近千张互相作用的卡。AutoTavern 是一套自我改进的研究系统——专职 LLM 研究 agent 共享类型化的研究记忆，每条论断都要过验证闸门，真实对局则用来闭环，于是模拟器、对手、策略以及研究流程本身被同时改进，人只负责定目标与裁决模糊机制。20 天内它构建了 TavernGym（首个内容完整的实况复刻），并产出 23 个版本的 TavernAgent，用 PPO 对着校准过的对手训练。该 agent 能自查天梯：评分从 6000 升到约 15000，最近 20 局平均名次 1.60、80% 拿第一，各项统计都高于服务器前十。TavernBench 上它答对 91%、决策 0.03 秒，前沿 LLM 至多 63% 且要 26 秒。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-24

本期推送：2026-10-27

Build, Don’t Play:
Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a
Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players

Abstract

Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback, their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days AutoTavern built TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of TavernAgent, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games. TavernAgent plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard’s measure, its last 20 records average a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server’s ten highest-rated players on every statistic (2.34, 59%). TavernBench, 960 tasks in 40 scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player: TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern.

1 Introduction

Games have long served as milestones for artificial intelligence, from Go and chess [(Silver et al., 2016; Silver et al., 2018)] to StarCraft II, Dota 2, poker, Mahjong and Stratego [(Vinyals et al., 2019; Berner et al., 2019; Brown and Sandholm, 2019; Li et al., 2020; Perolat et al., 2022)]. Each of these systems was the product of a large team of human experts who built the environment, designed the learning algorithm and debugged the countless ways in which a simulated training world differs from the real game. Today, LLM agents write and run much of the code behind such systems, and a growing line of work asks whether they can automate the research itself [(Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2026; Wijk et al., 2025; Srikanth et al., 2026)]. Existing evidence, however, comes from benchmark tasks or paper reviews; it remains open whether agents can carry a hard, real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people, where performance is ultimately measured in the real game.

We study this question in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, Blizzard’s eight-player auto-battler, played by millions. Each turn a player spends gold in a randomly stocked tavern to buy, sell and position minions, then fights an automatic battle against one opponent; players are eliminated in turn until one remains. The game combines stochastic shops and battles, hidden information about seven opponents, a shared card pool, a horizon of hundreds of decisions with a reward only at the end, and a content base of nearly one thousand interacting cards, heroes and trinkets that changes with every patch. No faithful simulator of the live game has been available, and existing AI work either advises human players or studies simplified versions of the game (Section2).

We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system in which a team of specialised LLM research agents iterates a model autonomously (Figure2). Its principle is reality-anchored self-improvement. Agents for the environment, training, opponent modelling, evaluation and deployment communicate only through a typed, versioned research memory; five verification gates stand between every claim and that memory; and live games on the real ladder close the loop, turning discrepancies between simulation and reality into fixes of rules, input encodings and opponent models. The same feedback improves the agents’ research process: errors they catch become lessons in the memory, loaded by every later session, or new gates, so each iteration starts from a better world and a better method. Because the loop does not pay for the same mistake twice, it took the agent from its first version to the level of the server’s best players in 20 days. The human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. Over 20 days the framework produced:

  • •

    AutoTavern, a self-improving research system in which LLM research agents improve a model, its training world and their own research process from the feedback of a real environment. In 20 days it ran about 10,000 experiments and delivered 23 agent versions with 418 human messages in all, and the errors it caught became lessons and gates that changed how it works (Sections4 and 8).

  • •

    TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game: all 978 game objects of patch 36.6.3, deterministic, 190–280 complete eight-player games per second on a single core, and aligned rule by rule with real games (Section5). We will open-source it.

  • •

    TavernAgent, the first Battlegrounds AI to play complete games on the live ladder, and the strongest. Its 23 successive versions, each passing an evaluation gate, raised the first-place rate against reality-calibrated opponents from 1.9% to 41.5% (random legal play and a scripted bot: 0%), and on the live ladder the deployed agent climbed by itself from a rating of 6,000 to about 15,000; on the public leaderboard’s measure its recent results are better than the server’s ten highest-rated players’ on every statistic (Section6 and AppendixD).

  • •

    TavernBench, the first decision benchmark for Battlegrounds: 960 tasks in 40 scenarios across eight categories, labelled by the simulator (Section7). We will open-source it.

    • The benchmark bears out our title (Figure1): asked to make the decisions themselves, the LLMs that built a ladder-level agent fall well short of the system they built, and decide far too slowly for a live turn (Section7). LLMs build far better than they play.

    2 Related Work

    AI for Hearthstone and Battlegrounds.

    Research on Hearthstone has focused on the two-player constructed mode [(Dockhorn and Mostaghim, 2019)]. For Battlegrounds, [Zolboot et al. (2022)] built a Monte Carlo tree search assistant on a simplified simulator, evaluated on the first turns of recorded games; an open-source simulator for reinforcement learning omits heroes [(Elimelech, 2019)]; community tools such as Firestone and Bob’s Buddy simulate only the combat phase to show win odds [(Zero-to-Heroes, 2017; HSReplay.net, 2020)]; and DeepBattler uses an LLM to give players advice during live games without an environment or an agent of its own [(William-Dic, 2025)]. None reproduces the full live game or trains an agent that plays it (Table2).

    Large-scale game RL.

    Superhuman systems for Go, StarCraft II, Dota 2, Honor of Kings, poker, Mahjong, DouDizhu and Stratego [(Silver et al., 2016; Vinyals et al., 2019; Berner et al., 2019; Ye et al., 2020; Brown and Sandholm, 2019; Li et al., 2020; Zha et al., 2021; Perolat et al., 2022)] combine self-play or human data with large-scale training and start from an existing environment. We use a standard learner, PPO [(Schulman et al., 2017)] with a transformer [(Vaswani et al., 2017)], and focus on building and correcting the training world itself, which here is done by agents.

    LLM research agents.

    The AI Scientist automates idea generation, experiments and paper writing [(Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025; Yamada et al., 2026)]; Eureka and AlphaEvolve use LLMs to propose reward functions and programs that an automatic evaluator scores [(Ma et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025)]; MLAgentBench, MLE-bench, RE-Bench and PaperBench measure agents on machine-learning tasks [(Huang et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025; Starace et al., 2025)]; and recent systems orchestrate coding agents or improve their own scaffolds [(Lange et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025; Srikanth et al., 2026)]; [Kirgis et al. (2026)] find that agents complete the engineering of open-ended projects but struggle with the research questions. AutoTavern differs in what improves and in how the improvement is judged. Its agents improve their research process through a memory of lessons and new verification gates rather than by rewriting their own code. Progress is measured on a live ladder against people, a reality loop re-anchors simulator and opponents to live games against proxy drift, and verification gates stand between every claim and the shared memory against false findings.

    LLMs as game players.

    Benchmarks evaluate LLMs on text, puzzle, video and strategic games [(Wu et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2024; Costarelli et al., 2024; Paglieri et al., 2025; Guertler et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025)] and on poker decisions [(Zhuang et al., 2025)]. TavernBench adds a stochastic multiplayer game of economy and combat with answers verified by a simulator, a strong specialised agent as reference and a real-time view: the decisions a model gets right within a live turn’s time.

    3 Hearthstone Battlegrounds

    A game has eight players, each with a hero, 30–40 health and a Hero Power. Every turn consists of a recruit phase and a combat phase. In the recruit phase the player spends gold (3 on turn 1, rising to 10) to buy minions from a tavern of random offers drawn from a pool shared by all players, sell minions, refresh or freeze the offers, upgrade the tavern tier (1–7, unlocking stronger minions), play cards from the hand, use the Hero Power and arrange the warband of up to seven minions. Three copies of a minion merge into a golden version that offers a discovery from the next tier. Battlecries, deathrattles, auras, magnetic attachments, tavern spells, trinkets and other mechanics interact across turns. In combat, the warband fights one opponent automatically, with random targets; the loser takes damage, and players are eliminated until one remains. The outcome is the placement, 1 to 8.

    We model a game as a partially observable stochastic game with a terminal utility of the placement. A player observes its own state and, for each opponent, only the public leaderboard and the warband last seen in combat. The current patch (36.6.3) contains 978 game objects: minions, heroes, trinkets, spells and other cards. A game lasts about 15 turns and about 450 atomic actions per player.

    4 The AutoTavern System

    AutoTavern is a self-improving research system: LLM research agents improve a model against an environment they cannot simulate exactly and, from the same feedback, their own research process. Its central idea is reality-anchored self-improvement: every proxy the agents optimise (the simulator, the opponent model, the exams) is re-anchored to the real game at a fixed cadence, every claim must survive a check designed to refute it before it changes the shared state, and the errors these checks catch change the process that made them.

    Problem setting.

    The research state at iteration t is a set of artifacts: an environment Eₜ, an opponent model Oₜ, a set of exams Xₜ and a policy πₜ, together with the research process itself: the memory Mₜ of findings and lessons and the gates Gₜ. The goal is the policy’s real performance J(π), its expected placement on the live ladder, observable only through a few slow, costly games. Inside the loop the agents can only improve a proxy Ĵ(π;Eₜ,Oₜ,Xₜ). Two failure modes follow. Proxy drift: Ĵ improves while J does not, because Eₜ or Oₜ is wrong in a way the policy exploits. False findings: a reading that reflects noise, a leak or selection is recorded as a result and steers later work. AutoTavern answers the first with a reality loop and the second with verification gates; both act on a shared memory, the only channel through which findings pass between agents. Self-improvement closes the loop: an iteration updates the artifacts and, when it catches an error, Mₜ and Gₜ, so that later iterations do not repeat it.

    Role agents.

    Long-running LLM research agents own the research roles (Figure2, Table5). A research lead chooses the next problem and dispatches work. An environment agent implements and verifies rules and repairs discrepancies found in live games, and an opponent agent builds human-like opponents from human statistics and live games. A training agent designs recipes and curricula, an evaluation agent measures, re-checks and audits, and a deployment agent maintains the client controller and the models’ input formats. Short-lived workers run probes and implement features.

    Typed research memory.

    Agents never talk directly; they read and write versioned, typed stores: a ledger of numbered findings in which a correction is a new entry pointing back, a registry of rule decisions and open questions, a hand-over note, an experiment registry, and a store of lessons loaded at the start of every session. A finding is never edited away, so the memory records how conclusions changed as well as what they are.

    Verification gates.

    Five gates stand between an idea and the shared state:

  • •

    G1 build: a code change passes the full test suite before it reaches the shared build;

  • •

    G2 contract: every model is tied to the simulator build it was trained on, and the controller refuses a model trained for another;

  • •

    G3 comparison: models are compared only within one build, over several seeds;

  • •

    G4 delivery: a candidate is delivered only after a re-check on seeds it was not selected on;

  • •

    G5 reality: delivered models play the live ladder, and their games are replayed in the simulator.

    • The gates acted throughout: candidates were held back after re-checks, findings were revised by later ones, and live games led to 184 fixes of rules, input encodings, the client controller and the opponents, counted in AppendixA.

    Reality loop.

    The controller logs every live game; game records are linked to the agent’s decisions; the evaluation agent replays real combats and real recruit steps in TavernGym and reports where simulation and reality part; the responsible agent fixes rules, input encodings or opponents, and the next iteration trains on the corrected world (Section8).

    Self-improvement.

    The loop improves the research process as well as its products. A finding that overturns an earlier one is recorded as a correction pointing back. A mistake the agents trace to their own method becomes a lesson that every later session loads at its start, or a new gate. Of the six errors in Section8, two became gates (the re-check on unseen seeds, G4, and the comparison of the two input encoders in G2) and two became standing rules (reseed copied games, and calibrate opponents on those the learner meets). Because a caught error changes the process and not only the current result, the loop does not pay for the same mistake twice: over the 20 days the 23 delivered versions raised the first-place rate from 1.9% to 41.5% (Figure2).

    4.1 The iteration cycle

    Algorithm1 shows one iteration. The cycle runs at three time scales: policy updates every few seconds to minutes (the training loop), experiments and findings within hours (the research loop), and live games feeding back into the environment within days (the ladder loop). A scheduler runs the registered experiments within a resource budget and keeps their successors queued, so the loop runs for days without a human present. The human researcher enters at two points only: setting goals, and ruling on mechanics that the game data leave ambiguous.

    4.2 Autonomy in numbers

    Table1 summarises the 20 days. Agents registered about 10,000 experiments, and 23 agent versions passed the delivery gate. The human typed 418 messages over the whole project, 0.6% of all messages. Labelled by their main intent (automatically, checked by hand on a sample), 42% ask for progress or a report, 24% set or change a goal, 11% concern resources, 8% approve a proposal, 6% correct an agent, 5% rule on a game mechanic and 5% report live games.

    5 TavernGym: Reproducing the Real Game

    Design.

    TavernGym is a Rust engine with thin Python bindings. One effect context serves the recruit and the combat phase, so every card is a table of event hooks that work the same in both; the state is an arena of entities, cheap to copy and serialisable; all randomness comes from one seeded generator, so a seed and an action sequence reproduce a game bit for bit. Card data are generated from the game’s own files, later patches are overlays, and a rule hash identifies every build.

    Fidelity to the live game.

    All 978 objects of patch 36.6.3 are implemented. 375 verification records and 220 confirmed rule decisions document how each mechanic was checked, and unit tests, fuzzing with invariant checks after every action and an exact legal-action mask guard the implementation. Live games led to 46 fixes of rules and card data and 73 of input encodings, found by replaying live turns, combats and offers in the engine (Sections8 and A).

    Speed and interface.

    A complete eight-player game with scripted bots takes 3.6–5.3 ms on one core (190–280 games per second), and a late-game combat 13–19 µs (52–76 thousand per second). The RL interface exposes 245 discrete actions with an exact legal mask, a player-view observation with only the information visible in the real client, batched environments and exact save and restore of running games for lookahead and replays.

    6 TavernAgent: Learning to Play the Live Game

    Model and training.

    TavernAgent is an entity transformer: each own minion, hand card, tavern offer, pending choice and opponent is a token (up to 56), a card is represented by an identity embedding, static features and an embedding of its rule text, and a pointer head produces the 245 masked action logits next to value and placement heads (d=384, 8 layers, 8 heads, 18M parameters, the best of three sizes in an early comparison, Table8). It is trained with PPO [(Schulman et al., 2017)] on about one million decisions per iteration with a terminal placement utility; each training stage of 300 iterations covers about 310 million decisions (570 thousand games) and starts from the previous stage under a KL anchor.

    Reality-calibrated opponents.

    Rather than self-play, the learner faces seven library seats: each turn, a seat takes a board (with hand and hidden counters) from a library built from statistics of top human players and recalibrated, turn by turn, to the opponents the agent actually met in live games; exam libraries are never used for training. This was the largest single gain: from the same checkpoint and with the same budget, training against the calibrated libraries raises the first-place rate from 20.9% to 27.2% on the main exam and from 10.3% to 13.5% on the harder one (Table3).

    Iterative improvement.

    The chart in Figure2 traces all 23 delivered versions (TA-1 to TA-23, Table6), re-measured on one simulator build, one exam and three unseen seeds: the first-place rate rises from 1.9% to 41.5% and the average placement from 3.40 to 2.33 (Table3).

    Live ladder.

    The deployed agent plays the live ranked ladder by itself: the controller feeds the live game’s state to the policy in the environment’s own encoding, the policy decides every operation, and a human presses the shortcut key the AI names, a feature of the game’s official plug-in (AppendixD). Most delivered versions entered this loop, so the agent’s iterations are also its climb on the ladder (Figures3 and 10): over 392 games on days 5–18 of the project the rating rose from 6,000 to 14,007. Games in which the client failed (96, flagged by the controller’s logs, never by the result; AppendixD) measure the client rather than the agent; without them the average placement is 3.22, with 16.4% first places and 77.1% top-four finishes. The latest versions (TA-19–23) averaged 2.37 with 32.6% first places and 91.3% top-four. A problem the ladder exposed paused testing until the loop fixed it (Figure3). By the end of the study the agent was rated about 15,000, in the server’s top 100; on the public leaderboard’s measure its last 20 records average 1.60 against 2.34 for the ten highest-rated players, better on every statistic, with no sign of a plateau (Table11).

    7 TavernBench: Build, Don’t Play

    Design.

    TavernBench asks whether general-purpose LLMs can make the decisions that TavernAgent makes: 960 tasks in 40 scenarios and eight categories (Table13). A task gives the player-visible state as text, the rule text of every card shown, an objective and an answer format. Labels come from TavernGym: rule tasks execute the actions; combat tasks simulate 4,096 combats; short-term decisions are scored by the simulated win rate of the next combat after the chosen option (correct within three points of the best); strategic decisions are turn plans cut from natural games (upgrade, buy, refresh or save the Gold), each played out 128 times by an earlier version (TA-21) and kept when one is better by a quarter place and two standard errors; hero and trinket choices are scored against top human players (AppendixE).

    TavernAgent’s interface.

    TavernAgent does not read the text: it receives the task’s engine state as in a game. Its policy answers the choices judged by playing the game out, its value head the hero offers. Combat questions and short-term decisions use TavernGym as the agent’s model of the game: it applies each option and simulates 256 combats after it (one-step lookahead). Rule tasks ask what the environment does, which TavernGym answers by construction; TavernAgent is not scored on them, and its row shows a dash.

    Protocol.

    LLMs answer with one JSON object within a fixed output budget, reasoning included (more is scored as wrong), in the fastest mode that answered a pilot of one task from each scenario (AppendixE). All systems answer the same 368 tasks (eight per scenario, all play-out tasks). Jev [(TypeSafe AI, 2026)], a decision model that picks among typed options without generating text, gets the same text with each task posed as a choice over its candidates (AppendixE).

    Results.

    Table4 and Figure1 give four findings. The system the LLM agents built is the strongest player.TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks; the best LLM playing directly, GPT-6 Astra, 63%, the Claude models 52–53%, GPT-6.1 Sol 46%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 44% and the remaining models 22–40%. It is near-perfect on combat, positioning, ordering and targets, where LLMs must simulate fights in their head; with TavernGym as a tool they recover most of that gap (GPT-6 Astra 62% to 97%, Table15).

    Latency rules out live play for the LLMs. A late recruit turn lasts about two minutes and holds up to about a hundred operations, so a decision that takes more than a second cannot be played. TavernAgent answers a task in 0.03 s (Table4). Gateway timings are not comparable across providers, so we time every LLM on one standard footing [(Artificial Analysis, 2026)]: the median time to its first answer token, which includes the model’s typical thinking, plus the task’s answer at its median output speed. Their median task takes 1.4–26 s, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash without reasoning 0.9 s. Within the one-second budget TavernAgent keeps 90%, DeepSeek its 26% and Jev its 37%, and every other LLM falls to 0%. Speed alone would not suffice: a turn chains dozens of decisions into one plan, so a model that errs on a third of them does not play a third worse, it loses the plan; per-decision errors compound over a turn rather than average out.

    Reading rules is not playing. The frontier LLMs execute rules well (GPT-6 Astra 95%, Claude Opus 92%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 90%), yet fall well short on the play tasks built from the same rules: knowing what each card does is not knowing which play wins.

    Judging a game is not computing a fight. On the turn plans scored by playing the game out, TavernAgent’s policy answers 75% in 0.03 s; the best LLM reaches 54% with seconds of reasoning, the others 19–43%. Its policy also leads on the choices cut from natural games (81%).

    8 Lessons from Self-Improvement

    The reality loop and the gates caught errors that no simulated metric revealed. We report six, each found and corrected inside the loop; four of them also changed the research process. (i) Copied games leak the future. A search over game copies appeared to add 23.6 points of first-place rate; the copies carried the random-number state, so the search saw the real future shop and combat outcomes. Reseeded per sample, the gain vanished (-0.65±1.14 points). (ii) Two errors can cancel. The exam once matched live results only because its late-game opponents were too strong while the agent’s growth was overstated; once both were fixed, the exam first-place rate rose to 43–49%. (iii) Winner’s curse. The best of many snapshots overstated its gain (+1.2–2.1 points on selection seeds, -0.7 on unseen ones); hence gate G4. (iv) Calibrate to the opponents you meet. Measure a library on the opponents the learner meets, not on uniform draws. (v) The ladder catches what simulation praises. TA-10 nearly doubled its predecessor’s exam first-place rate (24.2% against 12.8%), yet on the ladder the rating fell from 8,968 to 7,658 within 32 games, 18 of which also had client failures (Figure3). The loop paused live testing, traced the fall to client failures and an early- and mid-game weakness the exam had hidden, and retrained; TA-11 resumed the climb. (vi) Two encoders drift apart. Replays of live games showed the agent selling its whole warband on one turn far more often than in simulation; one input flag was encoded differently by the controller and the simulator after a trinket choice. The fix added a bit-level comparison of both encoders to gate G2.

    9 Conclusion

    We presented AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: LLM research agents improve a model, its training world and their own research process from the feedback of a real environment, in a closed loop of training, research and live games. In 20 days it built TavernGym, a faithful, full-content reproduction of Hearthstone Battlegrounds, and TavernAgent, which plays complete games on the live ladder at the level of the server’s best players. Asked to make the same decisions directly, frontier LLMs, including the models that built the system, fall well short of it and decide far too slowly for a live turn: LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern; limitations and ethics are discussed in AppendixD.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A The AutoTavern system in detail

    Conventions.

    Days count from day 1 of the project; all work targets patch 36.6.3.

    Agents.

    The research ran as several long-lived agent sessions inside our agentic research framework, each owning one role, plus short-lived sub-agents that a session dispatched for a probe, a feature with its own test gate, or a check.

    Shared research memory.

    All coordination goes through versioned text files: a ledger of numbered findings (date, configuration, readings, conclusion; corrections are new entries that point back), a registry of 220 confirmed rule decisions and a list of open rule questions, a hand-over note read at every change of hands, a persistent memory of lessons loaded at the start of every session, and an experiment registry (about 10,000 experiments, each with its module, resources, priority, dependencies and successors).

    Fixes from live games.

    Over the 20 days, discrepancies that live games exposed led to 184 fixes, each underlying defect counted once:

  • •

    35 of game rules and card behaviour in TavernGym, and 11 of card data and offer rules read from client records;

  • •

    73 of the input encoding, where the controller and the simulator described the same state differently;

  • •

    51 of the client controller: reading the game state, executing operations, recovery;

  • •

    14 recalibrations of the opponent libraries and exams to the opponents met in live games.

一句话：20 天重建完整模拟器并训练出超过服务器前十的 AI，说明 agent 在「造」上远强于「玩」。

要点：

  • 专职 LLM 研究 agent 共享类型化研究记忆，每个论断要过验证闸门，再用真实对局闭环，同时改进模拟器、对手、策略与自身研究流程
  • 20 天产出 TavernGym（首个内容完整的实况复刻）与 23 个版本 TavernAgent，用 PPO 对着校准到真实对局的对手训练
  • 天梯评分从 6000 涨到约 15000：最近 20 局平均名次 1.60、80% 第一，各项统计均优于服务器前十（2.34 / 59%）；TavernBench 上答对 91%、决策 0.03 秒

为什么值得看：结论值得反复读：LLM agent 在「造系统」上远强于「操作游戏」，把 agent 放在工程位而不是玩家位，收益高一个量级。对引擎团队来说，这更像一份「用 agent 重建并校准一个复杂模拟器」的流程样本。

中文摘要：作者把「LLM agent 能不能从原始数据一路做到能和人对抗的系统」放进炉石战棋这个硬场景：八人自动战斗、随机商店与战斗、隐藏信息、近千张互相作用的卡。AutoTavern 是一套自我改进的研究系统——专职 LLM 研究 agent 共享类型化的研究记忆，每条论断都要过验证闸门，真实对局则用来闭环，于是模拟器、对手、策略以及研究流程本身被同时改进，人只负责定目标与裁决模糊机制。20 天内它构建了 TavernGym（首个内容完整的实况复刻），并产出 23 个版本的 TavernAgent，用 PPO 对着校准过的对手训练。该 agent 能自查天梯：评分从 6000 升到约 15000，最近 20 局平均名次 1.60、80% 拿第一，各项统计都高于服务器前十。TavernBench 上它答对 91%、决策 0.03 秒，前沿 LLM 至多 63% 且要 26 秒。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-24

本期推送：2026-10-27

Build, Don’t Play:
Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a
Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players

Abstract

Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback, their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days AutoTavern built TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of TavernAgent, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games. TavernAgent plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard’s measure, its last 20 records average a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server’s ten highest-rated players on every statistic (2.34, 59%). TavernBench, 960 tasks in 40 scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player: TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern.

1 Introduction

Games have long served as milestones for artificial intelligence, from Go and chess [(Silver et al., 2016; Silver et al., 2018)] to StarCraft II, Dota 2, poker, Mahjong and Stratego [(Vinyals et al., 2019; Berner et al., 2019; Brown and Sandholm, 2019; Li et al., 2020; Perolat et al., 2022)]. Each of these systems was the product of a large team of human experts who built the environment, designed the learning algorithm and debugged the countless ways in which a simulated training world differs from the real game. Today, LLM agents write and run much of the code behind such systems, and a growing line of work asks whether they can automate the research itself [(Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2026; Wijk et al., 2025; Srikanth et al., 2026)]. Existing evidence, however, comes from benchmark tasks or paper reviews; it remains open whether agents can carry a hard, real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people, where performance is ultimately measured in the real game.

We study this question in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, Blizzard’s eight-player auto-battler, played by millions. Each turn a player spends gold in a randomly stocked tavern to buy, sell and position minions, then fights an automatic battle against one opponent; players are eliminated in turn until one remains. The game combines stochastic shops and battles, hidden information about seven opponents, a shared card pool, a horizon of hundreds of decisions with a reward only at the end, and a content base of nearly one thousand interacting cards, heroes and trinkets that changes with every patch. No faithful simulator of the live game has been available, and existing AI work either advises human players or studies simplified versions of the game (Section2).

We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system in which a team of specialised LLM research agents iterates a model autonomously (Figure2). Its principle is reality-anchored self-improvement. Agents for the environment, training, opponent modelling, evaluation and deployment communicate only through a typed, versioned research memory; five verification gates stand between every claim and that memory; and live games on the real ladder close the loop, turning discrepancies between simulation and reality into fixes of rules, input encodings and opponent models. The same feedback improves the agents’ research process: errors they catch become lessons in the memory, loaded by every later session, or new gates, so each iteration starts from a better world and a better method. Because the loop does not pay for the same mistake twice, it took the agent from its first version to the level of the server’s best players in 20 days. The human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. Over 20 days the framework produced:

  • •

    AutoTavern, a self-improving research system in which LLM research agents improve a model, its training world and their own research process from the feedback of a real environment. In 20 days it ran about 10,000 experiments and delivered 23 agent versions with 418 human messages in all, and the errors it caught became lessons and gates that changed how it works (Sections4 and 8).

  • •

    TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game: all 978 game objects of patch 36.6.3, deterministic, 190–280 complete eight-player games per second on a single core, and aligned rule by rule with real games (Section5). We will open-source it.

  • •

    TavernAgent, the first Battlegrounds AI to play complete games on the live ladder, and the strongest. Its 23 successive versions, each passing an evaluation gate, raised the first-place rate against reality-calibrated opponents from 1.9% to 41.5% (random legal play and a scripted bot: 0%), and on the live ladder the deployed agent climbed by itself from a rating of 6,000 to about 15,000; on the public leaderboard’s measure its recent results are better than the server’s ten highest-rated players’ on every statistic (Section6 and AppendixD).

  • •

    TavernBench, the first decision benchmark for Battlegrounds: 960 tasks in 40 scenarios across eight categories, labelled by the simulator (Section7). We will open-source it.

    • The benchmark bears out our title (Figure1): asked to make the decisions themselves, the LLMs that built a ladder-level agent fall well short of the system they built, and decide far too slowly for a live turn (Section7). LLMs build far better than they play.

    2 Related Work

    AI for Hearthstone and Battlegrounds.

    Research on Hearthstone has focused on the two-player constructed mode [(Dockhorn and Mostaghim, 2019)]. For Battlegrounds, [Zolboot et al. (2022)] built a Monte Carlo tree search assistant on a simplified simulator, evaluated on the first turns of recorded games; an open-source simulator for reinforcement learning omits heroes [(Elimelech, 2019)]; community tools such as Firestone and Bob’s Buddy simulate only the combat phase to show win odds [(Zero-to-Heroes, 2017; HSReplay.net, 2020)]; and DeepBattler uses an LLM to give players advice during live games without an environment or an agent of its own [(William-Dic, 2025)]. None reproduces the full live game or trains an agent that plays it (Table2).

    Large-scale game RL.

    Superhuman systems for Go, StarCraft II, Dota 2, Honor of Kings, poker, Mahjong, DouDizhu and Stratego [(Silver et al., 2016; Vinyals et al., 2019; Berner et al., 2019; Ye et al., 2020; Brown and Sandholm, 2019; Li et al., 2020; Zha et al., 2021; Perolat et al., 2022)] combine self-play or human data with large-scale training and start from an existing environment. We use a standard learner, PPO [(Schulman et al., 2017)] with a transformer [(Vaswani et al., 2017)], and focus on building and correcting the training world itself, which here is done by agents.

    LLM research agents.

    The AI Scientist automates idea generation, experiments and paper writing [(Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025; Yamada et al., 2026)]; Eureka and AlphaEvolve use LLMs to propose reward functions and programs that an automatic evaluator scores [(Ma et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025)]; MLAgentBench, MLE-bench, RE-Bench and PaperBench measure agents on machine-learning tasks [(Huang et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025; Starace et al., 2025)]; and recent systems orchestrate coding agents or improve their own scaffolds [(Lange et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025; Srikanth et al., 2026)]; [Kirgis et al. (2026)] find that agents complete the engineering of open-ended projects but struggle with the research questions. AutoTavern differs in what improves and in how the improvement is judged. Its agents improve their research process through a memory of lessons and new verification gates rather than by rewriting their own code. Progress is measured on a live ladder against people, a reality loop re-anchors simulator and opponents to live games against proxy drift, and verification gates stand between every claim and the shared memory against false findings.

    LLMs as game players.

    Benchmarks evaluate LLMs on text, puzzle, video and strategic games [(Wu et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2024; Costarelli et al., 2024; Paglieri et al., 2025; Guertler et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025)] and on poker decisions [(Zhuang et al., 2025)]. TavernBench adds a stochastic multiplayer game of economy and combat with answers verified by a simulator, a strong specialised agent as reference and a real-time view: the decisions a model gets right within a live turn’s time.

    3 Hearthstone Battlegrounds

    A game has eight players, each with a hero, 30–40 health and a Hero Power. Every turn consists of a recruit phase and a combat phase. In the recruit phase the player spends gold (3 on turn 1, rising to 10) to buy minions from a tavern of random offers drawn from a pool shared by all players, sell minions, refresh or freeze the offers, upgrade the tavern tier (1–7, unlocking stronger minions), play cards from the hand, use the Hero Power and arrange the warband of up to seven minions. Three copies of a minion merge into a golden version that offers a discovery from the next tier. Battlecries, deathrattles, auras, magnetic attachments, tavern spells, trinkets and other mechanics interact across turns. In combat, the warband fights one opponent automatically, with random targets; the loser takes damage, and players are eliminated until one remains. The outcome is the placement, 1 to 8.

    We model a game as a partially observable stochastic game with a terminal utility of the placement. A player observes its own state and, for each opponent, only the public leaderboard and the warband last seen in combat. The current patch (36.6.3) contains 978 game objects: minions, heroes, trinkets, spells and other cards. A game lasts about 15 turns and about 450 atomic actions per player.

    4 The AutoTavern System

    AutoTavern is a self-improving research system: LLM research agents improve a model against an environment they cannot simulate exactly and, from the same feedback, their own research process. Its central idea is reality-anchored self-improvement: every proxy the agents optimise (the simulator, the opponent model, the exams) is re-anchored to the real game at a fixed cadence, every claim must survive a check designed to refute it before it changes the shared state, and the errors these checks catch change the process that made them.

    Problem setting.

    The research state at iteration t is a set of artifacts: an environment Eₜ, an opponent model Oₜ, a set of exams Xₜ and a policy πₜ, together with the research process itself: the memory Mₜ of findings and lessons and the gates Gₜ. The goal is the policy’s real performance J(π), its expected placement on the live ladder, observable only through a few slow, costly games. Inside the loop the agents can only improve a proxy Ĵ(π;Eₜ,Oₜ,Xₜ). Two failure modes follow. Proxy drift: Ĵ improves while J does not, because Eₜ or Oₜ is wrong in a way the policy exploits. False findings: a reading that reflects noise, a leak or selection is recorded as a result and steers later work. AutoTavern answers the first with a reality loop and the second with verification gates; both act on a shared memory, the only channel through which findings pass between agents. Self-improvement closes the loop: an iteration updates the artifacts and, when it catches an error, Mₜ and Gₜ, so that later iterations do not repeat it.

    Role agents.

    Long-running LLM research agents own the research roles (Figure2, Table5). A research lead chooses the next problem and dispatches work. An environment agent implements and verifies rules and repairs discrepancies found in live games, and an opponent agent builds human-like opponents from human statistics and live games. A training agent designs recipes and curricula, an evaluation agent measures, re-checks and audits, and a deployment agent maintains the client controller and the models’ input formats. Short-lived workers run probes and implement features.

    Typed research memory.

    Agents never talk directly; they read and write versioned, typed stores: a ledger of numbered findings in which a correction is a new entry pointing back, a registry of rule decisions and open questions, a hand-over note, an experiment registry, and a store of lessons loaded at the start of every session. A finding is never edited away, so the memory records how conclusions changed as well as what they are.

    Verification gates.

    Five gates stand between an idea and the shared state:

  • •

    G1 build: a code change passes the full test suite before it reaches the shared build;

  • •

    G2 contract: every model is tied to the simulator build it was trained on, and the controller refuses a model trained for another;

  • •

    G3 comparison: models are compared only within one build, over several seeds;

  • •

    G4 delivery: a candidate is delivered only after a re-check on seeds it was not selected on;

  • •

    G5 reality: delivered models play the live ladder, and their games are replayed in the simulator.

    • The gates acted throughout: candidates were held back after re-checks, findings were revised by later ones, and live games led to 184 fixes of rules, input encodings, the client controller and the opponents, counted in AppendixA.

    Reality loop.

    The controller logs every live game; game records are linked to the agent’s decisions; the evaluation agent replays real combats and real recruit steps in TavernGym and reports where simulation and reality part; the responsible agent fixes rules, input encodings or opponents, and the next iteration trains on the corrected world (Section8).

    Self-improvement.

    The loop improves the research process as well as its products. A finding that overturns an earlier one is recorded as a correction pointing back. A mistake the agents trace to their own method becomes a lesson that every later session loads at its start, or a new gate. Of the six errors in Section8, two became gates (the re-check on unseen seeds, G4, and the comparison of the two input encoders in G2) and two became standing rules (reseed copied games, and calibrate opponents on those the learner meets). Because a caught error changes the process and not only the current result, the loop does not pay for the same mistake twice: over the 20 days the 23 delivered versions raised the first-place rate from 1.9% to 41.5% (Figure2).

    4.1 The iteration cycle

    Algorithm1 shows one iteration. The cycle runs at three time scales: policy updates every few seconds to minutes (the training loop), experiments and findings within hours (the research loop), and live games feeding back into the environment within days (the ladder loop). A scheduler runs the registered experiments within a resource budget and keeps their successors queued, so the loop runs for days without a human present. The human researcher enters at two points only: setting goals, and ruling on mechanics that the game data leave ambiguous.

    4.2 Autonomy in numbers

    Table1 summarises the 20 days. Agents registered about 10,000 experiments, and 23 agent versions passed the delivery gate. The human typed 418 messages over the whole project, 0.6% of all messages. Labelled by their main intent (automatically, checked by hand on a sample), 42% ask for progress or a report, 24% set or change a goal, 11% concern resources, 8% approve a proposal, 6% correct an agent, 5% rule on a game mechanic and 5% report live games.

    5 TavernGym: Reproducing the Real Game

    Design.

    TavernGym is a Rust engine with thin Python bindings. One effect context serves the recruit and the combat phase, so every card is a table of event hooks that work the same in both; the state is an arena of entities, cheap to copy and serialisable; all randomness comes from one seeded generator, so a seed and an action sequence reproduce a game bit for bit. Card data are generated from the game’s own files, later patches are overlays, and a rule hash identifies every build.

    Fidelity to the live game.

    All 978 objects of patch 36.6.3 are implemented. 375 verification records and 220 confirmed rule decisions document how each mechanic was checked, and unit tests, fuzzing with invariant checks after every action and an exact legal-action mask guard the implementation. Live games led to 46 fixes of rules and card data and 73 of input encodings, found by replaying live turns, combats and offers in the engine (Sections8 and A).

    Speed and interface.

    A complete eight-player game with scripted bots takes 3.6–5.3 ms on one core (190–280 games per second), and a late-game combat 13–19 µs (52–76 thousand per second). The RL interface exposes 245 discrete actions with an exact legal mask, a player-view observation with only the information visible in the real client, batched environments and exact save and restore of running games for lookahead and replays.

    6 TavernAgent: Learning to Play the Live Game

    Model and training.

    TavernAgent is an entity transformer: each own minion, hand card, tavern offer, pending choice and opponent is a token (up to 56), a card is represented by an identity embedding, static features and an embedding of its rule text, and a pointer head produces the 245 masked action logits next to value and placement heads (d=384, 8 layers, 8 heads, 18M parameters, the best of three sizes in an early comparison, Table8). It is trained with PPO [(Schulman et al., 2017)] on about one million decisions per iteration with a terminal placement utility; each training stage of 300 iterations covers about 310 million decisions (570 thousand games) and starts from the previous stage under a KL anchor.

    Reality-calibrated opponents.

    Rather than self-play, the learner faces seven library seats: each turn, a seat takes a board (with hand and hidden counters) from a library built from statistics of top human players and recalibrated, turn by turn, to the opponents the agent actually met in live games; exam libraries are never used for training. This was the largest single gain: from the same checkpoint and with the same budget, training against the calibrated libraries raises the first-place rate from 20.9% to 27.2% on the main exam and from 10.3% to 13.5% on the harder one (Table3).

    Iterative improvement.

    The chart in Figure2 traces all 23 delivered versions (TA-1 to TA-23, Table6), re-measured on one simulator build, one exam and three unseen seeds: the first-place rate rises from 1.9% to 41.5% and the average placement from 3.40 to 2.33 (Table3).

    Live ladder.

    The deployed agent plays the live ranked ladder by itself: the controller feeds the live game’s state to the policy in the environment’s own encoding, the policy decides every operation, and a human presses the shortcut key the AI names, a feature of the game’s official plug-in (AppendixD). Most delivered versions entered this loop, so the agent’s iterations are also its climb on the ladder (Figures3 and 10): over 392 games on days 5–18 of the project the rating rose from 6,000 to 14,007. Games in which the client failed (96, flagged by the controller’s logs, never by the result; AppendixD) measure the client rather than the agent; without them the average placement is 3.22, with 16.4% first places and 77.1% top-four finishes. The latest versions (TA-19–23) averaged 2.37 with 32.6% first places and 91.3% top-four. A problem the ladder exposed paused testing until the loop fixed it (Figure3). By the end of the study the agent was rated about 15,000, in the server’s top 100; on the public leaderboard’s measure its last 20 records average 1.60 against 2.34 for the ten highest-rated players, better on every statistic, with no sign of a plateau (Table11).

    7 TavernBench: Build, Don’t Play

    Design.

    TavernBench asks whether general-purpose LLMs can make the decisions that TavernAgent makes: 960 tasks in 40 scenarios and eight categories (Table13). A task gives the player-visible state as text, the rule text of every card shown, an objective and an answer format. Labels come from TavernGym: rule tasks execute the actions; combat tasks simulate 4,096 combats; short-term decisions are scored by the simulated win rate of the next combat after the chosen option (correct within three points of the best); strategic decisions are turn plans cut from natural games (upgrade, buy, refresh or save the Gold), each played out 128 times by an earlier version (TA-21) and kept when one is better by a quarter place and two standard errors; hero and trinket choices are scored against top human players (AppendixE).

    TavernAgent’s interface.

    TavernAgent does not read the text: it receives the task’s engine state as in a game. Its policy answers the choices judged by playing the game out, its value head the hero offers. Combat questions and short-term decisions use TavernGym as the agent’s model of the game: it applies each option and simulates 256 combats after it (one-step lookahead). Rule tasks ask what the environment does, which TavernGym answers by construction; TavernAgent is not scored on them, and its row shows a dash.

    Protocol.

    LLMs answer with one JSON object within a fixed output budget, reasoning included (more is scored as wrong), in the fastest mode that answered a pilot of one task from each scenario (AppendixE). All systems answer the same 368 tasks (eight per scenario, all play-out tasks). Jev [(TypeSafe AI, 2026)], a decision model that picks among typed options without generating text, gets the same text with each task posed as a choice over its candidates (AppendixE).

    Results.

    Table4 and Figure1 give four findings. The system the LLM agents built is the strongest player.TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks; the best LLM playing directly, GPT-6 Astra, 63%, the Claude models 52–53%, GPT-6.1 Sol 46%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 44% and the remaining models 22–40%. It is near-perfect on combat, positioning, ordering and targets, where LLMs must simulate fights in their head; with TavernGym as a tool they recover most of that gap (GPT-6 Astra 62% to 97%, Table15).

    Latency rules out live play for the LLMs. A late recruit turn lasts about two minutes and holds up to about a hundred operations, so a decision that takes more than a second cannot be played. TavernAgent answers a task in 0.03 s (Table4). Gateway timings are not comparable across providers, so we time every LLM on one standard footing [(Artificial Analysis, 2026)]: the median time to its first answer token, which includes the model’s typical thinking, plus the task’s answer at its median output speed. Their median task takes 1.4–26 s, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash without reasoning 0.9 s. Within the one-second budget TavernAgent keeps 90%, DeepSeek its 26% and Jev its 37%, and every other LLM falls to 0%. Speed alone would not suffice: a turn chains dozens of decisions into one plan, so a model that errs on a third of them does not play a third worse, it loses the plan; per-decision errors compound over a turn rather than average out.

    Reading rules is not playing. The frontier LLMs execute rules well (GPT-6 Astra 95%, Claude Opus 92%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 90%), yet fall well short on the play tasks built from the same rules: knowing what each card does is not knowing which play wins.

    Judging a game is not computing a fight. On the turn plans scored by playing the game out, TavernAgent’s policy answers 75% in 0.03 s; the best LLM reaches 54% with seconds of reasoning, the others 19–43%. Its policy also leads on the choices cut from natural games (81%).

    8 Lessons from Self-Improvement

    The reality loop and the gates caught errors that no simulated metric revealed. We report six, each found and corrected inside the loop; four of them also changed the research process. (i) Copied games leak the future. A search over game copies appeared to add 23.6 points of first-place rate; the copies carried the random-number state, so the search saw the real future shop and combat outcomes. Reseeded per sample, the gain vanished (-0.65±1.14 points). (ii) Two errors can cancel. The exam once matched live results only because its late-game opponents were too strong while the agent’s growth was overstated; once both were fixed, the exam first-place rate rose to 43–49%. (iii) Winner’s curse. The best of many snapshots overstated its gain (+1.2–2.1 points on selection seeds, -0.7 on unseen ones); hence gate G4. (iv) Calibrate to the opponents you meet. Measure a library on the opponents the learner meets, not on uniform draws. (v) The ladder catches what simulation praises. TA-10 nearly doubled its predecessor’s exam first-place rate (24.2% against 12.8%), yet on the ladder the rating fell from 8,968 to 7,658 within 32 games, 18 of which also had client failures (Figure3). The loop paused live testing, traced the fall to client failures and an early- and mid-game weakness the exam had hidden, and retrained; TA-11 resumed the climb. (vi) Two encoders drift apart. Replays of live games showed the agent selling its whole warband on one turn far more often than in simulation; one input flag was encoded differently by the controller and the simulator after a trinket choice. The fix added a bit-level comparison of both encoders to gate G2.

    9 Conclusion

    We presented AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: LLM research agents improve a model, its training world and their own research process from the feedback of a real environment, in a closed loop of training, research and live games. In 20 days it built TavernGym, a faithful, full-content reproduction of Hearthstone Battlegrounds, and TavernAgent, which plays complete games on the live ladder at the level of the server’s best players. Asked to make the same decisions directly, frontier LLMs, including the models that built the system, fall well short of it and decide far too slowly for a live turn: LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern; limitations and ethics are discussed in AppendixD.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A The AutoTavern system in detail

    Conventions.

    Days count from day 1 of the project; all work targets patch 36.6.3.

    Agents.

    The research ran as several long-lived agent sessions inside our agentic research framework, each owning one role, plus short-lived sub-agents that a session dispatched for a probe, a feature with its own test gate, or a check.

    Shared research memory.

    All coordination goes through versioned text files: a ledger of numbered findings (date, configuration, readings, conclusion; corrections are new entries that point back), a registry of 220 confirmed rule decisions and a list of open rule questions, a hand-over note read at every change of hands, a persistent memory of lessons loaded at the start of every session, and an experiment registry (about 10,000 experiments, each with its module, resources, priority, dependencies and successors).

    Fixes from live games.

    Over the 20 days, discrepancies that live games exposed led to 184 fixes, each underlying defect counted once:

  • •

    35 of game rules and card behaviour in TavernGym, and 11 of card data and offer rules read from client records;

  • •

    73 of the input encoding, where the controller and the simulator described the same state differently;

  • •

    51 of the client controller: reading the game state, executing operations, recovery;

  • •

    14 recalibrations of the opponent libraries and exams to the opponents met in live games.

item.title: 不动模型只改记忆：Memento 3 让冻结 LLM 用可修订规则手册反复重写自己的世界模型 ｜ Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks
item.description:
一句话：自然语言规则手册当持久记忆，编译成可执行代码，只有逐格重放复现观测才被接受。

要点：

  • 智能体维护一份自然语言规则手册作为持久语义记忆，记录可修订的动力学假设、显式留空未知部分，再把它编译成可执行代码用于预测与规划
  • 观察 → 反思 → 修订规则 → 编译 → 验证的持续闭环：只有当 LLM 判定代码忠于手册、且逐格重放能复现观测时，更新才被接受
  • 群体扩展并行维护多个世界模型并共享交互证据；ARC-AGI-3 上通关全部 25 个公开游戏的每一关，平均 RHAE 100.0，只用人类 44% 的动作数
